docs.title: Cortex
docs.text: An agent workbench for auto research, self-improvement loops, and other work that runs for days. You give it a mission with a success criterion. It plans the work, runs it with a team of agents across your machines and GPUs, keeps every result as plain files in your project, and checks the outcome against what you agreed, asking you only when a decision is yours to make.

docs.title: Why Cortex?
docs.text:
A coding agent in a terminal is built around one session: one task, one machine, done within the hour. Auto research and recursive self-improvement (RSI) need more. A study runs for days and outlives every session in it. Its results have to be kept and compared run after run. The work splits among several agents, and the experiments run on GPU servers rather than on the machine the agent started from.

Cortex runs coding agents (Claude Code, or PI with the provider you already pay for) as a long-lived service built for that kind of work:

  • Work continues across sessions — mission, status, and decisions live as plain files rather than in a chat history that accumulates and decays, so a new session picks up where the last one stopped.
  • Results are kept — every experiment is its own record of what ran, what came out, and what it means; confirmed findings and cross-experiment patterns collect beside them (Memory).
  • Agents work as a team — a lead hands bounded pieces to subagents and persistent workers that start with a fresh context, and keeps a live board of where the work stands (Team Mode).
  • Agents manage model training across your machines — they check which GPUs are free, launch training and evaluation runs on any connected machine, and wait on them without polling (Cross-Machine, Waitpoints).
  • The setup itself can improve — skills, rules, hooks, and Cortex's own source are files the agents can change, inside a safety boundary you write. Cortex itself is developed entirely inside Cortex.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Plans and approvals — non-trivial work starts from a plan you approve; questions, decisions, and operations that need sign-off arrive as cards you answer in place (Safety & Approvals).
  • Subagents and team mode — bounded work goes to subagents with a clean context; with team mode on, a session can lead persistent worker sessions (Team Mode).
  • Boards for long work — a long task keeps a live status page beside the conversation, showing its state, plan, what needs you, and the decisions taken (Boards).
  • Structured project log — every project keeps mission, roadmap, status, experiments, knowledge, patterns, and decisions as plain files (Memory).
  • Scheduling and waitpoints — schedule Cortex to scan, digest, or sweep on a recurring basis, and let a waitpoint wake a session when a training run, build, or evaluation it launched finishes (Scheduling, Waitpoints).
  • One agent across your machines — connect any Mac, Windows, or Linux machine via cortex-client; the workbench shows each machine's CPU, memory, disk, and per-GPU load and processes (Cross-Machine).
  • Editable skills and plugins — skills are plain SKILL.md files that Cortex and you can write, override, or revert, on disk or from Settings → Plugins; execution environments choose which plugins, rules, and tools each session gets (Skills & Plugins, Configuration).
  • Rebuilds itself from source — with CORTEX_REPO pointing at a source checkout, Cortex rebuilds, reinstalls, and restarts itself when its code changes (Hot rebuild).
  • A browser the agent drives — agents open, read and operate web pages in a Chrome on the server or on your own machine; you watch it live and take over for logins (Agent Browser).
  • Web, native app, chat, and terminal access — use the browser workbench, Linux/macOS/Windows desktop app, Android app, Slack, Feishu, or TUI against the same server. The workbench shows sessions, workers, boards, approvals, machines, and project memory side by side.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
The desktop app installs and starts a Cortex server on macOS, Linux, or Windows without a terminal. From a terminal:

npm install -g @cortex-agent/server
cortex init
cortex ui enable
cortex daemon

See Quickstart for detailed server and chat-platform setup. Once the server is running, open the workbench at http://127.0.0.1:3004 on the server, use Browser Access to reach it from elsewhere, or connect a native client as described in Desktop and Android Apps.

docs.title: Agent Browser
docs.text:
Agents in Cortex drive a real Chrome: they open pages, read them, click through them, fill in forms and take screenshots. The browser is the one Cortex manages on the server, or the Chrome on one of your connected machines, and you can watch it live in the app and take over when a page needs a human.

Agents control it with the cortex-browser command, which runs in their shell like any other tool. The built-in browser skill (in the cortex-system plugin) tells an agent when and how to use it, so asking for "check the page", "take a screenshot of the dashboard" or "log in and look" is enough.

docs.title: How an agent uses it
docs.text:
cortex-browser is agent-browser attached to a Chrome that Cortex manages. Every argument except --device goes to agent-browser, so the command set is agent-browser's: open, snapshot, click, fill, screenshot, get, eval and the rest. The usual loop is:

cortex-browser open http://127.0.0.1:5173
cortex-browser snapshot -i              # interactive elements as refs: @e1, @e2 …
cortex-browser click @e2
cortex-browser screenshot ./after.png

The full, version-matched command guide ships with the binary: cortex-browser skills get core (add --full for every command and option). The CLI reference lists what cortex-browser itself adds and refuses.

Relative file paths (screenshot ./page.png, pdf out.pdf, upload @e5 a.png) resolve against the agent's working directory. Files always land on the server, whichever machine's Chrome took them; the agent sends a screenshot to you with send_file.

docs.title: One tab per session
docs.text:
Each session gets its own tab, and so does each worker and subagent, because they run as sessions of their own. The tab stays between turns, so an agent continues on the page where it left off. Sessions never share a tab and cannot see each other's.

A session's tab closes after 10 minutes without a cortex-browser call. The next call starts on a blank page and says so; the agent reopens the URL it needs. If Chrome stops for another reason, such as a crash or a machine restart, the next call starts Chrome again and continues the same way. Chrome itself shuts down 10 minutes after the last session's tab on it closes.

Logins live in the browser profile, not in the tab, so a site you signed in to stays signed in for later tabs and later sessions. On the server the profile is $CORTEX_HOME/browser/profile/ (~/.cortex/browser/profile/ by default); on a device it is ~/.cortex/browser/profile/ in the home of the user running cortex-client. Each is separate from your everyday Chrome profile.

docs.title: Choosing the machine
docs.text:
• server (the default) is the Chrome on the Cortex server. There, localhost means the server. It runs on the server's display when there is one, otherwise on a virtual display (when Xvfb is installed) or headless. The live view and takeover in the app go through Chrome's debugging connection, so they work in every case.
  • --device <name> uses the Chrome on a connected machine instead: its localhost, its network and its logins. Cortex starts that Chrome through the machine's cortex-client and reaches its debugging port through the client's port forwarding, so nothing extra needs to be open on the machine. Chrome or Chromium has to be installed there.

The choice sticks: once a session has used a device, later calls go there without repeating --device. Choosing another machine closes the session's tab on the previous one. An agent picks a device when you ask for your machine, or when the page only exists there.

When the browser cannot be used, cortex-browser exits non-zero and says why and what to do: the device is offline or unknown, Chrome failed to start, or you are controlling the browser.

docs.title: Watching it in the app
docs.text:
When a session has a browser, the chat header shows a Browser capsule with the machine and the browser's state: starting, failed to start, on a page, or You are in control. Clicking it opens the session's Agent browser tab in the dock, which shows the page live. The command palette (⌘K / Ctrl+K) lists every live agent browser under Agent browsers, so you can open one from any session. The view streams only while the tab is visible.

On a phone, the chat's activity strip shows the browser chip, and tapping it opens a read-only view of the page.

docs.title: Taking over
docs.text:
Some pages need a person: a login, a captcha, a second factor, a cookie banner the agent cannot get past. The skill tells the agent to ask you rather than work around them. To step in:

  1. Open the session's Agent browser tab and press Take over.
  2. Use the page directly: clicks, scrolling and keys go to the page. The tab's text field types into the focused element, and pasting from the clipboard does the same.
  3. Press Hand back, then reply in the chat so the agent carries on in the same tab.

While you are in control, the agent's cortex-browser calls are refused with "the user is controlling this browser", and the agent waits for you. A takeover belongs to the window that made it; another window can take it over in turn. Cortex hands the browser back by itself 30 seconds after the controlling window's view goes away (the dock tab closed, the page reloaded, the network dropped) or after 10 minutes without a click, key or paste.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose CORTEX_AGENT_BROWSER_BIN the agent-browser binary shipped with Cortex Absolute path of the agent-browser binary cortex-browser runs. A path that does not exist is an error, not a fallback CORTEX_BROWSER_BINARY auto-detected Chrome or Chromium binary for the server's browser CORTEX_BROWSER_DISPLAY auto-detected X display the server's browser uses, skipping display detection

Cortex uses its own pinned agent-browser, never one found on PATH, so the command guide always matches the commands. See Configuration for where these variables live.

docs.title: Cortex Architecture
docs.text: Cortex is an autonomous research agent system for robotics and AI/ML. It runs as a server-client architecture: the agent-server orchestrates work — conversations and their agent runs, scheduling, chat integrations, the Web UI, and MCP tools — while remote agent clients connect via WebSocket to execute commands on remote machines. For deeper dives into these subsystems, see memory.md, scheduling.md, and mcp.md.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
The repository is a pnpm workspace. Two packages are published to npm; the others are built into them or deployed on their own.

Package Path Purpose @cortex-agent/server agent-server/ Main server: Slack and Feishu adapters, the Web UI host, the TUI gateway, LLM orchestration, scheduling, MCP tools. Provides five CLI binaries: cortex, cortex-browser, cortex-hook, cortex-evidence-export, cortex-signal. The published package also carries the built web app and the client bundle @cortex-agent/client client/ Lightweight remote agent daemon (cortex-client). Connects via WebSocket and executes shell/file commands locally @cortex-agent/web web/ Vite + React app for the browser, desktop and mobile layouts. Built to web/dist and served by the server's Web UI host @cortex-agent/desktop desktop/ Tauri v2 desktop and Android shell. Serves the web app through the cortexui:// scheme, from its bundled copy or a newer bundle downloaded from the server @cortex-agent/ui-contract packages/ui-contract/ Type-only re-export of the server's Web UI router and DTO types, which the web app compiles against @cortex-agent/deepseek-relay-worker packages/deepseek-relay-worker/ Cloudflare Worker that relays to DeepSeek for hosts that cannot reach it directly Plugins agent-server/defaults/plugins/ Built-in plugin bundles (cortex-system, cortex-board, cortex-feishu) containing skills. Not npm packages — read in place as directories at runtime

docs.title: Agent-Server Architecture: Six Layers
docs.text:
The agent-server code at agent-server/src/ is organized into six layers (L0 through L5), plus two adapter directories with rules of their own. A layer may import only from the layers below it at runtime; type-only imports may cross layers. These rules are enforced at test time by agent-server/.dependency-cruiser.cjs — npm test runs depcruise and fails on any runtime violation (npm run test:quick skips it).

L0  core/          → (no runtime dependencies)
L1  store/         → core
L2  events/        → core
L3  domain/        → core, store, events, platform, agent-adapter
L4  orchestration/ → core, store, events, domain, platform, agent-adapter
L5  entry/         → everything (composition root)

    platform/      → core, events
    agent-adapter/ → core, store, events

orchestration/ must also be free of import cycles.

  • agent-adapter/ — the two-LLM-backend abstraction (Claude Code and PI). domain/runs/adapters.ts is the one place the adapters are assembled.
  • platform/ — the messaging and transport layer: the Slack and Feishu adapters, the TUI gateway, the composite adapter that runs several platforms at once (adapters/), the Web UI HTTP host (ui-http/), and the server's Chrome and the agent-browser process runner (browser/).

A further directory, tui/, is the Ink terminal client that cortex tui runs. It talks to the server only over the TUI gateway's WebSocket, sharing the gateway's protocol types and the i18n strings, and has no layer rule of its own.

docs.title: Layer 0: core/ — Shared Kernel
docs.text:
The shared kernel every other layer builds on: types, path constants, settings, and the in-memory run and session state. It has no runtime imports of other layers; it may import their types, which is how core types such as the hook bus entry or the environment definition refer to shapes owned elsewhere.

File Purpose paths.ts Canonical path constants: INSTALL_ROOT, DEFAULTS_DIR, DATA_DIR (~/.cortex/), CONFIG_DIR, STORE_DIR (data/), CONTEXT_DIR, PROJECTS_DIR, WORKSPACE_DIR (tmp/), PLUGINS_DIR, PROMPTS_DIR, HOOKS_DIR, LOGS_DIR, AGENT_CWD, CLAUDE_CONFIG_HOME, and the daemon PID and restart-trigger files settings.ts, settings-spec.ts The runtime settings in config/settings.json: the key schema with defaults and legacy variables, validation, the cached snapshot, and hot reload (see configuration.md) utils.ts Utility functions: chunkText, formatDurationCompact, todayISO, listProjectDirs, readableTimestamp, npm prefix resolution atomic-write.ts atomicWrite(filePath, data) / atomicWriteSync — write to .tmp.<pid>.<ts>.<rand> then fs.rename; mutateFileAtomically for read-modify-write json-repository.ts Generic JsonRepository<T> base class: read(), write(), mutate(fn), flush(). Lazy orphan .tmp.* sweep on first I/O. Corrupt-JSON backup mechanism async-mutex.ts AsyncMutex class — promise-based mutex for serializing async disk writes. Used throughout the store layer to prevent concurrent file corruption log.ts createLogger(tag) — console + daily-rolling file sink with 14-day retention i18n.ts, locales/ English and Chinese strings for system-generated messages; CORTEX_LANG or the !lang preference picks the locale cli-utils.ts formatHelp, formatError, readStdinSync, readStdinBufferSync, cliError — shared CLI formatting status-format.ts Pure formatting: computeElapsed, formatMetricsSuffix, buildSessionTag, buildUserProcessingMessage, renderTurnStatus rebuild-progress.ts The hot-rebuild progress record the supervisor publishes to daemon-rebuild.json: pure step transitions (planRebuildProgress, startRebuildStep, finishRebuildStep, settleRebuildProgress) plus a read that never throws run-registry.ts RunRegistry — the single in-memory index of the executions that are live right now, keyed by executionId and indexed by channel. Publishes the agent.* lifecycle events to the EventBus session-holds.ts SessionHolds — the other half of "is this session busy": a turn that ended while background work continues, with per-owner handles, supersede and stop session-state.ts sessionState(sessionId) / channelEngineBusy() — the one join of live executions and holds, and the only place that answers whether a session is busy agents/ Subagent role loading (roles.ts) and the shared delegation schema, model choice and orchestration (subagent/) used by both backends types/agent-types.ts Backend, AgentResult, AgentProgress, AskUserQuestionInfo, and the todo, context-usage, attachment and notice shapes types/environment-types.ts Execution environment types: AgentDefinition (one config/environments/*.json file) and the ResolvedEnvironment a run opens with config-generator.ts Config file initialization for new installs, and the MCP configs written at every start gateway-generator.ts API gateway YAML generation models-generator.ts Default model and favorites JSON generation

docs.title: Layer 1: store/ — Persistence
docs.text:
All write operations are serialized through AsyncMutex to prevent corruption from concurrent writes. The layer uses two repository patterns:

  • Pattern A (JsonRepository delegation): Simple CRUD wrappers around JsonRepository<T>. Used for schedule-repo, cost-repo, board-repo, waitpoint-repo, provider-state-repo and most other repositories. All writes go through atomicWrite().
  • Pattern B (in-memory Map + fire-and-forget persist): Synchronous in-memory Map for reads, with async persist chain for writes. Used for execution-repo where read latency matters and stale-on-crash is acceptable.
File Purpose outbound-queue.ts WAL-based durable outbound message queue. 30-min TTL, 200-entry compaction, 5-second drain loop. Coalesces consecutive updates to the same message conversation-ledger-repo.ts Façade over session-registry-repo.ts — same per-channel turn API (initConversation, beginTurn, addResponseTs, completeTurn, rollbackTo) with no file of its own session-registry-repo.ts JSONL-backed UUID session registry and single owner of session records, channel→session bindings, and per-channel conversation headers and turns. Replays an append-only journal (put/patch/delete-intent/delete-commit/bind/unbind/turn/conversation), admits sessions, and compacts snapshots when the log grows conversation-history-repo.ts Per-session transcript JSONL under data/conversation-history/, the record the Web UI renders a conversation from execution-repo.ts Pattern B repository: startLocalExecution, completeExecution, failExecution, cancelExecution. At startup markMissingRunningExecutionsStale marks runs that are not alive any more as stale; terminal records older than seven days are archived to data/archive/ project-dir-repo.ts projectName → machineName → dirPath with reverse channel lookup schedule-repo.ts Schedule persistence. ScheduleTask interface; schedules.json is shared with out-of-process writers cost-repo.ts Costs in JSONL (append-only), budget in JSON. 90-day pruning at startup models-repo.ts Synchronous cached reader. startModelsWatcher() for hot-reload waitpoint-repo.ts, provider-state-repo.ts, board-repo.ts Waitpoints, provider throttle state and the resume queue, and the board registry team-inbox-repo.ts, team-outbox-repo.ts Messages between team leads and their workers, kept across restarts hook-registry.ts, hook-writer.ts The hook registry: built-in declarations with config/hooks/ laid over them, and the writer behind hook switches version-migrations.ts One-time upgrade migrations of $CORTEX_HOME, run at startup

docs.title: Layer 2: events/ — Event Bus
docs.text:
A synchronous, type-safe event bus with JSONL logging.

File Purpose event-types.ts The CortexEvent discriminated union, grouped below, plus two meta events (event-bus.handler-failed, event-logger.dropped) event-bus.ts EventBus class — subscribe(type, handler) / publish(event). Synchronous fan-out. Async handlers fire-and-forget. Re-entrant guard for event-bus.handler-failed. Close hooks for SIGTERM drain event-logger.ts Subscribes to '*', ring buffer of 1024 entries, 100ms flush interval, daily rolling JSONL under logs/events/, 14-day retention. Gated by the eventLog setting in config/settings.json (legacy env CORTEX_EVENT_LOG=off is read as a deprecated fallback)

Event categories:

  • Session: session.message, session.message.delta, session.message.delivered, session.status, session.turn, session.turn.completed, session.todos, session.context-usage, session.context-compacted, session.rewound, session.decision, session.board, session.interaction, session.tool-images, session.debug.updated
  • Interaction: plan.submitted, plan.approved, ask-user.requested, ask-user.answered
  • Agent lifecycle: agent.started, agent.completed, agent.failed, agent.superseded
  • Auth: auth.required, auth.recovered
  • Board: board.updated, board.style-updated
  • System: system.notice, config.changed, llm.active-count-delta, rate-limit.changed, ui.mutate-invoked, and scheduler.tick (declared for the TUI dashboard; no server component publishes it)

docs.title: Layer 3: domain/ — Business Logic
docs.text:
The thickest layer. Contains one subdirectory per domain concern.

Subdirectory Purpose agents/ Engine selections, favorites, model memory, execution environments (agents/environments/), subagent runners and credentials: what a run may be configured as. Starting one belongs to runs/ runs/ The run layer: startRun and the AgentRun ownership object, RunRequest selection/spec/prompt resolution and its shared builders (builders.ts), the backend-neutral RunEvent stream, and the SessionEngines pool sessions/ Session lifecycle and records, the session hook pipeline (onNew, onMessageEnd, pre-close) with optional agent injection, team sessions, and the retention sweep executions/ Execution registry access over store/execution-repo.ts, plus teardown and stop of live executions auth/ Claude Code, PI and Codex credentials and login flows, auth status and expiry watching, and gateway sync after a login pi-providers/ Custom PI providers: the model catalog entries and gateway routes behind cortex auth provider costs/ Cost tracking, gateway management, usage collection, account readings and banked resets, rate limiting with per-provider awareness scheduling/ Persisted schedule engine plus settings-backed built-in job controller. Scheduler hot-reloads user schedules and opens a new session for each fire; built-in jobs such as the memory-index rebuild own daemon timers waitpoints/ Waitpoint service: arming, signal resolution, expiry, and the notices that wake a session (see waitpoints.md) boards/ Board service, paths and slugs, the file watcher that re-renders open boards, and the projection of decisions onto a board plugins/ Plugin catalog, built-in and user plugin loading, skill projection, and plugin MCP servers projects/ Project registry: scaffolding, scanning context/projects/, and project metadata memory/ Memory/index management. index-regen.ts rebuilds the generated index.md files from YAML frontmatter and the access log (CLI: cortex memory regen). File watcher for context changes. AGENTS.md scanning and injection, and the rules loader hooks/ Read-only view of the hook registry for the Web UI monitor/ GPU and disk resource monitoring system/ Host-level concerns: doctor checks, update state and prompts, system notices and their history, and rebuild-hold.ts — the supervisor-pushed "no new turns" state consulted by admission browser/ The agent browser broker (broker.ts): one lease per session that binds it to its own tab in the server's or a device's Chrome, closes the tab after 10 idle minutes, and holds the user's takeover state (see agent-browser.md) remote/ Remote device management via WebSocket. SSH-based client bootstrap; clients self-update from server-pushed bundles mcp/ The bundled Cortex MCP server and its tool modules (see mcp.md) ui-service/ The backend of the Web UI: the tRPC AppRouter (app-router.ts), its query and mutation handlers, and the event-bus subscription that streams live events to the UI (subscribe.ts) tui-session/ Session handshake and switching for the TUI gateway benchmark/ Production benchmark evidence: attempt identity and journals, and the export behind cortex-evidence-export

docs.title: Layer 4: orchestration/ — Message Routing and Execution
docs.text:
Connects platform messages to domain logic. The hook-bridge (part of this layer) is detailed in hooks.md.

File Purpose conduit-queue.ts Per-conduit serial Promise queue. Ensures only one turn runs per conversation at a time and lets !cancel discard a pending tail orchestrator.ts Hands each inbound message to AgentRunner agent-runner.ts Admission for the default-agent path: routing, mid-turn injection, queueing, and the session and lease resolution a turn needs. The turn body itself belongs to turn/turn.ts session-gateway.ts deliverToSession() — the one door into a conversation turn for everything that is not an inbound platform message (web sends, scheduled fires, agent results, resumes, waitpoint wakes) session-events.ts Publishes the session.* events the Web UI and TUI render: messages, deltas, status, turns, todos, context usage runtime.ts The PlatformAdapter + EventBus orchestration holds, injected once by the composition root conversation-request.ts prepareConversationRequest() — assembles a plain chat turn's RunRequest: agent spec plus the first-turn ambient blocks turn/turn.ts Turn / openTurn() — the single owner of one conversation turn: status message, ledger turn tracking, session lease, startRun, observer fan-out, terminal render, the running:true/false bracket turn/turn-prep.ts What a caller resolves before openTurn: the turn's files and its session record and use lease turn/terminal.ts A turn's terminal rendering: status seal, the ledger's turn completion, the error body, error-session persistence turn/turn-tracking.ts The ledger half of a turn's bookkeeping: begin, snapshot, accept, and the supersede-while-pending window turn/active-turns.ts Per-channel turn state: the streaming callback a turn registered, the edit-supersede flag turn/background-hold.ts One hold lifecycle for "the turn is over but the session is not": busy bracket, SessionHolds registration, run subscription, six terminal verdicts turn/hold-render-platform.ts The Slack/Feishu rendering of a held turn — the status line while the background phase runs, and its seal turn/hold-render-web.ts The web rendering of a held turn — the continuation's prose, tools and notices on the session event stream mid-turn-inject.ts, session-compact.ts, session-rewind.ts Steering a message into a running turn, compaction on request, and rewinding a conversation to an earlier turn subagent-*.ts, team-*.ts Delivery of background subagent results and of team worker reports into their parent or lead session waitpoint-*.ts Waitpoint signal ingress, the periodic sweep, draining spooled signals from connected devices, and wake notices session-retention-controller.ts Runs the session-retention sweep at startup, every 6 hours, and on a retention setting change resume-dispatcher.ts Rate-limit resume queue: continues the sessions a usage limit interrupted once the window resets busy-tracker.ts Tracks active LLM count, sends IPC busy/idle to parent daemon process human-answer-backstop.ts Leaf registry of channels waiting on a human's free-text reply, consulted by every entry into a session so the answer is consumed instead of opening a turn routing/message-router.ts Platform message entry point: registers the inbound message handler on the adapter and delegates to the orchestrator routing/commands/ !command handlers, one module per family: cancel, channel, compact, cost, device, lang, login (with login-custom), mode, nvtop, orient, restart, schedule, sendfile, session, status, tail, usage (with usage-reset). index.ts maps the command words — !agent, !backend, !model, !thinking, !new, !resume, !usage and the rest — to them routing/webhook.ts The loopback webhook server (WEBHOOK_PORT, default 3001): hook callbacks, cortex-signal, cortex-browser leases (browser-webhook.ts), subagent, team and board callbacks routing/hook-bridge.ts PreToolUse hook → EventBus bridge. Publishes plan.submitted and ask-user.requested routing/hook-bridge-subscribers.ts Subscribers that turn a question or a submitted plan into an interaction record, which each surface renders as a card interactions/ AskUserQuestion flow, plan approval state machine, button/modal action routing

docs.title: Layer 5: entry/ — Composition Root
docs.text: File Purpose app.ts Composition root. Loads .env and migrates legacy settings, then wires EventBus → event logger → hook bridge → RunRegistry/plan approvals/busy tracker → platform adapters → outbound queue → auth watch → scheduler → commands → interactions → message handler → Web UI host → platform connect → client manager → webhook → memory watcher shutdown.ts SIGTERM handling: an ordered list of shutdown steps, each run even when an earlier one fails, then exit daemon.ts Process supervisor. Forks app.js, watches $CORTEX_REPO/src for auto-rebuild (when CORTEX_REPO is set), watches .restart trigger file, crash recovery with exponential backoff (1s→30s max). Publishes per-step rebuild progress, waits for an idle app before install/restart, and holds new turns across that window (see below) daemon-notice.ts The app side of the downward IPC: turns rebuild-aborted into a system notice and rebuild-hold into the admission hold, and lifts the hold if the supervisor disconnects cortex-cli.ts, cli.ts cortex CLI entry point. Dispatches to init, config, auth, doctor, feishu, restart, setup-gateway, ui, client, install, schedule, memory, start, daemon, tui, each implemented in its own *-cli.ts module (see cli-reference.md) browser-cli.ts, hook-cli.ts, signal-cli.ts, production-evidence-export-cli.ts The cortex-browser, cortex-hook, cortex-signal and cortex-evidence-export binaries init.ts Interactive first-time initialization start-ui-http.ts, ui-http-gate.ts, ui-service-wiring.ts Start the Web UI host when CORTEX_UI_HTTP is on, and wire the UiService it serves startup-helpers.ts Cleanup logs, ensure MCP config startup-notify.ts Send startup DM to admin channel platform-connect.ts Start the platform adapters. The TUI gateway is bound before boot continues; Slack and Feishu connect in the background, so boot never waits on a network handshake (outbound posts use their HTTP APIs, not the socket). A failed connect is retried after 5 s, 30 s and 2 min, then reported as an error notice; a platform still connecting after 60 s is reported as a warning

docs.title: Hot Rebuild: Published Progress and the Turn Hold
docs.text:
With CORTEX_REPO set, a source change makes the supervisor rebuild the packages, reinstall itself, and replace the app process. The build runs as three concurrent lanes. One is an ordered chain — server, then ui-contract, then web-typecheck — because ui-contract re-exports the server's built types and web typechecks against ui-contract's built output. The other two, web-bundle and web-depcruise, read only web sources and start at once beside it. Every lane runs to its end, and any failed step stops the rebuild before the install, with a notice naming each step that failed. Two mechanisms make the rebuild visible and safe.

Progress lives in a file, not in memory. Before step one the pipeline writes its whole plan to $STORE_DIR/daemon-rebuild.json — the steps this checkout will run (the build steps above, then install and restart), which are in flight, and how each ended (done, failed, skipped), with the install step recording whether it took the fast staged-rename path or npm pack + npm install -g. A file is the only option: the pipeline's last act replaces the very process that would have held that state, so nothing in memory can tell the new app.js what the rebuild it was born from did. system.daemonStatus reads the record and the daemon page renders it, polling once per second while a rebuild runs. A running record whose daemonPid is not the live supervisor is dropped rather than shown forever; a terminal record is kept, so "the last rebuild failed at web-typecheck" is still readable after the restart. The terminal statuses are succeeded, aborted, and deferred.

The dangerous half of the pipeline waits for an idle app. The build steps read the repo and write dist/; the install step overwrites the files the running app.js loaded and restart kills it. So busy/idle is checked twice: once before the build, and again after it, because a build takes minutes and a turn can legitimately have started meanwhile. A busy child at the second gate parks the trigger in pendingRebuild, publishes the record as deferred, and the whole pipeline runs again on the next idle transition — real work is waited for, not refused, because a refused turn is not a delayed turn (a waitpoint wake or a background agent's result would be dropped outright).

No new turns in the seconds the process is being replaced. Entering install or restart — or queueing a restart — makes the supervisor send rebuild-hold down the fork IPC, and admission (agent-runner.ts) refuses before tracking, queueing, or mid-turn injection: a turn started now is orphaned by the SIGTERM a moment later, with its backend CLI left writing into a pipe no one reads. The scope is deliberately narrow — never the build — so the only messages it can catch are those landing in the tick-level race between the idle check and the SIGTERM. A person who typed gets an in-channel reply naming the current phase; a callback or system message nobody is waiting on becomes a warning-level system notice naming what was dropped. The hold carries a five-minute lease renewed by each phase message, so a supervisor that dies mid-pipeline cannot mute the app forever, and an IPC disconnect lifts it immediately.

docs.title: LLM Backend Adapter
docs.text:
The agent-adapter/ directory abstracts two LLM backends behind a unified interface:

Backend Adapter Notes Claude Code claude/adapter.ts Stateless engine adapter: opens a Claude process session (print mode), spawn-args builder, event parser and translator PI pi/adapter.ts Stateless engine adapter: opens an in-process PI session, MCP bridge, hook bridge, tool shims

The session pool lives in domain/runs/engines.ts (SessionEngines), not in either adapter.

Each adapter translates its backend's events into the unified NormalizedEvent shapes (normalize/) and the RunEvent stream (run-events.ts). The capabilities.ts file declares a Capability enum with capability sets for Claude and PI. See backends.md for how runs, sessions and engines fit together.

docs.title: Platform Adapter
docs.text:
platform/adapter.ts defines the PlatformAdapter interface. Slack (adapters/slack.ts), Feishu (adapters/feishu.ts) and the TUI gateway (adapters/tui/) implement it, and adapters/composite-adapter.ts combines whichever are online into one adapter that routes each outbound call to the platform owning the conduit (slack:, feishu:, tui-). The Web UI does not go through this interface; it reads and drives sessions through domain/ui-service/ (see Web UI Protocol).

Member Purpose name / capabilities Identity and what the platform supports start / stop Lifecycle onMessage / onMessageEdit / onAction / onModalSubmit Event registration postMessage / updateMessage / deleteMessage Outbound messaging postInteractive Interactive messages with buttons openModal Modals markQueued / unmarkQueued The queued marker on a message waiting behind a running turn uploadFile / downloadFile File operations openOutputStream A stream that renders an agent's output as it arrives bindProjectConduit / unbindProjectConduit / getProjectConduits / resolveInboundProject Project ↔ channel bindings ownsConduit Whether a conduit id belongs to this platform getPermalink / adminChannelKey / setAdminChannel Utility and the admin channel used for system notices

OutputStream (platform/output-stream.ts, with Slack, Feishu and chunked implementations under adapters/) carries a turn's output to a chat platform: committed text, mutable regions such as the status line that later edits update in place, and interactive messages, split into chunks the platform accepts and queued so updates arrive in order.

docs.title: WebSocket Protocol (Server ↔ Client)
docs.text: The WebSocket protocol is used for remote device command execution, not for chat or UI traffic. The server runs a WebSocket server (default port 3002, CORTEX_CLIENT_PORT) via startClientManager(). Every connection presents the client token in the x-cortex-token header. For the full cross-machine story — deployment, network topology, and security — see cross-machine.md.

docs.title: Message Flow
docs.text:
1. Client connects → sends { type: 'hello', device, platform, capabilities, gpuCount, bundleHash, pid? }
  2. Server validates → closes with 4001 when the device name is missing, 4005 when machines.json does not list it, and 4002 when that device is already connected
  3. Heartbeat → client sends { type: 'heartbeat', device, timestamp } every 5 seconds. Server closes a device silent for 15 seconds (code 4003)
  4. Command dispatch → server sends { type: 'command', commandId, action, params }. Client executes and replies with { type: 'result', commandId, success, data, error }
  5. Update → when the bundleHash differs from the server's client bundle, the server sends { type: 'update', hash, files }; the client installs it, answers update-result, and restarts on the new bundle
  6. Streams → open-stream (a TCP port forward) and open-file-stream (a file transfer) ask the client to dial back a separate WebSocket for the bytes; a callback naming an unknown stream is closed with 4004

docs.title: Command Actions
docs.text: The client supports these remote actions: bash (shell execution with timeout/background), read (file read with text/image/PDF support), write (file write with CRLF detection), edit (text replacement with replace_all), glob (file glob with VCS exclusion), grep (ripgrep with pagination), file.stat (pre-transfer metadata probe).

docs.title: Client Architecture
docs.text: The client (client/src/client.ts) is a lightweight WebSocket daemon that maintains a persistent connection. It supports automatic reconnection with exponential backoff (1s→30s max). It does not launch or supervise long-running jobs: those run independently and report back through a waitpoint.

docs.title: Web UI Protocol
docs.text:
The browser workbench, the desktop app and the mobile app all talk to the server through one HTTP host (platform/ui-http/), started when CORTEX_UI_HTTP is on. It listens on 127.0.0.1:3004 (CORTEX_UI_PORT); remote access goes through a tunnel or a LAN proxy (see browser-access.md and desktop-app.md).

  • tRPC under /trpc/. Queries and mutations are plain HTTP requests against the AppRouter in domain/ui-service/app-router.ts; the web app gets its types from packages/ui-contract.
  • Live events use one subscribe subscription over Server-Sent Events. The client names the event types it wants, optionally scoped to a project or session, and the server forwards matching CortexEvents from the bus through a bounded queue, sending ui-subscribe.dropped if the client falls behind. A subscriber to streamed text first receives a snapshot of the assistant message in progress.
  • Authentication, checked in order: the x-cortex-token header carrying the client token (the desktop and mobile apps), a cortex_ui session cookie from token login (/api/ui/login, /api/ui/logout, /api/ui/session), or a Cloudflare Access JWT. Browser origins outside the same origin need an entry in the uiCorsOrigins setting.
  • Other routes: file download and attachment upload (/api/files/download, /api/attachments/upload), board assets (/api/boards/asset), the web-bundle update the desktop app downloads (/api/ui-ota/manifest.json, /api/ui-ota/bundle.zip), the native app update manifest (/api/app-update/manifest.json), port forwarding to remote machines (/api/forward/*, with the /forward WebSocket), and the agent browser: its sessions, takeover and typed text (/api/browser/*) and the live view over the /api/browser/stream WebSocket.
  • The same host serves the built web app, so a browser loads the UI and its API from one origin.

The TUI uses a separate WebSocket gateway on port 3003 (CORTEX_TUI_PORT), and hooks and signals reach the server through the loopback webhook on port 3001.

docs.title: Event Bus Topology
docs.text:
The EventBus is created in app.ts. runRegistry, planApprovals and busyTracker are constructed with no dependencies and wired with setBus(bus); every other component receives the bus as an argument.

Component Publishes Subscribes runRegistry agent.started/completed/failed/superseded — eventLogger event-logger.dropped '*' (all events → JSONL) hookBridge plan.submitted, ask-user.requested — routing/hook-bridge-subscribers.ts — plan.submitted, ask-user.requested planApprovals plan.approved — interactionHandlers ask-user.answered — busyTracker llm.active-count-delta (pending background tasks) llm.active-count-delta, counted to send IPC busy/idle orchestration/session-events.ts session.* — domain/auth/ auth.required, auth.recovered auth.* (auth watch) domain/boards/ board.updated board.updated (board watcher) domain/system/system-notice.ts system.notice — app.ts config.changed, rate-limit.changed session.status (session holds) resume-dispatcher.ts — agent.completed/failed/superseded team-delivery.ts, subagent-delivery.ts — session.turn.completed, session.status domain/ui-service/ ui.mutate-invoked the event types each UI subscription asks for

docs.title: State Storage
docs.text:
Cortex stores all state on the filesystem under ~/.cortex/. There is no database — everything is JSON or JSONL on disk, with the session registry and history paths intentionally append-oriented. Paths below are relative to ~/.cortex/; configuration.md lists the whole tree.

Path Purpose data/agent-state.json Channel selections, model memory, new-session choice, and default agent config/models.json Default engine selection and favorite models config/budget.json Daily and monthly budget limits config/environments/ Execution environments — one JSON file per environment data/schedules.json Persistent schedule list data/boards.json Board registry: each board's project, slug, title, creation time and last use (created, attached to by a session, or its files changed). The page itself lives in the project context under boards/<slug>/ data/session-registry.jsonl Append-only JSONL journal and single owner of session records, channel→session bindings, and per-channel conversation headers and turns. Events: put/patch/delete-intent/delete-commit/bind/unbind/turn/conversation; startup replays the stream to rebuild live and pending state. Compaction keeps live records + bindings + live turns; it runs once the journal holds more than max(512, live×4, 2×compacted) events — where compacted is the number of events a compaction would write — or exceeds both 16 MB and twice its size after the last compaction. A one-time upgrade migration imports the retired sessions.json and conversation-ledger.json and renames them to *.pre-2026.9.14.bak data/retention-candidates.json Two-sweep orphan retention candidates for history and PI cleanup data/conversation-history/ Per-session transcript/history JSONL keyed by stable Cortex session id data/executions.json Unified execution registry data/archive/ Terminal execution records older than a week, moved out of executions.json data/provider-state.json Provider usage, throttle windows, and the provider-attributed resume queue data/waitpoints.json Waitpoints and their signals data/team-inbox.json, data/team-outbox.json Messages between team leads and workers data/ui-sessions.json Browser login sessions for the Web UI browser/profile/ Profile of the server's agent browser: its cookies and logins data/daemon-rebuild.json The supervisor's published hot-rebuild record: plan, per-step status and timings, and the terminal outcome of the last rebuild data/costs.jsonl Per-call cost records (90-day rolling) logs/sessions/ Claude capture logs used for retention protection/cleanup logs/sessions-pi/ PI transcript bundles keyed by backend session id logs/ Daemon and backend logs, and the daily event log under logs/events/

The session registry is an append-only journal rather than a mutable JSON file. session-registry-journal.ts owns an append-only JSONL file whose events carry the full session record for put and delete-intent, plus a final delete-commit. A delete intent also freezes the validated Claude turn-backup cleanup manifest, so a later retry does not depend on a ledger that an earlier partial cleanup already removed. Startup first migrates any legacy session-registry.json file into the journal, writes a backup of that legacy file, truncates any unterminated tail, and then stream-replays the journal line by line into in-memory live and pending maps. When the journal grows too large, compaction rewrites a minimal snapshot consisting of one full-record event per live session plus one delete-intent event per pending deletion.

Session retention is coordinated separately from registry mutation. session-retention-controller.ts starts a session-retention.ts sweep in the background at app startup — boot does not wait for it, and the session registry's own lock serializes it against other session mutations — then runs it every 6 hours, with an immediate debounced rerun when sessionRetentionDays hot-reloads. The startup sweep begins after any ready provider-resume dispatch, and queued direct resumes retain their stable tracking id as a liveness guard. The coordinator retries pending delete commits, writes registry delete intents for all expired idle sessions in one append, then works through them in batches of 100 — one append each releases their channel bindings and their conversations, their files are deleted, and one append commits the sessions whose cleanup succeeded. Stopping the controller aborts the sweep between batches, leaving uncommitted deletions pending for the next sweep. It also prunes orphan conversation-history, prunes orphan PI transcript bundles, prunes inactive Claude capture logs, prunes orphan tmp/tool-images/ session directories, and syncs Claude user cleanupPeriodDays.

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Execution IDs: exec_<kind>_<base36-ts>_<4-rand> (e.g., exec_local_1a2b3c_xyzw)
  • Schedule IDs: 8 hex characters (from randomBytes(4))
  • Session IDs: UUIDs identify sessions in the registry and UI. Unlabeled sessions display the first 8 characters of the UUID. /resume accepts a full UUID or a unique prefix of at least 6 characters.
  • Board IDs: 8 hex characters (from randomBytes(4)). A board's directory is a slug of its title, with a numeric suffix when the slug is taken, or board-<id> when the title has no slug-safe characters.
  • Waitpoint IDs: wp_ followed by 12 hex characters (from randomBytes(6)); each waitpoint also carries its own secret for cortex-signal.
  • File format: All TypeScript uses .ts with ESM import style (import { X } from './foo.js')

docs.title: Backends
docs.text: A backend is Cortex's adapter for a specific coding agent. Cortex does not call LLM APIs directly. It drives a coding agent — Claude Code as a child process, PI as a session inside the server process — sends messages to it, and consumes a normalized event stream. Each backend implements the EngineAdapter interface defined in agent-server/src/agent-adapter/types.ts.

docs.title: Supported backends
docs.text: Backend Status Engine Requirement Feature level Claude Code Supported @anthropic-ai/claude-code the claude binary on PATH Full PI Supported @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent, installed with the server package none beyond a logged-in provider Full

docs.title: How backends work
docs.text:
Three nouns cover the path from a message to a backend process: a run, a session, and an engine.

A run is one execution of one user request: a conversation turn, a hook-injected turn, an edit retry, an ask-user resume, or a subagent child. startRun (domain/runs/service.ts) opens one from a fully resolved RunRequest — engine selection, prompt, policy, and context — plus the observers that watch it, and returns the AgentRun (domain/runs/run.ts) that owns the run's event stream, its cancel and steer handles, and its result.

A session is the conversation identity a run continues: the stable Cortex session id, the backend's own resume id, its engine selection, and the channel it is bound to. A session owns the engine it resumes into. A run reuses its session's pooled engine; a hook-injected turn gets an engine key, and an engine, of its own.

The engine is the backend process itself — a pooled claude subprocess or an in-process PI SDK session. SessionEngines (domain/runs/engines.ts) is the only owner of pooled engines: acquire(spec) reuses the session for a spec's engine key when it is alive and was opened from the same session identity, and otherwise retires it and opens a new one. The adapter is stateless; it opens a session from an EngineSpec and translates what that session emits.

Configuration is resolved once per run. resolveRunSelection (domain/runs/config-resolver.ts) uses an explicit complete selection, then the session's recorded selection, the channel's selection, then models.json's default. The selection supplies backend, model, provider, gateway mode, and thinking level. buildEngineSpec (domain/runs/engine-spec.ts) produces a backend-neutral EngineSpec, which the adapter translates into Claude Code command-line arguments or in-process PI session options. Each run uses one engine selection.

From there the engine emits one RunEvent stream (agent-adapter/run-events.ts). Each adapter translates its backend's native events into the NormalizedEvent shapes declared in agent-adapter/normalize/, and toRunEvent tags them with the run's phase, so the run layer never needs to know which backend is running.

A run outlives its turn. Claude opens a turn of its own when a background task finishes, so a run has two endings and both are on the same stream. The foreground result is the answer to the request: it lands as soon as the backend finishes the turn, which is what await run.result gives a surface — the reply is rendered and the status message can go into its waiting state while the run is still alive. The settled result is the whole run with every continuation folded in; it is what the terminal tally, the execution record and the cost attribution read. A policy decides what happens after the foreground result (RunRequest.policy.background): an interactive turn holds the session open for the continuation (hold), and a run that cannot produce one, or whose caller has no use for it, ends at the first result (none).

The wait itself is bounded, the work is not. ContinuationPhase (agent-adapter/continuation-phase.ts) arms a grace timer for work the backend reported finished but never announced (CORTEX_BG_GRACE_S, 90s) and a cap for work still running (CORTEX_BG_WAIT_MAX_S, 30min); both defaults live in agent-adapter/bg-wait.ts. The grace period expiring ends the run; the cap expiring only ends the waiting — a tunnel or a monitor that runs for an hour still streams its continuation into the same session when it finishes.

docs.title: Feature matrix
docs.text:
Cortex defines four capabilities that a backend may support. The orchestration layer checks capabilities before attempting backend-specific operations.

Capability Claude Code PI Description mid-turn-inject yes yes Accept user input into a turn already in flight usage no yes Report scoped provider usage from a pull source or push cache background-continuation yes no Open a continuation turn of its own after the foreground result subagents yes yes Host a delegated subagent child, streamed and billed under its parent

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
The reference backend. Each session runs a persistent claude -p process with stream-json input and output. Cortex pools the process by session key and sends later turns over the same NDJSON stream until the session is closed, times out, or its spawn identity changes.

Claude Code sessions are pooled by engine key for reuse (SessionEngines, domain/runs/engines.ts). Each turn's cost is the growth of the CLI's own cumulative total_cost_usd, measured from the total a resumed session starts with (see Cost reporting).

Every claude process Cortex starts runs with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$CORTEX_HOME/data/claude, Cortex's own Claude Code config directory, so its transcripts, user settings, plugins and login stay apart from a terminal claude using ~/.claude. A pinned benchmark trial keeps the config directory its own environment names. The directory, its one-time seed from ~/.claude/settings.json, and the plugin install command are described in Configuration → Claude Code config directory. The session-retention coordinator keeps that directory's cleanupPeriodDays equal to the sessionRetentionDays runtime setting, preserving every other key.

docs.title: PI
docs.text:
PI runs inside the Cortex server process. The engine (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent) is bundled into the published server package, so there is no separate pi command-line install and no PI process to supervise. agent-server/src/core/pi-sdk.ts imports the SDK once per daemon — on the first PI session or provider scan, since the entry pulls in every provider client — and every PI session is created from that one handle.

Sessions. Each Cortex session runs on one PI SDK AgentSession. session-options.ts resolves the spawn configuration into a session request, and runtime.ts builds the session from it: a SettingsManager for the working directory, a ModelRuntime reading auth.json and models.json from Cortex's private PI agent directory, then createAgentSessionServices and createAgentSessionFromServices. Sessions are pooled by session key and reused across turns. A pooled session is retired when its spawn identity changes — a different model, tool surface, or MCP set cannot be applied to a live session — and when it goes idle or an explicit teardown closes it. pi-session.ts owns the turn loop, mid-turn steering through the SDK's steer path, compaction, and re-pointing a live session at another transcript. Resume names a session id or a transcript path; session-files.ts maps the id to its file. Transcripts are written under $CORTEX_HOME/logs/sessions-pi/.

Mid-turn compaction. A single Cortex turn is one whole PI agent loop, so a long tool-driven turn must be able to compact from inside that loop. PI does this itself: after the tool results land and before the next assistant response, it compacts if the context has passed contextWindow - reserveTokens, then resumes the same run, so the turn is never aborted and stays one Cortex turn. Cortex only sets the threshold — piCompactReserveTokens (default 16384, PI's own default) is mirrored into the private agent dir's settings.json when a session is created, and a larger reserve makes PI compact earlier, leaving more working headroom. Claude needs none of this: the CLI compacts inside a turn by itself.

Context cap. maxContextTokens caps the usable window of every model on both backends. Claude receives it as CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW. On PI, Cortex leaves the model's own window untouched, since PI also uses it to detect overflow, and instead widens the reserve that runtime-settings.ts reports by the window's excess over the cap. PI then compacts at cap - piCompactReserveTokens, with the reserve bounded to half the cap so a large reserve cannot compact every turn.

Cortex's glue. Everything Cortex adds is a set of inline PI extensions assembled per session in extensions.ts:

  • Image first (image-first.ts) — moves the images in a tool result ahead of its text in each request.
  • MCP bridge (mcp-bridge.ts) — serves the composition-scoped Cortex tool bundles in-process over an in-memory MCP transport pair, bound to a tool context built for that one session. Assigned plugin MCP servers keep their own stdio children or remote connections.
  • Tool shims (tool-shims.ts) — registers the PI-local web_fetch, web_search and todo_write tools, each subject to the session's tool allowlist under its Claude name (WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite), and the agent and agent_stop delegation tools where the session may delegate (see Subagents).
  • Hook bridge (hook-bridge.ts) — mounts the hook-registry entries that target the pi backend as native PI event handlers, so Cortex hook scripts see PI tool events. See hooks.md.
  • Quota probe (quota-probe.ts) — reads provider quota off response headers on gateway-routed runs and hands each reading to the throttle.

System prompt override, appended prompts, and Cortex plugin skill directories are session options (systemPrompt, appendSystemPrompt, additionalSkillPaths), not command-line flags.

Interaction tools. User-initiated direct PI sessions add the interaction bundle to their in-process Cortex tool set, so PI exposes the same cortex_ask_user, cortex_plan_enter, and cortex_plan_exit tools as Claude TUI and Claude print. Their dialogs travel over PI's extension UI protocol, which ui-context.ts answers inside the server; see safety-and-approvals.md.

Cache warming. Cortex disables PI's automatic prompt-cache warming in both main and subagent sessions. Ordinary provider prompt caching remains available; Cortex does not issue extra warming requests whose usage is outside its cost accounting. This is a runtime override and leaves the terminal PI settings intact.

Credentials. PI provider credentials are managed by Cortex — !login pi in chat or Settings → Accounts on the web — and stored in PI's own auth file at ~/.pi/agent/auth.json. Cortex makes that file visible inside its private PI agent directory (a symlink on Linux and macOS, a copy on Windows) so the SDK reads it, and it reads user-defined providers from ~/.pi/agent/models.json. An installation that also has the terminal pi CLI therefore shares one set of credentials and one provider catalog with Cortex.

PI transcript retention is filesystem-based. Active PI backend session ids are protected during retention sweeps, while orphan transcript bundles under $CORTEX_HOME/logs/sessions-pi/ are deleted only after they stay unreferenced past the retention cutoff and survive a second confirmation sweep.

PI provider names are independent of Cortex backend names. In particular, openai-codex is a supported PI provider (including the openai-codex-responses API kind); engine selections using it set "backend": "pi".

docs.title: Subagents
docs.text:
Both backends delegate through one tool, one role table, and one runner, and either backend can be the parent or the child. A Claude turn can hand work to a PI model and a PI turn can hand work to Claude.

The tool. PI registers agent and agent_stop in-process. Claude gets the same pair as MCP tools (mcp__cortex-core__agent, mcp__cortex-core__agent_stop) and its own built-in Agent tool is stripped from every spawn, so there is no second delegation path the daemon cannot see. One call runs a single task, up to eight in parallel, or up to eight chained; {previous} in a chained prompt is replaced with the previous link's output.

Roles. A role is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter. explore, general-purpose, and plan are built in and read from the install's agent-server/defaults/agents/; a file in $CORTEX_HOME/config/agents/ adds a role, or replaces the built-in role of the same name, and deleting it brings the built-in one back. The role body is appended to the child's system prompt. Its frontmatter must set name and description — a file without them is ignored — and may set:

Key Meaning tools Canonical tool names, translated into each backend's own spelling model provider/model[:thinking] for a PI child, a bare model id for a Claude child backend claude or pi; absent means "whatever the parent is running" mode PI child route: role value, then the PI parent’s route on the same provider, then the provider name. Claude children use their Claude parent’s route or the configured Claude-backend default route

When $CORTEX_HOME/config/agents/ does not exist yet, roles found in an agents/ directory inside Cortex's private PI agent directory are moved into it at startup, and that directory is renamed to agents.migrated so an edit there cannot silently do nothing.

Choosing the model. The model is the task's explicit model when given, then the role's model, then the parent's own model — but only when the child runs the same backend, since a Claude model id means nothing to PI and a PI provider/model means nothing to Claude. A Claude child without an explicit or same-backend parent model uses the Claude-backend default (the configured default if Claude, otherwise the first Claude favorite). A PI parent starting a Claude child also uses that Claude default’s route and requires a Claude default or favorite to be configured.

What the caller can see. The subagent_type, model, and backend field descriptions are rendered at tool-registration time rather than hardcoded, from what this host actually has. Roles come from the live role table — the built-in roles with $CORTEX_HOME/config/agents/ laid over them — so a role you add shows up in the next session. Claude model ids come from the same table Cortex builds the gateway's Anthropic routes from, plus the daemon's current model. A PI parent reads its own live model registry; a Claude parent cannot, because its MCP tool runs in a sidecar process that has no PI SDK, so the daemon passes down the provider/model pairs of its cached scan through the spawn environment. A cold cache simply means no PI models are listed yet — the scan is never provoked just to decorate a Claude spawn. Roles and models each have a character budget, and overflow renders as (+N more). The lists are a snapshot, so they do not change mid-session, and they are hints rather than a whitelist: an unlisted model id is still accepted and passed through. When nothing is known, the descriptions fall back to the generic wording, so the tool never fails over a missing catalog.

Isolation. A pi child is a nested in-process session that writes no transcript and runs headless. A claude child is a frozen one-shot claude run: no session to resume, no hooks, no ambient rules, no transcript log. Either way the child's MCP surface is the cortex-core bundle with the delegation tools removed, so it cannot fan out further.

What the parent sees. A child's tool calls, results, and text are streamed into the parent's live transcript attributed to the subagent, and its token usage is rolled into the parent's. Attribution is best-effort: a run whose parent turn has already ended simply stops streaming and still returns its answer.

Background runs. run_in_background: true returns an agent_id immediately. Cortex holds the session open for the length of the run — the Stop button reaches it, and a deferred daemon restart waits for it — and delivers the answer as an ordinary turn when it is ready, folding into a live turn if one is running. agent_stop cancels a run early and discards what it had produced. Stopping a session stops its delegated runs too, foreground and background alike: children never outlive the turn that asked for them.

docs.title: Remote login
docs.text:
Backend login can be completed remotely without SSH access to the Cortex host. The same login flow is exposed through three channels:

Channel Entry Interaction Slack Send !login, !login cc, or !login pi [provider] Selectors and secret fields open in Slack modals; authorization links are posted to the channel. Feishu Send !login, !login cc, or !login pi [provider] Selectors and secret fields use inline card forms; authorization links are posted to the chat. Web (desktop and mobile) Desktop: open Settings → Accounts. Mobile: tap Settings → Accounts to drill in to /m/settings/accounts. The Accounts section shows Claude Code credentials and every PI provider, with status plus login/logout actions that open the same selector-driven login flow.

The chat command forms are:

!login
!login status
!login cc
!login pi
!login pi <provider>
!login custom

!login custom manages self-hosted endpoints that have no login flow; see Custom providers below.

!login with no arguments and !login status both show the authentication status overview. !login cc selects Claude Code. !login pi opens a PI provider selector; adding a provider skips that selector. Authentication type is also selected interactively when a provider supports more than one type. Do not append oauth, API keys, authorization codes, or provider-specific OAuth flags to the command.

One backend/provider pair has at most one login in progress. Starting a login cancels an unfinished one for the same pair, whichever channel started it, unless that login is already saving a submitted credential; then the new start is refused until it finishes. A failed login shows Cortex's message followed by the first line of the provider's own reason.

OAuth is offered only when the installed PI provider exposes provider.auth.oauth.login as a function. The list is discovered from the installed PI runtime, so API-key-only providers never show a non-functional OAuth option. Claude Code similarly offers API-key and subscription choices through the selector.

For a Claude Code subscription, Cortex starts claude auth login --claudeai against its own Claude config directory, sends the command's authorization URL to the initiating channel, and writes the returned code to that command's standard input. Claude Code owns the OAuth exchange and credential persistence. Cortex marks the flow complete only after an authentication-environment-scrubbed claude auth status --json reports loggedIn: true; it never reads or stores the resulting token. Subscription logout similarly delegates to claude auth logout and verifies the logged-out postcondition. A legacy Cortex-managed subscription token remains a removable runtime credential while Claude Code is logged out, but it does not make the account appear logged in and is suppressed as soon as Claude owns a credential.

When a running backend reports expired authentication, Cortex posts a card that names the provider and offers one-click re-login, pre-filled with the authentication type that failed: for Claude Code, the API key when the run used api mode and the subscription otherwise. While that login runs, the button reopens it; after it fails, is cancelled or expires, the button starts a new one. A daily expiration scan checks in-use accounts and sends the same actionable warning for credentials that are expiring, expired, or missing. The daily scan skips any provider the runtime notification already reported within the reminder window, so a scheduled warning never repeats a notice you just received. The reverse is deliberate: a runtime failure always notifies, even if the daily scan warned about that provider earlier, because an in-session failure is the message you most need at that moment.

For a read-only status check from the host, use:

cortex auth status
cortex auth status --json

The text form is a concise overview; --json returns the complete normalized status snapshot. Both are credential-free. See CLI Reference for the exact command contract.

docs.title: Custom providers
docs.text:
A custom provider is an endpoint PI does not ship a definition for: a local inference server, a lab GPU box, or a company proxy. It has no login flow — there is no vendor to authenticate against — so it is defined rather than logged into, and it is managed from the same three surfaces as everything else:

Surface Entry CLI cortex auth provider list \| add \| remove Web (desktop and mobile) Settings → Accounts → Custom providers Slack / Feishu !login custom [list \| add <name> <api> <url> <model…> \| remove <name>]

A definition needs four things: a name, the request protocol the endpoint speaks (anthropic-messages, openai-completions, openai-responses, or google-generative-ai), the upstream URL, and at least one model id. An upstream key is optional; without one the gateway passes the caller's own key through.

Saving writes two files. ~/.pi/agent/models.json gets a providers.<name> entry whose baseUrl points at the gateway, so the terminal pi and Cortex share one definition. ~/.aistatus/gateway.yaml gets the route that forwards to the real endpoint, carrying the upstream key. The key lives only in the gateway config — the PI catalog holds a placeholder, so copying the catalog around never copies a secret. Every call therefore goes through the gateway and is accounted and throttled like any other route. The generated gateway config sets max_body_size_mb: 100. With aistatus 0.0.8 or newer, this caps each buffered request body in MiB; edit the top-level value to use a different limit. The gateway reloads its config by itself, so route and body-limit changes need no restart.

The chat command deliberately has no key argument: a channel transcript is a poor place for a secret. Add the key from the CLI with --key - (read from stdin) or from the Web form, both of which keep it off any transcript.

To use a custom provider, choose its model in the picker or enter !model my-vllm/Model-27B. You can favorite it and make it the default (see configuration.md). Deleting a provider removes its catalog entry and gateway route; first move sessions, the default, favorites, and schedules using it to another provider.

docs.title: Selecting a backend
docs.text:
Each session stores a concrete engine selection: backend, provider, model, thinking, and mode. backend is claude or pi; Claude uses a null provider, while PI requires a provider id that selects its request protocol and gateway endpoint. The default selection and favorites live in config/models.json.

!backend <claude|pi> selects the configured default if it belongs to the target backend, otherwise the first favorite on that backend with its remembered settings. If neither exists, favorite a model there first. A conversation with history cannot change backend; start a new session for that.

docs.title: Per-session model, thinking level and route
docs.text:
The Web and mobile composer's engine picker lists favorite models at its root, showing each model and its remembered thinking level, grouped by backend and provider. Open the full model list to choose another model or use a row's star to add or remove a favorite. The thinking picker includes a default option, which stores null and lets the backend choose. /model opens model selection. The execution environment is a separate choice; see configuration.md.

A selection is saved on the session. Choosing a model restores that model's remembered thinking and route; without a memory, thinking is null, Claude uses the first Anthropic route in gateway.yaml (plan if none is declared), and PI uses its provider name. User changes update the model's memory. A fresh Web conversation starts from the last selected engine on this host.

A conversation with history cannot change backend. The picker disables models on the other backend; a new draft can choose either backend.

Route is the gateway endpoint's billing lane: for example, plan for an Anthropic subscription or api for a metered key. The picker offers routes declared for the endpoint in gateway.yaml, and hides the route choice when only one is available. The model catalog supplies each endpoint's backend, provider, routes, and models. Thinking levels use the backend's range, narrowed to the model's own levels where PI reports them.

Settings → Models manages the default model and the favorites list. Platform channels use the same selection rules through these commands:

Command What it does !model Shows the current selection and favorites, with favorite buttons !model <id> Selects a model on the current backend !model <provider/model> Selects a PI model with an explicit provider !model reset Restores the complete configured default selection !thinking [level] Shows or sets the reasoning level !thinking reset Sets thinking to null, using the backend default !mode [route] Shows or sets the gateway route, validated against the endpoint's routes

docs.title: Thinking level
docs.text: thinking sets reasoning depth in the backend's native value set. Claude Code accepts low/medium/high/xhigh/max, passed as --effort. PI accepts off/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh/max, passed as the session's thinking level. A null value uses the backend's own default. A level the selected model does not accept is clamped by PI to the nearest one it does.

docs.title: Usage-limit throttling and auto-resume
docs.text:
Cortex tracks rolling usage windows by provider. Provider identifiers are opaque strings, so the throttle can track any number of providers without a fixed provider enum. Each provider keeps its own window types and reset times. A provider and route mode are gated without blocking another provider that happens to use the same mode name.

The policy is configured in config/settings.json as providerRateLimits, an object keyed by provider id. Each provider can hold a windows array of { type, label?, enabled, threshold? } entries, so 5-hour, weekly, weekly-overage, Codex primary/secondary, and labeled model windows are independently configurable. threshold is a ratio greater than 0 and at most 1; an omitted value uses 0.95 for the weekly windows (seven_day, seven_day_overage_included) and 0.90 for every other window, five_hour included. Exact window policy takes precedence over the visible, clearable legacy provider fallback. Desktop and mobile Usage edit these rows; spend-only providers do not show quota controls.

docs.title: Why a rate-limit signal is injected, not streamed
docs.text:
The adapter reports a provider's rate-limit window to the host through an injected callback (RateLimitReporter), not as a RunEvent. The backend emits its rate_limit_event between turns and during a spontaneous continuation turn, i.e. exactly when no turn is in flight — routing it through the per-turn event stream would drop the observation that matters most. RunEvent therefore carries rate_limit only as a transcript-level notice (agent-runner ignores it), and the throttle itself is fed by the injected reporter. Quota observations take the same path.

Interrupted conversations are stored with the provider that limited them. When one provider fully recovers, Cortex resumes only that provider's work; entries belonging to other active providers remain queued. A conversation resumes in its own channel with the prior context intact. Resume starts are staggered so a freshly opened window is not immediately exhausted.

The active rate-limit details show the number of waiting conversations for each provider and preserve labels for simultaneous model-scoped windows. The provider key is the isolation boundary: multiple accounts or quota pools reported under the same provider key share one provider record, and windows with the same type and label retain the later reset time. Timed throttling requires a reset-bearing observation. Claude live account-usage pulls submit every reported window for each configured Anthropic mode, while stale PI cache reads are never replayed; PI response-header observations arrive through their push path, and the OpenAI Codex and Claude account reads of each usage collection are described below.

Policy edits apply only to future quota observations. They do not rewrite a window that is already active. An active quota window or outage retry window stays in force until its reset time or a manual Resume now clear; a Codex or Claude quota window also lifts when a fresh account reading shows it below its threshold. Outage retry behavior uses its own outage windows and is unaffected by quota-policy threshold edits.

Throttle windows and provider-attributed resume entries persist in data/provider-state.json. On startup Cortex re-arms active timers and immediately resumes entries whose provider window expired during downtime, even when a different provider remains limited. Provider-less entries from older data wait until every active provider clears. A channel that already has an active conversation is skipped; elapsed age alone does not discard work.

Auto-resume is on by default. Set "autoResume": false in config/settings.json to drop ready resume entries instead of dispatching them automatically; the change takes effect without a daemon restart. The legacy CORTEX_AUTO_RESUME=0 variable in .env is still read as a deprecated fallback.

docs.title: Account usage and banked resets
docs.text:
Every usage collection — the built-in provider-usage job, opening a Usage screen, or Refresh — reads two subscription accounts directly:

  • OpenAI Codex, with a ChatGPT-plan sign-in. The reading fills the Codex primary and secondary windows on the Codex subscription row. When the read fails, the row keeps the windows last observed in Codex response headers and carries a note saying so.
  • Claude, signed in with claude login. The reading fills the five-hour and seven-day windows on the Anthropic subscription row, plus the weekly limit the account scopes to one model, shown with that model's name, such as 7 days (Fable). That model window is the one Claude Code reports as seven_day_overage_included, so its threshold control is the policy that window's throttle uses. Cortex uses the access token Claude Code stores and cannot refresh it, so with an expired token, an API-key setup, or no login the row falls back to the gateway's quota observation; a failed read falls back the same way and adds a note. The account offers resets only to a current Claude Code client, so these requests identify as the installed claude CLI version.

Each reading also lists the account's banked resets: how many are available and when the earliest one expires. An account reading never starts a throttle, but it lifts that provider's throttle windows that have fallen below their threshold, so a reset spent from another device also releases work Cortex paused.

A banked reset applies to the whole account, on every device, and cannot be undone. A Codex reset restores the Codex usage windows and expires about 30 days after it is granted. A Claude reset clears the windows its grant names — typically the five-hour, seven-day, and seven-day-including-overage limits — for claude.ai and every other Claude client as well. Cortex never spends a reset on its own. On the Codex and Anthropic cards in desktop and mobile Usage, Reset appears while a reset is available and asks for confirmation first; the Claude confirmation names the windows the reset clears and, while the account is not at a limit, shows their current use. Cortex spends the reset the account offers next, otherwise the one that expires first. In chat, !usage shows the same count and expiry with a Reset Codex or Reset Claude button that posts a confirm prompt in the thread, and a Codex or Claude throttle notice carries that button next to Resume now while the account holds a reset. After a reset Cortex clears that provider's throttle, resumes the work it paused, and re-reads usage for a few seconds until the account shows the cleared windows restored. When the account declines — nothing to reset, a reset already used, a cooldown, or an account that cannot use resets right now — no reset is spent and Cortex says which case applies.

docs.title: Cost reporting
docs.text:
