Cost reporting differs by backend:

  • Claude Code — reads the cumulative total_cost_usd the CLI reports at the end of each turn and records the increase since the previous turn, with the token counts from the same result. A resumed session starts from the total the CLI restores, so its history is not billed again. Records are written to $CORTEX_HOME/data/costs.jsonl.
  • PI — reads the usage the session reports on each assistant message (input, output, cacheRead, cacheWrite, and cost.total) and sums it per turn into one record naming the provider and model that served it. A token field the provider does not report is recorded as unknown rather than as zero. Records land in the same $CORTEX_HOME/data/costs.jsonl.

All cost records follow the same JSONL format and are subject to a 90-day rolling retention window. Cost queries via MCP tools aggregate across all backends — see mcp.md for the cost_query tool.

docs.title: Adding a new backend
docs.text:
New backends implement the EngineAdapter interface in a new directory under agent-server/src/agent-adapter/. The required surface:

  1. adapter.ts — implements EngineAdapter with open(spec), returning an EngineSession. The adapter is stateless: SessionEngines owns the pool.
  2. EngineSession — carries its backend, identity and backendSessionId, and exposes run(prompt, opts) for one turn, returning an EngineRun whose events is an async iterable of RunEvent, whose result is the foreground AgentResult and whose settled result folds in any continuation, with cancel(); plus steer(), respondToDialog(), ingestExternal(), compact(), close(), and kill().
  3. Event translation — turns the backend's native event format into NormalizedEvent / RunEvent members (for Claude, event-parser.ts and event-translator.ts).
  4. Registration — add the adapter to the assembly in domain/runs/adapters.ts and a branch to SessionEngines.acquire in domain/runs/engines.ts; add capabilities to capabilities.ts; include the backend label in the Backend type union in core/types/agent-types.ts. A backend that hosts subagents also needs a branch in domain/agents/subagent/runner.ts.

Shared pieces live beside the adapters: the normalized event types, prompt building and tool-result image handling in agent-adapter/normalize/, the RunEvent queue in agent-adapter/run-events.ts, and tool-name translation in core/tool-names.ts.

docs.title: Browser Access & Deployment
docs.text:
Cortex ships a browser workbench — the same SPA the desktop app wraps — reachable from any browser without installing anything. This page covers both the deployment runbook (building the SPA and enabling the Web UI endpoint on your server) and the browser access path (reaching it through Cloudflare Access edge login).

There are three independent ways to reach the workbench, and they authenticate differently:

Path Who Authentication Holds clientToken? Browser + Access Anyone with a browser Cloudflare Access edge login (email / IdP), verified as a JWT by the server No — the browser never sees the token Browser + token login Anyone who knows the token The token is pasted once and exchanged for an HttpOnly session cookie No — only the server sees it, and only once Desktop (Tauri) The installed desktop app Bearer x-cortex-token (the clientToken) stored in the OS keychain Yes

This page is the browser + deployment reference. For installing the native desktop app, see Desktop App.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Help → Check for updates (or Settings → Check for updates in the mobile layout) checks the connected server for a fresh release and compares the loaded page's production entry scripts and stylesheets with fresh, same-origin HTML fetched without using the browser cache. It does not call native app commands. Development pages and unsupported entry layouts report a skipped page check; network, authentication, and invalid-page responses report a failed check, not “up to date.”

Server prompts take priority and are visible on desktop and mobile browsers. Update authorizes server installation and a restart, which briefly interrupts the connection. Later hides the prompt; another manual check can reopen it. Skip this version, disabled server checks, and development-mode policies remain in effect.

After the server reconnects, the browser checks only the page assets again. Changed assets offer Refresh page; nothing reloads automatically. Refresh can lose unsaved page state but does not stop running server tasks. Choosing Later keeps the loaded page, and a later check can offer refresh again. The server update and page refresh have separate confirmations.

docs.title: The in-core Web UI transport
docs.text:
The Web UI transport ships in-core with @cortex-agent/server and is loaded on demand behind the CORTEX_UI_HTTP flag. It pulls @trpc/server and jose, but these are runtime-lazy: the server imports the transport only through a dynamic import that is reached solely when the flag is set. When the flag is unset, neither the transport code nor @trpc/server / jose ever enter the runtime module graph, so a Slack- or TUI-only deployment pays zero UI weight — while installing and upgrading stay a single npm install -g @cortex-agent/server.

When enabled, the transport:

  • serves the built SPA (web/dist) same-origin with the tRPC API — one port, one origin, so the browser loads index.html + assets and calls /trpc with no cross-origin plumbing;
  • exposes the tRPC API at /trpc (HTTP batch for queries/mutations, SSE for subscriptions), connected in-process directly to the server's domain services (no proxy, no sidecar);
  • gates every /trpc request behind an auth check that accepts any of three credentials (see Authentication).

It runs in the same process as the server, binds to 127.0.0.1, and is meant to be exposed to the internet only through a tunnel.

docs.title: Deployment runbook (source → running server)
docs.text: These steps take you from a fresh checkout to a Cortex server serving the browser workbench.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Node.js ≥ 22.19.0 and pnpm (this repo is a pnpm workspace).
  • A running Cortex server (see Quickstart).

docs.title: 2. Build the SPA
docs.text:
The web SPA is built to web/dist. From the repo root:

pnpm install            # install workspace dependencies
pnpm -r run build       # build every workspace package, including web → web/dist

To build only the SPA and its dependencies:

pnpm --filter @cortex-agent/ui-contract run build
pnpm --filter web run build      # produces web/dist

web/dist is a plain static bundle (index.html + hashed assets). When the @cortex-agent/server package is published, web/dist is staged into the package (via a prepack step) and shipped in its files, so an installed server can serve the SPA with no extra build. From a source checkout you build it yourself with the step above.

docs.title: 3. Where web/dist is served from
docs.text:
The server resolves the SPA directory in this order:

  1. an explicit directory you pass to it;
  2. the CORTEX_UI_SPA_DIR environment variable;
  3. the package-root web/dist (present in an installed/published package);
  4. the monorepo's web/dist (when running from a source checkout).

If you deploy an installed package, option 3 works out of the box. If you deploy from a repo checkout, option 4 works with no configuration — build web/dist in place and it is served automatically. If you deploy the built SPA to a different location, point CORTEX_UI_SPA_DIR at it. If the directory is absent (SPA not built), non-/trpc paths return a 404 placeholder while /trpc still works.

docs.title: 4. Enable the Web UI endpoint
docs.text:
On the server, run:

cortex ui enable          # optional: --port <n>, --home <dir>, --json

The command generates CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN if .env has none, sets the endpoint variables, and adds the native apps' origins to uiCorsOrigins. It is safe to repeat, and it reports whether the configuration changed. To configure the endpoint by hand instead, add to ~/.cortex/config/.env:

CORTEX_UI_HTTP=1          # opt-in: start the tRPC HTTP + SSE endpoint (required)
CORTEX_UI_PORT=3004       # optional; defaults to 3004

This alone is enough to open the workbench from a browser: token login is on by default, so the SPA will ask for the clientToken and exchange it for a session (see Browser access with a token).

CORTEX_UI_HTTP accepts 1, true, on, or yes. With it unset, the endpoint — and the Web UI transport, along with @trpc/server / jose — never loads.

docs.title: 5. Restart the daemon to apply
docs.text:
The daemon reads the SPA and env at startup, so a new build or env change takes effect on restart. Start the daemon with cortex daemon if it is not running yet; otherwise restart it:

cortex daemon restart

Restarting interrupts the connection

A graceful cortex daemon restart waits until no turn is running and holds new turns until the server is back, but every connected client loses its connection while the server restarts. cortex daemon restart --hard and --force restart at once and interrupt running agents. Restart when the system is idle, and if your Cortex instance runs under an approval policy, route the restart through that approval step.

At this point the server is reachable at http://127.0.0.1:3004 on the server host only. Exposing it to a browser is the next section.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The /trpc auth gate accepts a request if any of three credentials is valid, and returns 401 before tRPC runs otherwise:

  1. x-cortex-token header equal to the server's clientToken — the desktop / machine path. Checked first, with a constant-time comparison.
  2. A live cortex_ui session cookie — the token-login browser path. Minted by POST /api/ui/login after the browser proves, once, that it knows the token.
  3. A valid Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion header — the Cloudflare Access browser path. The edge injects this JWT after it authenticates the user; the server verifies it.

Either browser path keeps the clientToken out of the page: the cookie is HttpOnly, so the SPA's own JavaScript cannot read it, and the Access JWT is issued by the edge.

The server verifies the Access JWT against your Cloudflare Access team-domain JWKS, checking the signature (RS256 / ES256 only), the audience (AUD) tag, the issuer, and expiry. If Access is not configured on the server, the JWT path is disabled and the gate securely degrades — an unconfigured Access path never admits a request.

The port forward is token-only, on purpose

/forward (the desktop shell's raw TCP tunnel to a loopback service on the server) accepts only the x-cortex-token header. Neither browser credential opens it. A browser attaches cookies to a WebSocket handshake automatically, so admitting the session cookie there would hand every logged-in page a raw socket to every loopback service on the host.

docs.title: Browser access via Cloudflare Access
docs.text:
The browser path puts a Cloudflare Access edge login in front of a dedicated UI hostname, so users log in with email / IdP at the edge and the server only ever sees an already-verified request.

browser
  │  https (Cloudflare Access: email / IdP login at the edge)
  ▼
Cloudflare Tunnel   (cortex-ui.example.com  →  server localhost:3004)
  │  edge injects  Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion  on every request
  ▼
agent-server Web UI transport  (verifies the JWT; the browser never holds clientToken)
  ├─ serves web/dist  (same-origin SPA)
  └─ serves /trpc     (same-origin real data, in-process)

docs.title: 1. Create a dedicated UI hostname and tunnel route
docs.text:
Point a Cloudflare Tunnel route from a new public hostname (for example cortex-ui.example.com) to the server's loopback endpoint (http://127.0.0.1:3004, or your CORTEX_UI_PORT).

Use a separate hostname from the cortex-client endpoint

The hostname your remote cortex-client instances connect to must not be placed behind Cloudflare Access — Access would block the WebSocket clients. Always give the browser UI its own hostname and apply Access only to that one.

docs.title: 2. Add a Cloudflare Access application (account-side ops)
docs.text: In the Cloudflare Zero Trust dashboard, create a self-hosted Access application for the UI hostname with a policy that allows your login email (or IdP group). This is an account-level operation performed in the Cloudflare dashboard, not in Cortex config. Note the application's AUD tag — you need it below.

docs.title: 3. Configure the server to verify Access JWTs
docs.text:
Add to ~/.cortex/config/.env on the server:

CORTEX_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN=your-team      # bare team name, or your-team.cloudflareaccess.com
CORTEX_ACCESS_AUD=<your-access-app-AUD>  # the Access application's AUD tag
# CORTEX_ACCESS_CERTS_URL=...            # optional: override the derived JWKS URL

From CORTEX_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN the server derives the issuer (https://your-team.cloudflareaccess.com) and the JWKS URL (https://your-team.cloudflareaccess.com/cdn-cgi/access/certs). If either CORTEX_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN or CORTEX_ACCESS_AUD is unset, the browser path stays disabled (token-only). Restart the daemon after changing these values.

docs.title: 4. Open the workbench
docs.text: Navigate to https://cortex-ui.example.com. Cloudflare Access challenges you for email / IdP login; after you authenticate, the edge forwards every request with a verified Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion, the server serves the same-origin SPA, and the workbench loads real tRPC data — no token, no local install.

docs.title: Browser access with a token (no Cloudflare)
docs.text:
If you do not run Cloudflare Access — or you just want to open the workbench from a laptop on the LAN or through an SSH forward — a browser can authenticate itself by pasting the server's clientToken once.

This is on by default on any server with CORTEX_UI_HTTP=1. Open the UI, and if the browser holds no session yet the SPA shows a sign-in screen instead of the workbench:

browser  ──POST /api/ui/login {token}──▶  server   (constant-time compare vs clientToken)
        ◀──Set-Cookie: cortex_ui=… ; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Secure──
browser  ──every later /trpc, /api request carries the cookie──▶  server

What that buys, and what it costs:

  • The token is submitted once. It is exchanged for an opaque 32-byte session id. The cookie is HttpOnly, so page JavaScript — including an XSS payload — cannot read it back out.
  • SameSite=Strict keeps the session off requests from other sites. Every subdomain of a shared parent domain still counts as the same site, and a Cloudflare Access assertion is attached regardless, so the server also checks Origin: any request other than GET, HEAD or OPTIONS to /trpc or to an /api route — login included — whose Origin is neither this server's own nor listed in uiCorsOrigins is refused with 403, and Origin: null is always refused. Requests that carry no Origin (the CLI, devices, the native shells' own HTTP clients) are left to the credential check. "Own" means the Origin host equals the request's Host header, so a reverse proxy in front of the server must pass Host through unchanged (cloudflared does unless httpHostHeader is set; nginx needs proxy_set_header Host $host).
  • Served files open sandboxed. An HTML, XHTML, SVG or XML file opened directly from a download link (workspace files, attachments, board assets and memory files alike) is served with Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-scripts and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so it runs in an opaque origin and cannot read the session or call the API as you.
  • Sessions survive a daemon restart. They live in ~/.cortex/data/ui-sessions.json (mode 0600) and expire 30 days after sign-in; using a session does not extend it. Settings → Advanced has a Sign out of this browser button, on desktop and mobile layouts alike, which revokes the session server-side.
  • A session is strictly weaker than the token. It carries exactly the authority of a Cloudflare Access login: tRPC and the /api routes, never /forward.
  • The login endpoint is public. It has to be — a browser with no credential must be able to reach it. A wrong token costs the caller a fixed 250 ms and is logged; the token itself is 32 random bytes, so online guessing is not a realistic attack. There is deliberately no IP ban (behind a tunnel every request appears to come from 127.0.0.1) and no global lockout (which would let anyone lock you out of your own server).

docs.title: Tuning or turning it off
docs.text:
CORTEX_UI_TOKEN_LOGIN=0          # 0, false, off or no: remove the login routes and the cookie leg
CORTEX_UI_SESSION_TTL_DAYS=30    # optional; session lifetime in days, default 30

With token login off, the login and logout routes are not mounted and session cookies are not accepted, so only the header token and, if configured, Cloudflare Access admit requests. The SPA says so on the sign-in screen rather than offering a form that could not work.

docs.title: Where to use which
docs.text:
Put Cloudflare Access in front of a UI hostname when you want IdP-managed access for people who should never see the token, or when the UI is exposed to the open internet. Use token login for your own access — over a tunnel, a VPN, Tailscale, an SSH forward, or plain loopback. The two coexist: a server can have both, and each request is admitted by whichever credential it carries.

Plain HTTP on a LAN

The session cookie is marked Secure when the request arrived over HTTPS (or from localhost). Over plain HTTP to a LAN address it cannot be — a browser would silently drop a Secure cookie — so the cookie is issued without it and the daemon logs a warning. Anyone on that network path can read the session. Use HTTPS for anything beyond a trusted LAN.

docs.title: The three paths side by side
docs.text:
All three reach the same /trpc API and the same workbench, but they differ in where and how they authenticate:

Browser + Access Browser + token login Desktop (Tauri) Hostname Dedicated UI hostname behind Cloudflare Access Any hostname that reaches the port A hostname not behind Access Login Cloudflare Access edge login (email / IdP) Paste the clientToken once Enter serverUrl + clientToken once Credential on requests Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion (issued by the edge) cortex_ui session cookie x-cortex-token header Where auth is checked JWT verified by the server Session verified by the server Token verified by the server clientToken exposure Never touches the browser Typed once, never stored in the page Stored in the OS keychain Opens /forward No No Yes SPA origin Same-origin (SPA + /trpc on one host) Same-origin Direct connection to /trpc (CORS-enabled)

Because the desktop app sends x-cortex-token, it must connect through a hostname that is not behind Cloudflare Access (Access would block the bearer request at the edge). Choose the desktop app when you want a native window, the port forward, and are comfortable storing the token locally; Access when other people need in and should never see the token; token login when it is your own browser and the path to the server is already private or encrypted.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Browser gets a Cloudflare login loop or 403 at the edge

The Access application policy does not allow your identity. Check the policy on the UI hostname's Access application in the Cloudflare Zero Trust dashboard.

Browser logs in at the edge but the workbench shows 401 / no data

The edge authenticated you but the server rejected the JWT. Confirm on the server that CORTEX_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN matches your team and CORTEX_ACCESS_AUD matches the Access application's AUD tag exactly, and that the daemon was restarted after setting them. With those unset, the browser path is disabled and every browser request is 401.

The sign-in screen says token sign-in is turned off

CORTEX_UI_TOKEN_LOGIN is set to 0 on the server. Either remove it (token login is on by default) and restart, or reach the UI through Cloudflare Access / the desktop app instead.

The token is correct but signing in does nothing / it asks again on every page load

Check the daemon log for ui-http cross-origin request refused. A reverse proxy that rewrites the Host header makes the page's own origin look foreign, so the server refuses the sign-in request with 403. Make the proxy pass Host through unchanged (cloudflared does unless httpHostHeader is set; nginx needs proxy_set_header Host $host).

The page shows Cortex UI not built

web/dist was not found, so every path except /trpc returns 404 with that text while the API keeps working. Build the SPA (pnpm --filter web run build) or point CORTEX_UI_SPA_DIR at your built bundle, then restart.

Nothing is reachable at the UI hostname

  1. Confirm CORTEX_UI_HTTP=1 is set and the daemon was restarted after adding it.
  2. On the server, confirm the endpoint is up: curl http://127.0.0.1:3004/trpc should answer 401 Unauthorized (not connection-refused).
  3. Confirm the Cloudflare Tunnel is running and its route points at the correct port.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text:
Cortex ships five binaries, registered in agent-server/package.json:

Binary Entry point Purpose cortex dist/entry/cortex-cli.js Server management and initialization cortex-browser dist/entry/browser-cli.js Drive the session's agent browser cortex-evidence-export dist/entry/production-evidence-export-cli.js Production benchmark evidence v2 export cortex-hook dist/entry/hook-cli.js Hook inspection, switching, test runs, and blocking user asks cortex-signal dist/entry/signal-cli.js Resolve a waitpoint from an external program

All five accept --help (or -h) to print their usage.

docs.title: cortex
docs.text:
cortex <command> [options]

Server lifecycle and initialization CLI. cortex --help lists every command.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
cortex init [--home <path>] [--gateway-config-dir <path>] [--force] [--answers <file>] [--json]

Initialize CORTEX_HOME. The interactive wizard uses bundled PI by default without a backend-selection prompt, collects platform (Slack / Feishu), machine, usage-reporting, and service settings, writes .env, copies default configs, and generates the mcp-config*.json files, machines.json, preferences.json and agent-state.json. It also seeds schedules.json, creates a git repository in CORTEX_HOME when git is available, and can enable the local Web UI and install a system service when those answers ask for it.

After writing configs, it detects local provider credentials and offers login, rescan, continue with configured providers, or a warned skip. Login uses the same flow as cortex auth login; choosing Claude Code reuses an existing installation or asks permission to install a missing copy. Continue configures gateway routes and asks for a default model and favorites from detected endpoints. The recommended default is preselected and included among favorites. Detection makes no paid inference request and does not verify model access.

--answers and --json runs do not start provider login or wait for input. They report credential status and can finish with provider setup incomplete.

Options: - --home <path> — set CORTEX_HOME (default: $CORTEX_HOME or ~/.cortex/) - --gateway-config-dir <path> — gateway config output directory (default: ~/.aistatus/) - --force — overwrite existing configs (.env, budget.json, agent-state.json, etc.) - --answers <file> — read answers from a JSON document without prompting. Omitted fields use defaults; {} creates a single-machine installation using PI, with provider login still required if no credentials are detected. Used by the desktop installer. An explicit backends array retains its selection and installation semantics (claude, pi, or both); an explicit empty array selects Claude. - --json — emit newline-delimited progress events on stdout and move human-readable output to stderr. The final event reports the home directory, the version, the client token, and the local Web UI URL.

Model answers use this shape (the selected pair must be among detected models):

{
  "defaultChoice": { "mode": "openai-codex", "model": "gpt-5.5" },
  "favorites": [{ "mode": "openai-codex", "model": "gpt-5.5" }]
}

An explicit defaultChoice replaces the saved default; otherwise it is preserved. Favorites are merged and include the selected default. The positional stdin protocol ends with two model lines: default mode:model, then comma-separated favorite mode:model pairs.

cortex ui enable [--port <n>] [--home <path>] [--json]

Make this install reachable by the Cortex desktop app. Generates the client token if it is missing, sets CORTEX_UI_HTTP=1 and CORTEX_UI_PORT, and adds the app's origins to uiCorsOrigins. Idempotent — running it twice changes nothing the second time. ui has no other subcommand.

Restart the daemon when it reports that the configuration changed: .env is read once at process start.

Options: - --port <n> — the port to listen on. Without it, a CORTEX_UI_PORT already in .env is kept, and 3004 is used when there is none; an invalid port exits 1 - --home <path> — set CORTEX_HOME (default: $CORTEX_HOME or ~/.cortex) - --json — print { ok, home, url, token, port, changed }

cortex client remove --device <name> [--keep-remote] [--dry-run] [--home <path>]

Retire a remote machine. The command deletes the machine's entry from config/machines.json, connects to the machine over SSH, stops every process running its client bundle, and deletes the bundle (client/), config/cortex-client.json, and the logs/client-*.log files from the client's CORTEX_HOME. It then drops the machine from data/client-pids.json and data/client-routes.json. The registry entry goes first, so a running server releases the machine's tunnel and restart timer on hot-reload instead of relaunching the client that is being stopped.

The client's CORTEX_HOME comes from the bundle path in clientCommand and defaults to ~/.cortex (%USERPROFILE%\.cortex on Windows). A home that also contains config/machines.json belongs to a Cortex server; there the client process is stopped and every file stays in place. A machine that cannot be reached is still removed locally, with remote.status: "unreachable" in the result and a warning on stderr. The server's local machine (an entry without ssh) is refused.

Output is JSON with the device, removed_at, the removed machine_entry, the runtime pid and route that were dropped, and remote — cleaned (with the killed pids and files: removed | kept-server-home), unreachable, or skipped. --dry-run prints the plan under would_remove and changes nothing.

Options: - --device <name> — machine name in machines.json (required) - --keep-remote — only unregister locally; leave the remote process and files alone - --dry-run — print what would be removed and change nothing - --home <path> — set CORTEX_HOME

cortex path <install|remove|status> [--home <path>] [--dry-run] [--json]

Make this install's commands available in new terminals. install writes a launcher for each binary above into $CORTEX_HOME/runtime/bin. The launcher runs the Node.js that executed the command against this install's entry file, so the terminal does not need Node.js on PATH. It then registers that directory on PATH. On Linux and macOS it uses a block marked # >>> cortex >>>. The block goes at the end of ~/.profile, and of ~/.bash_profile and ~/.zshenv (under $ZDOTDIR when set) where those shells are in use. It goes at the top of ~/.bashrc, so that non-interactive SSH commands see it. On Windows the directory goes at the front of the user Path, which keeps its registry type and announces the change to new processes. Running install again rewrites only what differs. New terminals use this install even when another cortex is on PATH; the result lists those under shadowed. fish is not configured.

At startup the server re-points existing launchers when its Node.js or entry path has changed. A server that the desktop app installed in $CORTEX_HOME/runtime/prefix also runs install itself when no launchers exist, unless remove was the last choice. install and remove record that choice in $CORTEX_HOME/runtime/terminal-cli.json. remove deletes only the files this command wrote and takes the directory back off PATH, which leaves the profiles and the user Path as they were before install. status reports whether the launchers exist, which are out of date, and where the directory is registered.

Options: - --home <path> — set CORTEX_HOME, which also becomes the launchers' default CORTEX_HOME (default: $CORTEX_HOME or ~/.cortex) - --dry-run — for install and remove, report the changes and write nothing - --json — print { ok, action, dry_run, dir, … }: written and shadowed for install, removed for remove, and path_targets with each profile file or HKCU\Environment\Path and whether it changed

cortex start

Run the server in the foreground: fork dist/entry/app.js with inherited stdio and $CORTEX_HOME as its working directory, and exit with its exit code. The process runs the platform adapters, the Web UI host, the webhook server, and all agent orchestration, with no supervisor to restart it.

cortex daemon

Start the supervisor in the background and return at once. The command forks dist/entry/daemon.js detached from the terminal, with no stdio (the daemon writes its own logs under logs/), and exits 0. The daemon runs app.js as its child, restarts it after a crash with exponential backoff, and drains and respawns it when $STORE_DIR/.restart is touched. cortex daemon --version prints the version.

cortex daemon stop

Send the daemon SIGTERM and wait up to 10 seconds for it to exit; a daemon still alive after that is killed with SIGKILL and the command exits 1. The daemon is stopped together with the client it launched on this machine (the local client), so no Cortex process keeps running or keeps files of the runtime in use; a local client that survives also exits 1. Clients on SSH and custom-command machines keep running, and the next cortex daemon launches the local client again. A daemon that is not running, including a stale PID file, which is cleaned up, exits 0.

cortex daemon status

Print the daemon's PID and uptime and the state of its app.js child (PID and uptime, starting..., or none).

cortex daemon restart [--hard | --force]

Without a flag, touch the restart trigger so the daemon drains and respawns app.js. --hard sends SIGTERM straight to app.js and --force sends SIGKILL; either way the daemon starts a new child. All three exit 1 when no daemon is running; the flags also exit 1 when no app.js child is alive.

cortex daemon restart-self

Stop the daemon as cortex daemon stop does, then start a new detached daemon.

cortex restart

Touch the restart trigger at $STORE_DIR/.restart and print its path. A running daemon drains and respawns app.js; with no daemon running the command only creates the file. It exits 1 when the file cannot be written.

cortex tui [--resume] [--project <id>] [--port <n>]

Open the terminal chat client against a running server. The command checks that the TUI gateway is listening on 127.0.0.1:<port> and exits 1 with a hint to start the daemon when it is not; otherwise it runs the client in the terminal and exits with its exit code.

Options: - --resume — open the resume-session picker on connect - --project <id> — start a fresh session in that project - --port <n> — the gateway port (default: $CORTEX_TUI_PORT, else 3003)

cortex install latest

Update the server from npm. The command asks npm for the latest @cortex-agent/server version, prints Already on the latest version when the running install is current, and otherwise runs npm install -g for that version into CORTEX_NPM_PREFIX, else the running install's own prefix. Restart the daemon afterwards with cortex daemon restart. A failed lookup or install exits 1.

cortex config

Print resolved paths and initialization status. Shows INSTALL_ROOT, all data directories, and whether .env, mcp-config.json, and agent-state.json exist.

cortex doctor [--fix] [--json]

Health-check the whole installation in one pass and report what is wrong. The default run is read-only and safe at any time. It inspects four areas:

  • Runtime & process — Node version, git on PATH (a failure on Windows, a warning elsewhere), the claude binary on PATH (a warning when missing; PI always passes, since it runs in-process from the bundled SDK), and whether the daemon is running.
  • Backend install / login — data directories exist and are writable, .env is present, the client and webhook tokens are set, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY status, and that agent-state.json, models.json, and mcp-config.json are present and valid. A missing models.json is a warning; invalid JSON, an invalid default selection, or a missing or invalid favorites array is a failure. It also smoke-tests the installed PI runtime and its login export, then summarizes expired or logged-out in-use providers from the credential-free backend auth snapshot. These two checks warn rather than fail. In API mode, a healthy gateway with no local key is reported as gateway-backed information instead of a false logged-out warning.
  • Messaging platform — resolves CORTEX_PLATFORM and validates the credentials for each enabled platform (Slack xoxb-/signing/xapp-, Feishu app id/secret).
  • Gateway — ~/.aistatus/gateway.yaml presence and a health probe of http://127.0.0.1:9880/status. The probe is reported as a failure only when the gateway is actually in use; otherwise it is skipped.

Each check prints [OK], [WARN], [FAIL], or [--] (skipped) with a short detail and, for problems, a fix hint. The command exits 1 when any check fails, else 0; warnings do not fail the run.

Options: - --fix — apply safe, idempotent repairs only: create missing data directories, create a missing .env, generate missing auth tokens, and rebuild mcp-config.json. The JSON report lists them under fixes. It never deletes configuration or overwrites existing credentials. After fixing, diagnostics re-run so the summary reflects the repaired state. - --json — emit the full report (sections, checks, counts) as JSON for scripting.

cortex auth status [--json]

Read the normalized Claude Code and PI authentication snapshot. The default text output shows a concise status overview, while --json returns the full AuthStatusSnapshot for scripting. Both forms omit credential values and fragments.

This subcommand is read-only and reports local credential state, not live inference validation. Sign in locally with cortex auth login. Remote login starts from !login in Slack or Feishu, or Settings → Accounts in the Web UI; mobile users drill in at /m/settings/accounts.

Options: - --json — print the complete credential-free status snapshot as JSON - --help, -h — show auth command help

See Backends: Remote login for login commands, provider capability rules, and expiration handling.

cortex auth login [--backend pi|claude] [--provider ID] [--auth-type oauth|api_key]

Sign in to a provider from an interactive terminal without a running daemon. Omitted options are selected interactively from the backend's supported providers and authentication methods. PI is bundled. For Claude Code, an existing installation is reused; a missing installation requires confirmation before Cortex installs it and starts login.

Login requires TTY stdin and stderr, even when all selectors are supplied. API keys and authorization responses are entered through secret prompts; this command accepts no key, token, or authorization-code arguments. Browser links and device instructions appear on stderr. Non-TTY login fails promptly without starting an authentication flow; help works without a TTY.

The result is JSON on stdout, with human prompts and errors on stderr; no --json flag is needed or accepted. Results omit secrets. A successful login synchronizes gateway/model configuration and reports the sync result with inferenceVerified: false: credentials are configured, not inference-tested, and no paid model request is sent.

Options: - --backend pi|claude — choose the backend; omitted means select interactively - --provider ID — choose a provider supported by that backend's runtime - --auth-type oauth|api_key — choose a supported authentication method - --help, -h — show login help without starting login

cortex auth login
cortex auth login --backend pi --provider anthropic --auth-type api_key
cortex auth login --backend claude --provider anthropic --auth-type oauth
cortex auth login --help

cortex auth provider <list|add|remove> [options]

Manage custom PI providers — self-hosted or proxied endpoints that have no login flow of their own. add is an upsert, so re-running it with a changed URL or model list edits the stored definition in place.

Options: - --name <name> — provider name; letters, digits, - and _ only - --api <api> — request protocol: anthropic-messages, openai-completions, openai-responses, or google-generative-ai - --url <url> — upstream endpoint, stored in the gateway route - --key <key|-> — upstream API key; - reads it from stdin so it never appears in shell history - --model <id> — a model id the endpoint serves; repeat for several - --dry-run — on remove, report what would be deleted without deleting it - --json — print the result as JSON - --help, -h — show provider command help

# define a local endpoint that speaks the Anthropic protocol
cortex auth provider add --name my-vllm --api anthropic-messages \
  --url http://127.0.0.1:8100 --model Model-27B

# take the key from a secret store instead of the command line
pass show my-endpoint | cortex auth provider add --name my-proxy \
  --api openai-completions --url https://proxy.example.com/v1 --model small --key -

cortex auth provider list --json
cortex auth provider remove --name my-vllm --dry-run

See Backends: Custom providers for what the two writes contain and how a definition reaches an agent.

cortex setup-gateway [--dry-run] [--output-dir <path>]

Auto-detect Claude Code and PI configurations from their local config files, generate ~/.aistatus/gateway.yaml (with backup of existing), and write $CORTEX_HOME/config/models.json. Run this whenever you add a new API key or change models.

Options: - --dry-run — print the generated gateway.yaml to stdout without writing - --output-dir <path> — write gateway.yaml and models.json under <path> instead of defaults

Setup preserves an existing default selection and merges favorites. Its summary shows the default model and favorites; use Settings → Models to change the default. Provider-login sync also preserves existing choices, supplies a missing default, and adds a recommended favorite for each newly connected backend/provider group without one. Its result includes defaultSet and favorites.

cortex schedule <list|get|add|edit|pause|resume|remove> [<id>] [options]

Manage scheduled tasks — the same records !schedule and the Web UI manage. Each fire opens a new session in the schedule's project and sends it the message; see Scheduling. Changes are written to schedules.json, and a running daemon picks them up within a second.

Agents use this CLI through the schedule skill. For a session-project request, resolve the project from session context or cortex_context and pass --project explicitly; if the requested current project is missing, ask which one to use. The CLI does not infer session scope from Bash environment variables. Daily/weekly times use the daemon's local timezone (including TZ overrides); convert the user's timezone and weekday explicitly and report the next run in their timezone. There is no per-schedule timezone or automatic cross-timezone daylight-saving adjustment.

Every command prints JSON with ok: true and the schedule (schedule, or schedules and count for list); timestamps are ISO 8601. Invalid input exits 1 with the valid values on stderr.

  • list [--project <id>] — all schedules, or one project's
  • get <id> — one schedule; an unknown id exits 1
  • add --type <type> … — create a schedule; prints created: false and the existing schedule when --idempotency-key matches one. A timing flag that does not belong to the type is rejected
  • edit <id> … — change the message, project, model selection, pre-check, or the timing fields of the schedule's type; the type itself is fixed
  • pause <id> / resume <id> — pause or resume a recurring schedule; repeating either changes nothing
  • remove <id> [--dry-run] — delete a schedule (removed: false when it does not exist); --dry-run prints would_remove and deletes nothing

Options: - --type interval|daily|weekly|once — schedule type (add only) - --interval <duration> — interval: repeat period, e.g. 30m, 2h, 1d - --time <HH:MM> — daily/weekly: 24-hour time, server local time - --day <day> — weekly: sun..sat or 0-6 - --delay <duration> — once: fire this long from now; on edit, moves the fire time - --message <text|-> — the prompt for the fired session; - reads it from stdin - --project <id> — project the fired session belongs to (default: general) - --model <[provider/]model> — model to run; PI accepts an explicit provider/model. Creation without model flags stores the configured default selection, which may differ from the active session - --thinking <level> — backend-native thinking level. With no model flag, applies to a copy of the configured default on creation or the schedule’s stored selection on edit; omitted on a model change, uses that model’s remembered level - --pre-check <cmd> — shell gate run before each fire; a non-zero exit skips that fire - --idempotency-key <key> — add: a retry with the same key returns the first schedule - --help, -h — show schedule help

cortex schedule add --type interval --interval 30m --project nimbus \
  --message "Check GPU usage on lab2 and report a one-line summary"
cortex schedule add --type weekly --day mon --time 21:00 --message "Weekly review"
echo "Check training run r42 on lab2" | cortex schedule add --type once --delay 2h --message -
cortex schedule list --project nimbus
cortex schedule edit a1b2c3d4 --time 10:30
cortex schedule remove a1b2c3d4 --dry-run

cortex memory <regen|consolidate> [--project <name>]... [--text]

Maintain project memory under $CORTEX_HOME/context/projects/*/ (its experiments/, knowledge/ and patterns/ directories; see Memory). --project limits the run to one project and can be repeated; without it every project with memory directories is processed, and an unknown project exits 1 with the valid names.

  • regen — rebuild the generated index.md files from entry frontmatter and the access log, never touching the EXP/K/PAT entries themselves. Prints { ok: true, projects: [{ project, indexes }] }.
  • consolidate — report contradictions, stale entries, anti-pattern signals and consolidation candidates as { ok: true, reports }; --text prints a readable summary instead.

cortex feishu <login|status|logout> [--scope <scopes>] [--manual] [--redirect-uri <url>]

Manage the Feishu user identity that Feishu document tools act as.

  • login — authorize a Feishu account with the OAuth device flow: the command prints a URL and a code to open in any browser. It needs FEISHU_APP_ID and FEISHU_APP_SECRET. On success it stores the user token and writes FEISHU_AUTH_MODE=user to .env; restart the daemon to apply it.
  • status — show the auth mode (user or bot) and the stored token's validity and expiry.
  • logout — delete the stored user token.

Options: - --scope <scopes> — the scopes to request (default: $FEISHU_USER_SCOPE, else a document, sheet, base and wiki set that needs no app review; offline_access is always added) - --manual — use the authorize-URL and paste-the-code flow instead of the device flow - --redirect-uri <url> — redirect URI for --manual (default: $FEISHU_REDIRECT_URI)

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Error (invalid command, missing config, runtime failure) 130 init or auth login cancelled, or the Claude Code install declined

cortex start and cortex tui exit with the code of the process they run.

docs.title: cortex-browser
docs.text:
cortex-browser [--device <name>] <agent-browser command> [args...]

Drive the calling session's tab in the agent browser. Agents run it from their shell; every argument except --device is passed to the pinned agent-browser, attached to the session's own tab. Its output and exit code are agent-browser's. cortex-browser skills get core prints agent-browser's command guide for the shipped version, and --full adds every command and option.

Options: - --device <name> — whose Chrome: server or a connected device. The choice sticks for the session (default: the session's last device, else server) - --help, -h — show usage; cortex-browser <command> --help shows one agent-browser command

Each call asks the daemon for the session's browser over the loopback webhook (http://127.0.0.1:$WEBHOOK_PORT/webhook/browser, authenticated with CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN). The session comes from CORTEX_SESSION_ID (or CORTEX_EXECUTION_ID). Agent shells carry all three, so the command needs no setup there. skills, help and --version run without a browser.

Relative paths given to file commands (screenshot, pdf, download, upload, record, trace, har, state, …) and to --screenshot-dir, --download-path and --baseline resolve against the caller's working directory.

cortex-browser sets --cdp, --session and the tab binding itself, and refuses flags that would leave the session's tab: --cdp, --session, --no-pin-tab, --auto-connect, --provider/-p, --namespace, --engine and --executable-path. It also refuses connect, install, upgrade, dashboard, mcp and close --all, each with the reason and what to use instead.

When the session's tab is gone (closed after 10 idle minutes, or Chrome restarted), the call opens a new blank tab, prints a note on stderr, and runs the command there.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success 1 The agent-browser command failed, or no browser could be used: unknown or offline device, Chrome failed to start, the user is controlling the browser, the daemon is unreachable or rejected the token. The reason and a hint are on stderr 2 Usage error (a refused flag or command, --device without a name) or no session in the environment

Once the browser is attached, the exit code is agent-browser's own.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Open a page and list what can be clicked
cortex-browser open http://127.0.0.1:5173 && cortex-browser snapshot -i

# Click a ref from the snapshot, then capture the result
cortex-browser click @e2 && cortex-browser screenshot ./after-click.png

# Use the Chrome on the user's machine (its localhost, its logins)
cortex-browser --device my-pc open https://example.com

# Read the version-matched command reference
cortex-browser skills get core --full

docs.title: cortex-evidence-export
docs.text:
cortex-evidence-export --input-file <path|->

Publish immutable terminal/composite benchmark evidence v2 from the production stores under CORTEX_HOME. The command initializes the production attempt identity and journal stores, loads data/executions.json, reads attributed costs, then delegates validation and atomic publication to exportProductionBenchmarkEvidence. Cortex benchmark arms always run through the production server, as one direct session per trial; this command records that runtime's stores and does not define a second orchestration path.

Evidence is keyed by session and execution: every run the trial's session opened is one attempt, identified by its session_id and execution_id, and each later run of the session is a spawn child of the run before it.

--input-file contains one JSON-encoded ProductionEvidenceExportInput; use - to read it from stdin. The arguments must be exactly --input-file <value>; anything else is a usage error. The launcher owns every field: outputDirectory, trialId, rootRunId, armName, armCanonicalSha256, bundleManifestHash, proxyExport, and optional evaluatedChecks. Hashes, proxy trial identity, and predicate results are validated before publication. Missing or malformed input, incomplete durable records, or an existing output directory fail closed with exit code 1.

cortex-evidence-export --input-file production-evidence.json
cat production-evidence.json | cortex-evidence-export --input-file -

Success writes one JSON object to stdout:

{"ok":true,"directory":"/evidence/run-1","composite_path":"/evidence/run-1/composite-manifest.json","composite_sha256":"<sha256>","terminal_paths":["/evidence/run-1/execution-root.terminal.json"]}

Failure writes {"ok":false,"error":"..."} to stderr and does not publish a partial directory. The public output path appears only after all terminal and composite bytes are written, fsynced, and verified in a hidden staging directory.

docs.title: cortex-hook
docs.text:
cortex-hook <list|show|enable|disable|test|ask> [options]

Inspect and operate the hooks mounted from the built-in registry and $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/. Every command prints JSON on stdout and errors on stderr. Hooks: the cortex-hook CLI covers the registry these commands act on.

  • list — every mounted hook: id, event, enabled, source (builtin or user), and whether a user file overrides a built-in one
  • show --id <id> — one complete declaration; an unknown id exits 1 and lists the valid ones
  • enable --id <id> [--dry-run] / disable --id <id> [--dry-run] — switch a hook, idempotently; the result says whether anything changed, and --dry-run reports would_set without writing
  • test --id <id> --payload <file|-> — run the hook once with the payload on stdin and print its exit_code, stdout and stderr; the command exits with the hook's own exit code
  • ask (--question <text> | --payload <file|->) — post an ask-user card and block until it is answered, then print { ok: true, answers }. --header, --options "a|b|c", --multi and --level info|warn|warning|error shape a single question; --payload takes a JSON array of question objects. The card goes to --channel (default: $CORTEX_HOOK_CHANNEL) or the channel of --session-id (default: $CORTEX_HOOK_SESSION_ID), both of which a hook's environment already carries. --dry-run resolves synthetically without posting. See Asking the user from a hook

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success, or an answered ask 1 Usage or runtime error 2 ask timed out unanswered

test exits with the code of the hook it ran.

docs.title: cortex-signal
docs.text:
cortex-signal [--id wp_…] [--secret …] [--status ok|fail|progress] [--message TEXT] [--exit-code N]

Tell Cortex that something it is waiting for has finished. Run without arguments, it prints its usage. The agent arms a waitpoint with the wait_create MCP tool and ends its turn; this command resolves that waitpoint and wakes the session. See waitpoints.md for the full picture.

--id and --secret default to $CORTEX_SIGNAL_ID and $CORTEX_SIGNAL_SECRET, so the usual integration is two lines: export them once, then append one command.

Options: - --id <wp_…> — waitpoint id (default: $CORTEX_SIGNAL_ID) - --secret <hex> — the capability issued with that waitpoint (default: $CORTEX_SIGNAL_SECRET) - --status <s> — ok, fail, or progress (default: ok). ok/fail are terminal: they count toward the quorum and wake the session. progress records a heartbeat without resolving anything and without waking anyone — the difference between the two is entirely "is this worth a turn" - --exit-code <n> — derive the status from a command's exit code (0 = ok, anything else = fail) and default the message to exit=<n> - --message <text> — one-line summary shown in the wake message - --member <name> — which member of a multi-job waitpoint this signal is for - --data <@file|-|text> — extra payload from a file, stdin, or the literal text; it reaches the agent labelled as data, never as instructions - --url <url> — daemon signal endpoint (default: http://127.0.0.1:$WEBHOOK_PORT/webhook/signal) - --no-spool — fail instead of spooling to disk when the daemon is unreachable - --help, -h — show usage

The endpoint is loopback-only and does not accept CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN: the per-waitpoint secret is the only credential, and it can do nothing except resolve its own waitpoint. To signal from another machine, drop a JSON file in ~/.cortex/tmp/signals/ there instead — see waitpoints.md.

docs.title: Spooling
docs.text: If the daemon cannot be reached, the signal is written to $CORTEX_HOME/tmp/signals/<name>.json (.tmp first, then renamed, so a half-written file is never picked up) and the command still exits 0. The daemon drains that directory on its next sweep, so a signal sent during a restart is delayed, not lost. --no-spool turns this off and exits 1 instead.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Accepted, spooled, or the waitpoint was already resolved 1 Refused (bad secret, unknown id, rate-limited) or unreachable with --no-spool 2 Usage error (missing id/secret, unknown flag, missing value, bad --status or --exit-code, unreadable --data file)

An already-resolved waitpoint exits 0 on purpose: a retrying script should not treat "someone already reported this" as a failure.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Report the exit code of the command that just ran
export CORTEX_SIGNAL_ID=wp_1a2b3c4d5e6f CORTEX_SIGNAL_SECRET=…
python train.py; cortex-signal --exit-code $?

# Report one arm of a multi-job waitpoint
cortex-signal --member arm2 --status ok --message "33,120 steps"

# Attach the tail of a log as data
python train.py; s=$?; tail -c 2000 train.log | cortex-signal --exit-code $s --data -

# Heartbeat without waking anyone
cortex-signal --status progress --message "epoch 12/40"

# Signal when a process that is already running exits
(while kill -0 12345 2>/dev/null; do sleep 5; done; cortex-signal --status ok) &

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Cortex reads configuration from $CORTEX_HOME/config/. Messaging integrations are optional: browser and app sessions can run without a Slack or Feishu bot. Each enabled messaging platform needs its own credentials.

docs.title: File hierarchy
docs.text:
All paths below are relative to $CORTEX_HOME (default: ~/.cortex/).

$CORTEX_HOME/
├── AGENTS.md                     # Root instructions for agent sessions (scaffolded once)
├── config/
│   ├── .env                      # Secrets, platform credentials, startup variables
│   ├── settings.json             # Runtime behavior settings (hot-reloaded)
│   ├── preferences.json          # UI language for system messages (`!lang`)
│   ├── models.json             # Default engine and favorite models
│   ├── environments/             # Execution environments — one JSON per environment
│   ├── machines.json             # Machine registry for remote clients
│   ├── budget.json               # Daily/monthly budget limits
│   ├── mcp-config*.json          # Generated MCP configurations, rewritten at every start
│   ├── board.css                 # Optional stylesheet for every board (absent by default)
│   ├── agents/                   # Your subagent roles and overrides of the built-in ones
│   ├── archive/                  # Configuration an upgrade retired, moved aside
│   └── hooks/                    # Your hook declarations and overrides of the built-in ones
├── data/
│   ├── agent-state.json          # Channel selections, model memory, new-session choice, default agent
│   ├── schedules.json            # Persistent schedule list
│   ├── boards.json               # Board registry
│   ├── executions.json           # Unified execution registry
│   ├── costs.jsonl               # 90-day rolling cost records
│   ├── provider-state.json       # Provider usage, throttle windows, resume queue
│   ├── waitpoints.json           # Armed and resolved waitpoints
│   ├── session-registry.jsonl    # Session records, channel bindings, conversation headers + turns (single owner)
│   ├── retention-candidates.json # Two-sweep orphan retention markers
│   ├── ui-sessions.json          # Browser login sessions for the Web UI
│   ├── conversation-history/     # Per-session transcript/history JSONL
│   ├── archive/                  # Terminal execution records older than a week
│   ├── claude/                   # Cortex's own Claude Code config dir (CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR)
│   └── pi/                       # Cortex's PI agent dir
├── .claude/
│   └── settings.json             # Cortex-scaffolded Claude Code project settings
├── hooks/                        # Your hook scripts (.mjs)
├── plugins/                      # Your plugins, and your layers of the built-in ones
├── prompts/                      # Your system prompts, directives, templates
├── rules/                        # Your context rules for agent sessions
├── context/                      # Dense Context knowledge repository
│   └── projects/                 # Research project files
├── logs/                         # Daemon and backend session logs
│   ├── events/                   # Daily event-bus JSONL (the `eventLog` setting)
│   ├── sessions/                 # Claude capture logs
│   └── sessions-pi/              # PI transcript bundles
└── tmp/                          # Temporary workspaces, spooled signals, tool images

The gateway configuration, ~/.aistatus/gateway.yaml, lives outside $CORTEX_HOME; cortex setup-gateway and provider logins write it.

docs.title: Loading order and precedence
docs.text:
1. Built-in defaults (agent-server/defaults/) ship with the npm package and provide fallback values for every config file. The built-in plugins, hooks, rules, agent roles and system prompts are read from there in place, with your files in $CORTEX_HOME laid over them (see Built-in assets and your overrides).
  2. $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env is loaded at daemon startup via dotenv. Existing launcher environment variables take precedence over the file, and the worker inherits the daemon environment.
  3. $CORTEX_HOME/config/settings.json holds the runtime behavior settings. It is cached, re-read whenever the file changes, and each setting takes effect at its own point of use. For every key it defines, it overrides the legacy environment variable of the same setting.
  4. $CORTEX_HOME/config/models.json is cached and watched for changes to the default engine selection and favorite models.
  5. $CORTEX_HOME/.claude/settings.json is the Cortex-scaffolded Claude Code project settings file. Claude Code may also read <spawn cwd>/.claude/settings.local.json, <spawn cwd>/.claude/settings.json, and its user settings file, which for every Cortex-started claude is $CORTEX_HOME/data/claude/settings.json (see Claude Code config directory). The terminal's ~/.claude/settings.json is not read.

The .env file supports standard KEY=VALUE syntax and # comments. Environment variables already set in the shell take precedence over the .env file (dotenv default behavior).

docs.title: Platform settings in the Web UI
docs.text:
Settings → Platform provides Feishu/Lark and Slack connection forms in the browser, desktop app and mobile app. Enable the platform, fill its required credentials and save. Secrets are write-only: a blank secret field preserves the saved value, entering a value replaces it, and Clear saved value explicitly queues its removal for the next save. Disabling a platform keeps its credentials. Credential entry requires HTTPS or a loopback API address; a native app's local webview origin does not make a remote HTTP server secure.

The configuration check lists missing required fields; it does not test the connection or account permissions. Connection changes are saved to config/.env and require a daemon restart, not just a worker restart. The page compares saved configuration with the running server environment and marks differences. If differences remain after restarting the daemon, check its launcher environment for overriding variables. Saving does not restart any process.

Each card also edits its notification destination (adminChannel for Slack, feishuAdminChannel for Feishu). These runtime settings apply to subsequent notifications. Saving an empty destination clears the route; Feishu may register a destination automatically on the next first-contact private message.

The Feishu card's Feishu skills in Web / apps switch controls settings.feishuSkillsInWeb (default false). Enabling it allows web: sessions to load an assigned cortex-feishu skill plugin, including desktop and mobile app sessions. Feishu sessions retain their normal scope; Slack and CLI sessions do not gain the plugin. Start a new session to verify. Agent plugin assignment, lark-cli login and permissions remain necessary; this setting does not change Feishu MCP loading or grant account access.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
All values are loaded from the .env file at $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env. Every variable is optional; a platform's credentials are needed only to bring that platform online.

Server behavior settings belong in config/settings.json, where they hot-reload. A legacy variable for one of those settings is read as a deprecated fallback and moved out of .env automatically at the next daemon start (see Automatic migration out of .env).

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose CORTEX_HOME ~/.cortex/ User data root (config, context, logs, store) CORTEX_PROJECTS_DIR <CORTEX_HOME>/context/projects/ Override project directory CORTEX_AGENT_CWD $CORTEX_HOME Working directory of every agent backend process. Must be an absolute path to an existing directory; anything else stops the server at startup CORTEX_REPO — The agent-server/ directory of a source checkout. The daemon watches its src/ and rebuilds, reinstalls and restarts on change (see Hot rebuild); the server update check is skipped while it is set CORTEX_CLIENT_REPO — A client/ source directory that remote client bundles are built from instead of the packaged bundle CORTEX_NPM_PREFIX the running install's prefix npm prefix used when Cortex installs or updates itself

docs.title: Startup
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose CORTEX_MACHINE os.hostname() Machine label for startup DM CORTEX_LANG config/preferences.json, else en Language of system-generated messages (en or zh). Outranks the preference that !lang writes CORTEX_CLIENT_PORT 3002 WebSocket port for cortex-client manager CORTEX_CLIENT_HOST Unspecified (all interfaces) Bind address for the cortex-client WebSocket listener only; read at server startup CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN generated Shared secret that remote clients, the desktop app and the Web UI present. cortex init and the first server start generate it CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN generated Bearer token of the loopback webhook (hook callbacks, cortex-hook ask). Generated the same way

A new Windows local App installation writes CORTEX_CLIENT_HOST=127.0.0.1 to config/.env. Existing installations, ordinary CLI init, and other platforms keep their existing defaults and configuration. For intentional LAN-direct clients, explicitly set this variable to an appropriate bind address (for example, 0.0.0.0 for all IPv4 interfaces) and restart the server. Cortex does not configure firewall policy automatically. This setting does not affect Web UI, TUI, or other server listeners.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
CORTEX_PLATFORM selects the messaging platform(s). It accepts a single value (slack, feishu) or a comma-separated list to run several at once (slack,feishu), and defaults to slack. Each listed platform whose credentials are present is brought online and the others are skipped, so a server with no credentials at all runs without a chat platform and serves the Web UI, desktop app and TUI only. The TUI gateway runs alongside every platform unless CORTEX_TUI=0. With multiple platforms, messages route by platform and system notices fan out to each platform's admin channel.

Variable Required Purpose CORTEX_PLATFORM no slack (default). Comma list for multi-platform, e.g. slack,feishu SLACK_BOT_TOKEN for slack Slack Bot OAuth token (xoxb-...) SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET for slack Slack app signing secret SLACK_APP_TOKEN for slack Slack app-level token for Socket Mode (xapp-...) FEISHU_APP_ID for feishu Feishu app ID (cli_...) FEISHU_APP_SECRET for feishu Feishu app secret FEISHU_ENCRYPT_KEY no Feishu event encrypt key (optional with long-connection) FEISHU_VERIFICATION_TOKEN no Feishu event verification token (optional) FEISHU_DOMAIN no feishu (default) or lark for the international edition FEISHU_AUTH_MODE no bot (default) or user. cortex feishu login sets user, so Feishu document tools act as the signed-in user FEISHU_USER_SCOPE no Scopes cortex feishu login requests when --scope is not given FEISHU_REDIRECT_URI no Redirect URI for cortex feishu login --manual

The admin channels for system notices are settings, not environment variables: see adminChannel and feishuAdminChannel in config/settings.json. The legacy variables SLACK_ADMIN_CHANNEL, CORTEX_ADMIN_CHANNEL, and FEISHU_ADMIN_CHANNEL are still read as a deprecated fallback.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Variable Purpose ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Anthropic API key used by Claude Code runs on a metered (api) route ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL Anthropic endpoint for Claude Code runs while the local gateway is down. With the gateway healthy, each run's base URL is its gateway route instead

docs.title: Web UI and TUI
docs.text:
The Web UI host serves the browser workbench, the desktop app and the mobile app. Browser access covers token login and Cloudflare Access in depth.

Variable Default Purpose CORTEX_UI_HTTP off 1, true, on or yes starts the Web UI host. cortex ui enable sets it CORTEX_UI_PORT 3004 Port of the Web UI host, bound to 127.0.0.1 CORTEX_UI_SPA_DIR the packaged web/dist Directory of the web app the host serves CORTEX_UI_TOKEN_LOGIN on Browser login by pasting the client token. 0, false, off or no removes the login routes CORTEX_UI_SESSION_TTL_DAYS 30 Lifetime of a browser login session, in days CORTEX_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN, CORTEX_ACCESS_AUD, CORTEX_ACCESS_CERTS_URL — Cloudflare Access JWT verification for browsers; both of the first two are needed to enable it CORTEX_PORT_FORWARD on 0 disables the Web UI's port forwarding to remote machines CORTEX_TUI on 0 stops the TUI gateway CORTEX_TUI_PORT 3003 Port of the TUI gateway, also the one cortex tui connects to

docs.title: Rate limiting (Slack)
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose CORTEX_SLACK_RL_GLOBAL_CAPACITY 20 Global API call bucket capacity CORTEX_SLACK_RL_GLOBAL_REFILL_PER_SEC 1 Global refill rate per second CORTEX_SLACK_RL_CHANNEL_CAPACITY 1 Per-channel bucket capacity CORTEX_SLACK_RL_CHANNEL_REFILL_PER_SEC 1 Per-channel refill rate per second

docs.title: Webhook
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose WEBHOOK_PORT 3001 Port of the loopback webhook server that receives hook, waitpoint, subagent and board callbacks

docs.title: Data file overrides
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose CORTEX_EXECUTIONS_FILE <STORE_DIR>/executions.json Execution records CORTEX_COSTS_FILE <STORE_DIR>/costs.jsonl Cost tracking CORTEX_BUDGET_FILE <CONFIG_DIR>/budget.json Budget configuration CORTEX_SESSION_TOTALS_FILE <STORE_DIR>/session-totals.json Per-session cost and token totals carried over from archived executions

<STORE_DIR> is $CORTEX_HOME/data and <CONFIG_DIR> is $CORTEX_HOME/config.

docs.title: Tuning and debugging
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose DEBUG — Enable server-wide debug mode. In addition to debug-level logs, the desktop transcript shows hover inspectors for the exact agent message and each tool call's complete input/result. Only DEBUG=1 enables it; all other values disable it. Settings → Advanced has a switch for it; restart agent-server after changing it CORTEX_DEBUG_TOOL_WARNING_CHARS 10000 In DEBUG transcripts, mark a tool-name badge amber when its formatted complete parameters plus complete result strictly exceed this Unicode character count. Positive integers only; invalid values use the default. Restart agent-server after changing it CORTEX_BG_GRACE_S 90 Seconds a run waits for a background task the backend reported finished but never announced (see How backends work) CORTEX_BG_WAIT_MAX_S 1800 Seconds a turn waits on still-running background work before it stops waiting; the work itself continues CORTEX_STREAM_DELTA_MS 120 Flush interval, in milliseconds, for streamed assistant text CORTEX_AGENT_BROWSER_BIN the bundled binary agent-browser binary that cortex-browser runs (see Agent Browser). A path that does not exist is an error CORTEX_BROWSER_BINARY auto-detected Chrome or Chromium binary for the server's agent browser CORTEX_BROWSER_DISPLAY auto-detected X display the server's agent browser uses, skipping display detection CORTEX_GPU_MONITOR_MOCK — Mock GPU data JSON for testing (overrides real nvidia-smi queries)

The event log, tool-call rendering, user-context injection, update check, compaction notice, turn notification, and auto-resume switches are settings keys — see config/settings.json.

DEBUG persists unabridged prompts, tool parameters, and tool results in per-session conversation-history files. These values can contain secrets, private file contents, or large outputs, and storage grows with their full size. Enable this mode only on a trusted development server and turn it off when inspection is complete. Turning it off immediately removes debug fields and buttons from transcript responses, but it does not delete records captured earlier.

docs.title: models.json
docs.text: Located at $CORTEX_HOME/config/models.json. It stores the default engine selection and a list of favorite models. Settings → Models manages the default and favorites; the composer's full model list also lets you star or unstar models. For backend details, see backends.md.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
{
  "default": {
    "backend": "claude",
    "provider": null,
    "model": "opus",
    "thinking": "high",
    "mode": "plan"
  },
  "favorites": [
    { "backend": "claude", "provider": null, "model": "opus" },
    { "backend": "pi", "provider": "deepseek", "model": "deepseek-v4-pro" }
  ]
}

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description default object yes Complete engine selection used when a session or channel has none default.backend string yes claude or pi default.provider string or null yes null for Claude; an explicit provider id for PI, such as openai-codex, deepseek, or a custom provider default.model string yes Non-empty model identifier, as the backend names it default.thinking string or null yes Backend-native reasoning level; null uses the backend's default default.mode string yes Gateway route, such as plan or api for Claude; PI uses its provider name favorites object[] yes Ordered model references, each with backend, provider, and model. Each model identity occurs at most once

Favorites store model identities, not thinking levels or routes. The default need not be a favorite, and the favorites list may be empty. thinking accepts low/medium/high/xhigh/max on Claude and off/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh/max on PI.

docs.title: Selection resolution
docs.text:
An ordinary turn uses the session's recorded selection, then the channel's selection in data/agent-state.json, then models.json's default. An explicit run request, such as a scheduled fire, can supply a complete selection directly. Each selection contains backend, provider, model, thinking, and mode; execution environments are independent of this choice.

data/agent-state.json stores channelSelections, per-model modelMemory (thinking and mode, keyed by the JSON array [backend, provider, model]), and selectionDefault, the last Web engine choice used to seed new conversations. Selecting a model restores its remembered thinking and route. Without a memory, thinking is null; Claude uses the first Anthropic route in gateway.yaml (plan if none is declared), and PI uses its provider name. User selection changes update this memory. See per-session controls.

!backend <claude|pi> uses the configured default when it belongs to the target backend; otherwise it uses the first favorite on that backend, with its remembered settings. If neither exists, favorite a model on that backend first.

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text: mode and PI provider must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$. Claude requires a null provider. Thinking must be null or one of the backend's allowed values, and favorite identities must be unique. Selection writes validate the route against gateway.yaml when it is available. A file that parses but fails schema validation is rejected as a whole until corrected.

docs.title: Execution environments
docs.text:
An execution environment decides how a conversation runs, apart from which model runs it: the system prompt, the built-in tool list, which plugins load, which Cortex MCP tools the session gets, and how much ambient context (rules, hooks, the project block, the backend's own skills) comes with it. Each environment is one file, config/environments/<name>.json, and the file name is its name.

Cortex ships two:

Environment What it is for main General-purpose work on the session’s selected engine, with the built-in Cortex system, board, and Feishu plugins. It is the default: a session that has not picked an environment runs in main, and main cannot be deleted creative A clean-room surface for writing, image prompts, naming, and copy, with the operational context stripped out (see A minimal surface)

The shipped files are copied into config/environments/ at cortex init, and again at every server start when they are missing (a sealed home, with CORTEX_CONFIG_IMMUTABLE=1, skips that start-time copy). A file you already have is never overwritten, so your edits survive upgrades, and a file you add is an environment like any other. Changes to the directory are picked up about 300 ms later without a restart. A file that is not valid JSON, or whose name does not match its file name, is skipped and logged.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description name string yes Must equal the file name without .json description string no One line describing what the environment is for, shown in pickers directive string no Role or identity text prepended to the prompt systemPrompt string no Replaces the backend's default system prompt promptTemplate string no Wraps each message; {{input}} stands for what was sent claudeAgent string no Claude Code agent name, passed as --agent. Claude only outputStyle string no Claude Code output style. Claude only tools string no Comma-separated built-in tool list that replaces the backend's default set pluginDirs string[] no Plugin directories to load, relative to $CORTEX_HOME unless absolute. They load first, in the order listed, followed by the built-in plugins disabledPlugins string[] no Built-in plugin ids this environment leaves out. Every other built-in plugin loads, unless skills is false, in which case only pluginDirs loads mcpComposition "direct" | "none" no direct (default) gives the session the Cortex MCP tools; none gives it no MCP at all, plugin servers included mcpToolAllowlist string[] no Narrows the Cortex MCP tools to the names listed. Absent keeps the full surface loadRules boolean no Default true: prepend the global rules from rules/ disableHooks boolean no Default false. true runs the session without lifecycle hooks skills boolean no Default true. false removes the backend's skill layer, including the Skill tool settingSources string[] no Which Claude setting files to read: any of user, project, local. Absent uses the CLI default; [] reads none projectContext boolean no Default true: tell the session which project it belongs to on its first turn

The three prompt fields accept file:<name> instead of literal text. The text is then read from prompts/directives/, prompts/systemPrompts/, or prompts/promptTemplates/ respectively, and from the built-in prompt of that name when $CORTEX_HOME has none; the shipped main uses "systemPrompt": "file:direct.md". A field the schema does not know, a missing prompt file, or a missing plugin directory is reported as a warning, and the environment still loads.

docs.title: Plugins and the Environments panel
docs.text:
Plugins attach to environments. An environment's sessions load the plugins its pluginDirs lists and every built-in plugin its disabledPlugins does not name; the environment's Plugins tab writes those same fields, and Settings → Plugins shows which environments use each installed plugin (see Skills and Plugins).

In the Web workbench and the desktop app, Settings → Environments lists every environment and edits one at a time: the JSON body with live validation, a Validation tab for errors and warnings, and a Plugins tab for its plugin set. A new environment starts from a skeleton that already validates, and an existing one can be duplicated under a new name. Errors block a save, warnings do not, and a save made against a file that changed on disk in the meantime is refused rather than overwriting it. Editing a shipped environment that still matches its default warns first, because from then on it stops following the shipped version. main cannot be deleted. On Android, Settings shows Environments as a desktop-only entry.

The System prompt tab edits the text an environment's systemPrompt resolves to, which replaces the backend's default system prompt as a whole. When the field is a file: reference, the tab edits that file under prompts/systemPrompts/ and names any other environment that references the same file, since a save changes the prompt for all of them. When the field is literal text or absent, saving writes the text to prompts/systemPrompts/<name>.md and points the environment at it. Empty text leaves the environment on the backend's default prompt. A prompt file that ships with Cortex shows its built-in text until you save your own version, which is written to prompts/systemPrompts/ and used in its place; Restore default loads the built-in text into the editor, and saving it removes your version. New sessions start with the saved prompt. A session already open on the PI backend switches to it on its next turn; one on Claude Code keeps its prompt until its backend process restarts.

docs.title: Environments and engine selection
docs.text: The engine selection decides backend, provider, model, thinking, and mode. An execution environment decides the prompt, tools, plugins, MCP surface, and ambient context. They change independently: !model <id> changes the model; !agent <name> changes the environment. !agent reset also leaves the engine selection intact.

docs.title: Choosing an environment per conversation
docs.text:
The environment is chosen per conversation, over a host-wide default.

Command What it does !agent Shows this conversation's environment, the host-wide default it falls back to, and the list to pick from — as buttons on Slack and Feishu !agent <name> Runs THIS conversation in <name>, from its next turn !agent reset Hands this conversation back to the host-wide default. clear, off, none and disable say the same thing !agent global <name> Sets the host-wide default: what every conversation that has not chosen one runs !agent global off Clears the host-wide default, leaving main

Every bare form is scoped to the conversation it is typed in; the host-wide default moves only behind the explicit global prefix.

In the Web app and the desktop client the same choice is the composer's own control: a chip of its own, immediately left of the engine chip — where the turn runs, before what runs it. It names the environment the conversation is in, or, when the conversation has picked none, the host-wide default it falls back to, drawn muted so a choice reads differently from a fallback. Clicking it opens one flat list: a default row meaning "follow the host-wide default", then every environment this host declares, each with what it is for. A host declaring a single environment shows no chip — there is nothing to choose between.
