A pick on a new conversation travels with its first message; on a live one it applies at once and takes effect on the next turn.

A turn resolves its environment through this chain: the session's own choice, then the conversation's, then the host-wide default, then main. A name that no longer resolves, because the environment was renamed or deleted, is skipped.

Switching environments leaves the backend unchanged. It takes effect on the next turn and preserves history, so the model sees turns from the previous environment; use !new for a fresh context.

docs.title: A minimal surface
docs.text:
The shipped creative environment is the smallest one Cortex ships — writing, image prompts, naming and copy, with the operational context stripped out:

{
  "name": "creative",
  "description": "Clean-room creative environment: writing, image prompts, naming, copy. No skills, no project rules, minimal tools.",
  "promptTemplate": "{{input}}",
  "systemPrompt": "file:creative.md",
  "tools": "Read,Write,Edit",
  "pluginDirs": [],
  "skills": false,
  "settingSources": [],
  "mcpComposition": "direct",
  "mcpToolAllowlist": ["send_file", "send_view", "cortex_ask_user"],
  "loadRules": false,
  "disableHooks": true,
  "projectContext": false
}

Three built-in tools, no Cortex plugins, no ambient rules, no hooks, no project block, and an MCP surface of exactly three tools: send_file and send_view to deliver, cortex_ask_user to ask. A session opened under it reports three tools and zero skills when asked what it can see.

mcpToolAllowlist is an upper bound, not a requirement. It narrows a session's MCP surface to the names it lists; a name the session does not compose on the surface it opened on is simply absent there. One list therefore runs everywhere: this creative keeps all three tools in the Web and desktop app, and only cortex_ask_user on Slack and Feishu (their file delivery is a tool of its own, which this list does not name). A name that exists in no bundle on the host is still refused at spawn — that is a typo, not a surface.

docs.title: Skills outside pluginDirs
docs.text: pluginDirs is not the whole skill layer. Claude Code loads its own on every spawn no matter what Cortex passes: the plugins enabled in its setting files (installed under Cortex's Claude config directory, $CORTEX_HOME/data/claude), anything under $CORTEX_HOME/data/claude/skills/, and the CLI's built-in skills. Two environment fields reach them. settingSources: [] stops the setting files being read at all, which removes the enabled plugins' skills; skills: false removes the layer outright, built-ins included, and takes the Skill tool with it. An environment that sets both sees no skills and no slash commands.

docs.title: config/settings.json
docs.text:
Located at $CORTEX_HOME/config/settings.json. This file holds the runtime behavior settings of the server: switches, limits and notification routes. Editing this file takes effect without a daemon restart, except for the few keys read once at startup, which the table marks.

It is a flat JSON object that stores only the keys you explicitly override. Any key you leave out falls back to its legacy environment variable when one exists, and then to the built-in default. The file itself is optional — a fresh install has none and runs entirely on defaults. It is created the first time something writes it: the startup migration below, admin-channel auto-detection, or the Web workbench settings panels.

{
  "turnNotify": false,
  "turnNotifyThresholdS": 120,
  "uiCorsOrigins": ["cortexui://localhost"]
}

Values are checked against the schema below when the file is read. A key whose JSON type does not match, or whose value is outside its documented range (the job intervals, sessionRetentionDays, piCompactReserveTokens, maxContextTokens, cacheKeepWarmHours, the shape of providerRateLimits), rejects the whole file: at startup Cortex falls back to environment variables and defaults, and on a reload it keeps the last valid settings. Either way the reason is logged. Unknown keys are ignored.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Type Default Effect Legacy env variable turnNotify boolean true When a long-running turn finishes, post a fresh message to the conversation so you get a push notification (the inline status seals to "✓ Done" with an edit, which Slack and Feishu do not notify on). Both success and failure are announced CORTEX_TURN_NOTIFY turnNotifyThresholdS number 60 Minimum turn duration, in seconds, before that completion notification is posted. Shorter turns stay quiet CORTEX_TURN_NOTIFY_THRESHOLD_S notifyCompaction boolean true Post a chat notice when an agent's context is compacted. Covers the Claude Code (print mode) and pi backends CORTEX_NOTIFY_COMPACTION showToolCalls boolean false Inline tool-call rendering in VirtualMessage tails CORTEX_SHOW_TOOL_CALLS statusNewqButton boolean false Show the "New (quiet)" button on status messages (=!newq, which skips the pre-close hook) CORTEX_STATUS_NEWQ_BUTTON autoResume boolean true When a usage-limit window resets, automatically continue the conversations the limit interrupted, injecting a note to pick up where they left off. Set to false to leave interrupted work paused for manual continuation CORTEX_AUTO_RESUME providerRateLimits object {} Per-provider, per-quota-window throttle policy. Provider entries contain a windows array of { type, label?, enabled, threshold? }; threshold is a ratio greater than 0 and at most 1 — showThinking boolean true Capture model-provided thinking for Web and mobile chat. Disable to stop capturing new thinking; saved rows remain visible. Claude requests a thinking summary; PI displays the text the provider returns CORTEX_SHOW_THINKING streamDeltas boolean true Stream assistant text and captured thinking token by token. Disable to deliver only complete blocks CORTEX_STREAM_DELTAS bgContinuation boolean true Forward the output of background tasks back into the conversation when they finish CORTEX_BG_CONTINUATION eventLog boolean true Write the event bus to the daily rolling JSONL event log CORTEX_EVENT_LOG diskMonitor boolean true Check free space on the filesystem containing $CORTEX_HOME every five minutes and send a system notice below 500 MiB. false stops the timer; switching back to true runs an immediate check CORTEX_DISK_MONITOR disableUserContext boolean false Set to true to stop injecting USER.md context into direct conversation turns (injected by default) CORTEX_DISABLE_USER_CONTEXT serverUpdateDisable boolean false Set to true to disable the server auto-update check (enabled by default) CORTEX_SERVER_UPDATE_DISABLE serverAutoUpdate boolean true When the update check finds a newer server release, install it without asking. Installation starts only once no turn is running, and the server restarts right after. false asks for confirmation first; an agreed update waits for idle the same way. A skipped version stays skipped — clientHotReloadEnabled boolean true Push the server's client bundle to connecting remote clients that run a different one, so they update themselves. Read at startup — feishuSkillsInWeb boolean false Let web: sessions, including desktop and mobile app sessions, load an assigned cortex-feishu skill plugin (see Platform settings in the Web UI) — teamEnabled boolean true Experimental team mode: any web session can start and manage persistent worker sessions with the worker_* tools. Turning it off removes those tools from the next turn and leaves existing workers as ordinary sessions. See team.md CORTEX_TEAM_ENABLED waitpointSweepMs number 30000 Interval, in milliseconds, of the waitpoint sweep: it drains spooled signals (locally and from connected devices), expires overdue waitpoints, and retries deliveries that failed. See waitpoints.md CORTEX_WAITPOINT_SWEEP_MS waitpointTtlMs number 604800000 Default lifetime of a waitpoint (7 days) when the agent does not set one. A waitpoint may ask for less, or for more up to a hard ceiling of 30 days; past it the waitpoint expires and the session is told nothing arrived CORTEX_WAITPOINT_TTL_MS waitpointMaxWakesPerHour number 12 Cap on how many times a single waitpoint may wake its session per hour. A runaway signalling loop is throttled (and says so once) rather than flooding the conversation CORTEX_WAITPOINT_MAX_WAKES_PER_HOUR injectWaitMaxS number 600 Upper bound, in seconds, on how long an injected mid-turn message waits for a reply before the busy gate is released. Prevents a wedged process from holding the daemon restart gate forever CORTEX_INJECT_WAIT_MAX_S anthropicSubscriptionModes string[] ["plan"] Gateway modes whose Anthropic account quota is polled for the Usage screens. [] turns the polling off — subscriptionBillingModes string[] ["plan", "openai-codex", "google-gemini-cli", "google-antigravity"] Gateway modes paid by a subscription. The gateway still prices their requests, but usage rows for these modes show quota only and no cost — providerUsageCollectionEnabled boolean true Run the built-in provider-usage collection job that refreshes quota and spend readings — providerUsageCollectionIntervalMs number 300000 Interval between provider-usage collections, in integer milliseconds — claudeWindowWarmupEnabled boolean false Claude on a subscription mode (see anthropicSubscriptionModes) only. Claude's five-hour usage window opens with the first request after the previous window closed. With this on, once the window has closed and no Claude run has started for ten minutes, Cortex sends one tiny request (Haiku, no tools, through Claude Code on the first subscription mode's route) to open the next window, so it closes five hours later instead of five hours after work resumes. The request also lets Claude Code refresh its login, which keeps the Anthropic usage reading current. The window's close time comes from the Anthropic usage reading; a failed warm-up is retried after 30 minutes. Also on Settings → Advanced — storeArchiveEnabled boolean true Once a day, move terminal execution records older than a week from data/executions.json to data/archive/. Read at startup — memoryIndexRegenEnabled boolean true Run the built-in experiment/knowledge/pattern index rebuild. Switching from false to true runs it immediately — memoryIndexRegenIntervalMs number 86400000 Interval between memory-index rebuilds, in integer milliseconds — sessionRetentionDays number 30 Whole safe-integer retention window in days (valid range 1 through 104249991). The retention coordinator starts a sweep in the background at daemon startup (boot does not wait for it), runs every 6 hours, and runs again after a hot-reload change; it prunes expired session-registry entries, orphan conversation-history, orphan PI transcript bundles, orphan Claude capture logs, orphan tool-image directories, and syncs Claude user cleanupPeriodDays, while skipping active sessions/captures — piCompactReserveTokens number 16384 PI backend only: the context headroom PI keeps in reserve, in tokens. PI compacts once the context passes contextWindow - reserveTokens — both between turns and, since PI 0.84.4, inside a running turn at a tool-batch boundary — so a larger reserve compacts earlier and leaves more working room in a long tool-driven turn. A whole number from 1024 through 131072. Cortex mirrors it into the private PI agent dir's settings.json, which is the only way in: PI exposes no setter for it CORTEX_PI_COMPACT_RESERVE_TOKENS maxContextTokens number | null null Cap on every model's usable context window, in tokens, for both backends: the usable window is the smaller of the model's own window and this value, and each backend compacts before reaching it. A whole number from 100000 through 1000000 (Claude Code's own accepted range), or null to leave every model at its own window. Claude receives it as CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, which outranks any autoCompactWindow in Claude's settings files; PI compacts at cap - piCompactReserveTokens once a model's window exceeds the cap. Context-usage percentages use the capped window — cacheKeepWarmHours number 6 Claude on a subscription mode (see anthropicSubscriptionModes) only, where the prompt cache lasts one hour after its last use. While an idle session with at least 100k tokens of context still expects a wake (an open waitpoint, a worker that has not reported back, a background agent run), Cortex reads its cache about every 50 minutes so the wake does not re-send the whole context at the cache-write price. Each refresh is one short request on a fork of the session that leaves the conversation unchanged; it costs roughly a tenth of the context's input price and is recorded in costs under the cache-refresh trigger. Refreshing stops this many hours after the session last called the model. A cache that may already have expired, such as one whose last refresh came before a server restart, is not refreshed; that session's wake resumes cold. 0 turns it off; 0 through 24 — coldResumeClearToolResults boolean true Claude only. When a session with at least 100k tokens of context resumes after its prompt cache has expired (more than 65 minutes since the cache was last used), Cortex replaces the output of all but the 10 most recent tool calls since the last compaction with a short placeholder in its transcript before Claude re-reads it, so the uncached request is smaller. Tool calls, the model's replies, your messages, subagent records, and short tool output that the placeholder would not shrink stay as they were; the model does not see the old tool output and re-runs a tool when it needs that output again. The transcript is left unchanged when this would remove less than 40,000 characters. Rewinding or retrying the turn restores the full transcript — uiCorsOrigins string[] [] Origins that receive CORS headers from the Web UI HTTP host. See desktop-app.md CORTEX_UI_CORS_ORIGINS (comma-separated) adminChannel string | null null Slack channel for system notices (startup, rate-limit, disk alerts). The first DM to the bot is auto-detected and persisted here SLACK_ADMIN_CHANNEL, then CORTEX_ADMIN_CHANNEL feishuAdminChannel string | null null Feishu admin chat_id (oc_...) for the same notices. Independent of adminChannel — Slack channel ids are not usable on Feishu FEISHU_ADMIN_CHANNEL

The Web workbench writes a subset of these from Settings → Notifications (turnNotify, autoResume, notifyCompaction), Settings → Advanced (eventLog, diskMonitor, showToolCalls, disableUserContext, serverUpdateDisable, serverAutoUpdate, teamEnabled, sessionRetentionDays, maxContextTokens, piCompactReserveTokens, memoryIndexRegenEnabled and memoryIndexRegenIntervalMs), Settings → Platform (adminChannel, feishuAdminChannel, feishuSkillsInWeb), and the desktop/mobile Usage screens (providerRateLimits). Every other key is edited by hand in the file.

providerRateLimits is a settings.json object keyed by provider id. Each provider entry can contain a windows array whose entries are { type, label?, enabled, threshold? }. The identity of an ordinary quota row is its provider-reported type; a model-scoped row uses both type and its exact provider-reported label. An exact window entry takes precedence over older provider-level enabled/threshold fields. Those root fields remain a backward-compatible fallback and, when non-default, appear in Usage with an action to clear them.

Desktop and mobile Usage place separate controls on every displayed 5-hour, weekly, weekly-overage, Codex primary/secondary, and labeled model row. Leaving threshold out uses the row default: 0.95 for seven_day and seven_day_overage_included, 0.90 for other rows. Spend-only cards have no quota controls. Model policy identity follows the reported display label; if a provider renames that label, the old entry stops matching. Policy edits apply only to future quota observations; an already-active quota or outage window keeps its current state until its reset time or a manual Resume now clear. The Codex and Anthropic cards also show the account's banked resets and a confirmed Reset action; see Account usage and banked resets.

Built-in job intervals must be integer milliseconds from 1000 through 2147483647, the safe range for Node timers. Enabled jobs run once at daemon startup. Memory-index runs never overlap; a changed interval takes effect after an active run finishes.

sessionRetentionDays is the one numeric retention control in Settings → Advanced. The desktop Web UI writes it through the same config.set { section: 'settings' } path as the boolean runtime toggles, and the client enforces the same upper bound the server validates. piCompactReserveTokens sits in the same card and takes the same path; the client accepts 1024–131072, exactly what the server validates. Cortex writes it into PI's private settings.json when a PI session is created, so a new value reaches the next PI session without a restart — sessions already pooled keep the reserve they were built with.

maxContextTokens sits in the same card. Its field accepts 100000–1000000; clearing the field saves null, which leaves every model at its own window. PI reads the cap each time it decides whether to compact, so running PI sessions follow a new value at once. Claude takes it when its CLI process starts, so it reaches the next Claude session; a pinned CLI compatibility trial never receives it.

The retention coordinator has six housekeeping surfaces on that clock: live session-registry expiry (via delete-intent then delete-commit), orphan data/conversation-history/*.jsonl, orphan PI transcript bundles under logs/sessions-pi/, orphan Claude capture files under logs/sessions/, orphan per-session image directories under tmp/tool-images/, and the synced Claude user cleanupPeriodDays helper. An image directory goes once its session is neither live nor pending deletion and nothing in it changed inside the retention window. Orphan history and PI files use a two-sweep confirmation before deletion. Active direct sessions, running executions, pending interaction/bg-held sessions, live PI backend session ids, and active Claude capture pairs are protected.

Registry expiry writes the delete intents for every expired session in one journal append, then cleans up and commits them in batches of 100 sessions; each batch costs three registry appends however many sessions it holds. A daemon shutdown stops a running sweep between batches. Sessions whose deletion was not committed stay pending, and the next sweep finishes them first.

docs.title: Hot reload
docs.text:
The config directory is watched. A change to settings.json is debounced for 300 ms, the file is re-read, and the new values are used from then on — no daemon restart. Two consequences worth knowing:

  • Each setting takes effect at its own point of use: the next turn, the next agent spawn, the next built-in job run, or the next HTTP request. uiCorsOrigins is resolved per request; adminChannel and feishuAdminChannel are pushed into the running platform adapter as soon as they change. diskMonitor=false stops its timer, while restoring true starts the timer and checks immediately. Each built-in job switch likewise cancels or starts its timer immediately, and interval edits reschedule its next idle run.
  • A broken file never takes the server down. Invalid JSON or a type mismatch leaves the previous settings in place and logs the error; fix the file and the next write reloads it.

docs.title: Legacy environment variables and deprecation
docs.text:
Keys with a legacy environment variable in the table keep it as a fallback, parsed with its established semantics — CORTEX_EVENT_LOG=off, CORTEX_TURN_NOTIFY=0/false/off/no, CORTEX_NOTIFY_COMPACTION=0/false/off/no, a comma-separated list for CORTEX_UI_CORS_ORIGINS, and so on. Precedence is always: key in settings.json → legacy variable → built-in default. For adminChannel the original chain is preserved: SLACK_ADMIN_CHANNEL is consulted before CORTEX_ADMIN_CHANNEL.

The first time a legacy variable supplies a value, the daemon logs a deprecation warning naming the variable and the setting it feeds (Deprecated env <VAR> supplies settings.<key>; move it to settings.json). The fallback exists for compatibility during migration — new configuration belongs in settings.json.

docs.title: Automatic migration out of .env
docs.text:
On every daemon start, right after .env is loaded, Cortex scans $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env for the legacy variables listed above. If it finds at least one:

  1. .env is copied to .env.bak-<timestamp> in the same directory, where <timestamp> is an ISO 8601 instant with : and . replaced by - (for example .env.bak-2026-07-30T09-12-33-482Z).
  2. Each legacy value is parsed with its old semantics and written into settings.json. A key already present in settings.json is never overwritten — the file wins over .env.
  3. The migrated assignments are removed from .env, which keeps its original file permissions and gains the header comment # Legacy server settings migrated to settings.json; secrets remain in .env.
  4. The dead variable CORTEX_SERVER_UPDATE_ENABLE, which nothing reads any more, is dropped in the same pass.

The migration is idempotent: a .env with no legacy variables is left untouched, and later starts do nothing. If any step fails, the error is logged, .env keeps its variables, and the server keeps running on whichever source supplies each value — so a failed migration costs nothing but the deprecation warnings.

docs.title: What stays in .env
docs.text:
Three categories of variables deliberately remain in .env:

  • Secrets and credentials — SLACK_BOT_TOKEN, SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET, SLACK_APP_TOKEN, FEISHU_APP_ID, FEISHU_APP_SECRET, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN, CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN. They are settings in a loose sense, but keeping them out of a file that the Web UI can read and write keeps the blast radius small.
  • Variables consumed by child processes — CORTEX_HOME, CORTEX_PROJECTS_DIR, WEBHOOK_PORT, DEBUG, CORTEX_LANG, and the data file overrides. Hooks, MCP servers, the CLI, and cortex-client inherit the daemon's environment; a server-side JSON file would never reach them.
  • Startup topology — CORTEX_PLATFORM, CORTEX_MACHINE, CORTEX_UI_HTTP, CORTEX_UI_PORT, CORTEX_UI_SPA_DIR, CORTEX_UI_TOKEN_LOGIN. These decide which adapters and listeners exist at boot, so hot-reloading them would have no meaning; they require a restart by construction.

docs.title: Not the same file as .claude/settings.json
docs.text: $CORTEX_HOME/config/settings.json (this file) configures the Cortex server. $CORTEX_HOME/.claude/settings.json configures Claude Code's hooks and permissions and is read by the Claude CLI, not by Cortex. Same file name, different directory, different owner, different schema — see the next section.

docs.title: .claude/settings.json (Claude Code)
docs.text:
Located at $CORTEX_HOME/.claude/settings.json. This is the Cortex-scaffolded Claude Code project settings file under the Cortex data root. cortex init seeds it from defaults/.claude/settings.json once and Cortex never overwrites that path on later runs.

Claude Code itself can also read higher-precedence project files in the spawn cwd (.claude/settings.local.json, then .claude/settings.json) and its user settings file in Cortex's Claude config directory (next section). Cortex does not scaffold, sync, or overwrite those project-local cwd files at all; "never overwrite" here applies only to the $CORTEX_HOME/.claude/settings.json seed path above.

The file follows Claude Code's settings format with hooks and permissions sections. See hooks.md for the hook system documentation. It has nothing to do with the Cortex runtime settings in config/settings.json.

docs.title: Claude Code config directory
docs.text:
Every claude process Cortex starts — session engines, subagent children, and the claude auth login, status and logout commands behind the login flow — runs with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$CORTEX_HOME/data/claude, whatever the daemon's own environment holds. It is Cortex's private Claude Code home, the counterpart of PI's $CORTEX_HOME/data/pi: transcripts (projects/<encoded cwd>/<id>.jsonl), the user settings file, user- and local-scope plugins, .claude.json and the login all live there. A terminal claude working from ~/.claude and Cortex never see each other's sessions, settings or plugins. The claude binary itself still comes from PATH.

Login. The directory has a login of its own; Cortex never copies or links the terminal's .credentials.json, because each OAuth refresh rotates the token and two copies would invalidate each other. Sign in from Settings → Accounts, with !login cc in chat, or with cortex auth login --backend claude (see Remote login). On macOS the CLI keeps the login in the keychain item Claude Code-credentials-<first 8 hex of sha256(config dir)>.

settings.json. The user settings file belongs to Cortex. When it does not exist, the server creates it at startup from the model, effortLevel, modelSettings, autoCompactWindow, autoMemoryEnabled, env and attribution keys of ~/.claude/settings.json; once it exists the terminal file is never read again. The session-retention coordinator keeps one key in it current — cleanupPeriodDays, from the sessionRetentionDays runtime setting — and leaves every other key as it is. Edit the file directly to change what Cortex's Claude sessions use.

Plugins. Plugins Cortex's Claude sessions should load are installed into this directory:

cd ~/.cortex
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.cortex/data/claude claude plugin install <plugin>@<marketplace> --scope project

Project- and local-scope installs record the plugin in $CORTEX_HOME/.claude/settings*.json and the plugin files under $CORTEX_HOME/data/claude/plugins/.

Sessions from ~/.claude. At startup the server moves, once, every file a live Claude session in the session registry owns under ~/.claude/projects — its transcript, its turn backups and its sidecar directory — to the same path under $CORTEX_HOME/data/claude/projects, so those sessions keep resuming. A destination that already exists is never overwritten, and files no registry session owns stay where they are.

docs.title: Boards
docs.text:
A board is the status page of a long task, kept by the agents working on it (see Boards in the team guide). Each board lives in <project context>/boards/<slug>/, and data/boards.json lists every board with its project, title and when it was last used. On upgrade, registered commissions from earlier Cortex releases become boards: their directories move from commissions/ to boards/, and their files are moved, never deleted.

Boards are styled by a preset stylesheet that ships with Cortex in agent-server/defaults/board/board.css. It is read from the package and never copied into $CORTEX_HOME, so every upgrade brings its current version. The preset uses only the app's theme variables (--proto-*, --material-*, --border-card, --r-*, and the faces --font-ui and --font-code), so boards follow light and dark mode, the palette and the accent.

To restyle every board, create $CORTEX_HOME/config/board.css. The file does not exist by default. It loads after the preset, so it can redefine any variable, the preset's own --b-* or a theme --proto-*, or override any rule:

:root { --proto-accent: #0f766e; --b-gap: 16px; }
.h { font-size: 14px; }

Open boards pick up a save within a few seconds, and deleting the file restores the preset.

docs.title: Built-in assets and your overrides
docs.text:
Cortex's plugins, hooks, rules, subagent roles and system prompts ship in the install's agent-server/defaults/ and are read from there at runtime. They are never copied into $CORTEX_HOME, so they always match the running version, and $CORTEX_HOME holds only your own files. A file of yours at the matching place replaces the built-in one, a new name adds to them, and deleting your file brings the built-in one back.

Asset Built in Yours How yours combine with the built-in ones Plugins defaults/plugins/<id>/ plugins/<id>/ Same id: your skills replace or add to the built-in ones and your mcp.json replaces the built-in one; the manifest stays built in. Any other id is a plugin of its own. See Built-in plugins Hook declarations defaults/config/hooks/*.json config/hooks/*.json Same file name: each top-level field it sets replaces that field of the built-in declaration as a whole, so { "enabled": false } switches a built-in hook off. See the hook registry Hook scripts defaults/hooks/*.mjs hooks/*.mjs Same file name: replaces the built-in script Rules defaults/rules/*.md rules/*.md Same file name: replaces the built-in rule Subagent roles defaults/agents/*.md config/agents/*.md Same file name: replaces the built-in role System prompts defaults/prompts/systemPrompts/*.md prompts/systemPrompts/*.md Same file name: replaces the built-in prompt

Rules are Markdown files for agent sessions. A rule without paths frontmatter is prepended to every session whose environment loads rules (loadRules); a rule whose paths globs match a file the session reads is injected then by the rules-loader hook, once per session.

Settings edits — a skill, a hook switch, a system prompt — are written to $CORTEX_HOME in the same way, and Cortex never writes to the install. A sealed home (CORTEX_CONFIG_IMMUTABLE=1, as in a benchmark trial) declares its whole surface itself and uses none of the built-in plugins, hooks or rules.

A home set up by a release that kept copies of these files in $CORTEX_HOME is converted on its first start: copies identical to the shipped files are removed, plugin and hook copies that differ are moved to config/archive/builtin-overlay-<timestamp>/, edited rules, roles and prompts stay as your overrides, a switched-off built-in hook keeps its switch, and each environment keeps loading the same plugins.

docs.title: defaults/ layout
docs.text:
The agent-server/defaults/ directory in the npm package contains the shipped defaults. The scaffold files are copied to $CORTEX_HOME/ during init, and the execution environments are also merged at every server start; the built-in assets are read in place:

Source Destination Overwrite behavior defaults/AGENTS.md $CORTEX_HOME/AGENTS.md Never defaults/gitignore $CORTEX_HOME/.gitignore Never defaults/.claude/settings.json $CORTEX_HOME/.claude/settings.json Never — this applies only to the $CORTEX_HOME/.claude/settings.json scaffolded path; arbitrary repository-local .claude/settings.json files are outside Cortex's copy/sync loop defaults/config/budget.json $CORTEX_HOME/config/budget.json Only with --force defaults/config/environments/ $CORTEX_HOME/config/environments/ Per-file copy-if-missing, at init and again at every server start: a shipped environment you do not have yet is added; a file you already have is never overwritten — --force does not apply to this tree defaults/data/schedules.json $CORTEX_HOME/data/schedules.json Never (unless --force) defaults/context/ $CORTEX_HOME/context/ Index AGENTS.md files: never overwritten. The decisions/ scaffold: only with --force defaults/plugins/, defaults/config/hooks/, defaults/hooks/, defaults/rules/, defaults/agents/, defaults/prompts/ — Not copied: read in place, with your files laid over them (see Built-in assets and your overrides) defaults/board/ — Not copied: the board preset stylesheet and the scaffold of a new board are read from the package

Init also generates config/machines.json, config/preferences.json and data/agent-state.json when they are missing (or with --force), writes the config/mcp-config*.json files, and sets up the gateway configuration and models.json (see cortex init). The server rewrites the mcp-config*.json files at every start, so edits to them do not persist.

An upgrade therefore brings the current built-in plugins, hooks, rules, roles and prompts with it, and newly shipped environments reach existing installs without touching your edits. Whole-file config such as budget.json requires --force to replace.

docs.title: Hot-reload behavior
docs.text:
Watcher-backed files under config/ automatically switch to filesystem snapshot polling every 5 seconds if the watcher cannot start or reports a runtime error. Each loader keeps the same validation and failure behavior in polling mode as it uses with filesystem events.

  • config/settings.json — watched via file watcher, debounced 300 ms. New values apply at the next point of use without a restart; a broken file keeps the previous settings. See config/settings.json.
  • schedules.json — watched via file watcher. Changes are picked up within seconds without restart. See scheduling.md for the full scheduling system.
  • models.json — cached and watched for parseable JSON changes. An update refreshes the cache before the next agent spawn; malformed JSON keeps the previous model configuration.
  • machines.json — watched and reloaded after valid changes. Invalid entries keep the previous machine registry.
  • environments/ — watched. Changes are debounced (300 ms) and every environment is reloaded without a restart. See Execution environments.
  • .env — requires a daemon restart to pick up changes (loaded once at startup via dotenv). Behavior settings live in config/settings.json, which does not.
  • Hook declarations (config/hooks/*.json) — the registry is re-read on every agent spawn, so a new agent:* / cc:* / pi:* entry applies to the next agent that starts. cortex:* entries are snapshotted at server start and need a restart. See hooks.md.
  • Hook scripts — read fresh on every hook invocation.
  • Plugins, prompts, rules, subagent roles — read fresh on each agent session spawn.
  • config/board.css — watched together with every board's directory. Open boards re-render within a few seconds of a change. See Boards.

docs.title: Where each file lives
docs.text: File Purpose Path .env Environment variables $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env settings.json Runtime behavior settings (hot-reloaded) $CORTEX_HOME/config/settings.json models.json Default engine and favorite models $CORTEX_HOME/config/models.json environments/ Execution environments — one JSON per environment $CORTEX_HOME/config/environments/ machines.json Machine registry $CORTEX_HOME/config/machines.json budget.json Budget limits $CORTEX_HOME/config/budget.json preferences.json UI language for system messages $CORTEX_HOME/config/preferences.json mcp-config*.json Generated MCP server configs (rewritten at every start) $CORTEX_HOME/config/ .claude/settings.json Claude Code hooks/permissions (not the Cortex settings file) $CORTEX_HOME/.claude/settings.json agent-state.json Channel selections, model memory, new-session choice, default agent $CORTEX_HOME/data/agent-state.json schedules.json Schedules $CORTEX_HOME/data/schedules.json boards.json Board registry $CORTEX_HOME/data/boards.json provider-state.json Provider usage, throttle windows, resume queue $CORTEX_HOME/data/provider-state.json waitpoints.json Waitpoints $CORTEX_HOME/data/waitpoints.json board.css Optional stylesheet for every board $CORTEX_HOME/config/board.css session-registry.jsonl Append-only session registry journal $CORTEX_HOME/data/session-registry.jsonl retention-candidates.json Two-sweep orphan cleanup candidates $CORTEX_HOME/data/retention-candidates.json conversation-history/ Per-session transcript/history JSONL $CORTEX_HOME/data/conversation-history/ logs/sessions/ Claude capture logs $CORTEX_HOME/logs/sessions/ logs/sessions-pi/ PI transcript bundles $CORTEX_HOME/logs/sessions-pi/ hooks/*.json Your hook declarations and overrides $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/

docs.title: Cross-Machine Operation
docs.text: Cortex can dispatch work to remote machines: run commands, read and write files, search code, and execute long-running training jobs. This is done through cortex-client, a lightweight WebSocket daemon that runs on each remote machine and connects back to the agent-server. This document covers deployment, the network topology, and the security model.

docs.title: Why remote clients
docs.text:
The agent-server process (which runs the agent sessions, the chat platforms, and scheduling) may not be on the machine with the GPUs or the project files. A typical setup:

  • hub — the agent-server host (GPU training, simulation, the Cortex daemon itself)
  • trainer — a dedicated training box on the LAN with its own GPU
  • cluster — a remote training cluster reached through a tunnel
  • desk — a Windows workstation for Unity, VR, and documentation

Each remote machine runs cortex-client, which connects to the agent-server and executes commands on that machine's behalf. The agent sees all machines as a flat pool and selects which device to target per tool call.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
For the full server-side architecture including the six-layer structure, event bus, and WebSocket protocol details, see architecture.md.

┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Agent-Server (hub)             │
│                                 │
│  client-manager.ts              │
│  ┌───────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ WebSocketServer :3002     │  │
│  │ devices Map<name, ws>     │  │
│  │ - hub (local)             │  │
│  │ - trainer (remote, SSH)   │  │
│  │ - cluster (remote, tunnel)│  │
│  │ - desk (remote, Win/SSH)  │  │
│  └───────────────────────────┘  │
│                                 │
│  MCP core-server                │
│  ┌───────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ remote_bash/read/write    │──┼──→ HTTP :3001 → client-manager → WS → device
│  │ remote_edit/glob/grep     │  │
│  └───────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
         ▲ WebSocket              ▲ SSH
         │ (port 3002)            │ (port 22)
┌────────┴────────┐    ┌──────────┴──────────┐
│ cortex-client   │    │ cortex-client        │
│ (hub, local)    │    │ (trainer, remote)    │
│ ws://127.0.0.1  │    │ ws://192.0.2.10      │
└─────────────────┘    └─────────────────────┘

Each cortex-client instance: - Connects to the agent-server's WebSocket server (port 3002), presenting CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN - Registers itself with a device name on connect (hello message) - Sends a heartbeat every 5 seconds - Receives command messages and executes them on the local machine - Returns results over the same WebSocket connection, and opens separate callback sockets for file transfers and port forwards

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Node.js ≥ 20
  • Either a direct WebSocket path from the remote machine to the agent-server, or an SSH path from the agent-server to the remote machine for a managed reverse route
  • Network path from the agent-server to the remote machine on port 22 (SSH), if the server needs to start/restart the client remotely

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The client ships as one self-contained bundle — client.mjs — that lives on each device under the managed layout. A second file, cortex-run-watcher.mjs, is shipped alongside it as an empty compatibility stub: the update package is validated by file name on both ends, so a client installed before cortex-run was removed would otherwise refuse every future update.

~/.cortex/client/
├── current/    # the running version (client.mjs + a compatibility stub)
└── previous/   # the prior version, kept for manual rollback

New local desktop installations explicitly request client preparation during init. The server package carries the two client files built from the same source checkout; init prepares them under <CORTEX_HOME>/client/current/ and creates the local client configuration. The server records ownership in client/local-install.json and recovers interrupted preparation when starting its client. Existing unowned client files or user-edited configuration are not taken over. Ordinary init and remote connections do not request this preparation. The local client uses the server's Node and selected environment, with the loopback WebSocket URL and token supplied at launch. App-only reopen preserves the running daemon; server startup handles client recovery.

Nothing is installed through npm on a remote device; the only requirement is Node.js. The server's bootstrap script installs the remote device files — it checks SSH and Node.js, ships the bundle into ~/.cortex/client/current/, and writes a client config with serverHost, serverPort and deviceName. It does not start the client or create a device-side service. It runs from the agent-server/ directory of a source checkout, targets Linux and macOS devices, and takes --host, --device-name and --server-host (all required) plus --server-port (default 3002):

node --import tsx src/domain/remote/client-bootstrap.ts \
  --host user@machine --device-name trainer --server-host 192.0.2.10

For a device that dials a serverUrl instead, edit cortex-client.json after bootstrap.

Bootstrap is also the rescue path when a device's managed install is broken or wiped. Register the device in the server's machines.json, run bootstrap, then start or restart the agent-server. The server owns client startup and recovery; do not create a systemd, launchd, scheduled-task, tmux, or screen autostart entry on the client device.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Create ~/.cortex/config/cortex-client.json on the remote machine:

{
  "serverHost": "192.0.2.10",
  "serverPort": 3002,
  "deviceName": "trainer"
}
  • serverHost — the IP or hostname of the agent-server machine, reachable from this remote machine
  • serverPort — the WebSocket port (default 3002)
  • serverUrl — (optional) a full WebSocket URL the client dials, taking precedence over serverHost/serverPort. Use it for a Cloudflare Tunnel or any reverse-proxied route, e.g. "wss://cortex.example.com" — this lets a client reach a server that has no public IP (see Cloudflare Tunnel below)
  • clientToken — the server's CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN shared secret; the WS upgrade is rejected with 401 without it. The server injects this automatically when it launches the client, so set it here only for a temporary hand-started diagnostic process
  • deviceName — a unique name for this machine, matching the key in the server's machines.json. Defaults to the machine's hostname

The environment variables CORTEX_SERVER_URL and CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN, when set, take precedence over serverUrl and clientToken. The client honors CORTEX_HOME for its config, install and log directories, and writes its log to ~/.cortex/logs/client-YYYYMMDD.log, kept for 14 days.

For diagnostics, cortex-client can be run in the foreground with the token in its environment. Production clients are started and supervised by the agent-server; a second device-side supervisor creates competing lifecycle owners and must not be configured.

docs.title: Registering machines on the server
docs.text:
Machines are registered in ~/.cortex/config/machines.json on the agent-server host:

{
  "hub": {
    "cortexPath": "/home/user/Cortex",
    "gpuCount": 2
  },
  "trainer": {
    "cortexPath": "/home/user/Cortex",
    "gpuCount": 1,
    "ssh": "user@192.0.2.10"
  },
  "desk": {
    "cortexPath": "D:\\Projects\\Cortex",
    "gpuCount": 0,
    "ssh": "user@desk.example.com",
    "win": true
  },
  "cluster": {
    "cortexPath": "/home/user",
    "gpuCount": 4,
    "ssh": "user@cluster.example.com"
  }
}

Each entry: - cortexPath (required) — the working directory path on that machine - gpuCount (required) — number of GPUs (0 for non-GPU machines). Each client probes its own machine with nvidia-smi and reports the count when it connects; the server writes a differing value straight back into this file, so a stale number corrects itself on the next connection. A machine where nvidia-smi cannot run reports nothing and keeps the value you set here. - ssh (optional) — user@host for SSH connections. If omitted, the machine is assumed to be local and no SSH is needed - win (optional) — set to true for Windows targets (changes the SSH command syntax) - clientCommand (optional) — the command the server runs (over SSH) to launch the client on this machine. Defaults to node "$HOME/.cortex/client/current/client.mjs" (Linux) or node "%USERPROFILE%\.cortex\client\current\client.mjs" (Windows). Override it when node isn't on the machine's non-login SSH PATH — most commonly an nvm install, where node lives under ~/.nvm/...; set an absolute node path, e.g. "/home/u/.nvm/versions/node/v20.19.5/bin/node /home/u/.cortex/client/current/client.mjs". The server wraps this command with its token injection and the nohup/echo $! (Linux) or cmd.exe-wrapped WMI (Windows) launch machinery.

clientConnection selects the route. Its default, direct, uses the URL from cortex-client.json. Setting it to ssh-reverse makes the server maintain an SSH reverse tunnel and inject a loopback WebSocket URL when it launches the client. clientReversePort optionally selects the loopback port on the remote machine; it is valid only with ssh-reverse, defaults to the server's client port, and must be between 1024 and 65535. An SSH reverse route requires ssh.

An invalid machines.json stops the server at startup. When an edit made while the server runs fails validation, the server keeps the previous registry and sends an admin notice. The file is watched via fs.watch(). General registry readers see updates within a few hundred milliseconds. Managed client route fields are snapshotted when client startup begins, so changes to clientConnection, clientReversePort, or the associated ssh target require a server restart. Deleting an entry takes effect on the same reload: the server stops that machine's SSH reverse tunnel and cancels its pending client restart. cortex client remove --device <name> deletes the entry and also stops and uninstalls the client on the machine (see the CLI reference).

docs.title: Network topology
docs.text: The connection from the remote client to the server requires a TCP path to port 3002. Several options exist depending on the network layout.

docs.title: Same LAN
docs.text:
The simplest case. Use the server's LAN IP as serverHost:

{ "serverHost": "192.168.1.100", "serverPort": 3002, "deviceName": "trainer" }

If the connection fails, check the server's firewall:

sudo ufw allow 3002

docs.title: Tailscale (recommended for cross-network)
docs.text:
Tailscale assigns each machine a stable CGNAT IP (100.x.y.z) regardless of physical network. The client connects to the server's Tailscale IP:

{ "serverHost": "100.64.12.34", "serverPort": 3002, "deviceName": "cluster" }

To find the server's Tailscale IP:

tailscale ip -4

Tailscale works through NAT and firewalls without port forwarding. This is the recommended option for machines on different networks.

docs.title: Cloudflare Tunnel
docs.text:
When both the server and the client are behind NAT with no public IP, run cloudflared on the server to expose its WebSocket port through a tunnel, and point the client at the tunnel hostname with serverUrl. The server's cloudflared ingress maps a hostname to the local WS port:

ingress:
  - hostname: cortex.example.com
    service: http://localhost:3002
  - service: http_status:404

The client then dials the tunnel over wss/443:

{ "serverUrl": "wss://cortex.example.com", "deviceName": "desk", "clientToken": "<token>" }

Both sides connect outbound to Cloudflare's edge, so neither needs a public IP or port forwarding, and WebSocket upgrades pass through the tunnel transparently.

docs.title: Managed SSH reverse route
docs.text:
When the server can SSH into the remote machine, Cortex can carry the client WebSocket back through a persistent reverse forward. Configure the machine on the server as follows:

{
  "worker": {
    "cortexPath": "/srv/workspace",
    "gpuCount": 1,
    "ssh": "user@worker",
    "clientConnection": "ssh-reverse",
    "clientReversePort": 13002
  }
}

The server supervises an OpenSSH master connection that carries -R 127.0.0.1:13002:127.0.0.1:3002 to user@worker, with ExitOnForwardFailure=yes and a 15-second keepalive. Before each start it frees a stale listener left on the remote port by an earlier tunnel, then waits for the SSH control socket and launches the client with CORTEX_SERVER_URL=ws://127.0.0.1:13002. The remote listener binds only to loopback. Tunnel failure has its own retry loop, backing off from 1 to 30 seconds, while the client keeps its normal WebSocket reconnect behavior. The token remains required inside the SSH tunnel. Control sockets live under $CORTEX_HOME/data/client-ssh-tunnels/, and the route each client was started on is recorded in $CORTEX_HOME/data/client-routes.json, so a client left running on a route that no longer matches the configuration is stopped and relaunched.

Use a different clientReversePort if the default port is already occupied on the remote machine. SSH aliases and ProxyCommand entries in ~/.ssh/config work because the configured ssh value is passed as one OpenSSH host argument.

docs.title: Externally managed reverse tunnel
docs.text:
A separately supervised SSH tunnel can provide the same network path:

ssh -N -R 127.0.0.1:3002:127.0.0.1:3002 user@server

In that arrangement, configure the client with "serverUrl": "ws://127.0.0.1:3002" and leave clientConnection as direct, because Cortex does not own the tunnel process.

docs.title: Connection troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause Fix Client won't connect Port 3002 blocked Check firewall: sudo ufw allow 3002 Client connects then disconnects NAT timeout Use Tailscale or enable TCP keepalive SSH works but WebSocket doesn't SSH only opens port 22 Open port 3002 or use Tailscale/reverse tunnel Tailscale installed but can't connect ACLs blocking Check tailscale status and ACL rules "Device already connected" (code 4002) Stale connection or duplicate Kill the old client process on the remote machine "Unknown device" (code 4005) deviceName not in machines.json Add the machine, or fix deviceName HTTP 401 on connect Missing or wrong CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN Let the server launch the client, or copy the token from the server's config/.env

The client's own log, ~/.cortex/logs/client-YYYYMMDD.log on the device, records each connection attempt and close code.

docs.title: WebSocket protocol
docs.text: The protocol between agent-server and cortex-client is a JSON message stream over WebSocket. Every HTTP upgrade must carry the shared CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN in the x-cortex-token header; missing or mismatched tokens are rejected with HTTP 401. TLS depends on the selected route: a wss:// endpoint provides TLS, while direct loopback and SSH-reverse routes use ws:// inside their protected transport.

docs.title: Client → Server
docs.text:
Hello (sent immediately on connect). bundleHash identifies the client's running bundle (sha256 over the bundle files in order); the server compares it against the desired bundle to decide whether to push an update. gpuCount is the client's own nvidia-smi count, or null when it cannot probe, and pid is the client's process id, which the server records for a client on its own machine: 

{ "type": "hello", "device": "trainer", "platform": "linux", "capabilities": ["file-stream", "rg"], "gpuCount": 1, "bundleHash": "cebdfcd6…", "pid": 41822 }

Heartbeat (every 5 seconds): 

{ "type": "heartbeat", "device": "trainer", "timestamp": 1716154200000 }

Command result (in response to a server command; error replaces data when success is false): 

{ "type": "result", "commandId": "cmd-abc123", "success": true, "data": { "stdout": "..." } }

Update result (in response to a server update push): 

{ "type": "update-result", "device": "trainer", "hash": "cebdfcd6…", "ok": true }

docs.title: Server → Client
docs.text:
Command: 

{ "type": "command", "commandId": "cmd-abc123", "action": "bash", "params": { "command": "nvidia-smi", "timeout": 120000 } }

Supported actions: bash, read, write, edit, glob, grep, file.stat. A bash time limit travels in params.timeout in milliseconds. The server keeps its own timer for every command — the call's own limit when it sets one, otherwise 120 seconds for bash and 30 seconds for file actions — and fails the call if no result arrives in time.

Open stream (a port forward: the client dials back and pipes a raw TCP connection to a loopback port on the device; see Port forwarding): 

{ "type": "open-stream", "streamId": "4be1…", "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 6006 }

Open file stream (sent when the server wants a whole file off the device, e.g. send_file device="trainer"). Like open-stream, it is answered on a new outbound socket rather than on this one, so a large transfer neither blocks commands nor has to be base64'd through the control channel: 

{ "type": "open-file-stream", "streamId": "9f3c…", "path": "/home/x/report.csv" }

Update (pushed when a device's hello reports a diverged bundle; files carry the complete artifact as base64): 

{ "type": "update", "updateId": "a1b2c3", "version": "2026.7.30-dev", "hash": "cebdfcd6…", "files": [ { "name": "client.mjs", "data": "…" }, { "name": "cortex-run-watcher.mjs", "data": "…" } ] }

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 4001 Missing device name in hello 4002 Device already connected 4003 Heartbeat timeout (15 seconds) 4004 Unknown stream: a callback socket named a stream the server is not expecting 4005 Unknown device: hello name is not registered in machines.json 1001 Server shutting down

docs.title: Server-side client lifecycle
docs.text:
Two modules in agent-server's domain/remote/ share the remote client lifecycle: client-manager.ts holds the device connections (heartbeats and command routing), and client-lifecycle.ts launches, tracks and restarts the clients:

  1. At startup — startAllRemoteClients() iterates machines.json and spawns or SSH-launches the client on each machine. For local machines (no ssh field), it spawns node ~/.cortex/client/current/client.mjs directly. For remote machines, it runs the launch command over SSH with nohup/echo $! (Linux) or WMI (Windows). An ssh-reverse machine first gets a supervised reverse tunnel; startup and automatic restart share the same route-aware launcher and remote PID tracking. If the launch returns a PID but the client has not yet sent hello, the server keeps the per-device recovery timer armed until that connection arrives.

  2. Heartbeat monitoring — every 5 seconds, the server checks that each connected device has sent a heartbeat within the last 15 seconds. Missed heartbeats trigger a disconnect and automatic restart attempt.

  3. Automatic restart — after initial launch, disconnect, or heartbeat timeout, an offline device gets another start attempt after a 60-second delay. The server retries until the client connects. A per-device timer prevents duplicate restart attempts.

  4. PID tracking — the server records each launched client's PID, local or remote, in ~/.cortex/data/client-pids.json so it can check whether the process is still alive before attempting a restart.

  5. Command routing — when the agent calls remote_bash({ device: "trainer", ... }), the MCP server sends an HTTP request to client-manager, which looks up the WebSocket connection for trainer in its devices map and sends the command. Only online devices receive commands — if the target device is offline, the tool call returns an error.

docs.title: Client updates
docs.text:
Clients update themselves; the server publishes the desired bundle. For an App-enrolled local client, that bundle comes from the installed server package, with its ordered file hash verified; a missing or invalid payload does not fall back to npm. For other clients, a server running from a source checkout (CORTEX_REPO or CORTEX_CLIENT_REPO set) builds the client repo with esbuild, and an installed server fetches the latest published @cortex-agent/client from npm, cached per version under $CORTEX_HOME/data/client-bundles/. Every device hello carries the client's own bundle hash; when it differs from the desired hash, the server pushes an update message with the complete artifact over the existing WebSocket. Successful and failed installs are announced as chat notices. Setting clientHotReloadEnabled to false in settings.json turns update pushes off, and an existing local client version is then preserved rather than replaced during preparation.

The client writes the files into ~/.cortex/client/next/, verifies the hash, rotates current/ to previous/ and next/ to current/, reports update-result, closes its socket, spawns its successor from current/ and exits. The successor reconnects with the new hash, which the server logs as convergence. Any failure (bad hash, unwritable disk) leaves the running version untouched — the device stays online on its old bundle and the server is told why. A failed install is not retried on the same device for 10 minutes, and a push that is in flight or has just been installed is not repeated for 2 minutes.

Because the trigger is the hello itself, devices converge whenever they connect: after a server restart with a new build, after a device comes back from days offline, or right after a bootstrap. There is no scheduled update job. If a new bundle crashes on startup, the SSH supervision keeps relaunching current/. For manual recovery, move the failing version aside, then restore previous/ on the device, or run a fresh bootstrap. These are real directories, not symlinks: current/ must be absent before moving previous/ into its place. The commands below keep the failing version in broken/ and require that name to be unused; choose another unused name if needed. Use your client install root if it differs from ~/.cortex/client.

Linux/macOS (Bash):

cd ~/.cortex/client &&
  test -d previous && test ! -e broken &&
  mv current broken && mv previous current

Windows (PowerShell):

& {
  Set-Location "$HOME/.cortex/client" -ErrorAction Stop
  if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath previous -PathType Container)) { throw 'previous/ is missing' }
  if (Test-Path -LiteralPath broken) { throw 'Choose an unused backup name for broken/' }
  Move-Item -LiteralPath current -Destination broken -ErrorAction Stop
  Move-Item -LiteralPath previous -Destination current -ErrorAction Stop
}

docs.title: Client-side reconnect behavior
docs.text:
The cortex-client process handles reconnection automatically:

  • On disconnect, it waits 1 second before the first reconnect attempt
  • Uses exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, capping at 30 seconds
  • If the server rejects with code 4002 ("Device already connected"), the client exits. This prevents two clients from fighting over the same device name
  • If the server rejects with code 4005 ("Unknown device"), the client exits. Its deviceName must match an entry in machines.json, including for a local client whose entry has no ssh field
  • For all other disconnects (network errors, server restart, heartbeat timeout), the client keeps retrying indefinitely

docs.title: Remote command execution
docs.text: Each command from the server includes an action and params. The client dispatches to the appropriate handler:

docs.title: bash
docs.text: Executes in a login shell: /bin/bash -l -c "<command>". On Windows, commands run through Git Bash, found at CORTEX_GIT_BASH_PATH when that is set, then in the standard Program Files locations, then on PATH. The timeout parameter uses integer seconds from 1 to 600 and defaults to 120. A foreground timeout returns exit code 124 and kills the command's process group on POSIX or its process tree on Windows. Output is cut to its head and tail beyond 200 KB of stdout or 50 KB of stderr. run_in_background: true returns the detached shell PID immediately and ignores timeout. Cortex does not supervise long-running jobs: start one yourself and have it report back through a waitpoint. These remote execution tools are exposed to agents via the cortex-core MCP server — see mcp.md.

docs.title: read
docs.text: Reads a file from disk. Paths must be absolute, and files over 10 MB are refused. Text is returned with line numbers, 2,000 lines by default, and a range over about 25,000 words is refused with a suggested limit. Image files (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP) and PDFs come back whole as base64; the server's remote_read tool then downscales large images when sharp is available.

docs.title: file.stat
docs.text: Metadata probe — size, base name, mtime — used before a file transfer so a bad path or an oversized file fails with a real error message instead of an aborted stream. Paths must be absolute.

docs.title: Sending a device's file to the chat
docs.text:
send_file (and slack_send_file / feishu_send_file) take an optional device. With it, the path is read on that device and the bytes are streamed back over the reverse channel, then delivered as an ordinary attachment:

send_file({ device: "trainer", file_path: "/home/x/runs/loss.png", caption: "latest curve" })
send_file({ device: "trainer", files: [{ file_path: "/home/x/runs/loss.png" }, { file_path: "/home/x/runs/eval.csv" }] })

The server refuses before transferring anything if the device is offline, the path is not a readable file, or it exceeds the 200 MB cap, and it rejects a transfer that ends short rather than delivering a truncated file. Devices running a client older than this feature report no file-stream capability and are refused with a message saying so; they gain it on their next client update.

docs.title: write and edit
docs.text: write creates or overwrites a file, creating parent directories if needed. edit finds and replaces a string in an existing file. Successful mutations return a compact confirmation; session activity records the target path and device without copying file contents.

docs.title: glob and grep
docs.text: glob finds files by pattern (e.g., **/*.ts), limited to 500 results and excluding VCS directories, node_modules, __pycache__, .tox and .mypy_cache. grep uses rg (ripgrep) when available, with head_limit (default 250) and offset for pagination. When rg is not installed it falls back to grep -rn, which ignores the pagination, glob, type and context options.

docs.title: Remote AGENTS.md files
docs.text: On read, write and edit, the client also walks up from the target file and returns the AGENTS.md and AGENTS.local.md files it finds (up to 20 levels, each up to 200 KB), plus the one at the device's ~/.cortex/AGENTS.md. The remote_read, remote_write and remote_edit tools add each of them to their result once per session, so instructions that live next to a project on a device reach the agent the same way local ones do.

docs.title: Port forwarding
docs.text:
The server can map a loopback port on a device to a loopback port on its own machine (at most 32 at a time): each connection to the server-side port makes the server send open-stream, and the client dials back and pipes the bytes to 127.0.0.1:<port> on the device. Two features use it:

  • The agent browser on a device. cortex-browser --device <name> starts Chrome there through the client and reaches its debugging port through a forward. Sessions using that device share its one Chrome, each in its own tab, and Chrome closes 10 minutes after its last tab (see Agent Browser).
  • The docked browser's ports panel lists ports listening on the server or a connected device and previews them in the desktop app, with a remote port forwarded first.

docs.title: Long-running jobs
docs.text: Cortex does not launch, supervise or adopt processes on a device. Start the job the way you normally would (nohup, setsid, tmux, a scheduler) and arm a waitpoint so the session is woken when it finishes. On a device the job drops a small JSON file in ~/.cortex/tmp/signals/. On each sweep the server lists, reads and removes those files with ordinary bash commands over the connection this client already holds open — only on devices that have an armed waitpoint — so nothing extra has to be installed there.

docs.title: Checking device status
docs.text:
The agent sees the registered devices in the description of its remote tools, and a call to an offline device fails with the list of devices that are online. A quick probe:

remote_bash({ device: "trainer", command: "hostname" })

In the Web UI and desktop app, the machines button in the top bar shows how many machines are online and opens a sheet with each machine's GPUs, processes, load, memory, disk and uptime, probed on demand with one shell command over the client. In Slack or Feishu, !devices (alias !clients) lists the registered and connected machines with their platform, connection age and last heartbeat.

From the server's CLI:

# Check machine registry
cat ~/.cortex/config/machines.json

# Check which clients are connected (via the server logs)
tail -f ~/.cortex/logs/daemon.log | grep client-manager

docs.title: Security boundary
docs.text:
The remote client system operates with these security constraints:

  • The client runs as the same user who started it — no privilege escalation
  • Every client WebSocket upgrade requires CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN. Network controls such as a firewall, Tailscale ACL, localhost binding, or an SSH reverse route remain defense in depth
  • The server's SSH access to remote machines is governed by the SSH key of the user running agent-server. The agent cannot escalate beyond what that user can do
  • MCP tools that target remote devices are subject to the same safety boundary rules documented in safety-and-approvals.md
  • The cortex-client npm package installs no postinstall scripts, uses no native addons beyond what Node.js ships, and has no external dependencies beyond ws
  • Port forwards bind to loopback on the server and reach only loopback ports on the device

docs.title: Multi-client routing
docs.text:
There is no automatic device selection. The agent explicitly specifies which device to target in each tool call via the device parameter. It learns the available devices from the catalog in the remote tools' description, built from machines.json with Windows machines marked.

For GPU-aware workloads (training), the agent can read each machine's gpuCount from the registry and check GPU utilization on the device before choosing where to run.

docs.title: The client-manage skill
docs.text:
Cortex includes a client-manage skill (in the cortex-system plugin) that provides step-by-step operational guidance for: - Bootstrapping a new device (register, install, configure, verify, restart) - Checking online status and connectivity - Viewing client logs - Updating client configuration - Troubleshooting common symptoms with root causes and fixes

The skill is available to the agent automatically and serves as the operational reference for cross-machine management.

docs.title: Desktop and Android Apps
docs.text:
Cortex provides a Tauri v2 native shell for Linux, macOS, Windows, and Android. The desktop shell presents the three-pane workbench; Android presents a phone-specific interface built around the session list and a swipe-in Projects panel. Both connect directly to a Cortex server over the Web UI HTTP transport and use the same projects, sessions, approvals, files, and memory as the browser workbench.

The native apps require a reachable Web UI endpoint and the server's CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN. Browser access uses a separate Cloudflare Access path described in Browser Access.

The desktop app can either install a Cortex server on the computer it runs on or connect to one that already exists. The first screen asks which, and the local path needs no terminal: it installs the package, writes the configuration, starts the daemon, and connects. Android is remote-only, since it has no place to run a Node process.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
For server releases that include native packages, download the platform asset from the GitHub Releases page. The release policy assigns the native UI exactly the same CalVer as the corresponding server release: YYYY.M.D[-N]. The version embedded in the app and shown in the asset name must match the server-v<version> tag.

Platform Native release package Installation Linux x86_64 AppImage, DEB, or RPM Run the AppImage directly after chmod +x, or install the distribution package. Windows x86_64 NSIS setup.exe Run the installer and launch Cortex from the Start menu. macOS Apple Silicon macOS-aarch64 DMG Open the DMG, then drag Cortex into Applications. macOS Intel macOS-x86_64 DMG Open the DMG, then drag Cortex into Applications. Android arm64 Signed APK Open the APK and allow installation from the selected file source when Android asks.

Linux AppImage builds require WebKitGTK and GTK at runtime. Ubuntu and Debian users can install the common runtime libraries with:

sudo apt-get install libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 libgtk-3-0

Windows 10 and 11 normally include WebView2. If Cortex reports that WebView2 is missing, install the Microsoft Evergreen WebView2 runtime before launching the app. Release installers without an Authenticode certificate may also trigger a Microsoft Defender SmartScreen warning; review the publisher and release checksum before choosing to run one.

A macOS package without a Developer ID certificate is ad-hoc signed but not notarized. Gatekeeper may prevent the first normal double-click launch. Open Cortex once with Finder's Open action or approve it under System Settings → Privacy & Security. Ad-hoc signing verifies the bundle structure but does not establish a trusted publisher identity.

The Android APK is intended for arm64 devices and is distributed outside the Play Store. Android therefore asks for permission to install from the browser or file manager used to open it.

docs.title: Installing a server from the app
docs.text:
Choose Install Cortex on the first screen and wait for installation to finish. Setup needs no terminal, Homebrew, Command Line Tools, or administrator access. Progress stays brief; Activity log is a folded troubleshooting entry. If installation fails, follow the message and choose Try again. Cancel during installation stops the active installation step, not an existing server; it does not undo files already installed.

Each desktop installer carries the runtime the local server needs: the official Node.js 24 build for its platform and, on Windows, Git for Windows (PortableGit) with Git Bash. Setup unpacks them into versioned directories under ~/.cortex/runtime, then uses that npm to install the Cortex server package into the private prefix ~/.cortex/runtime/prefix. Only the server package, and Claude Code when you choose to install it, come from the npm registry; npm follows your .npmrc registry, proxy, and credential settings. Setup does not change global npm settings, and it neither uses nor modifies a Node.js, npm, Git, or cortex already installed on the computer. The server adds the cortex command to new terminal windows itself, described in Using cortex in a terminal.

The local server always runs on the bundled runtime. When a runtime directory is missing or damaged, the app unpacks it again during setup, or at launch before it starts the daemon. A saved server installation that no longer runs, or is older than the app requires, is reinstalled into the private prefix. On Windows, Cortex runs shell commands with the bundled Git Bash. On macOS and Linux, Git is optional and setup does not install it; Git-based history and Git-sourced extensions require it.

The bundled Node.js determines where local installation works: macOS 13.5 or later, Linux x86_64 with glibc 2.28 or later, and Windows 10 or 11 on x86_64. On other systems the app can still connect to an existing server.

Installation continues automatically through initialization, server startup, and connection. A new installation uses this computer's hostname, port 3004, no login service, and the cortex terminal command. There is no machine-settings page or Start Cortex confirmation on this path. Progress remains one installation row, with technical details in Activity log. A new installation opens provider setup at /setup/providers for login and a default model before entering the workbench. PI is bundled with Cortex; setup does not ask you to choose backends.

If initialization, startup, or connection fails, Try again reuses the original setup choices. Edit settings opens the repair form; starting from this form can restart the local server to apply an explicitly selected port. Automatic setup preserves a responding server. Installation failures offer retry, not machine settings.

Local setup belongs to the native app and the setup page bundled with it; updating the Web frontend or replacing web/dist does not change it.

For local development, launch the native app with CORTEX_SETUP_SERVER_PACKAGE set to an absolute path to a locally packed .tgz. The installer uses that package through npm and checks its reported version against the app's minimum. This does not publish the package; use an isolated home, npm prefix, credential store, and network for fresh-install testing.

The installation step asks nothing about Slack or Feishu: the app is the interface, and a server with no messaging platform runs on its built-in gateway. Provider login and the default model are configured after the server connects.

A machine that already has a Cortex configuration keeps its machine identity and service settings. Automatic setup enables the local connection endpoint without overriding its configured port or running initialization again. It checks the saved installation even when it is already usable, so later launches use the same runtime. Existing installations and connections open the workbench unless a new local installation still has unfinished provider setup.

The app starts the local daemon at launch whenever it is not already answering. Automatic setup does not create or change a login service. If initialization needs repair, the new-install settings form offers Start at login: the native app writes and registers a systemd user unit on Linux or a launchd agent on macOS, so scheduled tasks can fire while the app is closed. Registration takes effect at the next login and does not replace the daemon already running. Existing service settings are preserved. Windows has no service registration, so the app's launch-time start is the only autostart there.

To enable the endpoint on an existing install without the wizard, run one command on the server:

cortex ui enable

This generates the client token if needed, sets CORTEX_UI_HTTP and CORTEX_UI_PORT, and adds the app's origins to uiCorsOrigins. Restart the daemon afterwards when it reports that the configuration changed. Server configuration describes the same settings by hand.

docs.title: Using cortex in a terminal
docs.text:
A server running from the app's runtime checks for its terminal launchers each time it starts. If they are missing, it runs cortex path install itself. New installations get the command this way, and so do existing ones after a server update. The command writes launchers for cortex, cortex-signal, cortex-hook and cortex-evidence-export into ~/.cortex/runtime/bin. Each launcher starts the bundled Node.js with the installed server, so a terminal needs no Node.js of its own. That directory is on PATH in every terminal opened afterwards:

  • Linux and macOS: a block marked # >>> cortex >>> sits at the end of ~/.profile, and of ~/.bash_profile and ~/.zshenv where those shells are in use. The same block sits at the top of ~/.bashrc, so ssh host cortex … works as well. fish is not configured; add the directory with fish_add_path ~/.cortex/runtime/bin.
  • Windows: the directory is part of the user Path, which Command Prompt, PowerShell and Git Bash all read.

When the server starts on a different bundled Node.js, for example after an app update, it rewrites the launchers to match. cortex path status shows the launchers and where they are registered. cortex path remove deletes them and takes the directory back off PATH. The removal is recorded in ~/.cortex/runtime/terminal-cli.json, and the server does not add the command again until cortex path install runs. The Use cortex in the terminal switch on the repair form runs one command or the other.

Agent sessions do not depend on any of this. The server puts its own node, cortex and cortex-signal on the PATH of every session it starts, so skills and waitpoint commands work even with the terminal command turned off. If adding the command fails, the server logs the error and tries again at its next start. When the repair form's switch is on, setup also shows a warning.

docs.title: Provider setup
docs.text:
The provider setup page, Connect a provider, runs top to bottom: a Claude Code card, the Model providers card, a default-model choice, and the optional leaderboard card. Model providers lists the providers whose credentials are already detected under Connected, and the rest under Add a provider: a search box above a two-column grid, with a Popular group first and More providers below it. Choose a provider and a supported OAuth or API-key method to open the same login modal used by Settings → Accounts. PI needs no separate installation. OAuth may open your browser and require authorization or MFA; login is not guaranteed to stay inside the app.

Claude Code is optional and separate from the Anthropic provider in PI. In local desktop setup, Install and sign in authorizes installing Claude Code on this computer, then opens its login flow. This is the only onboarding step that offers its installation. An existing Claude Code installation is reused.

Credential detection is not a live inference test: setup sends no paid inference request and does not prove that a model call will succeed. Missing, expired, or unknown credentials need attention even when the runtime is installed.

After login, the page refreshes credentials and synchronizes gateway and model configuration. Rescanning also picks up credentials configured elsewhere. Sync supplies a recommended default when none is configured and adds a recommended favorite for each connected backend/provider group that has none. Existing defaults and favorites are preserved. First-run setup asks you to choose a default model from favorites with a matching configured account before entering the workbench; login alone is not enough.

The optional Public usage leaderboard card puts your token usage on the public aistatus.cc leaderboard, which shows your name, organization, and token counts. It is off unless you have already joined. Switch it on, enter a name and an email (the organization is optional), and choose Save; the email only identifies you and is never displayed. The card does not affect Enter workbench or Set up later, and the same card stays available under Settings → Usage.

Choose Enter workbench when the configuration is ready, or Set up later to skip. The skip warning explains that the Agent may be unavailable until you finish Settings → Accounts and Settings → Models.

After a new local installation connects, quitting on this page and reopening the app resumes provider setup—even if you have not signed in. Login alone does not finish setup. Enter workbench and deliberate Set up later save your choice before leaving, so later launches open the workbench. If saving fails, stay on this page and try again. Older unmarked installations and remote connections keep their usual startup behavior.

docs.title: Server configuration
docs.text:
The native shell talks to the server's opt-in Web UI endpoint. The endpoint itself is startup topology, so it stays in $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env on the server:

CORTEX_UI_HTTP=1
CORTEX_UI_PORT=3004

The allowed CORS origins are a runtime setting. Add or confirm the uiCorsOrigins key in $CORTEX_HOME/config/settings.json (see configuration.md):

{
  "uiCorsOrigins": [
    "cortexui://localhost",
    "http://cortexui.localhost",
    "tauri://localhost",
    "http://tauri.localhost"
  ]
}

The legacy comma-separated CORTEX_UI_CORS_ORIGINS variable in .env is still read as a deprecated fallback.
