cortex init generates CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN in .env. The native app uses that exact value; CORTEX_TOKEN is not the server-side client-token setting. Retrieve the configured token with:

grep CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN "${CORTEX_HOME:-$HOME/.cortex}/config/.env"

Restart the daemon after changing the endpoint in .env. A change to uiCorsOrigins needs no restart — it is resolved per request. A native app connects to an HTTP or HTTPS URL that reaches this endpoint. When the endpoint is exposed through a tunnel, use a hostname that accepts the Cortex token directly rather than one that requires an interactive browser SSO page.

Current builds serve the shell through the cortexui custom protocol, which appears as cortexui://localhost or http://cortexui.localhost depending on the WebView platform. The two tauri origins keep older native builds connectable. The server returns CORS headers only for origins explicitly listed in uiCorsOrigins.

docs.title: First connection
docs.text:
Choose Connect an existing server on the first screen, then enter the server URL, including https:// or http://, together with CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN. The connection test distinguishes an unreachable endpoint from an unauthorized token. A successful connection opens the workbench and stores the credentials for later launches. A server installed by the wizard skips this screen — it connects with credentials it generated itself.

Linux, macOS, and Windows store the connection JSON in the operating-system keychain: Secret Service, Keychain, or Windows Credential Manager. Android stores it in the app's private data directory because the desktop keychain library has no Android backend. Disconnecting clears the platform store and returns to the connection screen.

docs.title: Desktop workbench
docs.text:
The desktop app uses the same workbench as the browser. The left rail lists projects and project-scoped sessions and links to the selected project's Overview. The center pane contains chat, streamed agent output, tool activity, attachments, question cards, and plan approvals. A slim rail along the chat's left edge marks every prompt in the session. The marks nearest the pointer stretch as it travels down the rail, the one under it previews what was asked, and clicking it scrolls the transcript back to that point. Marks stay lit for every turn the view currently shows, whether it holds the whole turn or only its head or tail.

Each turn of the agent reads as its work, its answer and what it produced. The work — tool calls, thinking, short working notes, subagents — folds into one line above the answer, such as Worked for 3m 20s · 49 tool calls · 1 subagent; click it to open the work in order. While the turn runs, that line reads Working and stays open, and the text being written already sits where the answer will stay; once a tool call follows it, it was a working note and joins the work. Everything that needs the reader stays in view: plan and question cards (folded to one line once settled), notices, files and decisions the agent sent, boards it opened, workers it started, waitpoints it armed, and long notes the agent clearly wrote for the reader (a heading, a table, or a few paragraphs). While the turn runs, those that arrive once the work has begun sit in the open work where they happened, so the work reads in order and only the text being written sits below it; when the turn ends and its work folds, they stand below the folded line. A turn starts at your message, at a lead's message to its worker, and at a system turn that woke the agent — a waitpoint's signal, a worker's report or question, or a background agent's result that arrived after the turn ended; a resume after a rate limit, or a background result folded into a turn still running, continues the same work. Settings → Appearance → Work in chat can keep every turn's work open. When the turn has ended but the session is not done, the end of the chat says so: background work still running (the agent continues when it finishes), or the waitpoint it is waiting on; the waitpoint's own line in the turn reads waiting until its signal arrives as a turn of its own.

Model-provided thinking appears separately from the answer, collapsed by default. A standalone Thinking row previews its first line; click it to read the full text. Thinking beside tool calls stays inside their collapsed group, which counts it as Thinking, and expands in its original position. While it streams, Thinking… shows the latest line until the saved row replaces it. Desktop, browser, and mobile chat share this display. Claude supplies a thinking summary; PI supplies the text its provider exposes. Empty, redacted, and subagent thinking is omitted. Slack, Feishu, and the terminal do not display thinking. The server setting showThinking controls capture; saved thinking survives a refresh, and unavailable past thinking is not reconstructed.

The chat header carries the session's title and, for a lead, its team capsule, and for a session bound to a board, the board capsule (Team Mode, Boards). The Notes button (⌘⇧N) opens the private notes as a card beneath the header, leaving the composer in view. Directly above the composer, one row of capsules shows what the session is doing: the agent's task list, as a progress ring with the current item, and anything it waits on outside Cortex. The task capsule stays while the list has open items and leaves once a finished list's turn ends. Each capsule opens its detail as a popover, so the composer never moves. On a phone the same row also carries the lead's team and the bound board; each capsule names itself in words (Tasks 3/7, 2 workers, Board) and opens a sheet. The phone's chat header says what the session is doing in plain words, such as Running · 1m 12s · 2 workers or Plan waiting for your approval, and carries context usage beside the ⋯ menu as a small gauge that fills like a pie. Clicking the status line under the composer opens Session stats: runs, agent turns, active time, total cost, and the part of the cost spent by subagents.

The composer's engine picker lists favorite models with their remembered thinking levels, grouped by backend/provider. Each row in the full model list has a star to add or remove a favorite, and thinking includes an option to use the backend default. Settings → Models manages the default model and favorites; the schedule editor selects a model and thinking level. See Backends for the selection rules.

Typing / in the composer opens the slash palette: /new, /cancel, /compact, /model, /settings, and /usage, followed by the skills the session can load. The arrow keys move through it, and Enter or Tab picks an entry. The composer's + menu attaches files, lists the same commands, and sets browser control for a new session: the agent gets tools to drive Chrome on the server (this host) or on a connected device, where the window opens on that machine's screen with the logins already in its profile. Browser control is chosen before the session's first message, because the agent's tools are fixed when it starts; the chosen device then shows as a chip in the composer.

The machines button in the top bar shows how many registered machines are online, such as 2/3, beside a server icon whose dot is green when every machine is online, amber when some are offline, and red when none are. Clicking it, or choosing View → Machines, opens the Machines menu, headed by how many are online, with one row per machine: a status dot (green when online, a hollow ring when offline), its name and last heartbeat, and a line with its GPUs, operating system, and how long it has been connected. Expanding a row probes the machine live while the menu stays open. It shows CPU load, RAM, and free disk as thin aligned bars, then one row per GPU with utilization and temperature, with its memory, power draw, and process count beneath; click that line to list the heaviest processes. The machine's uptime closes the row. An offline machine shows Offline — no live telemetry. Manage › opens Settings → Machines. On Android, Machines is a drill-in screen with one card per machine, the same vitals, and a GPU grid.

The right-hand dock (View → Dock pane, ⌘J or Ctrl+J) holds tabs beside the chat: pinned file previews, boards, web pages, and agent browsers. An Agent browser tab shows the page a session's agent is driving, live, and lets you take it over; Agent Browser covers it. A web tab takes a port or a URL. Its Ports list shows the ports listening on the server or on a connected device, and the desktop app forwards a chosen port through its token-authenticated /forward tunnel, so a development server on a remote machine opens as if it ran locally. A browser cannot forward, and opens those ports as plain localhost addresses.

Consecutive tool calls collapse into one row that says what they did — Ran 6 commands · Edited parser.ts · Called send_decision — and opens to one line per call with its command or path. Thinking between the calls belongs to the same row, including a thought still being written right after one. While the row is what the agent is doing right now, it ends with the step under way — Running pnpm test, Reading parser.ts, Thinking — and the line rolls to each new step. Calls whose result returned images — Read on an image file, PI's read, remote_read, or any MCP tool that answers with an image — form rows of their own, labelled Read N images: consecutive image reads share one row, and rows keep the order the calls ran in, so reads interleaved with other tools alternate with them. Expanding it lists each of those calls with its images beneath it, at most 120 px high; clicking an image opens it in the media viewer. A read call's image carries the name of the file it read. The row shows only what the model received: a PI model that takes no image input is never sent a tool's images, so its calls stay in the ordinary row. Mobile chat and subagent blocks show the same rows. The images are kept under $CORTEX_HOME/tmp/tool-images/<session id>/.

The chat header's ⋯ menu offers Star / Unstar, Rename, and Session ID on desktop and mobile. Session ID shows the session's stable ID and the backend's own UUID, each with a copy button; Edit → Copy session ID copies the first directly. In the desktop session list, hovering a row replaces its time with the same actions under ⋯, without opening that conversation; the control is also available by keyboard focus. Each project's session list has a collapsible Stars section; starring moves a session there, and unstarring returns it to its ordinary group. Empty Stars sections are hidden. Names and stars are saved on the server. Rename changes only the display title, not either session ID, and accepts a nonblank title of up to 60 characters.

Execution rows on a project's Overview open a drawer with live logs and cancellation controls. ⌘K on macOS or Ctrl+K on Linux and Windows opens the command palette, which searches commands, pages, sessions, boards, and live agent browsers. The Help menu holds Documentation, Send feedback (which opens the GitHub issue tracker), Daemon status, Check for updates, Developer tools, and About Cortex.

Code blocks in chat show a copy button while the pointer is over them; on touch screens the button stays visible. On Windows, text copied in the app with Ctrl+C, the context menu, or a copy button appears in Clipboard History (Win+V) like a copy from any other application. WebView2 writes these copies from its own browser process, which Windows leaves out of the history, so the app shell writes the same data back under its own window. Content its writer marks as excluded from history stays excluded (desktop/src-tauri/src/clipboard_history.rs).

docs.title: Plugin settings
docs.text:
Settings → Plugins shows every plugin on the connected Cortex server, the built-in ones and your own, and edits them in place. Plugins and skills carry a built-in, local, or modified tag. A plugin's Overview tab shows its portable or legacy format, manifest metadata, location, validation issues, and the environments that use it. The Skills tab opens each skill's SKILL.md for editing and offers New skill, Move or rename, and Delete. Saving a built-in skill keeps your version in its place, and Revert to built-in restores the shipped one; built-in skills cannot be moved or deleted, and a built-in plugin cannot be deleted but can be switched off per environment. The MCP tab edits a portable plugin's root mcp.json servers (Add server, transport, command or URL, environment, and headers); saved secrets stay hidden and are kept unless you Replace them. New plugin, Delete plugin, and Convert to portable manage whole plugins. The desktop shell keeps no separate local catalog because it renders the same server-backed SPA as the browser (web/src/features/settings/panels/PluginsPanel.tsx).

Settings → Environments edits the execution environments in four tabs: Body, Validation, Plugins, and System prompt. The Plugins tab assigns plugins to the environment. Adding a portable plugin with at least one valid inventoried mcp.json server requires confirmation before save, and unsaved assignment edits block navigation and closing the Settings modal. If server data changes during editing, the draft stays visible as stale and must be reset before saving. The System prompt tab replaces the environment's entire system prompt for new sessions; it names the file that holds the prompt, warns when other environments share that file, and offers Restore default. Skills and Plugins describes package formats, runtime behavior, and the trusted-code boundary.

To change servers, open the daemon or connectivity status, choose Disconnect, and enter the new endpoint and token on the connection screen.

docs.title: Desktop and browser notifications
docs.text:
Settings → Notifications → System notifications · this device controls notifications on this device and defaults to on. Browser permission is separate: click Allow notifications to grant it. Browsers require HTTPS or localhost and a supported Notifications API; a denied permission must be changed in the browser's site settings.

While the desktop app or browser page is running and connected, completed replies, sessions that start waiting for your answer or approval, and system notices use operating-system notifications when the window is hidden or unfocused. In the foreground, Cortex keeps its in-app notifications and suppresses those for the conversation being viewed. Team workers raise neither; their lead's reply does (Team Mode). Disabling system notifications, missing permission, or a delivery error leaves the in-app notifications available.

Clicking a session notification restores/focuses the app or browser page and opens that conversation. A system notice without a conversation only focuses the window. Desktop click routing requires the native notification bridge in the installed app; a frontend update alone cannot add it to an older shell. Switching servers invalidates pending desktop notification targets.

Desktop and browser notifications require the app or page to remain running; closing it stops delivery. Browser tabs receive events independently. System notification settings, Do Not Disturb, and Linux notification-server/window-manager support can restrict display, click actions, or focus. Some mobile browsers do not support page-created notifications and keep the in-app fallback. Android has its own background service, described below.

docs.title: Android interface
docs.text:
The Android home screen is the current project's session list, in sections: Needs you (a question or plan waiting on you), In progress (running, holding background work, or waiting on a signal) and Recent, with starred sessions in their own section on top. Each row shows its status as a dot, its title, what it is doing, and when it last ran; New session sits at the bottom right. Swiping right anywhere on the list slides in the Projects panel from the left: the current project's budget, approvals, issues, notes and memory, the other projects to switch to, and the usage and settings buttons. The panel follows your finger and opens or closes depending on how far or how fast you swipe. A mostly vertical swipe scrolls the list. Swiping left, tapping the dimmed list, or pressing Back closes the panel. The Cortex mark in the top-left corner also opens the panel, with an amber count beside it while approvals are waiting for you. Session chat, plan review, approvals, issues, notes, memory files, machines, settings, hooks, and daemon status open as drill-in screens, and Back from a screen opened in the panel returns to the open panel. The Android back action closes overlays first, then returns through the app's navigation stack.

With notification permission granted, Settings → Notifications → Background notifications on this device enables an Android-owned connection that continues listening when the page is in the background. A silent ongoing notification shows the running direct-session count across projects, including background continuations. At zero it shows that background notifications are connected; while reconnecting it reports unavailable state rather than a stale count. Disabling this device-local switch or disconnecting stops the service and clears its notifications (desktop/tauri-plugin-cortex-notifications/android/src/main/java/dev/cortex/notifications/NotificationService.kt; Reconciler.kt).

Pending questions and plan approvals raise separate notifications. Session notifications open the related conversation, including from a cold launch. Approval-center entries open the approvals screen and select the entry. The native owner retains tap targets until the page handles them, and reconciles pending requests on reconnect and periodically. Notifications hide private content on the lock screen. The background connection requires HTTPS and is subject to Android Doze, manufacturer battery restrictions, network availability, and user force-stop; it is not a guarantee of delivery while the app is forcibly stopped. Pending question details currently require a Web-origin session channel (NotificationsPlugin.kt; Protocol.kt).

The background service also announces finished turns. Once a direct session's run reaches a completed state on the server and that session is no longer running, waiting for an answer, or holding a background task, the notification shows the session label (or a short session ID) and a short line inviting you to open it; no transcript text is fetched. Cancelled, failed, and still-waiting runs stay silent, as do team workers' runs, and the session currently on screen raises nothing. The first connection to a server records the runs it finds without announcing them, so turning the feature on never replays old conversations. While the background service owns these notifications the page stops posting its own; with the device switch off, or on an app shell or cached page that predates them, the page's live feed keeps generating them (Completions.kt; Reconciler.kt; web/src/mobile/screens/MNotificationMount.tsx).

Files downloaded by Cortex are handed to Android's DownloadManager, which writes them to the public Downloads collection and shows the system completion notification.

docs.title: Files and downloads
docs.text:
Surface Download behavior Browser Uses the browser's normal download manager. Linux, macOS, Windows Uses the operating system Downloads directory when available, falls back to app-local downloads, and offers Open file and Open folder actions after completion. Android Uses the system DownloadManager and public Downloads collection.

The workbench previews images and videos, pages through PDFs, and displays text files without requiring a separate download. Desktop users can pin a preview beside chat while continuing the conversation.

docs.title: Versions and frontend updates
docs.text: A tagged native release uses the same version as @cortex-agent/server. This shared CalVer identifies the server release and all native packages built from its tagged commit.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Help → Check for updates (or Settings → Check for updates on Android) checks the connected server for a fresh release, then checks the frontend workbench and native app shell. Repeated clicks share the running check. Results distinguish available, current, skipped, and failed checks; disabled checks, development runs, and skipped versions are not reported as current.

Update prompts are ordered: server first, native app next, then the frontend workbench. With serverAutoUpdate on (the default), a newer server release is installed without a prompt once no task is running, and the server then restarts; only a failed install raises the dialog. With it off, checking does not authorize installation or a restart: Update on the server prompt authorizes them, and they wait until no task is running; Later hides the prompt until another manual check, while Skip this version retains the skipped-version policy. Server checks respect serverUpdateDisable and development mode.

After the server reconnects, the app checks only its frontend and native channels again. Each restart or installer keeps its own confirmation and platform permissions: this is an ordered flow, not an atomic installation of all components. Browsers use a page refresh confirmation rather than native installers.

docs.title: Frontend workbench
docs.text: After launch, the shell compares its installed SPA with the content-addressed frontend bundle served by the server. It downloads a newer bundle in the background, verifies its SHA-256 digest, stages it, and prompts when a restart can apply it. This channel updates the Web workbench without replacing the native executable or APK. Installing an Android APK with a different bundled frontend refreshes the local page once; subsequent launches preserve compatible frontend OTA updates. A cached legacy page without the native notification bridge falls back to the bundled page so notification taps remain usable (desktop/src-tauri/src/seed.rs). While no server is connected, the shell serves the frontend bundled with the app instead of the downloaded one, so the connection and setup screens always match the installed app, whichever server's bundle is on the device (desktop/src-tauri/src/frontend.rs).

docs.title: Native app shell
docs.text:
A server release can also carry native packages as GitHub Release assets. The server advertises the newest installable release that is not newer than its own version. The shell selects the asset matching its operating system, architecture, and package kind, downloads it directly from GitHub without forwarding the Cortex token, and verifies the GitHub-provided SHA-256 digest before offering it. The update dialog supports installing now, skipping that version, or postponing the decision.

Platform Native update behavior Linux AppImage Replaces the running AppImage in place, retains one .old backup, relaunches, and exits the old process. Linux DEB or RPM Copies the verified package to Downloads and opens the system package installer. Windows Launches the verified NSIS installer and exits so the installer can replace the app. macOS Copies the verified DMG to Downloads and opens it; installation finishes by dragging Cortex into Applications. Android Opens the system package installer over the verified APK; Android requests install-source permission when required.

Sessions run on the server, so restarting or reinstalling a client does not stop them. Native shell update checks are disabled when CORTEX_FRONTEND_DIR marks a development run, when the installed app does not carry a CalVer release version, or when CORTEX_APP_UPDATE_DISABLE=1 is set.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
Settings → Advanced → Uninstall Cortex opens the uninstaller: a separate window that asks what to remove, removes it, and lists each step's result. On Windows, uninstalling Cortex from Settings → Apps opens the same window before the program files are removed.

The window offers two choices:

  • What to remove appears when the app installed a server on this computer. App and local server, the default, turns off start at login, stops the daemon and the local client it launched, takes the cortex terminal command off PATH, and deletes ~/.cortex/runtime. App only leaves the server running and reachable from a browser or other devices. An app that connects to a remote server shows no such choice and never touches that server.
  • Also delete data is off by default. Together with the server it deletes the whole Cortex home (~/.cortex, or CORTEX_HOME): configuration and tokens, conversations, project context, plugins and logs. It also deletes the app's own data directories, named dev.cortex.desktop, and the connection saved in the system keychain. With App only it deletes just the app's own data and saved connection. The window lists every path before you confirm; deletion cannot be undone.

With the data kept, installing Cortex again picks up where it left off: setup unpacks the runtime, reinstalls the server package, and connects to the existing configuration and sessions.

The app itself is removed the way it was installed. The Windows uninstaller deletes the program files once the window closes. macOS moves Cortex.app to the Trash. An AppImage deletes its file. A DEB or RPM install is removed by its package manager after a system authorization prompt. A copy that no package owns shows its folder for you to delete. When stopping the server or deleting its files fails, the app stays installed and the window offers Try again. A login service the app did not write, such as a cortex.service created by cortex init on the command line, is reported and left in place.

Windows app updates and silent uninstalls (/S, /P, /UPDATE) do not open the window; they only replace or remove the program files.

Removing the app any other way, by dragging Cortex.app to the Trash, running apt remove, or deleting the AppImage, leaves the server and its data in place. To remove the server afterwards, turn off its login service, stop it, and delete the runtime:

# Linux
systemctl --user disable --now cortex.service && rm ~/.config/systemd/user/cortex.service
# macOS
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/cc.cortex.agent-server && rm ~/Library/LaunchAgents/cc.cortex.agent-server.plist
# Both
cortex daemon stop
cortex path remove
rm -rf ~/.cortex/runtime

Deleting the rest of ~/.cortex removes the data as well.

docs.title: Unauthorized
docs.text: Confirm that the app contains the value of CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN, not the webhook token or a legacy variable. Re-enter the token after using Disconnect if the server token changed.

docs.title: Network error
docs.text: Confirm that the daemon is running, CORTEX_UI_HTTP=1 is loaded, the URL reaches the configured port, and the tunnel is active. A successful page load with failed API calls usually indicates a token or CORS problem. Confirm that the current cortexui origins are present in the uiCorsOrigins setting in config/settings.json; retain the tauri origins when older app builds also connect to the server.

docs.title: Local installation cannot finish
docs.text: Choose Try again first: setup unpacks missing runtime files again and reinstalls a server that cannot run. When the server package cannot be downloaded, check the network connection and the registry and proxy settings in .npmrc. If the app reports that it is incomplete, download the installer for your platform again and reinstall it. An unsupported system can connect to a server on another computer instead. Open Activity log only when you need diagnostic details.

docs.title: The server does not answer after the wizard starts it
docs.text:
A cold start loads the whole agent runtime and can outlast the wizard's wait on a slow machine. The streamed log shows what the daemon reported. Check the state from a new terminal:

cortex daemon status
cortex doctor

A terminal opened before setup finished does not see the command yet. When the terminal command is turned off, call the launcher directly, for example ~/.cortex/runtime/bin/cortex doctor. If there are no launchers, run the CLI with the absolute node path recorded in ~/.cortex/runtime/selection.json: "<node path>" ~/.cortex/runtime/prefix/bin/cortex doctor (or daemon status).

On Windows without launchers, use PowerShell with the saved runtime:

$runtime = Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\.cortex\runtime\selection.json" -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
& $runtime.node "$env:USERPROFILE\.cortex\runtime\prefix\node_modules\@cortex-agent\server\dist\entry\cortex-cli.js" daemon status
& $runtime.node "$env:USERPROFILE\.cortex\runtime\prefix\node_modules\@cortex-agent\server\dist\entry\cortex-cli.js" doctor

If you set CORTEX_HOME, substitute that directory for ~/.cortex or $env:USERPROFILE\.cortex in these paths.

The app also starts a local server at launch, so reopening it retries.

docs.title: Credentials do not persist on Linux
docs.text:
A headless Linux environment may not provide a Secret Service daemon. Fresh local setup cannot finish until it can save credentials; ordinary connections fall back to credentials that last only for the current process. Enable the system keyring, or launch the app with an explicit connection to the running server:

CORTEX_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:3004 CORTEX_TOKEN='<client-token>' ./Cortex.AppImage

Use the value of CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN in $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env (default ~/.cortex/config/.env) as <client-token>. CORTEX_TOKEN is the native-shell fallback variable; it does not replace the server setting. This fallback connects to an already-running server and does not start it automatically.

docs.title: App window does not open on Wayland
docs.text:
Tauri supports Wayland, but a system-specific WebKitGTK issue may require X11 compatibility:

GDK_BACKEND=x11 ./Cortex.AppImage

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A hook is a command Cortex runs when something happens — a tool is about to execute, a session starts, a schedule fires, an assistant turn ends. Every hook is a declaration: one JSON file that names an event, an optional matcher, and the command to run. The built-in declarations ship with Cortex and are read from its install; yours live in $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/. The server loads those declarations at startup, and each consumer compiles the subset it cares about: the Claude Code backend, the PI backend, and the server's own event dispatcher. Adding a hook means adding a file, not changing code. For where hooks sit in the overall system, see architecture.md.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
defaults/config/hooks/*.json + $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/*.json
              — one declaration per file, built-in and yours
                            │
                            │  load + validate (store/hook-registry.ts)
        ┌───────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
        ▼                   ▼                        ▼
 Claude compiler       PI hook bridge            HookBus
 hooks-builder.ts      pi/hook-bridge.ts         core/hook-bus.ts
 agent:* + cc:*        agent:* + pi:*            cortex:*
        │                   │                        │
        ▼                   ▼                        ▼
 --settings JSON at    pi.on(<native event>)    server-side dispatch
 Claude spawn time     at extension load
        └───────────────────┴────────────────────────┘
                            │
                            ▼
     $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/*.mjs, then defaults/hooks/*.mjs — the scripts

docs.title: The hook registry
docs.text:
The registry has two layers. The built-in declarations are the .json files in the install's agent-server/defaults/config/hooks/, read in place, so they always match the running version. Yours are the .json files in $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/. Each file is one declaration. Files from both layers are read in sorted filename order, which is also the order hooks run in for the same event — the built-in declarations carry numeric prefixes (05-…, 06-…) so their relative order is explicit.

A file in $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/ with the same name as a built-in declaration overrides it rather than adding a hook. It is merged over the built-in declaration one top-level field at a time, so it only needs the fields it changes — { "enabled": false } switches a built-in hook off — and the built-in id is kept. A field the override sets replaces the built-in field whole: an override of run must restate the complete run object, script included. Deleting the file restores the built-in declaration. A sealed home (CORTEX_CONFIG_IMMUTABLE=1, as in a benchmark trial) mounts only its own declarations.

Loading is fail-soft and loud. A file that isn't valid JSON, fails schema validation, or reuses an id already claimed by an earlier file is skipped with [hook-registry] skipped <file>: <reason> on stderr; the rest of the registry still mounts. An override that cannot be parsed is reported the same way, and the built-in declaration it was meant to change mounts unchanged. At startup the server logs how many enabled hooks mounted, in the form Startup: mounted 7 hooks (0 cc / 1 cortex). The Web UI settings panel reads the same list.

The desktop Settings → Hooks panel is a full view of that registry rather than a listing: it groups declarations by event namespace in load order, shows where each one actually mounts (claude / pi / server), whether a change takes effect on the next agent spawn or only after a server restart, and flags a run.script that neither scripts directory has. What you may change there follows the entry's source. A user entry is fully editable and can be created or deleted. A built-in entry offers only the enabled switch; flipping it writes the minimal override to $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/, and flipping it back removes that override again. The result choice is constrained to the modes the event can actually carry, and an entry created from the UI is always a user entry. Each entry can also be run against an editable sample payload, with the exit code, stdout and stderr shown inline; a test run from the panel stops after 15 seconds whatever the declared timeout. Filter chips and a search box narrow the list.

On mobile the same registry is read-only: the hooks screen shows the grouped inventory and the full declaration behind each row, but no editing, creation or test run. Change hooks from a desktop session.

docs.title: Entry schema
docs.text:
{
  "id": "status-md-guard",
  "event": "agent:pre-tool",
  "matcher": "Edit|Write",
  "run": { "script": "status-md-guard.mjs", "timeout": 10 },
  "enabled": true
}
Field Type Meaning id string, required Unique across the registry. Used by cortex-hook and in log lines event string, required One of the agent:* events, or any cc: / pi: / cortex: prefixed name matcher string or object Regex for agent:* / cc:* / pi:* events; equality filter object for cortex:* events. Omit to match everything run.script string Script filename, looked up in $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ and then in the built-in scripts. Absolute paths and .. segments are rejected run.command string A raw shell command instead of a script. Exactly one of script or command must be present run.timeout number Timeout in seconds, a positive number. Defaults to 30 on PI and the server; on Claude an absent timeout leaves Claude Code's own default scope.backends array Narrows which of claude / pi an agent:* hook compiles to scope.requiresTool string On Claude, mounts the hook only when the agent's tool list contains that tool blocking object { "mode": "webhook", "ttlMin": <positive number> }. Descriptive metadata for a hook that blocks on a webhook round trip: the loader validates it and the settings panel shows it, but nothing enforces it at runtime result string How a cortex:* hook's stdout is used: stdout-as-prompt (accepted only on cortex:session.new and cortex:session.messageEnd) or none. The loader rejects a mode the event cannot carry version string Optional CalVer version of the declaration, shown read-only in the settings panel enabled boolean false removes the hook from every consumer without deleting the file. Defaults to true

The loader also rejects a matcher regular expression that does not compile, an object matcher whose values are not plain strings, numbers or booleans, and an event that is neither one of the seven agent:* names nor a cc:, pi: or cortex: prefix followed by a name.

docs.title: Built-in and user entries
docs.text: An entry declared in the install is built-in, whether or not a file in $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/ overrides some of its fields; cortex-hook and the settings panel report it as such. An entry declared only in $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/ is a user entry. Cortex never writes to the install, and it writes to $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/ only when you edit, add, delete or switch a hook.

docs.title: agent:* — backend-neutral agent events
docs.text:
These are the events both coding-agent backends genuinely agree on. One declaration compiles to Claude Code and to PI at the same time, and the payload handed to the script is Claude-shaped in both cases, so a single script serves both.

agent:* event Claude event PI event agent:pre-tool PreToolUse tool_call agent:post-tool PostToolUse tool_result agent:session-start SessionStart before_agent_start agent:session-end — session_shutdown agent:pre-compact — session_before_compact agent:user-prompt — input agent:turn-end — turn_end

The Claude compiler emits settings for the first three; the last four reach PI only. To hook the corresponding Claude mount points, declare them natively as cc:SessionEnd, cc:PreCompact, cc:UserPromptSubmit, or cc:Stop.

docs.title: cc:* — Claude Code passthrough
docs.text: Everything after cc: is used verbatim as the Claude settings event name, so any Claude Code mount point is reachable without code changes — cc:PermissionRequest, cc:SessionEnd, cc:PreCompact, cc:UserPromptSubmit, cc:Stop. These declarations mount on the Claude backend only. Note that Cortex spawns Claude with --permission-mode bypassPermissions, so cc:PermissionRequest never fires as things stand.

docs.title: pi:* — PI passthrough
docs.text: Everything after pi: is registered directly as a PI extension event, so PI-only mount points such as pi:session_start or pi:before_provider_headers are reachable the same way. These mount on the PI backend only, and the script receives the raw PI event object, with hook_event_name, session_id and cwd added, rather than a Claude-shaped payload.

docs.title: cortex:* — server-side events
docs.text:
These fire inside the agent-server process itself, dispatched by the HookBus.

Event Fires when Payload fields cortex:server.start The server finishes wiring and starts serving version, pid cortex:server.shutdown The server receives SIGTERM version, pid, reason cortex:schedule.fired A schedule fires scheduleId, name, project cortex:client.connected A remote device client registers device cortex:client.disconnected A remote device client drops device, reason when known cortex:session.new A session is closing via !new or the "New" status button channel, sessionId, backendSessionId, executionId, backend, model, trigger (new), timestampIso cortex:session.messageEnd An assistant turn completes same shape, with trigger set to messageEnd

In cortex:schedule.fired, name carries the schedule's message and project its projectId. The event fires once the schedule's preCheck has passed, before Cortex checks whether the run can start, so it also fires for a run that is then skipped.

docs.title: Matchers
docs.text:
For agent:*, cc:*, and pi:* events the matcher is a regular expression tested against the tool name. agent:* and cc:* matchers use Claude's PascalCase names (Edit|Write, Read|Grep); on the PI side the bridge maps PI's edit / read / web_fetch style names up to those canonical names before testing, so one matcher covers both backends. pi:* matchers are tested against PI's native tool names as-is. Non-tool events match differently: Claude tests a SessionStart matcher against the start reason (startup|resume|clear|compact), and the PI bridge applies matchers only to tool events, ignoring them on lifecycle events.

For cortex:* events the matcher is an object of equality filters, and every key must be present in the payload with exactly that value. A cortex:client.disconnected hook with {"device": "gpu-box"} fires only when that one device drops, not for every client.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
At spawn time, buildHooksSettings() in agent-adapter/claude/hooks-builder.ts loads the registry, keeps the entries that are enabled, mount on the claude backend, and pass their scope.requiresTool check against the agent's tool list, then emits a Claude settings object injected through the --settings CLI flag. run.script becomes node <script path> — the script in $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ when there is one, otherwise the built-in script in the install, and a script from $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ also gets the --import preload that resolves its imports of the built-in helpers. run.command is passed through verbatim, and run.timeout becomes Claude's per-hook timeout in seconds. Consecutive entries on the same event with the same matcher are merged into one matcher group:

{
  "PreToolUse": [
    { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [
        { "type": "command", "command": "node <install>/defaults/hooks/status-md-guard.mjs", "timeout": 10 }
    ]}
  ],
  "PostToolUse": [
    { "matcher": "Read|Grep", "hooks": [ ... ] },
    { "matcher": "Read|Edit|Write|Skill", "hooks": [ ... ] },
    { "matcher": "Read|Edit", "hooks": [ ... ] }
  ],
  "SessionStart": [ ... ]
}

Because the registry is read on every spawn, a new declaration takes effect on the next agent that starts.

docs.title: PI
docs.text:
agent-adapter/pi/hook-bridge.ts runs as the cortex-hook-bridge PI extension, inside the server process. On load it takes the registry entries that mount on the pi backend and calls pi.on() once per entry, with the native event name from the agent:* mapping table above or the literal suffix of a pi:* event. scope.requiresTool is not applied on PI.

For agent:* entries the bridge normalizes PI's shapes into the Claude form the hook scripts expect: the tool name is mapped to PascalCase (edit → Edit, web_fetch → WebFetch), and input.path is copied to input.file_path for the read / write / edit tools. The payload carries hook_event_name (the Claude name — SessionEnd, PreCompact, UserPromptSubmit and Stop for the four PI-only events), session_id, tool_name, tool_input, tool_use_id, and cwd; tool-result events add tool_output, tool_response, and is_error. Hook processes get CORTEX_SESSION_ID in their environment.

A run.script that exports a runHook(payload, env) function is imported and called in-process instead of being spawned as a child; its return value is treated like the JSON a spawned script prints.

Script output is honored natively. On tool_call, a hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision of deny blocks the tool and surfaces permissionDecisionReason, and hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput replaces the tool input. On tool_result, hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext is appended to the tool's content. On before_agent_start, that same field is appended to the system prompt. pi:* entries can additionally return {"block": true} on pi:tool_call, replace input wholesale, and rewrite headers on pi:before_provider_headers.

docs.title: The server-side dispatcher
docs.text:
core/hook-bus.ts dispatches cortex:* events. The server snapshots the registry into the bus at startup, so a newly added cortex:* declaration takes effect the next time the server starts.

When an event is emitted, the bus selects the enabled entries whose event matches exactly and whose object matcher is satisfied by the payload, then runs them one at a time. Each hook runs as sh -c '<command> "$@"' hook <args> with the working directory set to $CORTEX_HOME and the payload delivered as JSON on stdin. run.timeout seconds is the process limit — 30 by default, and session events use 60 unless the declaration says otherwise.

What the bus does with stdout depends on result:

  • stdout-as-prompt — trimmed stdout is used as a prompt. Session events use this to inject a turn.
  • none, or omitted — output is discarded; the hook is fire-and-forget.

A hook that times out or exits non-zero is logged to the daemon log with the tail of its stderr, and skipped; session-event hooks also log their stderr when they succeed. A hook never fails the surrounding operation.

docs.title: Session events and prompt injection
docs.text:
cortex:session.new fires before a session is torn down by !new or the "New" status button, when a hook is declared for it and the channel has an active session. cortex:session.messageEnd fires after each assistant turn of a session that has a live stream. Both are declared like any other hook; the built-in session-new-hook declaration points at new-session-hook.mjs with result set to stdout-as-prompt.

sessionId is the Cortex session id — the key of the session registry, from which the cortex-hook helpers resolve a channel. backendSessionId is the backend's own id for the session's conversation (the name of its transcript), or null while the session has had no turn; the two differ once the backend has assigned its own id or a rewind has moved the conversation.

Beyond the JSON payload on stdin, session hooks receive CORTEX_HOOK_CHANNEL, CORTEX_HOOK_SESSION_ID, CORTEX_HOOK_TRIGGER, and CORTEX_HOOK_EXECUTION_ID in the environment, plus CORTEX_HOOK_BACKEND_SESSION_ID when the session has a backend conversation. Non-empty stdout is injected as a fresh agent turn that resumes that conversation — for session.new on an isolated session key that is closed afterwards, so the pre-close turn cannot resurrect the old session under the channel; for session.messageEnd on the channel itself, so the follow-up continues the live conversation and its output threads under the reply that triggered it. A session with no backend conversation has nothing to resume, so its hook output is shown but not injected.

docs.title: The hook-bridge: blocking calls over HTTP
docs.text:
Two interactions need a human in the loop, which the agent process cannot do on its own: asking the user a question, and getting a plan approved. Both POST to the server's loopback webhook listener (WEBHOOK_PORT, default 3001) on /hook/ask-user-question and /hook/exit-plan-mode, authenticated with the CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN bearer token in the x-cortex-token header, and block on the response. A question posted with blocking: false returns as soon as the card is up.

Agents reach that bridge through the cortex_ask_user and cortex_plan_exit MCP tools, and hook scripts reach it through cortex-hook-api.mjs / the cortex-hook ask CLI (see Asking the user from a hook). Claude's native AskUserQuestion and ExitPlanMode are not part of a Cortex session that has the interaction tools, so no hook needs to intercept them.

On the server, orchestration/routing/hook-bridge.ts registers a pending promise with a 30-minute TTL and publishes ask-user.requested or plan.submitted on the event bus. The subscribers in hook-bridge-subscribers.ts present them on the session's platform — an inline card on the Web UI, interactive messages on Slack and Feishu (see safety-and-approvals.md). When the user responds, the interaction handler resolves the promise and the HTTP response returns to the waiting caller.

docs.title: Hook scripts
docs.text:
Scripts are ordinary Node.js .mjs files: read JSON context from stdin, write JSON (or, for stdout-as-prompt hooks, plain text) to stdout. The built-in scripts run in place from the install's agent-server/defaults/hooks/; yours live in $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/. A script name is looked up in $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ first, so a file there with a built-in script's name replaces it, and deleting the file restores the built-in one. A script in $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ can import the built-in helper libraries (./cortex-hook-api.mjs, ./cortex-context-lib.mjs, …) by the same relative path the built-in scripts use: an import that $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ cannot satisfy is resolved against the built-in scripts directory. The built-in scripts are:

Script Used by Purpose status-md-guard.mjs agent:pre-tool, Edit\|Write Keeps a project's STATUS.md and ISSUES.md and the memory tree's AGENTS.md indexes within their size caps (see below) memory-ref-tracker.mjs agent:post-tool, Read\|Grep Records experiment, knowledge and pattern accesses to _meta/access-log.jsonl (see Reference tracking) rules-loader.mjs agent:post-tool, Read\|Grep Injects path-scoped rules — the built-in ones and those in $CORTEX_HOME/rules/ — when a matching path is read, once per session per rule session-activity-tracker.mjs agent:post-tool, Read\|Edit\|Write\|Skill Appends activity records to logs/session-activity/<session_id>.jsonl agents-md-injector.mjs agent:post-tool (Read\|Edit) and agent:session-start Injects the AGENTS.md ancestor chain into agent context, deduplicated per session new-session-hook.mjs cortex:session.new Recalls valuable information from the closing session and writes it to the context files

A declaration may run an inline run.command instead of a script.

The size caps status-md-guard enforces:

File Warns at Denied above context/projects/<project>/STATUS.md, ISSUES.md 60 lines or 4 KB 80 lines or 6 KB Any AGENTS.md under context/ 90 lines or 6.5 KB 120 lines or 8 KB

An edit that crosses either limit is denied with advice on what to trim. An edit that shrinks a file already over its cap is allowed with a warning, so an oversized file can be cut down step by step.

Several files among the built-in scripts are not hook entries. cortex-hook-api.mjs is a helper library that hook scripts import (see below). cortex-context-lib.mjs holds the AGENTS.md dedup cache, the inline size budget and the rules paths: parser shared by agents-md-injector.mjs, rules-loader.mjs and the server, so the hooks and the MCP-side injection of remote AGENTS.md files read and write the same per-session cache. git-support.mjs is the Git helper memory-ref-tracker.mjs uses, and overlay/ holds the --import loader that lets a script in $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ import the built-in helpers.

docs.title: Asking the user from a hook
docs.text:
Any hook can pose an ask-user-question card on the message platform bound to the current session — Slack, Feishu, or the Web UI — and block until the user answers. The card is the same interactive form the cortex_ask_user tool produces, and it accepts an optional severity level (info, warning, or error, with warn as an alias) that renders with the Web UI's notice tones and an icon prefix on Slack and Feishu. Without a level the card keeps its neutral look.

Node hook scripts import the helper by its relative path, which a script in $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ can use too (see Hook scripts). askUser takes questions, level, channel, sessionId, dryRun, and a client-side timeoutMs (60 minutes by default), and resolves to { answers, error? }; error is timeout, post_failed or bus_not_initialized.

import { askUser } from './cortex-hook-api.mjs';

const { answers, error } = await askUser({
  questions: [{
    question: 'Disk is almost full — clean old checkpoints?',
    header: 'Disk',
    options: [{ label: 'Clean' }, { label: 'Keep' }],
  }],
  level: 'warning',
});
if (error === 'timeout') process.exit(0); // user did not answer — pick a safe default

run.command hooks (and anything shell-based) use the CLI instead:

cortex-hook ask --question "Disk is almost full — clean old checkpoints?" \
  --options "Clean|Keep" --level warning
# → { "ok": true, "answers": { "Disk is almost full — clean old checkpoints?": "Clean" } }

Both entry points POST to the server's /hook/ask-user-question webhook with the CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN that hooks run by Cortex inherit, so they share one routing and blocking contract:

  • Routing. An explicit channel wins. Otherwise the helper and the CLI fall back to the hook environment: CORTEX_HOOK_CHANNEL (session hooks), then SLACK_CHANNEL (agent-side hooks). When only a sessionId is available (CORTEX_HOOK_SESSION_ID, or passed explicitly), the server resolves the session's channel from the session registry. Server events such as cortex:schedule.fired carry no channel, so their hooks must pass channel or sessionId themselves.
  • Blocking. The server holds the request in the hook-bridge with a 30-minute TTL. The response is { answers }, or { error: "timeout", answers: {} } when the TTL expires. cortex-hook ask exits 0 on answers, 2 on timeout, and 1 on other errors, so a shell hook can branch on $?. A hook that asks must set its run.timeout above the expected wait, and should declare blocking: { "mode": "webhook", "ttlMin": 30 } so the settings panel shows that it blocks.
  • Multiple questions. askUser takes any non-empty question array; cortex-hook ask --payload <file|-> accepts the same array as JSON, e.g. cat questions.json | cortex-hook ask --payload - --session-id <id>. Cortex does not impose a question-count maximum; the destination platform may still reject a payload that exceeds its own limits.
  • Smoke tests. --dry-run (CLI) or dryRun: true (helper) journals the event and resolves synthetically without posting a card.

Agents themselves get the same severity option through the cortex_ask_user MCP tool's level parameter.

docs.title: The cortex-hook CLI
docs.text:
cortex-hook inspects and operates the mounted hooks. Every command prints JSON on stdout; --help prints text, and an error is reported on stderr with exit code 1.

Command Flags What it does cortex-hook list — Lists every mounted hook as id, event, enabled, source (builtin or user), and overridden for a built-in hook with an override file cortex-hook show --id <id> Prints one complete declaration, including source cortex-hook enable --id <id>, --dry-run Sets enabled: true, idempotently: in the declaration file for a user hook, in the override file for a built-in one cortex-hook disable --id <id>, --dry-run Sets enabled: false the same way cortex-hook test --id <id>, --payload <file\|-> Runs the hook once with the payload on stdin, in $CORTEX_HOME, with a 30-second default timeout cortex-hook ask --question, --header, --options "a\|b", --level, --channel / --session-id, --payload <file\|->, --multi, --dry-run Posts an ask-user card on the session's platform and blocks for the answer (exit 2 on timeout). --header defaults to the first 12 characters of the question

--help / -h works on the root command and on each subcommand.

cortex-hook list
cortex-hook show --id session-new-hook
cortex-hook disable --id rules-loader --dry-run
cortex-hook test --id status-md-guard --payload payload.json
cat payload.json | cortex-hook test --id status-md-guard --payload -

enable and disable report changed so you can tell a real state change from a no-op, and --dry-run adds a would_set block instead of writing. For a built-in hook the override file holds only the switch, and returning the switch to its built-in value deletes the file.

test returns ok, id, exit_code, stdout, stderr, and error when the process failed, and exits with the hook's own exit code.

docs.title: Adding a hook
docs.text:
1. Write the script into $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/, for example warn-sensitive-file.mjs:
#!/usr/bin/env node
const chunks = [];
for await (const chunk of process.stdin) chunks.push(chunk);
const input = JSON.parse(Buffer.concat(chunks).toString());

const path = input.tool_input?.file_path || '';
if (path.includes('.env') || path.includes('credentials')) {
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    hookSpecificOutput: {
      hookEventName: 'PreToolUse',
      permissionDecision: 'deny',
      permissionDecisionReason: `Refusing to edit sensitive file: ${path}`
    }
  }));
  process.exit(0);
}

console.log(JSON.stringify({
  hookSpecificOutput: {
    hookEventName: 'PreToolUse',
    permissionDecision: 'allow'
  }
}));
  1. Declare it. Drop $CORTEX_HOME/config/hooks/50-warn-sensitive-file.json into the registry — the numeric prefix places it after the built-in entries:
{
  "id": "warn-sensitive-file",
  "event": "agent:pre-tool",
  "matcher": "Edit|Write",
  "run": { "script": "warn-sensitive-file.mjs", "timeout": 5 }
}
  1. Verify with cortex-hook list (the id appears with source user) and cortex-hook test --id warn-sensitive-file --payload payload.json.

An agent:*, cc:*, or pi:* hook applies to the next agent that spawns. A cortex:* hook is picked up when the server next starts, because the bus snapshots the registry at startup.

The same three steps cover server-side events — declare "event": "cortex:schedule.fired" with a matcher such as {"project": "my-project"} to run something whenever one of that project's schedules fires.

docs.title: Reference tracking
docs.text:
The memory-ref-tracker hook implements automatic reference tracking for the atomized memory system (see memory.md for the full architecture). It records every Read and Grep that touches an experiment, knowledge, or pattern entry — EXP-NNN.md, K-NNN.md or PAT-NNN.md under context/projects/<project>/ — as one JSONL record of the entry's filename, the tool, and a timestamp:

{"file": "EXP-012.md", "tool": "Read", "ts": "2026-05-19T10:30:00.000Z"}

A Grep inside a project that matches no entry file is recorded as "file": "_directory_search". The log lives at <project>/_meta/access-log.jsonl. When $CORTEX_HOME is a Git repository, the hook stages every changed access-log.jsonl and commits them as chore: update access log, unless something else is already staged, in which case it only stages them. Without Git, access tracking still writes the log. Memory index regeneration reads it to compute access counts (refs) and last-access timestamps (last-ref), which drive index sorting and hot/cold classification.

docs.title: Debugging hooks
docs.text:
Start with cortex-hook list to confirm the hook is mounted and enabled, then cortex-hook test --id <id> --payload <file> to run it in isolation with a payload you control — that separates "the script is broken" from "the declaration never matched". Server-side hook failures are logged to $CORTEX_HOME/logs/daemon.log with the tail of the script's stderr.

  • Hook doesn't appear in cortex-hook list — the loader rejected it. Look for [hook-registry] skipped <file> in the log: invalid JSON, a schema violation, or an id already used by an earlier file.
  • Hook is listed but never fires — check the matcher. Tool matchers for agent:* and cc:* events use Claude's PascalCase names, and cortex:* matchers require every key to be present in the payload with exactly that value.
  • agent:session-end, agent:pre-compact, agent:user-prompt, or agent:turn-end has no effect on Claude — those four compile to PI only. Use the cc: form for the Claude mount point.
  • New cortex:* hook does nothing — the bus snapshots the registry at startup; restart the server.
  • JSON parse error — stdout wasn't valid JSON. Make sure nothing but the result is written to stdout; diagnostics belong on stderr.
  • Timeout — raise run.timeout (in seconds). The default is 30 seconds, or 60 for session events; on Claude an unset timeout falls back to Claude Code's own default.
  • scope.requiresTool has no effect on PI — the PI bridge mounts the hook regardless; narrow it with scope.backends instead.
  • Script not found — run.script is looked up in $CORTEX_HOME/hooks/ and then among the built-in scripts; absolute paths and .. segments are rejected by the loader.

docs.title: MCP — Model Context Protocol
docs.text: Cortex ships privilege-scoped and platform-scoped MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools that give agents access to remote machines, subagents, costs, waitpoints, team workers, boards, and platform integrations. This document explains what each server provides, how they are composed, and how to add third-party MCP servers.

docs.title: What MCP is
docs.text:
MCP is an open protocol that lets LLM applications expose tools to agents through a standardized JSON-RPC interface over stdio, HTTP, or an in-memory transport pair. Cortex uses MCP to bridge between the agent (which reaches no agent-server internals of its own) and the server's capabilities. MCP support varies by backend — see the feature matrix in backends.md.

Claude Code reads MCP server configurations from JSON files and spawns each stdio server as a child process. The agent then calls MCP tools just like built-in tools (Bash, Read, Edit, etc.), with the tool names prefixed by mcp__<server-name>__. PI connects MCP servers through Cortex's own bridge: the bundled Cortex tools keep their bare names, and a plugin server's tools are named plugin_tool_plugin_server_<server>_<tool>.

docs.title: Why Cortex ships its own MCP servers
docs.text: Cortex's agent-server maintains state that the agent process cannot reach directly: WebSocket connections to remote machines, running subagents and team workers, waitpoints, the chat platforms, cost records, and the execution registry. The Cortex MCP tools are a controlled bridge — the agent calls a tool, the tool asks the server (over the loopback webhook, or by reading the server's stores), and the result flows back to the agent.

docs.title: The bundled MCP servers
docs.text:
The names below are logical capability bundles, not separate processes. Unless a session's MCP composition is empty, the session gets exactly one Cortex-owned server built from agent-server/src/domain/mcp/bundled-server.ts, registering only the bundles selected for it. Claude Code starts that server as a stdio child; PI runs it inside the agent-server process over an in-memory transport pair, bound to a tool context built for that one session. Under Claude the server key is cortex-core, so every bundled tool carries that prefix — the remote tools are mcp__cortex-core__remote_*, and the context tool is mcp__cortex-core__cortex_context. PI exposes the same tools under their unprefixed names.

User-provided MCP is outside this bundle. Portable plugin servers, remote HTTP/SSE servers, and Claude-native MCP from an assigned legacy plugin keep independent configurations, transports, and failure boundaries.

docs.title: cortex-core
docs.text:
Exposes remote-machine operations, the read-only clock, and subagent delegation. Every session whose MCP composition is not none loads it, subagents included.

Tool Parameters Description remote_bash device, command, timeout? (seconds, 1–600, default 120), description?, run_in_background? Execute a shell command on a remote device via cortex-client remote_read device, file_path (absolute), offset?, limit? Read a file from a remote device (supports images and PDFs) remote_write device, file_path, content Write content to a file on a remote device remote_edit device, file_path, old_string, new_string, replace_all? Edit a file on a remote device by string replacement remote_glob device, pattern, path? Find files matching a glob pattern on a remote device remote_grep device, pattern, path?, glob?, type?, output_mode?, -A?, -B?, -C? (alias context?), -i?, -n?, head_limit?, offset?, multiline? Search file contents on a remote device using ripgrep current_time timezone? Get the current date/time; optional IANA timezone (defaults to server local). Returns Unix epoch, UTC ISO, and localized wall-clock with offset agent single (description, prompt, subagent_type) or parallel[] or chain[] (each item description, prompt, subagent_type, model?, backend?), plus model?, backend?, run_in_background? Delegate work to an isolated subagent on either backend agent_stop agent_id Stop a running subagent and discard whatever it had produced

The remote tools are registered by agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/remote-ops.ts; agent and agent_stop by agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/subagent.ts.

The remote tools share some behavior:

  • The first remote tool in a session's surface carries a catalog of the devices registered in machines.json in its description, Windows machines marked, so the agent knows which device values exist. A call to a device that is not connected fails with the list of devices that are online.
  • remote_read, remote_write and remote_edit add the target's AGENTS.md ancestor chain on that device to their result, once per file per session (see cross-machine.md).
  • remote_read returns images and PDFs as media; the server downscales large images when sharp is available.
  • Output above 30,000 characters (remote_bash), 20,000 (remote_grep) or 100,000 (remote_glob) is saved under $CORTEX_HOME/tmp/tool-results/, and the tool returns the path with a 2 KB preview.

agent replaces Claude Code's built-in Agent tool, which Cortex strips from every Claude spawn. It runs on the same role table as PI's own native agent, can place a child on either backend, and is visible to the daemon — so a delegated run appears in the parent's transcript, is billed to the parent, and can be stopped from the UI. A foreground call that is still running after 25 minutes is handed to the background and its result arrives later. See backends.md.

PI sessions never receive the MCP agent and agent_stop: PI registers its own agent, and two tools of that name cannot coexist. A subagent receives neither on either backend. That is enforced by the tool allowlist rather than by the prompt, so a child cannot fan out further no matter what it is asked to do.

docs.title: cortex-workers
docs.text:
The lead's side of team mode. A session selects this bundle when teamEnabled is on and it is a web direct session that is not itself a worker, on Claude and PI alike. Workers and subagents never load it. Every tool returns at once; worker reports and questions reach the lead as new messages.

Tool Parameters Description worker_spawn name, prompt, backend?, model? Start a persistent worker session with its first task; it runs the lead's current model unless backend/model (same format as agent) name another worker_send worker, message Deliver a message to a worker, folded into its running turn or opening a new one worker_list worker? The lead's roster, or one worker with its full last report worker_stop worker Stop a worker's current turn worker_answer request_id, answers?, approved?, feedback? Resolve a worker's pending question or plan approval

The bundle is loaded by agent-server/src/domain/mcp/bundled-server.ts; the tools are in agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/workers.ts and are served by the /webhook/team route.

docs.title: cortex-worker-report
docs.text:
A worker's side of team mode. Every worker session loads it, on Claude and PI alike; leads, ordinary sessions and subagents never do.

Tool Parameters Description mark_routine none Mark the current turn as routine: its final reply is recorded for the lead as an unread update and does not wake it. A failed or stopped turn reports anyway

The tool is in agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/workers.ts and is served by the /webhook/team route, which refuses it for a session that is not a worker.

docs.title: cortex-ext
docs.text:
Exposes Cortex management tools: cost queries, execution records, context resolution, and waitpoints. Every top-level session whose MCP composition is not none loads it, on Claude and PI alike. Claude subagents load it too; PI subagents do not.

Tool Parameters Description cost_query projectId? Query current cost: today/month spending, budget limits, remaining budget, API/plan split, source breakdown, token usage; with projectId, scoped to that project query_executions execution_id?, status? (running, completed, failed, cancelled, stale, all), project?, limit? Query execution records — filter by status, project, or look up by ID cortex_context (none) Return the current execution context: sessionId, project, backend, model, thinking, mode, and for a scheduled or callback-triggered run scheduleTaskId and callbackSource; in a Web session also board, the board it is bound to (id, title, dir) or null wait_create label, intent, members?, quorum?, fail_fast?, max_signals?, expires_in_hours?, device? Arm a waitpoint and return the id, a one-time secret, and ready-to-paste signal commands; then end the turn wait_check id? Inspect one waitpoint, or list everything this session is waiting on wait_cancel id Cancel a waitpoint so it can no longer fire

wait_create is how a session waits for something outside Cortex — a training run, a build, an eval — without polling it. The external program reports back with the cortex-signal CLI, a loopback POST /webhook/signal, or a file dropped in a spool directory, and the session is woken with the result. See waitpoints.md.

Schedules are not MCP tools: agents manage them with the cortex schedule CLI through the schedule skill, resolving the project with cortex_context and passing it with --project (see Scheduling).

The bundle is loaded by agent-server/src/domain/mcp/bundled-server.ts. Individual tools are in agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/.

docs.title: cortex-slack
docs.text:
Platform-specific MCP server for Slack. Loaded only when the session originates from Slack, providing platform-specific file upload and messaging capabilities.

Tool Parameters Description slack_send_file file_path, file_name?, title?, comment?, device? Upload a file to Slack; with device, the file is read on that remote device

The bundle is loaded by agent-server/src/domain/mcp/bundled-server.ts; the tool is in agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/slack.ts.

docs.title: cortex-feishu
docs.text:
Platform-specific MCP server for Feishu/Lark. Loaded only when the session originates from Feishu. It exposes a single tool — sending files to a chat.

Tool Parameters Description feishu_send_file file_path, file_name?, title?, channel?, device? Upload a file to a Feishu chat; with device, the file is read on that remote device

Document, table, spreadsheet, and knowledge-base operations are not MCP tools. They run through the official Lark/Feishu CLI (@larksuite/cli), driven by the feishu-doc skill of the built-in cortex-feishu plugin, which handles native tables and block-level edits. See the feishu-doc skill for the install/auth preflight and how to delegate to the CLI's embedded lark-doc / lark-sheets / lark-base skill guides.

The bundle is loaded by agent-server/src/domain/mcp/bundled-server.ts. The tool is in agent-server/src/domain/mcp/feishu/file.ts.

docs.title: cortex-web
docs.text:
Platform-specific MCP server for the Web workbench. Loaded only when the session originates from the Web UI (its channel carries the web: prefix), so a Slack- or Feishu-originated session never sees these tools.

Tool Parameters Description send_file file_path or files[] ({file_path, file_name?}), file_name?, caption?, device? Send one file, or several as one grouped message with a single caption, into the chat as downloadable cards (images and video preview inline); with device, the files are read on that remote device send_view title, html or file_path, caption?, height? (160–900, default 360), width? (narrow, wide, full) Render an HTML view inline in the chat as a live, interactive card send_decision decisions[] — each title, decision, context, reasoning Record decisions the agent just made and show them as lines in the chat board_open title or board (exactly one) Create a board, or attach to an existing one by id or slug, and bind the session to it

Assistant Markdown can place an image or video inside the reply with ![alt](src). Use a server path (/absolute/plot.png, ~/plot.png, or figs/plot.png relative to CORTEX_HOME, normally ~/.cortex), an existing workspace/... path, a registered device path such as gpu-box:/home/user/plot.png or win-pc:C:/Users/x/clip.mp4, or an external https://... URL. Local and device files are snapshotted per message, with a 200MB limit; reusing a source in a later message creates a separate snapshot. Workspace paths use the existing file. Video extensions are .mp4, .webm, .mov, and .m4v; other supported media extensions render as images, and an external URL without an extension is treated as an image. Previews load near the viewport and open the media viewer when clicked. During streaming, local and device references show a placeholder until the reply is saved. External media loads directly in the browser without a referrer; non-HTTPS, local-network hostnames and private IP literals are not embedded. This Markdown behavior is limited to assistant chat text in the Web UI and native apps; send_file remains the way to share downloadable attachment cards.

send_file, send_view and send_decision proxy their payload to the daemon over the loopback webhook rather than returning it as tool output: the normalized event stream carries tool results as flat strings, and the PI backend flattens rich MCP content to text, so anything richer than a string has to travel out of band. The daemon copies the bytes into workspace/outputs/<sessionId>/ (views land one level deeper, in views/), records an assistant message carrying the attachment, and publishes the live event. Only the path travels — a large document never enters the transcript or the event stream.

send_view takes either an inline html string (up to 256KB) or the path to an .html file the agent already wrote (up to 2MB). The view renders in a frame sandboxed to allow-scripts with no allow-same-origin, so the document has an opaque origin: no access to the page, storage, cookies, the Cortex API, or (in the desktop shell) the auth token and Tauri IPC. It may still load libraries and data over https. That isolation is why the rendering intent is carried by the attachment bucket the server mints and never by a file extension — an .html file that a user uploads or that an agent sends with send_file opens as source text, not as a running document.

width picks one of three inline card widths: narrow (the default) sits in the chat's text column, wide extends to about one and a half columns (up to 1040px), and full spans the whole chat pane. wide and full shrink with the pane, so on a narrow window both end up as wide as the pane. The tier is stored with the message, so a view keeps its width across reloads. Only the inline card on the desktop chat honours it; the expanded and docked views and the mobile chat always fill the space they have.

send_decision is non-blocking: the agent announces choices it made on the user's behalf and keeps working, rather than putting a question to the user the way cortex_ask_user does. Each decision (up to 10 per call, title ≤120 chars, other fields ≤1000) renders as one line under the reply that announced it: its title, and its status once the user has answered it. A batch shows three lines and folds the rest into one line that can also approve them all. Opening a line shows the decision, then why, then the context. The user can approve (recorded only — nothing is sent to the agent; on desktop also straight from the hovered line) or reply: one box that either asks why (the text is optional) or requests a change (the text is required). Both compose a templated message that is recorded on the decision and delivered to the agent as an ordinary user message. Decisions and their action log persist in the conversation history, so they keep their state across reloads and devices.

board_open opens the status page of a long task: who is bound to it, how agents write it, and how it shows in the chat and the workbench are described under Boards.

The bundle is loaded by agent-server/src/domain/mcp/bundled-server.ts. The tools are in agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/ui-file.ts, agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/ui-view.ts, agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/ui-decision.ts, and agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/ui-board.ts.

docs.title: cortex-interaction-bridge
docs.text:
Direct Claude TUI sessions, user-initiated direct Claude print sessions, and user-initiated direct PI sessions select this interaction bundle in their single Cortex MCP server. Where it is loaded, Claude's native AskUserQuestion, EnterPlanMode and ExitPlanMode are removed, so every question and plan goes through these tools.

Tool Parameters Description cortex_plan_enter reasoning? Enters the shared read-only planning protocol: investigate, write the plan under plan/, implement only after approval cortex_plan_exit plan_file_path, summary? Reads the plan file, submits it for human approval, and blocks until resolved cortex_ask_user questions[] (each question, header?, options?[] of {label, description?}, multiSelect?), level? (info, warning, error; warn is an alias), blocking? Asks one or more free-text or multiple-choice questions through the session platform, waiting for the answers or continuing without them

cortex_ask_user posts its question card the same way in either mode; the blocking parameter decides how the answer comes back. Blocking is the default: the tool call waits up to the 30-minute interaction TTL and returns the answers in its own tool_result, so the agent cannot proceed without them. With blocking: false the call returns as soon as the card is posted and the agent keeps working; when the human answers, the answer is delivered to the session as an ordinary user message — folded into the running turn if one is still live, otherwise opening a fresh turn. An unanswered non-blocking card expires on the same TTL and simply never produces a message. In the workbench, only a blocking question marks a session as awaiting user action; a session that asked without blocking keeps rendering as running.

How the cards look on each platform, and how plan approval and questions route in team mode, is described in safety-and-approvals.md. The plan and question handlers are in agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/interaction-plan.ts and agent-server/src/domain/mcp/tools/interaction-ask.ts.

docs.title: MCP configuration files
docs.text:
Cortex generates the Claude MCP config files at startup (via agent-server/src/core/config-generator.ts and the ensureMcpConfig() call in agent-server/src/entry/startup-helpers.ts). A sealed home (CORTEX_CONFIG_IMMUTABLE=1) keeps the files it was given.

File Purpose Server key Logical bundles $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-config.json The direct composition every ordinary Claude session uses cortex-core core + ext $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-config-empty.json The none composition: no MCP servers — — $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-config-core.json Explicit restricted composition cortex-core core $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-config-interaction.json Explicit interaction composition cortex-interaction-bridge interaction $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-config-slack.json Explicit Slack composition cortex-slack Slack $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-config-feishu.json Explicit Feishu composition cortex-feishu Feishu $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-config-web.json Explicit Web composition cortex-web Web

Claude sessions load mcp-config.json or mcp-config-empty.json; the other five serve callers that pass explicit config paths. Each file follows Claude Code's standard MCP config format:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cortex-core": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": [
        "<install>/agent-server/dist/domain/mcp/bundled-server.js",
        "[\"cortex-core\",\"cortex-ext\"]"
      ],
      "cwd": "<install>/agent-server"
    }
  }
}

The config files are rewritten on every agent-server startup, so manual edits to them do not persist. To customize MCP configuration, use a plugin (see Plugin-provided MCP servers).

A spawn that runs under a tool allowlist — a subagent, or an agent role that declares one — gets a merged config written to $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-tool-gates/mcp-composition-<digest>.json, carrying the allowlist to the bundled server.

docs.title: How the right config gets selected
docs.text:
