In agent-adapter/claude/spawn-args.ts, a session on the direct composition loads mcp-config.json, and one on none loads mcp-config-empty.json with --strict-mcp-config. The Claude adapter writes the final logical selection to CORTEX_MCP_BUNDLES for the stdio child it spawns: core and ext, plus the interaction bundle for user-initiated sessions, the workers bundle for a team lead, the worker-report bundle for a worker, and the platform bundle matching the session's channel (slack:, feishu: or web:). The plugin MCP configuration is added as a separate config file.

PI's bridge computes the same logical selection from the session's own environment and hands it directly to the in-process bundled server, alongside one independent connection per plugin server; on PI the interaction, workers and worker-report bundles require the direct composition. Subagents run under an allowlist: Claude subagents receive core (without agent and agent_stop) and ext, and PI subagents receive core alone, with no plugin servers. Allowlists are validated against the selected bundles before the bundled server registers tools.

docs.title: How MCP tools communicate with agent-server
docs.text:
User-provided stdio MCP entries are separate child processes under both backends, and Claude Code sessions run the Cortex-owned MCP server as a child too. Cortex MCP tools never reach agent-server in-process state (WebSocket connections, running sessions, waitpoints) directly, wherever their server runs. They communicate through two paths:

  1. Loopback webhook — most tools POST to the server's webhook at http://127.0.0.1:<WEBHOOK_PORT> (default 3001), authenticated with the CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN bearer token in the x-cortex-token header. Remote machine tools use /webhook/remote-command, whose handler in agent-server/src/orchestration/routing/webhook.ts forwards the request to client-manager.sendCommand() and on over WebSocket to the device. The subagent, team, board, waitpoint, Web delivery (ui-file, ui-view, ui-decision) and interaction (/hook/ask-user-question, /hook/exit-plan-mode) tools each have their own route.

  2. Store reads — cost_query reads cost records (data/costs.jsonl) through the same repository layer as the main server, and query_executions reads the execution registry (data/executions.json). Neither writes.

MCP calls and loopback HTTP requests share a 30-minute-30-second infrastructure deadline. Tool-specific business deadlines remain authoritative: shell commands use their timeout argument, while human interactions retain their 30-minute response window. The extra 30 seconds lets a business timeout return its result before an outer transport deadline closes the request.

docs.title: Plugin-provided MCP servers
docs.text:
Environment-scoped third-party MCP belongs in a portable Agent Plugins package under $CORTEX_HOME/plugins/<plugin-id>/. The package declares servers in root mcp.json, and the Plugins tab of an execution environment (Settings → Environments) assigns the package to it. The schema supports stdio, streamable-http, and legacy sse; Skills and Plugins documents the complete package and trust model.

A legacy plugin directory is passed through to its backend as it is. Claude can load a Claude-native root .mcp.json from such a directory, but Cortex does not inventory, summarize, or acknowledgment-gate those native servers, and PI does not receive them. The guarantees in this section apply to portable root mcp.json only (agent-server/src/domain/plugins/runtime.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/claude/spawn-args.ts).

Cortex validates and normalizes the package once at spawn time. Claude receives a private supplemental configuration layered after the normal Cortex files. Stdio entries remain separate processes; each remote entry becomes a local stdio proxy whose private configuration holds its URL and headers. PI receives the normalized server list with its session request, and its bridge opens each entry's own transport — a stdio child for a stdio entry, a direct HTTP or SSE connection for a remote one. Both remote paths use the same manual-redirect fetch and reject every redirect before a configured header or request body can be replayed. Connection and tool registration are isolated per server. Materialization follows declared dependencies: unavailable plugin-scoped PLUGIN_DATA omits its stdio dependents while preserving remote MCP, skills, and bundled tools (agent-server/src/domain/plugins/runtime.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/claude/mcp-config.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/claude/remote-mcp-proxy.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/pi/mcp-bridge.ts).

Portable MCP is omitted when the resolved MCP composition is none, and subagents load no plugins at all. Top-level Claude and PI sessions receive it only through an assigned plugin (agent-server/src/domain/plugins/runtime.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/pi/adapter.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/pi/mcp-bridge.ts).

The plugin catalog and Settings API expose sanitized summaries. Stdio summaries contain the executable basename, argument count, and environment key names; remote summaries contain the origin and header names. Environment values, full remote URLs, and header values remain server-side (agent-server/src/domain/plugins/mcp.ts; agent-server/src/domain/ui-service/plugins-shared.ts). Installed stdio commands and their working directories remain administrator-trusted package inputs; the private config and per-server isolation are not a code sandbox.

docs.title: Global custom MCP servers
docs.text:
The files under $CORTEX_HOME/config/mcp-config*.json describe Cortex's global and session-composed MCP layers. They are rewritten at server startup, so direct edits are temporary. A persistent global server requires an explicit builder and privilege-composition change in agent-server/src/core/config-generator.ts; it does not belong in an assignment-scoped plugin.

This distinction keeps global Cortex privileges separate from administrator-installed plugin capabilities. Use a portable plugin when the server should follow environment assignment, and change the global builders only when every eligible session composition should receive the server.

docs.title: Permission model
docs.text:
MCP tools cross the trust boundary from the agent process into agent-server internals and remote machines. Installed plugins are administrator-trusted code. For portable root mcp.json, the assignment confirmation makes the capability addition explicit, but it is not a sandbox or a separate authorization boundary. Legacy Claude-native MCP configuration remains outside that confirmation. Cortex applies the following controls:

  1. Registration-level availability — the bundled Cortex server registers only the logical surfaces selected for that session, and an optional canonical tool allowlist filters them further. Top-level sessions receive core and ext tools, user-initiated sessions add the interaction tools, a team lead adds the worker tools, a worker adds mark_routine, and the session's platform adds its delivery tools. Subagents receive no delegation tools.

  2. A separate Claude configuration — every Claude process Cortex starts runs with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$CORTEX_HOME/data/claude, so MCP servers and plugins configured for your terminal's Claude Code (~/.claude) are not part of a Cortex session. An execution environment's settingSources can narrow which settings files Claude reads further. Claude-native .mcp.json inside an explicitly assigned legacy plugin directory is still loaded by Claude.

  3. Bypass permissions — Claude Code is spawned with --dangerously-skip-permissions --permission-mode bypassPermissions, meaning it won't prompt for each MCP tool call. Access control happens at the MCP tool implementation level, through agent:pre-tool hooks, and through the server's webhook token.

  4. Network boundary — MCP tools that talk to remote machines go through the client-manager's WebSocket layer. Only devices registered in machines.json can connect, and only devices with an active WebSocket connection can receive commands.

docs.title: Environment variables passed to MCP servers
docs.text:
The bundled Cortex server builds its per-session context from these variables. Under Claude they are set in the environment of the stdio child; under PI the same values are passed to the in-process server directly.

Variable Source Used by SLACK_CHANNEL, FEISHU_CHANNEL The session's channel Platform-bundle selection, interaction tools, file delivery, subagent and team routing SLACK_BOT_TOKEN Server environment cortex-slack (slack_send_file) CORTEX_SESSION_ID Session context Interaction tools, cortex_context, waitpoints, Web delivery CORTEX_PROJECT, CORTEX_BACKEND, CORTEX_MODEL, CORTEX_PROVIDER, CORTEX_THINKING, CORTEX_MODE Session context cortex_context CORTEX_SCHEDULE_TASK_ID, CORTEX_CALLBACK_SOURCE Set for scheduled or callback-triggered runs cortex_context CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN, WEBHOOK_PORT Server environment Every tool that calls the loopback webhook CORTEX_MCP_BUNDLES Backend process composition Bundle selection in the bundled server CORTEX_MCP_TOOL_ALLOWLIST Agent role or subagent spawn Tool registration filter CORTEX_CLAUDE_MODEL, CORTEX_SUBAGENT_PI_MODELS, CORTEX_SUBAGENT_CLAUDE_MODELS Session model and model catalog The agent and worker_spawn model descriptions PLUGIN_ROOT Resolved selected plugin root Portable stdio plugin servers PLUGIN_DATA Private persistent per-plugin data directory Portable stdio plugin servers

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
MCP tools give the agent the ability to execute shell commands on remote machines, read and write files, delegate to subagents and workers, and post to the chat platforms. The security posture assumes:

  • The cortex-client WebSocket port (3002) requires CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN on every connection, and is still best kept off the public internet: use Tailscale, a VPN, a tunnel, or localhost-only binding (see cross-machine.md for network topology options).
  • The webhook HTTP port (3001) is bound to 127.0.0.1 only and requires CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN — MCP servers talk to it via loopback, not over the network.
  • The agent operates within the same blast-radius safety boundaries documented in safety-and-approvals.md. MCP tools do not exempt a high-privilege operation from that boundary.

docs.title: Cortex Memory System
docs.text: Cortex stores all knowledge on the filesystem as atomized, indexed markdown files — the Dense Context structure. There is no vector database, no RAG pipeline, and no external knowledge store. The filesystem is the database. For how this fits into the broader system architecture, see architecture.md.

docs.title: Why Atomized Memory
docs.text:
The core insight is that monolithic context files don't scale. A single EXPERIMENTS.md file grows unboundedly, making it expensive to load into agent context and hard to search. The solution is to atomize each experiment, knowledge entry, and pattern into its own file, with auto-generated indexes for fast lookup.

This design draws from academic work: Du 2026's survey of agent memory patterns, QMatSuite's layered knowledge hierarchy (finding → pattern → principle), and A-MEM's atomic notes with dynamic linking (< 4μs retrieval time at 1M memories).

docs.title: Directory Layout
docs.text:
The knowledge root is ~/.cortex/context/, structured as follows:

context/
├── AGENTS.md                    # Root index — entry point for finding anything
├── OVERVIEW.md                  # Global overview: one-line status per project + last scan date
├── decisions/                   # System-level design decisions (NNNN-title.md)
├── ideas/                       # Incubating research directions
├── scans/                       # Knowledge scan reports, one per date
├── user/                        # User preferences (maintained by /user-learn)
│   └── USER.md                  # Language, style, working habits (< 3KB)
└── projects/                    # One subdirectory per active research project
    └── <project>/
        ├── AGENTS.md            # Project-level index
        ├── mission.md           # Goal and success conditions
        ├── roadmap.md           # Milestones with testable checklist conditions
        ├── STATUS.md            # Present-tense state register (overwriting, max 80 lines / 6KB)
        ├── ISSUES.md            # Execution friction (append-only, resolved items deleted, max 80 lines / 6KB)
        ├── boards/              # One directory per board: board.html, assets/, decisions.jsonl
        ├── experiments/
        │   ├── index.md         # Auto-generated — do not edit manually
        │   └── EXP-NNN.md       # One file per experiment, YAML frontmatter
        ├── knowledge/
        │   ├── index.md         # Auto-generated
        │   └── K-NNN.md         # One file per knowledge entry
        ├── patterns/
        │   ├── index.md         # Auto-generated
        │   └── PAT-NNN.md       # One file per cross-experiment pattern
        ├── decisions/           # Project-level design decisions
        └── _meta/
            └── access-log.jsonl # Auto-tracked Read/Grep access log

cortex init seeds the root AGENTS.md and the indexes of ideas/, scans/, user/ and projects/. The other files and directories appear as Cortex creates them: OVERVIEW.md and decisions/ when there is something to record, USER.md from the user-learn skill, and each project's files from the project-init skill and the work that follows.

docs.title: Experiments (EXP-NNN.md)
docs.text:
Each experiment is an atomic file recording a single investigation. An experiment records what was done, what was observed, what was concluded, and what should change going forward.

YAML frontmatter:

---
id: EXP-NNN
date: 2026-01-15
project: my-project
summary: "Baseline success rate with the default controller"
tags: [baseline, grasping, evaluation]
status: valid
executor: Cortex
links: [PAT-NNN]
---

Required fields: id, date, project, summary (at most 300 characters), tags. The index generator skips a file without id; the other fields are convention, checked by the agent rather than the code.

Optional fields: status, executor, links (related entries).

Frontmatter is parsed as YAML, so quote any list item that contains a comma, a colon followed by a space, or braces: evidence: ["log.txt (55 configs, 10 seeds)", "run{1,2}/metrics.json"].

Body structure: The markdown body follows a standard template with sections: Background, Execution, Results, Conclusion, and Reflection (goal attainment, unexpected findings, process defects, behavioral adjustments).

Status lifecycle: experiments, knowledge entries and patterns share one status field. A status that points at another entry names it after a colon, such as superseded:EXP-012, and the index generator classifies a status by its prefix.

Status Meaning Index table active, valid, partial, or empty Normal, conclusions stand Active challenged:EXP-NNN Questioned by a newer experiment, pending review Active, and listed in Stats corrected:EXP-NNN Conclusion was corrected Active superseded:EXP-NNN Replaced by a better version Superseded / Deprecated deprecated No longer applies Superseded / Deprecated refined:EXP-NNN Fully replaced by an improved version Superseded / Deprecated stale No references for a long time, pending review Superseded / Deprecated invalidated:EXP-NNN Proven wrong; the body is replaced with a tombstone warning Invalidated

Any other status counts as active.

docs.title: Knowledge Entries (K-NNN.md)
docs.text:
Knowledge entries are atomic facts, anti-patterns, or heuristics distilled from experiments. Each must cite its source experiments in the evidence field.

YAML frontmatter:

---
id: K-NNN
date: 2026-02-01
project: my-project
summary: "ANTI-PATTERN: Comparing success rates across runs that used different random seeds and episode counts"
tags: [anti-pattern, evaluation, reproducibility]
evidence: [EXP-NNN, EXP-NNN, EXP-NNN]
---

Required fields: id, date, project, summary, tags, evidence.

Anti-pattern convention: Knowledge entries describing anti-patterns prefix the summary with ANTI-PATTERN: and include anti-pattern in tags.

docs.title: Patterns (PAT-NNN.md)
docs.text:
Patterns synthesize invariants across multiple experiments. A pattern states a reusable observation that holds across a cluster of experiments.

YAML frontmatter:

---
id: PAT-NNN
date: 2026-02-01
project: my-project
summary: "Policies trained with domain randomization lose less success rate when moved from simulation to the real robot"
tags: [sim-to-real, domain-randomization, transfer]
source-experiments: [EXP-NNN, EXP-NNN, EXP-NNN]
evidence: [EXP-NNN, EXP-NNN, EXP-NNN]
---

Required fields: id, date, project, summary, tags, source-experiments (the experiments the pattern was extracted from).

Body structure: Observation, Evidence (table citing experiments with specific findings), Pattern Statement, Scope & Limitations, Implications.

docs.title: Index Auto-Generation
docs.text:
Each directory under a project (experiments/, knowledge/, patterns/) has an index.md generated from the frontmatter of its atom files and the project's access log. The index opens with a # <Directory> Index — <project> heading and a Use when line, followed by the warning:

> Auto-generated from YAML frontmatter; Refs / Last ref come from _meta/access-log.jsonl. Do not edit manually. Not tracked by git.
> Last updated: 2026-02-15T09:00:00

The generator only reads the atom files; it never rewrites them. The server regenerates a project's indexes about two seconds after any .md file in one of its memory directories changes (projects created while the server runs are picked up as they appear), and the built-in regeneration job rebuilds every index on a schedule.

Index structure:

  • Active table — every active entry (see the status table above), sorted by reference count (descending), with its reference count and last access date
  • Superseded / Deprecated table — superseded, deprecated, refined and stale entries
  • Invalidated table — tombstoned entries proven wrong
  • Stats section — total counts, challenged entries under review, hot entries (refs >= 5), cold entries (refs = 0, age > 14 days), and any atom file whose frontmatter is not valid YAML (it is still indexed, read key by key, and should be fixed)

Rebuild command:

# For all projects
cortex memory regen

# For a specific project
cortex memory regen --project <project-name>

--project can be repeated, and an unknown project name is an error. The command prints JSON listing each project with the paths of its regenerated indexes.

docs.title: Access Tracking
docs.text:
Cortex automatically tracks which experiment, knowledge, and pattern files are accessed during research. This is implemented as the built-in memory-ref-tracker.mjs hook on agent:post-tool (see hooks.md for the full hook system).

How it works:

  1. After every Read or Grep tool call, the hook checks if the accessed file path matches the pattern /(experiments|knowledge|patterns)/(EXP-\d+[a-z]?|K-\d+|PAT-\d+)\.md$/
  2. If matched, it extracts the project name from the path and appends a JSON line to _meta/access-log.jsonl: 
    {"file":"EXP-NNN.md","tool":"Read","ts":"2026-02-15T09:00:00.000Z"}
  3. A Grep is tracked when its search path lies inside a project's experiments/, knowledge/ or patterns/ directory. The hook appends one line for each distinct atom file named in the output
  4. If such a Grep names no atom file, it records _directory_search instead
  5. When CORTEX_HOME is a git repository, the hook commits the access log with message chore: update access log; if other changes are already staged, it stages the log without committing

Reference counts exist only in the generated indexes: each rebuild counts a file's lines in the access log, so a file that is frequently read during research gets a higher count and appears higher in the index. Older atom files may still carry refs: and last-ref: frontmatter fields; nothing maintains or reads them.

docs.title: Project Log Files
docs.text: Each project has a set of governance files that together form its operational memory:

docs.title: mission.md — The Constitution
docs.text: Defines the project's goal, success conditions, and scope boundaries. This file is stable and should only change with explicit user approval. It answers: what are we trying to achieve, and how will we know we've succeeded?

docs.title: roadmap.md — Milestone Map
docs.text: Layered phases, each containing milestones with testable checklist conditions. Completed milestones are preserved with checkmarks (not deleted). The roadmap shows where the project has been, where it is now, and where it's going.

docs.title: STATUS.md — Current Snapshot
docs.text: An overwriting (not append-only) state register capturing the project's present tense — the minimal state a fresh session needs to continue correctly. Hard-capped at 80 lines and 6KB, with each bullet at most 2 lines. Required sections: current situation, in-flight work & new variables, blockers & pending decisions, next step. Facts that have a durable home elsewhere (experiments, knowledge entries, decision records, commits) appear only as pointers; the file grows with state complexity, never with project age. Updated when the situation changes — not on every task completion. This is the first file to read when resuming work on a project after a gap.

docs.title: ISSUES.md — Execution Friction
docs.text: An append-only log of problems that slow work, capped at 80 lines and 6KB with each entry at most 4 lines. An entry is a dated title, a one-line symptom, and a one-line root cause with a pointer to the detailed investigation (knowledge entry, report, or experiment record). Resolved issues are deleted from the file (not archived).

docs.title: decisions/ — Decision Records
docs.text: Each decision is one file named NNNN-title.md, headed # DR-NNNN: <Title>. System-level decisions live in context/decisions/, project decisions in the project's decisions/, and each level numbers its records from 0001. A record lists Date, Status (accepted, rejected, or superseded), an optional Supersedes, and Evidence, followed by the sections Context, Options Considered (at least two), Decision, and Consequences.

docs.title: Dense Context Conventions
docs.text:
The Dense Context system follows these operational conventions:

  1. Every directory has an AGENTS.md index — describing the directory's purpose, file list, and lookup rules. Indexes are pointer-style (one sentence + pointer per line, one line per atomic directory) and hard-capped at 120 lines and 8KB, matching the context-injection budget. The shipped status-md-guard hook rejects an Edit or Write that would push a context AGENTS.md, a STATUS.md or an ISSUES.md past its cap; a write that shrinks an oversized file is allowed
  2. Create file → update index — when adding a new file to a directory, update that directory's AGENTS.md
  3. Overwrite vs. append — STATUS.md overwrites (only current state); ISSUES.md appends then deletes; experiments/knowledge/patterns append and stay
  4. Provenance is mandatory — every factual claim must trace to a specific EXP-NNN, K-NNN, file:line, or inline calculation
  5. Persist after each work unit — save context updates to disk after each logical work unit. Git history is optional

docs.title: Who Loads AGENTS.md
docs.text:
AGENTS.md is the name both supported backends already look for, so most of the time Cortex does not inject anything — the backend does it.

Where the file sits Claude Code PI Loaded by An ancestor of the session working directory yes yes the backend A subdirectory of the working directory, when a file there is read yes no the backend on Claude, the agents-md-injector hook on PI Outside the working directory tree no no the agents-md-injector hook AGENTS.local.md, anywhere no no the agents-md-injector hook On a remote device, via remote_read / remote_write / remote_edit no no the cortex-client scanner, injected as extra tool-result blocks

Sessions run in the Cortex home directory by default, so ~/.cortex/AGENTS.md and every index under context/ is an ancestor or a subdirectory of the working directory and arrives natively. The hook exists for the remaining rows, and it records what the backend already loaded in a shared per-session cache so the same rules are never delivered twice.

Two consequences worth knowing:

  • A CLAUDE.md anywhere in the ancestor chain switches Claude's AGENTS.md fallback off completely — it is an all-or-nothing choice governed by the claude-md-or-agents-md setting, not a per-directory merge. The hook detects this and resumes injecting so no rules are lost, but mixing the two names in one tree is still best avoided.
  • Neither backend reads a .local variant. AGENTS.local.md is a Cortex-only convention for machine-specific rules, delivered by the hook and kept out of git.

docs.title: Browsing Memory in the Workbench
docs.text: The Web workbench shows a project's memory read-only. On desktop, View → Memory or Open in the Project memory section of the project's Overview opens it; the section also lists the memory files that changed most recently. On a phone, it is Project memory in the Projects panel. It lists mission.md, roadmap.md, STATUS.md, and the files in experiments/, knowledge/, patterns/ and decisions/ (without the generated index.md) and renders the selected file. On desktop the file reads as a document — its frontmatter becomes a property line, a title and the summary, and a wide pane lists the file's sections beside it — and, when the project is in a git work tree, the view shows how many lines differ from HEAD; Changes, next to Read in the header, shows the latest change behind each line.

docs.title: Fresh Session Test
docs.text: The acid test for Dense Context quality: if you start a fresh session with only read access to the repo, can you learn everything the previous session knew? If the answer is no, something wasn't recorded properly.

docs.title: Memory Index Regeneration Job
docs.text:
The built-in memory-index regeneration job rebuilds all index files from YAML frontmatter. memoryIndexRegenEnabled (default true) and memoryIndexRegenIntervalMs (default 24 hours) in config/settings.json control it. The job:

  1. Scans all projects under context/projects/
  2. Reads frontmatter from every EXP-*.md, K-*.md, and PAT-*.md
  3. Counts references per file from _meta/access-log.jsonl
  4. Writes each index.md atomically, leaving the atom files untouched

docs.title: Lifecycle: Knowledge Maintenance
docs.text:
cortex memory consolidate reviews every project's experiments, knowledge entries and patterns and reports what needs attention. It prints JSON, or a readable summary with --text, and changes no files. It reports:

  • Consolidation candidates — experiments that share tags or link to each other closely enough to merge, and chains of supersessions
  • Contradictions — knowledge entries and patterns whose evidence experiments are invalidated, superseded or deprecated, marked as fully or partially compromised
  • Stale candidates — active entries older than 30 days with no references in the access log
  • Anti-pattern signals — process deficiencies that recur across experiments' reflections

docs.title: Scale
docs.text: Index rebuilds stay cheap as projects grow. A rebuild parses only each file's YAML frontmatter, so regenerating every project's indexes at once — each project holding tens of experiments and a handful of knowledge entries and patterns — finishes in under a second.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
From zero to a Cortex agent answering you in chat in about 5 minutes, most of which is waiting for npm and clicking through your chat platform's app creation page.

Cortex talks to you through Slack or Feishu (飞书/Lark) — pick either, or run both at once. cortex init does almost everything. You will not edit a single config file by hand. This guide tells you what to expect at each prompt and shows you exactly where to click.

docs.title: Prefer not to use a terminal?
docs.text:
The desktop app can install and configure Cortex for you on macOS, Linux, and Windows. Choose Install Cortex and wait for installation and startup to finish automatically, then sign in and select a default model. New installations use the hostname, port 3004, and no login service; existing machine, port, and service settings are preserved. Only a failed initialization or start/connection offers repair settings. Slack and Feishu setup is skipped — the app is the interface. Login may open your browser for authorization or MFA, and macOS may require Gatekeeper approval when opening the app.

The installer carries its own Node.js and, on Windows, Git Bash, so no terminal, separately installed Node.js or Git, Homebrew, or administrator access is needed. Local installation supports macOS 13.5+, Linux x86_64 with glibc 2.28+, and Windows 10/11 x86_64; see the desktop guide for details. Continue below for terminal installation and chat-platform setup.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The following requirements and commands apply to terminal installation.

  • Node.js ≥ 22.19.0, required by the PI SDK included with the server.
  • A Slack workspace or a Feishu (Lark) organization where you can create an app.
  • About 2 GB of free disk for backends, plugins, and logs.

You do not need to install a coding agent beforehand. The PI engine ships inside the Cortex server package. Claude Code is optional; choosing its login flow offers installation if it is missing. You do not need to install Git on macOS/Linux. cortex init creates the directories and env files, and initializes version history only when usable Git is already installed. Git-based history and Git-sourced extensions require Git; Windows shell tools require Git Bash.

docs.title: Checking your Node.js version
docs.text:
Open a terminal and run:

node --version

You should see something like v22.19.0. If the version is below 22.19.0, or if you see command not found: node, install or upgrade Node.js using one of the methods below.

docs.title: Installing Node.js
docs.text:
macOS (Homebrew):

brew install node@22

Linux (nvm, recommended):

curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.3/install.sh | bash
# Restart your shell, then:
nvm install 22
nvm use 22

Linux (apt, only if your repository provides Node ≥22.19.0):

sudo apt update && sudo apt install nodejs npm

Windows:

Download the LTS installer from nodejs.org (choose an LTS version ≥22.19.0). Run the .msi installer and follow the prompts. After installation, restart your terminal.

Verify the installation:

node --version   # must print v22.19.0 or later
npm --version    # should print 10.x.y or later

docs.title: Step 1 — Install Cortex
docs.text:
npm install -g @cortex-agent/server

This puts the cortex command on your PATH, along with three helpers: cortex-signal, cortex-hook, and cortex-evidence-export.

If npm install -g fails with a permission error (common on Linux), prefix with sudo, or better, configure npm to use a user-local prefix:

mkdir -p ~/.npm-global
npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global
echo 'export PATH=~/.npm-global/bin:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
npm install -g @cortex-agent/server

docs.title: Step 2 — Run the setup wizard
docs.text:
cortex init

The wizard walks through the following prompts. Defaults are sensible; hit Enter to accept. Here is what each prompt does and how to answer.

docs.title: 2.1 Which language?
docs.text:
Select language / 选择语言
❯ English
  中文 (Simplified Chinese)

The first prompt picks the language Cortex uses for its system-generated messages and for the rest of this wizard. It defaults to your system locale, so a Chinese system pre-selects 中文. The choice is saved to config/preferences.json and you can change it later with the !lang command.

docs.title: 2.2 Bundled PI and optional Claude Code
docs.text:
Interactive cortex init uses PI by default without a backend-selection prompt. PI ships inside Cortex and needs provider credentials, not a separate installation. Continue with platform and machine settings; provider detection and login follow after configuration files are written in section 2.10.

Claude Code is optional and separate from the Anthropic provider in PI. Choosing Claude Code in the login step reuses an existing installation or asks permission to install it if missing.

docs.title: 2.3 Which interaction platform(s)?
docs.text:
? Which interaction platform(s) would you like to use? (space to toggle,
  enter to confirm, leave empty to skip)
❯ ◯ Slack (recommended)
  ◯ Feishu (飞书)

This is a multi-select. Toggle with space, confirm with Enter. Pick Slack, Feishu, or both — Cortex composes the platforms you choose and connects to all of them at once. Each platform you select triggers its own credential-collection steps below (Slack first, then Feishu).

Leaving the selection empty skips platform setup. You can configure a platform later by editing $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env and restarting the server.

docs.title: 2.4 Slack app setup (step by step in the browser)
docs.text:
Skip this section if you did not select Slack.

Cortex first prints a complete Slack App Manifest and asks if you want it copied to your clipboard. Press c — the manifest JSON is now in your clipboard.

docs.title: a) Open the Slack API apps page
docs.text: Go to https://api.slack.com/apps.

docs.title: b) Create a new app from manifest
docs.text: Click the green Create New App button, then click From a manifest. If you don't have a workspace yet, create one first.

docs.title: c) Pick your workspace and paste the manifest
docs.text:
1. Select your Slack workspace from the dropdown.
  2. Paste the manifest JSON into the text area (Ctrl+V / Cmd+V). The manifest was copied to your clipboard by cortex init, so just paste.
  3. Click Next.
  4. Review the summary and click Create.

docs.title: d) Copy the Signing Secret
docs.text:
After creation, Slack drops you on the app's Basic Information page. Under App Credentials, find the Signing Secret. Click Show and copy it.

Back in your terminal, paste this as SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET.

docs.title: e) Generate the App-Level Token (xapp-…)
docs.text:
Scroll down on the same Basic Information page to the App-Level Tokens section. Click Generate Token and Scopes.

  • Token Name: cortex-socket
  • Add Scope: connections:write
  • Click Generate

Copy the token that appears (starts with xapp-). It only shows once — copy it now.

Back in your terminal, paste this as SLACK_APP_TOKEN.

docs.title: f) Install to Workspace and copy the Bot Token (xoxb-…)
docs.text:
In the left sidebar, click OAuth & Permissions. Scroll up to the OAuth Tokens section and click Install to Workspace. On the authorization screen, click Allow.

After installation, the page shows a Bot User OAuth Token at the top (starts with xoxb-). Copy it.

Back in your terminal, paste this as SLACK_BOT_TOKEN.

docs.title: g) Enable the Messages Tab
docs.text:
In the left sidebar, click App Home. Scroll down to the Show Tabs section:

  • Check Messages Tab (so it appears in the bot's App Home).
  • Check Allow users to send Slash commands and messages from the messages tab (so you can DM the bot).

Without this checkbox, you can @cortex the bot in channels but you cannot send it DMs.

docs.title: h) Admin channel
docs.text:
Cortex sends startup notices, approval requests, and other operational messages to an admin channel. There is nothing to enter during setup — Cortex auto-detects the admin channel the first time you DM the bot and persists it.

If you'd rather route admin messages to a specific channel (e.g., a shared ops channel), grab the channel ID from Slack — right-click the channel name → View channel details → copy the Channel ID from the bottom of the dialog — and set the adminChannel key in $CORTEX_HOME/config/settings.json (see configuration.md). The legacy SLACK_ADMIN_CHANNEL / CORTEX_ADMIN_CHANNEL variables in .env still work as a deprecated fallback.

docs.title: 2.5 Feishu app setup (step by step in the browser)
docs.text: Skip this section if you did not select Feishu. Cortex prints a setup guide and then collects your app credentials.

docs.title: a) Create a Feishu app
docs.text: Go to https://open.feishu.cn/app and click Create Agentic App（创建 agentic 应用）. Enter an agent name (e.g. CortexAgent), pick an avatar, and click Create.

docs.title: b) Copy the App ID and App Secret
docs.text:
After creation, the app page displays the App ID and App Secret. Copy them.

Back in your terminal, paste them at the FEISHU_APP_ID and FEISHU_APP_SECRET prompts.

docs.title: c) Subscribe to message events
docs.text: In the app's event configuration, enable bot events and subscribe to im.message.receive_v1. Without this subscription the bot never receives your messages.

docs.title: d) Domain (optional)
docs.text:
? FEISHU_DOMAIN (optional, "feishu" or "lark"):
  feishu (leave blank to use default)

Enter feishu for the Feishu (mainland China) domain or lark for the international Lark domain. Leave it blank to use the default.

docs.title: e) Identity for document operations
docs.text:
? Identity for MCP document operations:
  bot   — documents owned by the app
❯ user (Recommended) — documents owned by your Feishu account

Cortex's MCP tools can create and edit Feishu documents (docx, wiki, bitable, sheets, drive). This prompt decides who owns those documents. Choosing bot makes the app the owner. Choosing user makes your own Feishu account the owner, which keeps documents in your personal space — this is the recommended choice.

If you pick user, cortex init immediately runs the Feishu user login (an OAuth device flow) so you authorize in one sitting. It prints a URL — open it in any browser, approve access, and Cortex polls for the token automatically. No redirect URI is needed. If you skip or abandon the login, your credentials are still saved and you can authorize later with cortex feishu login.

docs.title: 2.6 Machine name
docs.text: Defaults to your hostname. Hit Enter unless you want a custom label.

docs.title: 2.7 GPU detection
docs.text: Cortex runs nvidia-smi and prints the count. Nothing to type. If you don't have an NVIDIA GPU, it prints 0 — perfectly fine for most usage.

docs.title: 2.8 aistatus token-usage reporting?
docs.text:
Optional, and the prompt defaults to yes. Answering yes puts your token usage on the public aistatus.cc leaderboard, which shows your name, organization, and token counts; answer no to stay off it. If you join, provide a name and an email; the organization is optional. The email only identifies you and is never displayed.

The same choice appears as an optional Public usage leaderboard card on the desktop app's provider setup page, and you can turn it on or off at any time under Settings → Usage. Turning it off keeps your name, organization, and email for the next time you turn it on.

docs.title: 2.9 Register as a system service?
docs.text:
• macOS — creates a launchd plist at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/cc.cortex.agent-server.plist. The daemon starts automatically on login after you run the printed enable command.
  • Linux — creates a systemd --user unit (no sudo needed). The daemon starts automatically on login after you run the printed enable command. To keep it running after you log out, also run loginctl enable-linger.
  • Windows — not supported. Start manually with cortex daemon.

docs.title: 2.10 Detect credentials, sign in, and configure models
docs.text:
After writing the configuration files, Cortex automatically detects local Claude Code and PI credentials. This is credential detection, not a live inference test: it makes no paid inference request and does not guarantee that a model call will succeed.

The terminal offers these actions:

  • Continue with configured providers — shown once credentials are detected. Uses them to configure gateway routes and models.json from the discovered endpoints. Choose one default model (the recommended model is preselected), then select favorites. The default model is included among favorites even if you deselect it in this step.
  • Login / install and login Claude Code — choose a backend, provider, and supported OAuth or API-key method. PI is bundled. Claude Code is reused if installed; only choosing its login path prompts to install a missing copy. Login returns to credential detection.
  • Rescan credentials — detects credentials again, for example ones configured in another terminal, and returns to this menu.
  • Configure later (Agent may be unavailable) — finishes setup without configuring providers; the Agent stays unavailable until credentials and a default model are configured.

You can also sign in from a terminal without a running daemon:

cortex auth login
cortex auth login --backend pi --provider anthropic --auth-type api_key
cortex auth login --backend claude --provider anthropic --auth-type oauth
cortex auth status

Login requires an interactive TTY. Keys and authorization responses are prompted, never passed as command arguments. The command writes its JSON result to stdout and human prompts and instructions to stderr. cortex auth login --help lists the options. See the CLI reference.

With --answers <file> or --json, init detects credentials and reports status without starting provider login or waiting for input. Omitted backends defaults to PI; explicit backends answers retain their supplied selection and installation behavior. These runs can finish without a configured provider. Sign in later with cortex auth login or Settings → Accounts; a successful cortex auth login also configures the gateway routes, default model, and favorites. cortex setup-gateway runs that configuration again on its own. Remote login is also available through !login in Slack or Feishu; see Backends: Remote login.

For non-interactive model choices, --answers accepts defaultChoice and favorites, each choice an object with mode and model. An explicit defaultChoice replaces the saved default; otherwise it is preserved. Favorites are merged, with the selected default included. In the positional stdin protocol, the model-selection tail is two lines: mode:model for the default, followed by comma-separated mode:model favorites.

docs.title: 2.11 When the backend login expires
docs.text:
Backend credentials expire after a while. When they do, agent runs fail with an authentication error such as:

Failed to authenticate. API Error: 401 OAuth access token has expired.
Re-authenticate to continue.

Sign in again with cortex auth login, or use !login in Slack or Feishu or Settings → Accounts. Claude Code also supports claude plus /login.

Cortex also notices this for you. When a running agent hits expired authentication, it posts a card naming the provider with a one-click re-login button, and a daily scan warns about credentials that are close to expiring.

Once the login finishes, the refreshed credentials are picked up on the next agent run. If the endpoint or model changed, re-run cortex setup-gateway to refresh the gateway and model list, then choose the desired default in Settings → Models. Sync preserves an existing default.

When the wizard finishes you will see:

Cortex initialized at /home/you/.cortex. Run `cortex daemon` to launch.

docs.title: What cortex init created
docs.text:
Everything lives under CORTEX_HOME (default ~/.cortex/):

~/.cortex/
├── .git/                       # optional: created when usable Git is installed
├── .gitignore                  # keeps runtime state and secrets out of history
├── AGENTS.md                   # root agent context (seeded from defaults)
├── config/
│   ├── .env                    # CORTEX_PLATFORM list + platform tokens + CORTEX_MACHINE
│   ├── feishu-user-token.json  # Feishu user-identity token (only when FEISHU_AUTH_MODE=user)
│   ├── preferences.json        # operator UI language
│   ├── budget.json             # daily/monthly budget limits
│   ├── machines.json           # this machine's capabilities (gpuCount, path)
│   ├── mcp-config.json         # direct-session MCP servers
│   ├── mcp-config-core.json    # remote execution/time layer
│   ├── mcp-config-empty.json   # no MCP servers
│   ├── mcp-config-interaction.json # Shared interaction layer
│   ├── models.json             # default engine and favorites, once credentials are detected
│   └── environments/           # execution environments: main.json, creative.json
├── data/
│   ├── agent-state.json        # channel selections, model memory, new-session choice, default agent
│   └── schedules.json          # seeded built-in schedules
├── context/                    # the project log lives here
│   ├── AGENTS.md, projects/, decisions/, scans/, ideas/, retrospectives/, user/
├── plugins/                    # your plugins (built-in ones are read from the install)
├── prompts/                    # your directives, system prompts, templates
├── hooks/                      # your hook scripts (.mjs)
├── .claude/                    # Claude Code settings
└── logs/                       # daemon + LLM logs

You should not need to edit any of these by hand for normal use. Running cortex init again leaves an existing .env, machines.json, agent state, language preferences, schedules, and budget untouched, and regenerates the MCP configs. cortex init --force resets machines.json, agent state, language preferences, schedules, and budget, and updates the keys init writes in .env while keeping the existing client and webhook tokens and any keys you added by hand. Existing execution environments and scaffold files are preserved either way. Interactive setup asks before replacing an existing default model; favorites are merged with the saved list. Back up customized files before using --force. To add a platform to a working install, add its keys to .env and restart the daemon (see 2.3).

Cortex's built-in plugins, hooks, rules, subagent roles and system prompts are read from the install, not copied here, so plugins/, prompts/ and hooks/ start empty. A file you put there replaces the built-in one of the same name or adds a new one; see Built-in assets and your overrides.

~/.aistatus/ separately holds:

~/.aistatus/
├── gateway.yaml                # gateway routing config (generated once credentials are detected)
└── config.yaml                 # aistatus uploader settings (your name/org/email)

docs.title: Step 3 — Start the server
docs.text:
cortex daemon         # supervised in the background, restarts on crash + hot-reload
# or
cortex start          # foreground, Ctrl-C to stop

cortex daemon returns at once and leaves the server running in the background; cortex daemon stop stops it.

If you chose to register a system service in Step 2.9, init writes the service file and prints its enable command. Run that command to start it:

# Linux user service
systemctl --user enable --now cortex
# macOS
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/cc.cortex.agent-server.plist

Check the daemon with cortex daemon status. cortex config shows resolved paths and initialization status, and cortex doctor checks the runtime, login, platform, and gateway (--fix repairs what it can).

docs.title: Open the Web workbench
docs.text:
The browser workbench and the desktop and Android apps connect to the server's Web UI endpoint, which terminal setup leaves off. Turn it on with:

cortex ui enable
cortex daemon restart   # only if the daemon is already running

cortex ui enable generates the client token if needed, sets CORTEX_UI_HTTP=1 and CORTEX_UI_PORT=3004 in $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env, allows the native apps' origins, and prints the local address. Open http://127.0.0.1:3004 in a browser on the server and sign in with the value of CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN from .env, or enter the same address and token in the desktop app. To reach the workbench from another computer, see Browser Access.

docs.title: Step 4 — Send your first messages
docs.text: Now the fun part. Open Slack or Feishu, find the Cortex bot you just installed, and start a direct message with it. In the Web workbench, send the same messages from the composer of a new session.

docs.title: 4.1 Say hello
docs.text:
Send a DM to the bot:

hello

The first DM is what Cortex uses to auto-detect your admin channel (unless you set adminChannel explicitly in config/settings.json). You should get a reply within a few seconds.

docs.title: 4.2 Create your first project
docs.text:
Give Cortex a mission. Cortex will create the project, set up the directory structure, and confirm back to you:

create a project called "hello-world" — I want to build a
simple web dashboard that shows the weather in my city

Cortex replies with the project structure it created and what it understood the mission to be.

docs.title: 4.3 Check project status
docs.text:
status of hello-world

Cortex reads the project's STATUS.md, mission, and recent experiment records, then gives you a summary of where things stand.

When work runs on several workers or across many hours, Cortex opens a board in the Web UI: a status page beside the conversation with the task's state, plan, and decisions. You can also ask for one. See Boards.

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• The Slack app setup failed, or you want to do it before running cortex init — read slack-setup.md.
  • You want to know every config file and env var Cortex understands, or override one of the auto-generated paths — read configuration.md.
  • You want to know every CLI subcommand and flag — read cli-reference.md.
  • You want to switch backends or add another provider — read backends.md.
  • You want Cortex to hand work to subagents, or to lead persistent worker sessions — read backends.md and team.md.
  • You want to connect remote machines to Cortex — read cross-machine.md.
  • You want to understand the project log structure (experiments, knowledge, patterns) — read memory.md.

docs.title: Safety and Approvals
docs.text: Cortex can edit files, spawn processes, manage GPU training, and talk to multiple machines. Its safety model has four parts: a written safety boundary that tells the agent what it may do on its own, a queue for operations that need your sign-off, interactive cards for plan approval and questions, and a small set of mechanical guards around the server's own interfaces. The interactive cards run over the hook-bridge (see hooks.md) and the interaction MCP tools (see mcp.md).

docs.title: The three blast-radius classes
docs.text:
A safety boundary sorts agent operations into three classes. It is written in the root AGENTS.md of your Cortex home ($CORTEX_HOME/AGENTS.md), which every session loads, so it is guidance the agent follows rather than a check the server performs. The AGENTS.md that cortex init writes has no safety section; you add one in your own words. The judgment criterion that works best is behavioral impact, not file category: fixing a typo in a skill file and adding a new workflow step to it are different classes of operation even though both touch the same file.

A typical boundary, taken from a working installation, looks like this.

docs.title: Self-serve (autonomous)
docs.text:
Operations the agent performs without asking: read-only information gathering, local state updates, and low-risk maintenance.

  • Read files, check GPU status, read logs, run small test scripts
  • Update context files (STATUS.md, experiments/, knowledge/, OVERVIEW.md)
  • Web search, knowledge scans
  • Start training runs within budget, run analysis scripts
  • Skill maintenance changes (typo fixes, format alignment, description rewording — no behavioral change)
  • Agent-server non-behavioral fixes (syntax errors, log messages, comment updates)

docs.title: Needs approval (requires sign-off)
docs.text:
Operations that change system behavior, consume significant resources, or are hard to reverse. The agent writes them to the approval queue and leaves them unexecuted until you decide.

  • Modify AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.local.md
  • New skills or skill behavioral changes (new triggers, new workflow steps, capability expansion)
  • Agent-server behavioral or architectural changes (new features, protocol changes, API changes)
  • Over-budget training tasks, large-scale architecture modifications
  • Delete files or data
  • Modify model code or training configurations
  • Stop the Cortex server or daemon processes

docs.title: Forbidden (never permitted)
docs.text:
Operations the agent refuses even if you offer to approve them: system-level changes that could destabilize the machine.

  • Install system-level packages
  • Modify system configuration
  • rm -rf

docs.title: Classifying an edge case
docs.text:
Operation Class Reason Fix a typo in a skill's SKILL.md Self-serve Maintenance, no behavioral change Add a new workflow step to a skill Needs approval Changes behavioral logic Fix an agent-server syntax error Self-serve Non-behavioral fix Add new guard logic to agent-server Needs approval Changes behavior Start GPU training within budget Self-serve Within budget Modify AGENTS.md rules Needs approval System convention change

The boundary is advisory. Nothing in the server inspects a command before it runs: Claude Code is spawned with --dangerously-skip-permissions --permission-mode bypassPermissions, and PI runs its tools without a permission prompt. Budgets are advisory in the same way — budget.json limits are reported by cost_query and the UI, and no caller refuses work for exceeding them. The boundary holds because the agent reads it on every turn and because the queue below gives it a place to put what it should not do alone.

docs.title: How an operation reaches the queue
docs.text:
The approval queue is the Markdown file $CORTEX_HOME/context/PENDING_APPROVALS.md. An agent that judges an operation to need sign-off appends an entry and leaves the operation unexecuted. Each entry is a ## heading of the form <YYYY-MM-DD> <title> followed by bullet fields, with enough detail for you to decide without asking follow-up questions:

## 2026-10-14 Delete stale checkpoints on trainer
- **Operation**: Remove checkpoints older than 30 days under /data/ckpt
- **Reason**: The disk is 94% full and two runs are queued
- **Impact**: About 410 GB on trainer; no active run reads these files
- **Command/Action**: find /data/ckpt -mtime +30 -name '*.pt' -delete
- **Project**: nimbus
- **Status**: pending

Project is optional; an entry without one belongs to the global group. A free-form Provenance bullet may record where the request came from. The guiding principle is: when in doubt, queue it.

Settings also writes to this queue. Adding a machine or reconnecting a chat platform from Settings queues a request ("Queued for approval — review in the Approval Center") rather than performing the change from the browser. The file is created by the first entry written to it.

docs.title: In the Approval Center
docs.text:
On the desktop, a card with an amber dot at the foot of the left rail ("2 approvals pending") appears whenever the queue has pending entries, and opens the Approval Center. On a phone the same queue is the Approvals screen. Entries are grouped by project, with entries that name no project under GLOBAL, and each shows its operation, reason, impact and command.

Approving or rejecting there rewrites the entry's Status line — approved <date>, or rejected <date> (<feedback>) when you add feedback — and leaves every other line of the file untouched. The Approval Center records your decision; it does not run the operation or message a session. The operation is carried out by the agent that next works through the queue.

docs.title: Through the approval skill
docs.text: The approval skill (in the built-in cortex-system plugin) works through the queue inside a conversation, on any platform. Ask the agent to show pending approvals, or invoke the skill directly. It lists the pending entries with numbers and acts on replies such as approve 1, approve all, approve 1 3, reject 2, or approve 1 but change X to Y. For an approved entry the agent executes the operation, verifies the result, and records it.

docs.title: What happens after
docs.text:
Outcome Status line What the agent does Approved through the skill approved — executed <timestamp> Executes the operation and reports the result Approved in the Approval Center approved <date> Nothing until an agent acts on the decision Rejected rejected <timestamp>, optionally with feedback Does not execute; may propose an alternative Failed during execution failed — <reason> Reports the failure and keeps the entry

Resolved entries stay in the file as decision history. The Approval Center also treats a status that starts with resolved, deferred or superseded as decided, so an entry closed by hand stops counting as pending.

docs.title: Plan approval and questions
docs.text: Two interactions pause an agent until a person responds: approving a written plan, and answering a question. Both are MCP tools in the interaction bundle, which user-initiated sessions load on both backends (see mcp.md).

docs.title: Plan mode
docs.text:
cortex_plan_enter puts the agent into Cortex's planning protocol: it investigates read-only, writes the plan to a file under plan/, and does not implement anything until the plan is approved. The backends' native plan tools are disabled, so every plan goes through the same approval path and lands in the conversation's history.

cortex_plan_exit submits the plan file for approval and blocks until you decide:

  1. The tool reads plan_file_path and POSTs the plan to the server's loopback webhook at /hook/exit-plan-mode.
  2. The hook-bridge (agent-server/src/orchestration/routing/hook-bridge.ts) registers the request with a 30-minute TTL and publishes plan.submitted on the event bus.
  3. The subscriber (agent-server/src/orchestration/routing/hook-bridge-subscribers.ts) registers the plan and presents it on the session's platform.
  4. Your response resolves the pending request:
  5. Approve → the tool returns approval, plan.approved is published, and the agent proceeds.
  6. Reject with feedback → the tool returns your feedback and tells the agent to revise the plan and submit it again.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
cortex_ask_user poses one or more questions — single-choice, multi-choice, or free text — and takes an optional severity level (info, warning, error). It POSTs to /hook/ask-user-question, the bridge publishes ask-user.requested, and the subscriber presents the form.

A blocking question (the default) holds the tool call until you answer and returns the answers in its own result. With blocking: false the call returns as soon as the card is posted and the agent keeps working; your answer arrives in the session later as an ordinary user message, folded into the running turn if one is still live. An unanswered non-blocking card expires on the same TTL and never produces a message.

docs.title: Where the cards appear
docs.text:
Platform Plan approval Question Web UI and desktop An inline card in the chat with Approve plan and Request changes; requesting changes requires feedback and returns the plan for replanning An inline form; the agent continues after Submit answers Mobile The same cards, laid out for a phone The same form Slack The plan text, then a card with Approve and Provide Feedback; feedback opens a modal A summary with an Answer button that opens a modal form Feishu The plan text, then a card with Approve and Provide Feedback; feedback opens an inline form The form is posted inline in the chat

On the Web UI the card is part of the transcript, so its outcome — approved, rejected, answered, expired or cancelled — stays visible after a reload and on other devices. The first response wins wherever it comes from. A session blocked on a plan or a blocking question shows the amber marker in the session list, the one marker that means "waiting on you"; a non-blocking question leaves the session marked as running.

docs.title: Team mode
docs.text: A team worker that asks a question or submits a plan still shows its own card, and the request is also forwarded to its lead, which can answer with worker_answer. The first answer wins, whether it comes from the lead or from you on the worker's card. While the lead holds the request, the worker is shown as waiting on its lead rather than on you.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text: A pending plan or question expires after 30 minutes (the bridge sweeps every 5 minutes, so expiry lands between 30 and 35 minutes). A blocking call then returns a timeout to the agent; for a plan, the agent is told to revise and submit again. On the Web UI the card is marked expired.

docs.title: PI extension dialogs
docs.text: On PI, cortex_ask_user and cortex_plan_exit behave exactly as above; the interaction tools run in-process. PI extensions can also open their own dialogs (select, confirm, input) through PI's extension UI. Cortex hosts that UI inside the server (agent-server/src/agent-adapter/pi/ui-context.ts): each dialog becomes an extension_ui_request record with its own id, is presented as a question card through the hook-bridge's publish helper, and the answer travels back through sendExtensionUiResponse().

docs.title: What runs with which privileges
docs.text:
Cortex operates with the privileges of the user who launched it. It adds no escalation path of its own, and it adds no sandbox either: the forbidden class exists because the agent could otherwise do anything that account can do.

The server's own interfaces are guarded mechanically:

  • The webhook listener that MCP tools and hook scripts call (WEBHOOK_PORT, default 3001) binds to 127.0.0.1 only, and every route requires the CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN bearer token in the x-cortex-token header. The one exception is /webhook/signal, which authenticates each request with a secret scoped to a single waitpoint.
  • Every cortex-client WebSocket connection must present CORTEX_CLIENT_TOKEN; a missing or wrong token is rejected with HTTP 401. Both tokens are generated into $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env when absent. A remote client runs as the user who started it. See cross-machine.md.
  • The status-md-guard hook denies an edit that would push a project's STATUS.md or ISSUES.md, or a memory AGENTS.md index, past its size cap (see hooks.md).

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
Approvals and interactions leave records in four places:

  1. PENDING_APPROVALS.md — each queued operation with its full detail and final status. This is the human-readable decision history.
  2. Conversation transcripts — Web UI plan and question cards are stored in the session's history with their outcome and any feedback.
  3. Event log — plan.submitted, plan.approved and ask-user.requested are written with the rest of the event bus to daily $CORTEX_HOME/logs/events/events-YYYYMMDD.jsonl files, kept for 14 days. Setting CORTEX_EVENT_LOG=off disables the log.
  4. Slack and Feishu — each interaction leaves a visible message in the channel.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The safety boundary is the section you write in $CORTEX_HOME/AGENTS.md. The approval queue is $CORTEX_HOME/context/PENDING_APPROVALS.md. Neither needs further configuration: the agent reads the boundary as part of its instructions, and the queue, the Approval Center and the interaction cards are built in.

docs.title: Cortex Scheduling System
docs.text:
The scheduling system lets you set up recurring or one-time agent invocations. Schedules persist to disk, survive restarts, and hot-reload when changed externally. Each fire opens a new session that runs the schedule's prompt. Daemon infrastructure loops such as provider-usage collection and memory-index rebuild use the built-in job controller described below rather than schedule records.

Waiting for something to finish? Do not schedule a poll

A schedule that fires only to check whether a job is done costs a full agent turn every time, and almost every one of those turns finds nothing. Arm a waitpoint instead: the job reports back when it finishes and the session wakes exactly once. Schedules are for work that should happen on a clock, not for watching something else.

docs.title: Schedule Types
docs.text:
Four trigger types are supported:

Type Description Key Parameter Example interval Fire every N time units interval (e.g., "5m", "1h", "30s") Run a status check every 5 minutes daily Fire at a specific time each day time (HH:MM 24-hour format) Run a daily digest at 09:00 weekly Fire on a specific day of week at a time dayOfWeek (0-6, 0=Sun), time Run a weekly review Monday at 21:00 once Fire once after a delay delay (duration string) Send a reminder in 2 hours

Duration strings follow the format <number><unit> where unit is s (seconds), m (minutes), h (hours), or d (days), case-insensitive, and the number may have a decimal part. Examples: "30s", "5m", "1.5h", "1d". A bare number in a string is rejected, so "30" never turns into 30 milliseconds; callers that pass JSON numbers (such as the Web UI) give milliseconds. Weekdays are sun..sat (case-insensitive) or 0-6, and times are 24-hour HH:MM with a two-digit hour (09:00, not 9:00) in the server's local time. The message is trimmed and must not be empty.

docs.title: Managing schedules
docs.text:
Every entry point applies the same validation and writes the same schedules.json:

Entry point Who uses it schedule skill → cortex schedule Agents inside a session (see Agent workflow) cortex schedule Scripts and terminals (see CLI) !schedule Chat commands in Slack or Feishu (see Chat commands) Web UI / desktop app The schedule list and editor; it sets every field except preCheck, and a once schedule's time is fixed once created

The Web and mobile editor selects a model and thinking level. CLI and chat --model accept a model id or PI provider/model and restore its model memory; --thinking can override the level. Creation or editing stores the complete selection, and each fire uses that snapshot.

docs.title: Schedule Records
docs.text:
Each schedule is stored as a JSON object in ~/.cortex/data/schedules.json:

{
  "tasks": [
    {
      "id": "d6f1bb1e",
      "type": "interval",
      "message": "Check the active projects and report blockers",
      "projectId": "general",
      "selection": {
        "backend": "claude",
        "provider": null,
        "model": "haiku",
        "thinking": null,
        "mode": "plan"
      },
      "intervalMs": 3600000,
      "createdAt": 1747680000000,
      "nextRun": 1747683600000,
      "lastRun": 1747680000000
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: ScheduleTask Fields
docs.text: Field Description id 8-character hex identifier (auto-generated) type interval, daily, weekly, or once message The prompt to send when the schedule fires (a [Scheduled Task] prefix is added automatically at fire time) projectId Project the schedule belongs to; each fire's session opens in it selection Complete engine choice: backend, provider, model, thinking, and mode. Without an explicit choice, stores the configured default at creation; later default or model-memory changes do not alter existing schedules intervalMs For interval type: milliseconds between fires time For daily/weekly types: HH:MM 24-hour time dayOfWeek For weekly type: 0-6 (0=Sunday) runAt For once type: epoch milliseconds when to fire nextRun Computed epoch ms of next scheduled fire createdAt Epoch ms when the schedule was created lastRun Epoch ms of the last fire handed to the runner, including one the runner then skipped because the previous run was still going or the selected engine was rate-limited. A once schedule is deleted when it fires and never records one lastSkipped Epoch ms of last skipped fire (preCheck failed) isPaused Whether the schedule is currently paused pausedAt Epoch ms when paused pausedBy "user" while the schedule is paused dispatchType Reserved internal handler key; ordinary user schedules omit it preCheck Optional shell command; non-zero exit → skip this fire idempotencyKey Set by cortex schedule add --idempotency-key; a retry with the same key returns this schedule

docs.title: Built-in periodic jobs
docs.text:
Provider-usage collection and memory-index rebuild are daemon-owned jobs. They do not appear in schedules.json, !schedule list, cortex schedule list, or the Web schedule list. Their switches and intervals are the config/settings.json pairs providerUsageCollectionEnabled / providerUsageCollectionIntervalMs (on, every 5 minutes) and memoryIndexRegenEnabled / memoryIndexRegenIntervalMs (on, every 24 hours). The memory-index pair is also on Settings → Advanced → Built-in jobs.

Enabled jobs run once when the daemon starts. Settings edits hot-reload: disabling a job clears its next timer, enabling it runs immediately, and changing an interval reschedules the next idle run. See configuration.md for defaults and bounds.

docs.title: Where a fire lands
docs.text:
Every fire opens a new, ordinary session — the same kind you start from the Web UI or the desktop app — and sends the schedule's message, with a [Scheduled Task] prefix, as its first turn. The session is recorded as that schedule's run and labeled with the first 60 characters of the message. A fire never reuses an earlier run's session, so the runs of a recurring schedule stay in separate transcripts.

In the workbench, the session rail's Scheduled group shows one row per schedule. A recurring schedule's row opens the list of its runs; a once schedule's row opens its run. Replying to a run turns it into an ordinary conversation, which then moves to the regular session timeline.

The session opens in the schedule's projectId, settled when the schedule is created. cortex schedule and the Web UI take the project directly and default to general. Agents pass the intended project explicitly with --project; !schedule uses the creating channel's registered project, or general. If the project no longer exists when the schedule fires, the session opens in a project named in the message, or in general.

docs.title: PreCheck
docs.text:
The preCheck field is an optional shell command that acts as a gate: if the command exits with a non-zero status, the schedule's fire is skipped for that cycle. The schedule is rescheduled for its next normal interval — there is no fast retry.

The command runs in a shell, off the event loop, with a 15-second timeout. It receives the PRECHECK_LAST_RUN environment variable (epoch ms of the task's lastRun field). The working directory is DATA_DIR (~/.cortex/).

Use cases for preCheck:

  • Check if a required file exists before running: test -f ~/.cortex/data/schedules.json
  • Check if a process is running: pgrep -f "python train.py"
  • Check system load: [ $(cat /proc/loadavg | cut -d' ' -f1 | cut -d. -f1) -lt 8 ]

docs.title: Hot-Reload
docs.text:
The daemon's scheduler is the only process that fires schedules. The daemon and cortex schedule share the persisted records; the CLI writes schedules.json directly. The scheduler watches it with fs.watch and, 300ms after the last change:

  1. Reads the file from disk, bypassing its in-memory copy
  2. Removes timers for tasks no longer in the file
  3. Adds timers for new tasks
  4. Re-arms tasks whose scheduling config changed (detected via config hash comparison)
  5. Sends an admin notification: 🔄 schedules.json hot-reloaded: +N -M ~P task(s), T total

The scheduler's own writes trigger the watcher too; the reload that follows finds nothing changed and stays silent. Every write — the daemon's included — re-reads the file inside the write, so a change another process made a moment earlier is kept rather than overwritten by a stale copy.

docs.title: Config Hash for Change Detection
docs.text: Each task's scheduling-relevant fields are hashed: type, the type-specific timing (intervalMs, time, dayOfWeek, runAt), message, projectId, selection, dispatchType, preCheck, and whether it is paused. If the hash of a task in the file differs from the armed one, the timer is re-armed, so an edit, pause, or resume made by any writer takes effect without a restart.

docs.title: In-Flight Protection
docs.text: If a schedule fires while its previous run is still going, the new fire is skipped. This prevents overlapping runs of the same schedule. The skipped fire still counts as the schedule's lastRun, and the next fire follows the normal timing.

docs.title: Pausing
docs.text:
Schedules of type interval, daily, and weekly can be paused. Pausing or resuming a once schedule is refused with an error; it either fires or gets removed.

When paused: - isPaused is set to true, pausedAt records the timestamp, pausedBy records "user" - nextRun is set to null - The in-memory timer is cleared and not re-armed

A paused schedule stays paused until it is resumed. Pausing a paused schedule, or resuming a running one, changes nothing.

docs.title: Resuming
docs.text: When resumed: - isPaused is set to false, pausedAt and pausedBy are cleared - nextRun is recomputed based on the schedule type (for interval: now + intervalMs; for daily/weekly: the next occurrence) - The timer is re-armed

docs.title: Removing
docs.text: Schedules can be deleted by ID. The timer is cleared and the entry is removed from schedules.json. Removal is idempotent: cortex schedule remove reports "removed": false for an id that does not exist, while the Web UI and !schedule remove report that the schedule was not found.

docs.title: Startup Behavior
docs.text:
On server startup, the scheduler:

  1. Drops once tasks that are more than 1 minute overdue (past their runAt), with an admin notice for each: Schedule <id> skipped (<n>s overdue): <message>
  2. Schedules all remaining tasks with their computed nextRun times. An interval task whose nextRun passed while the server was down fires immediately; a daily or weekly fire missed during downtime is not caught up, and the next occurrence is scheduled
  3. Starts the file watcher for hot-reload
  4. Logs the total task count

docs.title: Agent workflow
docs.text:
The schedule skill uses cortex schedule for every scheduling operation. The CLI runs on the Cortex server with its CORTEX_HOME; it does not infer a project from the calling session or channel. Agents use the user's explicit project, or resolve the session project from session context or cortex_context, then pass --project <id> when adding a schedule. If the user requests the current project but none is available, ask which project to use rather than falling back to general. Bash is not guaranteed to carry session-specific environment variables, including on PI. Creating a schedule without model flags stores the configured default selection, which may differ from the active session. Use --model to pick a model and --thinking to set its backend-native reasoning level.

Each message must be self-contained: the fired session needs the project, run, machine, and file paths, not references to the conversation that created it.

Daily and weekly times use the server's local timezone. Convert a request in the user's timezone to the server timezone before setting --time and, for weekly schedules, --day; report nextRun in the user's timezone. Check the daemon's actual timezone, including any TZ override. There is no per-schedule timezone; differing daylight-saving transitions can shift the user's local recurring time. Clarify uncertain conversions and explain that limitation when it matters.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
cortex schedule manages the same schedules from an agent session, terminal or script. Its subcommands are list, get, add, edit, pause, resume and remove. Every command prints JSON with ISO timestamps, timing comes from explicit flags, and the long prompt can come from stdin:

cortex schedule add --type daily --time 09:00 --project nimbus --message "Summarize yesterday's sessions"
echo "Check training run r42 on trainer" | cortex schedule add --type once --delay 2h --message -
cortex schedule list --project nimbus
cortex schedule get a1b2c3d4
cortex schedule edit a1b2c3d4 --time 10:30
cortex schedule pause a1b2c3d4
cortex schedule remove a1b2c3d4 --dry-run

A timing flag that does not belong to the schedule's type is rejected, and edit cannot change the type; edit --delay on a once schedule sets its fire time to now plus the delay. A running daemon picks the change up within a second. See cli-reference.md for every option.

docs.title: Chat commands
docs.text:
The !schedule command manages schedules from Slack or Feishu. A schedule added here belongs to the channel's registered project, or general.

Command Description !schedule / !schedule list List all schedules with status and next run time. The first ten get a button: Pause or Resume for a recurring schedule, Remove for a once schedule !schedule add interval <duration> [--model <[provider/]model>] [--thinking <level>] <message> Repeat every duration (--model comes right after the timing words) !schedule add daily <HH:MM> [--model <[provider/]model>] [--thinking <level>] <message> Run every day at a time !schedule add weekly <day> <HH:MM> [--model <[provider/]model>] [--thinking <level>] <message> Run every week on a day !schedule add once <duration> [--model <[provider/]model>] [--thinking <level>] <message> Run once after a delay !schedule pause <id> Pause a recurring schedule !schedule resume <id> Resume a paused schedule !schedule remove <id> Remove a schedule

docs.title: Execution routing
docs.text: Ordinary schedule records use the scheduled-task runner, which opens a new session for each fire and sends the message with the [Scheduled Task] prefix. A record may instead name an internal handler in dispatchType; the registered keys are auth-expiry-scan and sync-public, and an unregistered dispatchType is logged and skipped rather than interpreted as an agent prompt. Daemon-owned periodic infrastructure uses the built-in job controller and is not routed through schedule persistence.

docs.title: Rate limits
docs.text: When the schedule’s selected engine is rate-limited, the fire is skipped with a warning notice. A recurring schedule keeps its timing and fires at its next scheduled time; a once schedule is deleted at fire time and is not retried. Other startup failures, such as an invalid route, also produce a notice. A run that hits a rate limit after starting is paused and resumed like any other session.

docs.title: Cortex Skills and Plugins
docs.text: Cortex uses skills for reusable agent instructions and plugins for installable capability bundles. A plugin can contribute skills alone or, when it follows the portable Agent Plugins format, skills together with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Plugins are assigned to execution environments, so each spawned backend receives only the surface its environment selects.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
A skill is a directory whose entry point is SKILL.md. Its YAML frontmatter describes when the skill applies, while the Markdown body provides the instructions expanded by the Skill tool. A minimal portable skill looks like this:

---
name: summarize
description: Use when a long artifact needs a concise technical summary
---

# Summarize

Read the complete artifact, preserve evidence links, and report the main result.

When the frontmatter has a name, it must match the directory name. Portable skill names use lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens — the Settings editor enforces that form when it creates or moves a skill — and Cortex discovers only immediate children of the plugin's skills/ directory. A skill can keep supporting files such as scripts and references below its own directory. Cortex validates the frontmatter of portable skills only; a legacy package's skills are handed to the backend as they are.
