The loader is deliberately lenient. A skill is dropped only when it cannot be used at all: no parseable frontmatter, a name that contradicts its directory, or an empty description. Everything else — an absent name, a non-canonical one, an over-long description, a malformed optional field, an allowed-tools list written as YAML, or a key outside the spec — is loaded and reported as an advisory issue on the plugin's detail page. Losing a working skill to a stray frontmatter key is a worse and quieter failure than tolerating the key.

docs.title: Supported plugin formats
docs.text:
Cortex inventories its built-in plugins and each immediate child directory of $CORTEX_HOME/plugins/. It recognizes the portable Agent Plugins 1.0.0 Working Draft and the existing Claude-compatible legacy layout.

Format Manifest Skills Cortex portable MCP Agent Plugins 1.0 plugin.json at the plugin root Immediate skills/<name>/SKILL.md children Root mcp.json Legacy .claude-plugin/plugin.json Immediate skills/<name>/SKILL.md children Not cataloged or mapped cross-backend

A root plugin.json takes precedence. If it exists but has a fatal validation error, Cortex reports the portable package as invalid rather than falling back to the legacy manifest. Unknown top-level fields and a non-object extensions value are reported and ignored as non-fatal exceptions. The legacy manifest is considered only when root plugin.json is absent. The portable format and its failure boundaries follow the Agent Plugins 1.0.0 specification, while Cortex retains the legacy layout for existing installations.

Legacy directories are passed through to the backend. Claude can therefore interpret Claude-native files such as a legacy package's root .mcp.json; those servers are not inventoried, summarized, or acknowledgment-gated by Cortex and are not mapped into PI. Use portable root mcp.json when MCP must be visible in Settings and consistent across Claude and PI.

docs.title: Built-in plugins
docs.text:
Cortex ships three portable plugins in its install, under agent-server/defaults/plugins/: cortex-system (approvals, schedules, project setup, client management, the agent browser, learning user preferences), cortex-board (boards) and cortex-feishu (Feishu documents, loaded in Feishu sessions and, with settings.feishuSkillsInWeb, in web sessions). Cortex reads them from the install and never copies them into $CORTEX_HOME, so they always match the running version.

A directory $CORTEX_HOME/plugins/<id>/ whose name is a built-in plugin's id is that plugin's user layer, not a plugin of its own. The built-in manifest stays in force, and the layer changes the plugin piece by piece:

  • skills/<name>/ with a SKILL.md, where the built-in plugin has a skill of that name, replaces that skill whole, support files included;
  • skills/<name>/ under any other name adds a skill to the plugin;
  • mcp.json replaces the plugin's MCP declarations whole.

Deleting a skill directory or mcp.json from the layer brings back the built-in one. The catalog reports where each skill comes from: built in, modified (the user's version in place of the built-in one), or local (the user's own).

Built-in plugins load in every environment that loads skills. An environment switches one off by naming it in disabledPlugins (see Assigning plugins). An environment with "skills": false loads only what its pluginDirs lists, and a sealed home (CORTEX_CONFIG_IMMUTABLE=1, as in a benchmark trial) has no built-in plugins.

docs.title: Portable package layout
docs.text:
A portable package has this shape:

my-plugin/
├── plugin.json
├── skills/
│   └── summarize/
│       ├── SKILL.md
│       └── references/
└── mcp.json

The minimal manifest selects the exact supported schema:

{
  "$schema": "https://agent-plugins.org/schemas/1.0.0/plugin.schema.json",
  "name": "my-plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Summarization skills and tools"
}

Cortex validates the manifest with a locally vendored schema and does not fetch schemas while loading a plugin. The package directory name is the Cortex assignment identity; the manifest name supplies the portable runtime namespace. Package files, manifests, skill entry points, plugin-relative commands, and plugin-root-based working directories must remain inside the resolved plugin root. A ${PLUGIN_DATA} working directory is contained under that plugin's data root instead. A symlink or equivalent path escape is rejected at the narrowest component boundary.

An invalid portable manifest makes the plugin unassignable. An invalid skill is skipped while valid sibling skills remain available. A top-level mcp.json error disables MCP for that plugin without disabling valid skills, and an invalid MCP server entry is skipped without removing valid sibling servers. The Plugins page shows these issues instead of silently hiding them.

docs.title: Portable MCP servers
docs.text:
A portable mcp.json declares stdio, Streamable HTTP, or legacy HTTP+SSE servers. The schema version must match plugin.json.

{
  "$schema": "https://agent-plugins.org/schemas/1.0.0/mcp.schema.json",
  "mcpServers": {
    "local-tools": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "./bin/server",
      "args": ["--data", "${PLUGIN_DATA}"],
      "env": {
        "CONFIG": "${PLUGIN_ROOT}/config.json"
      },
      "cwd": "${PLUGIN_ROOT}"
    },
    "remote-tools": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://tools.example.com/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "X-Tenant": "public"
      }
    }
  }
}

A stdio command is one executable token, not a shell command. It can be a bare executable name or a contained ./ path. Cortex expands only ${PLUGIN_ROOT} and ${PLUGIN_DATA} in args, environment values, and cwd; it supplies both variables itself and reserves their names. The dedicated persistent data directory is $CORTEX_HOME/data/plugin-data/<plugin-id>/ and is created only when a selected stdio server is materialized.

Remote servers require HTTPS except for loopback HTTP. URLs containing credentials or fragments are rejected, and configured headers are never treated as a portable secret mechanism. Both backends reject every remote MCP redirect: PI applies the shared redirect-rejecting fetch directly, while Claude reaches each remote server through a local stdio proxy with the same policy. This prevents configured headers and request bodies from being replayed to a redirect target (agent-server/src/agent-adapter/mcp-remote-fetch.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/claude/remote-mcp-proxy.ts). The Settings UI shows only the remote origin and header names; for stdio it shows only the executable basename, argument count, and environment key names. Environment and header values are not returned to the browser.

The detailed transport and isolation rules come from the Agent Plugins MCP runtime contract. Cortex implements all three declared transports for Claude and PI.

docs.title: Inspecting a plugin
docs.text:
The desktop and browser workbench expose the catalog at Settings → Plugins. The page reads the connected Cortex server, so its entries belong to that server rather than to the local desktop installation. It lists every installed package and opens each one on three tabs: Overview, Skills and MCP. New plugin creates a local portable package — a plugin.json at version 0.1.0 and an empty skills/ directory — under a name that is not a built-in plugin's id.

Overview carries the package's identity and health: format, manifest source and metadata, on-disk location, validation issues, and any spawn-time scope restriction. It also lists which environments currently reference the plugin, so the relationship stays discoverable from the package side without the page owning it.

docs.title: Managing a plugin's contents
docs.text:
The Skills tab lists what the package ships, each with its description and its path, and edits it. A skill opens into its SKILL.md, which saves against the hash it was opened with, so a file changed underneath the editor produces a conflict rather than a silent overwrite. New skills are created from a template with a name and a required description, existing ones can be renamed or moved to another plugin, and moving rewrites the frontmatter name (and only the frontmatter) so it keeps agreeing with the directory. A new or moved skill cannot take the name of a built-in skill. Deleting removes the skill directory and everything under it.

The MCP tab edits mcp.json as a form. Command, arguments, working directory and URL round-trip normally, but environment values and headers do not: this page is never told them. Each stored key shows as kept, and replacing one is an explicit action; keys you leave alone are merged back server-side from what is already on disk, and a key you remove from the form is removed from the file. Unlike the skill editor, the MCP form saves without a conflict check, so the last save wins. A legacy package cannot declare MCP servers at all, so its MCP tab offers the conversion instead — writing a root plugin.json while leaving .claude-plugin/plugin.json in place. Saving the MCP form of a built-in plugin writes mcp.json into its user layer.

Built-in plugins are marked in the list, and each skill shows whether it is built in, modified or local. A built-in skill opens and saves like any other: saving copies the skill directory to $CORTEX_HOME/plugins/<id>/skills/<name>/ with your edit, where it replaces the built-in skill, and the skill shows as modified with a Revert to built-in action that deletes your version after a confirmation. Built-in and modified skills cannot be moved, renamed or deleted; those buttons are disabled and say why. A built-in plugin cannot be deleted either: its delete dialog explains this and keeps the confirm button disabled. Skills you add to a built-in plugin are your own and can be moved and deleted. A local package can be deleted once no environment still references it.

docs.title: Assigning plugins
docs.text:
Assignment is a field of an execution environment rather than a property of the plugin, so it is edited on the environment: Settings → Environments, select an environment, then the Plugins tab (which appears once a new environment has been saved). Each environment has a single plugin set, shown as one switch per catalog plugin. Built-in plugins are marked and on by default; switching one off records it in the environment's disabledPlugins, while local plugins that are switched on are listed in its pluginDirs.

Saving uses the environment file's content hash as an optimistic concurrency guard. If the environment changes on disk, Cortex refreshes the target instead of overwriting the newer file. Existing plugin paths that are outside the managed catalog remain preserved and are reported as unmanaged. An already selected invalid catalog entry can be removed, but a new invalid entry cannot be assigned.

Adding a portable plugin with at least one valid root mcp.json server opens a confirmation that explains the local-code and network trust surface. The acknowledgment is required for that portable MCP addition, but it is not a sandbox or an independent authorization boundary. Reset discards the local draft, while Save persists it through plugins.assign. The Settings modal blocks section navigation and closing while an assignment draft is dirty. If a background refetch reports a different assignment hash, the page preserves the user's draft, marks it stale, disables Save, and requires Reset instead of silently replacing the edits (web/src/features/settings/vm/plugin-assign-vm.ts).

The assignment tab and the JSON body editor write the same file, so only one of them may hold a draft at a time: the tab is frozen while the body has unsaved edits. Assignment is also not the last word on whether a plugin loads. Scoped plugins are filtered again at spawn time, so a channel-scoped package shows an inline note saying it will not load outside that scope however it is assigned.

Assignments are stored in the environment's JSON file under $CORTEX_HOME/config/environments/, and can be written there directly:

{
  "name": "researcher",
  "pluginDirs": [
    "plugins/my-plugin"
  ],
  "disabledPlugins": [
    "cortex-feishu"
  ]
}

The environment's sessions load the plugins pluginDirs lists, in order, followed by every built-in plugin that disabledPlugins does not name. A built-in plugin written into pluginDirs by hand is placed earlier in that order; saving the Plugins tab rewrites the file with built-in plugins left out of pluginDirs. With "skills": false only pluginDirs counts. There is no inheritance between environments.

Relative paths resolve against $CORTEX_HOME; absolute paths remain supported as unmanaged legacy configuration. The Settings UI canonicalizes managed entries to plugins/<plugin-id> while preserving unmanaged entries.

docs.title: Backend loading
docs.text:
Cortex reloads the selected catalog at spawn time. Legacy plugin directories are handed to the backend at their own path. Portable skill support trees are containment-checked, content-hashed, and copied into private snapshots. Claude receives a compatibility projection of each portable plugin through --plugin-dir; PI receives one snapshot directory per skill as additional skill paths on its in-process session, followed by any legacy directories. Neither backend receives a portable skill path that points directly into the mutable installed package (agent-server/src/domain/plugins/skill-projection.ts; agent-server/src/domain/plugins/runtime.ts). Each skill is projected from the layer it comes from: a built-in skill from the install, a modified or local one from $CORTEX_HOME/plugins/<id>/.

Portable MCP declarations pass through one backend-neutral normalization layer. Claude receives a private supplemental configuration; remote entries in that file are local stdio proxies whose separate private files hold the remote URL and headers. PI's MCP bridge receives the normalized server entries on the session request and opens each connection itself (stdio, Streamable HTTP, or SSE). Components fail at their declared dependency boundary: an invalid or unmaterializable skill is omitted without removing sibling skills or valid MCP; unavailable plugin-scoped PLUGIN_DATA omits the stdio servers that share it while preserving remote MCP and skills; and remote/stdio processes connect independently from sibling processes and bundled tools (agent-server/src/domain/plugins/runtime.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/claude/mcp-config.ts; agent-server/src/agent-adapter/pi/mcp-bridge.ts). When a selected skill or MCP server cannot be materialized, a web session shows one warning notice for the run naming what is missing and why.

Projections, snapshots and the private MCP files live under $CORTEX_HOME/data/plugin-runtime/. $CORTEX_HOME itself may be reached through a symlink (a home relocated to another disk, for instance); a symlink anywhere below it is refused. Every projection and snapshot is content-addressed: one that a spawn reuses is marked live, and one that no spawn has used for a week is removed and rebuilt at the same path when it is next needed. The sweep runs during a spawn that selects plugins, at most once an hour per backend.

A capability fingerprint covers the effective plugin paths, portable skill content, projected manifest, and normalized MCP declarations. Claude pooled sessions reuse a process only when that capability matches, so assignment changes and changes to those covered inputs select a compatible process boundary. Legacy package contents and auxiliary portable files such as executable bytes are not content-hashed; changing only those files does not promise process replacement. A selected portable plugin whose plugin.json is invalid is left out of the spawn, and the run's notice names it; its issues are listed on the Plugins page. When two selected portable plugins offer the same skill name, the one that comes first in the environment's plugin order keeps it and the other plugin loads without that skill. When two selected portable plugins share a manifest name (their namespace), the first keeps it and the later plugin is skipped as a whole; the Plugins page flags a shared name on every package that carries it. These two collisions are recorded in the daemon log rather than in the run's notice. A portable and a legacy plugin that ship the same skill name both reach Claude, while PI keeps the portable one.

Portable MCP is suppressed for the explicit none composition, and subagents load no plugins at all — neither skills nor MCP. This keeps plugin capabilities out of execution modes that intentionally expose a narrower tool set.

docs.title: Trust and administration
docs.text:
Everything below $CORTEX_HOME/plugins/ is administrator-installed code. Assign only packages whose source and contents you trust: a stdio MCP server can execute local code with the backend process's account, and a remote MCP server can receive tool data over the network. Portable skills are copied into private snapshots, but stdio commands, arguments, working directories, and package data remain trusted administrator-controlled runtime inputs rather than a sandbox boundary. Manifest validation, path containment, private runtime files, redirect rejection, and assignment confirmation reduce configuration mistakes and secret exposure; they do not sandbox plugin behavior.

The Plugins page manages inventory and package contents, and an environment's Plugins tab manages assignment. Its MCP inventory and acknowledgment apply only to portable root mcp.json; a legacy Claude-native .mcp.json remains outside this managed view. Installation, marketplace search, update, OAuth, credential entry, per-tool permission policy, and live MCP health checks are outside this surface. Installing a package means placing its directory under $CORTEX_HOME/plugins/ through an administrator-controlled workflow.

docs.title: Skill discovery and invocation
docs.text:
The !skills command lists the skills the current conversation would load, grouped by plugin: the plugins of its environment after scope filtering. Portable plugins show the skills the catalog accepts; a directory handed to the backend as it is (a legacy package, or a path outside $CORTEX_HOME/plugins/) shows its skills/<name>/SKILL.md entries, labelled by the configured path when it is not a catalog plugin. The Skills view lists every catalog plugin's skills the same way.

The agent invokes a skill itself through its Skill tool when the skill's description matches the task. You can also invoke one explicitly. In the Web UI and desktop app, typing / in the composer opens a palette with Cortex's commands and the skills the conversation loads; choosing a skill inserts its invocation in the backend's form — /<namespace>:<skill> on Claude, where the namespace is the plugin's manifest name, and /skill:<skill> on PI — and the message goes to the agent as typed. PI resolves skills by bare name, so when two plugins ship a skill of the same name only the first is reachable there.

Each successful Skill call is recorded by the built-in session-activity-tracker hook as a skill_use event in $CORTEX_HOME/logs/session-activity/<session_id>.jsonl (see hooks.md).

docs.title: Implementation references

docs.title: Slack Setup
docs.text:
cortex init walks you through the entire Slack side interactively — it prints the App Manifest, copies it to your clipboard, gives you a 7-step Slack-side checklist, then collects the three tokens with validation. This document is the standalone reference for the same flow, useful when:

  • you want to read the steps before starting cortex init,
  • the bot was created by a teammate and you only need to know what permissions / events it requires, or
  • you need to rotate a token or move the bot to a new workspace.

If you have not run cortex init yet and you do not have a specific reason to read ahead, you can stop reading and just run cortex init — the wizard contains everything below.

docs.title: Why Socket Mode
docs.text:
Cortex uses Slack's Socket Mode. The bot opens an outbound WebSocket to Slack and receives events over it. No public ingress, no ngrok, no reverse proxy — Cortex works behind a corporate firewall, on a laptop, or in a private VPC with no inbound rules.

The App Manifest Cortex ships sets socket_mode_enabled: true and interactivity.is_enabled: false. You will not need to configure a Request URL.

docs.title: Create the Slack App (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Open https://api.slack.com/apps.
  2. Click Create New App → From a manifest.
  3. Pick your workspace.
  4. Paste the manifest (full content shown below — cortex init also prints it and offers to copy it to your clipboard with a single keypress). Click Next then Create.
  5. Slack drops you on the app's Basic Information page. Copy the Signing Secret under "App Credentials" — this is your SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET.
  6. Scroll further down to "App-Level Tokens" → Generate Token and Scopes. Name it cortex-socket, add the connections:write scope, click Generate, and copy the token (starts with xapp-) — this is your SLACK_APP_TOKEN.
  7. In the left sidebar go to OAuth & Permissions → Install to Workspace → Allow. After install you'll see the Bot User OAuth Token at the top of the page (starts with xoxb-) — this is your SLACK_BOT_TOKEN.
  8. In the left sidebar go to App Home → scroll to "Show Tabs" → enable the Messages Tab and check "Allow users to send Slash commands and messages from the messages tab". Without this checkbox you can @cortex the bot in channels but cannot DM it.

You now have all three secrets. Drop them into cortex init when it asks. If init is already done and you need to update one, edit $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env directly.

docs.title: The App Manifest Cortex uses
docs.text:
This is what cortex init will paste into your clipboard. You can also import it manually at https://api.slack.com/apps → Create New App → From a manifest.

{
  "display_information": {
    "name": "Cortex",
    "description": "Autonomous research agent",
    "background_color": "#2c2d30"
  },
  "features": {
    "bot_user": {
      "display_name": "Cortex",
      "always_online": true
    }
  },
  "oauth_config": {
    "scopes": {
      "bot": [
        "chat:write",
        "im:history",
        "im:write",
        "reactions:read",
        "reactions:write",
        "users:read",
        "commands",
        "app_mentions:read",
        "channels:history",
        "channels:read",
        "groups:history",
        "files:read",
        "files:write",
        "emoji:read",
        "pins:read",
        "pins:write"
      ]
    }
  },
  "settings": {
    "event_subscriptions": {
      "bot_events": [
        "message.im",
        "message.channels",
        "message.groups",
        "app_mention"
      ]
    },
    "interactivity": {
      "is_enabled": false
    },
    "org_deploy_enabled": false,
    "socket_mode_enabled": true,
    "token_rotation_enabled": false
  }
}

docs.title: What each scope is for
docs.text: Scope Why Cortex needs it chat:write Reply in channels and DMs im:history Read your DMs to the bot im:write Open DMs (e.g. to send the startup notification) app_mentions:read Receive @cortex mentions in channels channels:history Read messages in public channels the bot is in channels:read List channels the bot can post in groups:history Read messages in private channels the bot is in reactions:read/write Show ✅/❌ for command results and approval decisions users:read Map user IDs to names in transcripts files:read/write Receive uploaded files and post generated artifacts (plots, PDFs, logs) emoji:read Custom-emoji status indicators pins:read/write Pin / unpin key messages commands Reserved for future slash commands

docs.title: What each event is for
docs.text: Event Triggers message.im Direct messages to the bot (primary chat surface) message.channels Messages in public channels the bot is invited to message.groups Messages in private channels the bot is invited to app_mention @cortex mentions when the bot is in a channel

docs.title: Three tokens, where each one comes from
docs.text:
Token Looks like Where in Slack Goes into env as Signing Secret 32-char hex Basic Information → App Credentials SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET App-Level Token xapp-… Basic Information → App-Level Tokens → Generate Token (scope: connections:write) SLACK_APP_TOKEN Bot User OAuth Token xoxb-… OAuth & Permissions (only appears after "Install to Workspace") SLACK_BOT_TOKEN

cortex init validates that the App-Level Token starts with xapp- and the Bot Token starts with xoxb- before writing them to .env.

docs.title: Admin channel: auto-detected, no setup needed
docs.text:
The adminChannel setting is the channel Cortex DMs for startup notifications, approval requests, and other operator-facing chatter. cortex init does not ask for it. The first time you DM the bot, the Slack adapter records the channel ID and persists it to config/settings.json. See agent-server/src/platform/adapters/slack.ts for the auto-detection path.

If you want to pin it explicitly (e.g. you want admin chatter to land in a different channel than your DM), grab the channel ID from Slack (channel name → View channel details → bottom of the page) and set adminChannel in $CORTEX_HOME/config/settings.json (see configuration.md):

{
  "adminChannel": "C0123456789"
}

A change here reaches the running Slack adapter without a daemon restart. The legacy SLACK_ADMIN_CHANNEL and CORTEX_ADMIN_CHANNEL variables in .env are still read as deprecated fallbacks.

docs.title: After the bot is in your workspace
docs.text:
Invite the bot to any channel where you want it to listen:

/invite @Cortex

DMs work without invitation as soon as the Messages Tab is enabled.

To verify the install end-to-end, send the bot a DM. If you see no reply within ten seconds, check $CORTEX_HOME/logs/ for connection errors — the most common ones are an invalid xapp- token (Socket Mode failing to connect) or the Messages Tab still being disabled (DMs silently ignored). Cortex connects to Slack in the background after it starts; a connection that keeps failing, or is still not up a minute after startup, also raises a system notice in the Web UI.

docs.title: Rotating or replacing a token
docs.text:
Tokens live in $CORTEX_HOME/config/.env (see configuration.md for the full config reference). Edit the file directly, then restart the server:

cortex daemon restart   # drains running work, then restarts the server

Or, if you ran cortex start in the foreground, Ctrl-C and start again.

The admin channel auto-detection and DM trust model have safety implications — see safety-and-approvals.md.

docs.title: Server auto-update on Slack
docs.text:
When Cortex runs in release mode (no CORTEX_REPO environment variable), it periodically checks npm for a newer @cortex-agent/server version. The first check runs 60 seconds after startup, then every 24 hours.

The check is enabled by default. To disable it, set "serverUpdateDisable": true in $CORTEX_HOME/config/settings.json (see configuration.md); the legacy CORTEX_SERVER_UPDATE_DISABLE=1 variable in .env is still read as a deprecated fallback.

With serverAutoUpdate on (the default), a newer version is installed without asking. Installation waits until no turn is running; from then until the restart, Cortex refuses new turns and tells the sender to resend. It runs npm install -g @cortex-agent/server@<version> for the exact version it found, with --prefix pinned to the running install: CORTEX_NPM_PREFIX if set, otherwise the prefix the server is installed under, otherwise the prefix of the cortex binary on PATH. The package's post-install hook touches .restart, and the daemon restarts app.js. Remote clients receive the matching client release when they reconnect. A failed install is reported in the Web workbench and retried on the next check.

With "serverAutoUpdate": false, Cortex asks first. The Web workbench shows the question as a dialog; if nobody answers it within 10 minutes, Cortex also sends an interactive message to the admin DM:

Button Behaviour Update Agrees to the same install and restart, which wait until no turn is running. Release Note Posts the release notes for the offered version. Skip this version Dismisses the prompt and records the version in update-state.json. The same version will not be prompted again; the next release will trigger a new prompt. Cancel Dismisses the prompt. The next 24-hour check will re-prompt.

If no button is pressed within 24 hours, the prompt times out and is treated as a cancel.

In dev mode (CORTEX_REPO points to an existing directory), the check is skipped entirely since the developer manages the install directly.

docs.title: Team Mode
docs.text:
Team mode lets one conversation run a team. You talk to a single session, the lead, and it hands work to persistent worker sessions, continues them later, answers their questions and tells you what came back. You never open a session to give a piece of work its own context, or decide which conversation should carry on with what; the lead does that.

Team mode is experimental and on by default. Turn it off in Settings → Advanced → Team (experimental), or set teamEnabled to false in settings.json (CORTEX_TEAM_ENABLED=0).

docs.title: Leads and workers
docs.text:
With team mode on, every web session can lead. Nothing about a session changes until it starts a worker: one with no workers looks and behaves like any other session. The only difference is a set of worker_* tools in its tool list.

A worker is an ordinary session that belongs to a lead. It has its own transcript, context and resume history, runs on Claude or PI like any session, and has the full tool surface, including the one-shot agent tool. It cannot start workers of its own, so a team is one level deep. A worker inherits its lead's project and copies the lead's complete engine selection: backend, provider, model, thinking, and route. The lead can pass backend and model in the same format as the agent tool (provider/model[:thinking] for PI, a bare model id for Claude). On the same backend, only the named parts change. For another backend, the worker starts from models.json's default if it belongs to that backend, otherwise that backend's first favorite with its remembered settings. With neither available, creation fails and asks you to favorite a model on that backend. An explicit change of PI provider uses that provider's route. A Claude lead can run PI workers and vice versa. Creating a worker leaves the engine choice for new user conversations unchanged.

A lead uses workers only when there are several tasks (or the work splits into several) or the user switches to a different task; a single task stays in the lead's own session. For the work it hands off, the lead chooses between a worker and the one-shot agent tool by what happens next. Work that may need follow-up, runs long, or may need back-and-forth goes to a worker. Bounded reconnaissance or verification whose result the lead uses straight away goes to agent. When the work runs on several workers or across many hours, the lead also opens a board so you can follow it at a glance.

docs.title: How work flows
docs.text:
you ⇄ lead ── worker_spawn / worker_send ──────────▶ worker
        ▲  ◀── report at the end of each worker turn ──┤
        │  ◀── question / plan approval notice ────────┤
        └──── worker_answer ──────────────────────────▶ (pending request resolved)
you ─────────── open the worker and talk to it directly ──▶ worker

Dispatch never blocks. worker_spawn and worker_send return at once. The lead ends its turn, and the worker's report wakes it later. A message sent to a running worker is folded into its current turn; to an idle worker it starts a new one. While the server is about to restart, both tools return an error instead of dispatching, and the lead tries again after the restart.

Reports. Each worker turn ends in a report unless the worker marks it routine (below): its final reply reaches the lead as a message headed [Worker <name> · completed|failed|stopped] with a one-line status, and wakes it. A report that arrives while the lead is mid-turn is folded into that turn. Turns you start yourself by typing in a worker are not reported; the lead's roster marks that worker as one you have talked to. A server restart does not lose a report: one that ends while a restart is pending reaches the lead once the server is back. A worker's finished turn raises no notification on the web page, the desktop app or Android; you hear about it when the lead's own turn ends.

Routine updates. A turn with nothing new for the lead, such as a stale or duplicate signal, a routine check that found everything as expected, or work still running with no change, should not wake it. The worker marks such a turn by calling mark_routine before its final reply. The reply then shows in the lead's chat as a routine update and in worker_list, and goes into the lead's inbox of unread updates instead of waking it. A failed or stopped turn always reports, marked or not. The lead reads its unread updates the next time it hears anything: they are appended as the last section, headed [Unread routine updates], to the next report or question notice it receives, or added to the [Team] block of its next turn, whichever comes first. Each update is one line, the first line of the reply with its time, grouped by worker. The lead's chat does not display that section, since each of those updates already has its own row. Once given to the lead, an update counts as read and is not repeated. The inbox survives a restart and keeps the last five updates per worker, noting how many older ones it left out.

Questions and plans. When a worker calls cortex_ask_user or submits a plan with cortex_plan_exit, the request shows up as a card in the worker's session and as a notice in the lead's conversation. The lead answers with worker_answer. It may answer questions and approve plans on its own judgement, and asks you with cortex_ask_user when it is unsure what you would want. You can answer on the worker's card yourself; whichever answer arrives first is the one the worker gets.

Roster. While a lead has active workers or unread updates, each of its turns opens with a short [Team] block: a few working rules, one line per active worker (status, brief, last report, and whether you have talked to it), one line counting the inactive ones, and any unread updates. A worker with no turn running that still holds an open waitpoint is listed as waiting on external, not idle. A worker's first turn opens with a [Worker] block telling it who its lead is and how its replies are used.

Inactive workers. A worker counts as inactive once it has nothing running, no question or plan waiting, no open waitpoint, and no activity for three hours. Workers are never deleted; an inactive one simply folds out of view. The [Team] block counts it instead of listing it, worker_list names it on a single Inactive line, and the workbench lists it last. worker_send reaches an inactive worker like any other, and the new turn makes it active again.

Transcripts. Every session's first turn names the directory holding all session transcripts (<sessionId>.jsonl). When a report is not enough, the lead can read a worker's full transcript there, using the session id that worker_list shows.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
The lead's tools come from the cortex-workers MCP bundle (see MCP).

Tool Parameters What it does worker_spawn name, prompt, backend?, model? Starts a worker named by a short slug and gives it its first task worker_send worker, message Continues, redirects or briefs a worker, inactive ones included worker_list worker? The roster, or one worker in detail with its model and full last report worker_stop worker Stops the worker's current turn worker_answer request_id, answers? or approved? + feedback? Answers a worker's question, or approves or rejects its plan

Workers get one tool of their own from the cortex-worker-report bundle: mark_routine, which takes no parameters and marks the current turn as a routine update (see above).

docs.title: In the workbench
docs.text:
• The sidebar nests a lead's workers under it, behind a caret with a worker count. The lead's dot summarizes its workers, and inactive workers are listed last and dimmed.
  • A lead's chat header carries its team as one capsule: up to six status dots for its active workers, running ones first, then a summary such as 7 workers · 3 running. Clicking it opens the team list, headed Team · N. Each row shows a worker's status as its dot and how long it has been running or idle, and underneath it what the worker is doing: its current task while it runs, or the brief the lead spawned it with. A row opens that worker. Inactive workers are folded at the bottom of the list under Inactive N, and the capsule disappears once every worker is inactive.
  • On mobile, the Sessions list leaves workers out. The lead's row carries their state instead: it shows as running while any worker runs, and as unread while any worker has news. In the lead's chat, a team capsule above the composer shows up to three worker dots and the active workers in words (2 workers), and opens the same team list as a sheet. Inactive workers count toward neither state and are folded at the bottom of the list.
  • A worker's header starts with its lead's title, which takes you back to the lead. The composer works as in any session, so you can talk to a worker directly.
  • A worker never waits on you: its questions and plans go to its lead, and while it waits for the answer it shows as running, like any worker mid-turn. The amber dot is reserved for requests only you can answer, so it never appears on a worker.
  • In a worker's transcript, messages from the lead appear as your own messages labelled From lead session.
  • In the lead's chat, what the lead does to its workers shows as quiet rows of its own rather than tool calls. A spawn is one line with the worker and its model, with the first two lines of its brief under it; on a phone the model moves to the line's tooltip and the opened brief. A message or an answer is one line naming the worker; click it for the full text. A stop is one line too. An answer that directly follows its request folds into that request's line.
  • Worker traffic in between the lead's replies (reports, routine updates and requests) gathers into one line per worker per run: the worker's status dot, its name, its latest report or request (or the latest routine update in muted text when the run holds nothing else) and when it happened. Where a request stands, such as Question answered, and the worker's live status, such as running 3m, are in the line's tooltip and accessible name. Click it to open a timeline where routine updates read quieter than reports and each entry expands to the full text, with a link to the worker's session. Several workers in one run get a line each. A worker whose question or plan is still unanswered keeps its request's tag on the line. Live status appears only on a worker's latest line; older lines show when they happened.
  • When the lead is idle while workers are still running or waiting on something, the chat ends with a line naming who it is waiting on, such as Lead is waiting for docs to report.

docs.title: Boards
docs.text:
A board is a status page for long work. It sits beside the conversation and shows at a glance where a task stands, what comes next, what is waiting on you, and the decisions taken so far. A board belongs to a project and is attached to the sessions doing the work. It does not group sessions: organizing several sessions around one piece of work is what the lead and its workers are for. Boards work in every Web UI session, with or without team mode, on Claude and PI alike.

Opening a board. The agent opens a board when the work calls for one, typically when it is about to dispatch several workers or the task will run across many turns or hours. The board skill tells it when a board is worth opening and how to keep one. You can also simply ask for a board.

Tool Parameters What it does board_open title or board Creates a board titled title, or attaches to an existing board by id or slug. Binds the calling session, and a lead's workers (below)

The tool comes from the cortex-web bundle (see MCP). A board has no open or closed state: it stays available, and the page itself says where the work stands, including when it is finished.

Who is bound. A session is bound to at most one board. When a lead opens a board, each of its workers that is not inactive and has no board yet is bound along with it. A worker spawned later, or one the lead sends work to, joins the lead's board if it has none of its own. A worker that opens a board binds only itself. Once a session is bound, its next turn opens with a short [Board] block naming the board and its directory, and the block comes back after context compaction.

Writing the page. The page is board.html, an HTML fragment the agents edit like any other file. Every bound session may edit it, and Cortex neither locks the file nor tracks who wrote what; how the sessions share the page is up to them. Every time on the page, such as the updated stamp and the timeline entries, is read from the clock when it is written. A new board starts with a scaffold page whose heading carries the board's title and whose sections hold short examples for the agent to replace, next to an empty assets/. Each board has a directory in its project's context:

<project context>/boards/<slug>/
├── board.html        # The page body the agents edit
├── assets/           # Images and files the page shows or links
└── decisions.jsonl   # Decisions from the bound sessions

Cortex collects every bound session's send_decision calls into decisions.jsonl; agents never edit it. The list of all boards is data/boards.json.

In the chat. When the agent creates a board, the call appears in the conversation as a board card headed Board created, set apart from the folded tool calls. The card shows the board's flag and title, up to four bound sessions as a status dot and a name each with a count of the rest, how many requests are waiting on you (N awaiting you), and Open board. A worker goes by its worker name; any other session goes by lead, or by its title when more than one such session is on the board. Inactive workers are left out. The card updates live, and its flag turns amber while any bound session waits on you. When the agent attaches to an existing board, the conversation shows a single line: Attached to board followed by the title and an Open link. If the board has since been deleted, the card and the line keep its title and their buttons are greyed out.

On desktop, a board that the session on screen creates opens in the right-hand dock as it is created, in a new tab when the dock already holds something. Each board opens this way once per page load; reloading, switching sessions or scrolling back through the history does not open it again. On mobile, nothing opens by itself, and the card's button opens the board full screen.

In the workbench. A session bound to a board carries a board capsule among its chat header's actions. The capsule shows the board's flag and title; while a session on the board waits on you, its flag turns amber and it adds the count of those requests in amber. Workers never count here, since their requests go to their lead. Clicking the capsule opens the board in the right-hand dock, and the capsule stays hidden while the dock shows that board. On mobile the board sits in the row of capsules above the composer as its flag and the word Board, with the waiting count beside it once there is one, and tapping it opens the board full screen.

The command palette reaches every board, including those of old sessions. With an empty query it lists the eight most recently used boards, where a board is used when it is created, when a session attaches to it, and when its files change; typing searches all of them.

The top of the board is drawn by the app and updates live: one quiet line under the dock's tabs, which already name the board (on mobile the line starts with the title). It shows every bound session as a status dot, its name and how long since it was last active, with its state spelled out on hover; clicking a session opens it. While anything waits on you, an amber N awaiting you › link appears on the right: with one session waiting it opens that session, and with several it lists them with their pending questions. The Decisions N › link beside it unfolds the decision stream, newest first. The decision lines are the chat's, without its Decision label: each shows its status and the time of its latest answer, or of the announcement while unanswered, and offers Approve and Reply, answering the session that announced it. Approve records your acknowledgement without messaging the agent; a reply either asks why, with an optional question, or requests a change, with the change you want, and sends the session a message.

Below the strip, board.html renders in a sandboxed frame. Images in assets/ show inline. A link marked data-open opens a file from the board directory in the viewer the chat uses for files, which is the dock while it is open and a preview window otherwise; a file with no viewer downloads. Ordinary web links open in a new browser tab. The page re-renders within a few seconds of a save, with no reload.

Styling. Cortex ships a default stylesheet with components the agent is encouraged to use: sections (card), state labels drawn as a status dot and a word (chip), progress meters (meter), stages as rows with a status column (steps), row lists for acceptance criteria, decisions and risks (rows), and timelines (tl), among others. The page reads as one document: sections are set apart by space and a small heading rather than boxed, and only a callout is boxed, for something you have to act on. Text is in the app's face, with the mono face kept for code. The agent can also write its own HTML and SVG. The stylesheet takes its colours from the app's theme, so a board follows light and dark mode, the palette and the accent. To restyle every board, write ~/.cortex/config/board.css (see Boards in the configuration guide).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A lead runs at most eight workers at once.
  • Only web sessions lead. Slack, Feishu and scheduled sessions do not get worker tools.
  • A blocking question or plan waits at most 30 minutes, the same limit as any interaction, and pending requests do not survive a server restart.
  • Files, views and decisions a worker sends appear in the worker's own session. The worker names the paths in its report so the lead can pass them on. Decisions from a session bound to a board also gather on the board.
  • Workers live as long as their lead. Session retention removes a lead and its workers together.
  • With team mode off, leads lose the worker tools and the roster from their next turn, reports and request routing stop, and existing workers behave as ordinary sessions whose questions come to you. Their finished turns still raise no notification.

docs.title: Waitpoints
docs.text:
A waitpoint is a durable "wake me when this finishes" object. An agent arms one, hands its one-time secret to something running outside Cortex — a training run, a build, an evaluation — and ends its turn. When that thing reports, the session is woken with the result.

Cortex does not start, supervise or adopt the process. You run it exactly as you do today and append one line.

docs.title: Why not just poll
docs.text: A scheduled check costs a full agent turn every time it fires, and almost every fire only discovers that the job is still running. A waitpoint costs nothing while you wait: the session is idle, and the only turn that happens is the one that matters.

docs.title: The shape of it
docs.text:
agent                          your job                     Cortex
  │ wait_create(label, intent)
  │──────────────────────────▶ (id + secret)
  │ ends its turn
  ⋮                            runs for six hours
  ⋮                            cortex-signal --exit-code $?  ──▶ waitpoint fires
  ◀───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── session woken

docs.title: Arming one
docs.text:
wait_create takes a label (what it is) and an intent (what you are waiting for and what you will do about it). The intent matters more than it looks: you will read it hours later in a fresh turn with none of today's context, so write it for a stranger.

It returns the id, the secret, and ready-to-paste lines under how_to_signal. You never compose those yourself.

wait_create({
  label: "nightly training",
  intent: "the 33k-step run on cluster; when it lands, compare the loss curve against the baseline",
})

Arm it before you start the job, so the signal line goes into the same command. Nothing signals by itself — Cortex launches nothing and watches nothing, so a waitpoint whose callback was never wired just sits there until it expires. If the job is already running, the reply's attach_to_pid line watches its pid instead.

Once the callback is in place, end your turn. You are not supposed to wait around.

docs.title: wait_create parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning label Short name shown on the wake and in the UI intent What you are waiting for and what to do next; repeated back to you on the wake members Names of the jobs that will report; once set, every signal must name one of them quorum How many terminal (ok/fail) signals resolve the waitpoint: a number, or "all". Defaults to "all" with members, otherwise 1 fail_fast Wake on the first fail even if the quorum is not met. Default true max_signals How many times the waitpoint may wake you. Default 1; higher keeps it open as a monitor expires_in_hours Deadline after which you are told nothing (more) arrived. Default 168 (7 days), maximum 720 device The connected device the job runs on, so its signal files are collected there

The reply carries the waitpoint's state together with secret and how_to_signal, which holds env (the export line), cli, curl, shell (the file-drop form for a device), and attach_to_pid, plus recommended naming the form that fits — shell when device is set, otherwise cli. With members, every line carries a bare MEMBER placeholder and member_note lists the names to put there; attach_to_pid has a bare PID placeholder.

docs.title: Signalling it
docs.text:
On the machine running the daemon:

export CORTEX_SIGNAL_ID=wp_1a2b3c4d5e6f CORTEX_SIGNAL_SECRET=…
python train.py; cortex-signal --exit-code $?

--exit-code turns $? into both a status and a message, which is why the integration is one line. Everything else is optional: --message for a one-line summary, --member for which job this is (required once the waitpoint names its members), --data @file or --data - to attach a log tail.

Without the CLI, the same thing with curl:

curl -sS -XPOST http://127.0.0.1:3001/webhook/signal \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"id":"wp_1a2b3c4d5e6f","secret":"…","status":"ok","message":"33,120 steps"}'

To attach to a process that is already running, wait for the pid and then signal — the attach_to_pid line is exactly this:

(while kill -0 12345 2>/dev/null; do sleep 5; done; cortex-signal --status ok --message "pid 12345 exited") &

You do not get an exit code that way (the kernel only hands it to the parent), but you do get told when it is over.

docs.title: On another machine
docs.text:
The daemon's webhook listens on loopback only, so a job on a trainer box cannot call it. Pass device: "<name>" to wait_create and drop a file instead — the daemon collects it over the connection the device already holds open, within a sweep tick (30s by default):

python train.py; s=$?; d=~/.cortex/tmp/signals; f="$d/$(date +%s%N)-$$-$RANDOM"; mkdir -p "$d"
printf '{"id":"wp_1a2b3c4d5e6f","secret":"…","status":"%s","message":"exit=%s"}' \
  "$([ $s -eq 0 ] && echo ok || echo fail)" "$s" > "$f.tmp" && mv "$f.tmp" "$f.json"

Write to .tmp and rename — a same-directory rename is atomic, so the collector never reads a half-written file. Give every file a fresh name: the collector treats the name as the signal's identity, so a monitor that reused one name would be heard once. For a waitpoint with members, add "member":"arm2" to the JSON — without it the file is refused and parked under bad/. Nothing needs to be installed on the device. If the device is offline the files simply wait there.

That spool directory works on the daemon's own machine too, and cortex-signal falls back to it automatically when it cannot connect to the daemon, so a signal written during a restart is not lost. When the daemon starts, it drains the local spool and re-sends any wake whose delivery a restart interrupted.

docs.title: The cortex-signal CLI
docs.text:
Flag Meaning --id <wp_…>, --secret <hex> The waitpoint; default $CORTEX_SIGNAL_ID and $CORTEX_SIGNAL_SECRET --exit-code <n> Status from an exit code (0 → ok, else fail), and exit=<n> as the message unless --message is given --status <s> ok, fail or progress; overrides the status --exit-code derives. Default ok --message <text> One-line summary shown in the wake --member <name> Which member this is; required when the waitpoint names members --data <@file\|-\|text> Extra payload from a file, stdin, or the literal value; delivered as data, never as instructions --url <url> Signal endpoint. Default http://127.0.0.1:$WEBHOOK_PORT/webhook/signal --no-spool Fail instead of writing to the spool when the daemon cannot be reached

Run with no arguments, it prints its help and sends nothing. It exits 0 when the signal is accepted, when the waitpoint had already resolved, and when the signal was spooled; 1 when the signal is refused or, with --no-spool, the daemon is unreachable; and 2 on a usage error or a missing id or secret. The spool lives under $CORTEX_HOME/tmp/signals/.

The HTTP route answers 202 for an accepted (or duplicate) signal, 410 once the waitpoint has resolved, 401 for a wrong secret, 404 for an unknown id, 422 for a missing or unlisted member (the error lists the expected members), 413 for a body over 64 KB, and 429 when the miss budget below is spent.

docs.title: Other shapes
docs.text:
A waitpoint is not a completion notification; it is a wake with an address. Nothing about it assumes the sender is a job that just finished, so the other useful shapes need no extra feature — they are the same object with a different line pasted somewhere else.

An alarm clock. Nobody says the signal has to come from real work:

(sleep 3600; cortex-signal --message "an hour is up, look at the queue again") &

A monitor. Set max_signals above 1 and the waitpoint stays open, waking you on every report:

wait_create({ label: "nightly", intent: "…", max_signals: 24 })

while :; do sleep 1800; cortex-signal --message "$(tail -1 train.log)"; done &

The hourly wake cap still applies, so a chatty monitor cannot burn the session down: past the cap, reports are recorded and folded into one late wake once the hour has room again. Cancel it with wait_cancel once you have what you need — closing it is your decision, not the server's.

A heartbeat you are not woken for. --status progress records the report without resolving anything and without waking you; it shows up when you next look, and in the session's wait rail. Use it for "still alive at step 12000" and keep ok/fail for the moments actually worth a turn.

Both at once. Point the real job and a sleep loop at the same waitpoint. With the loop sending --status progress, the job's own signal is the one that wakes you and the check-ins tell you the run is still alive. With the loop sending ok, whichever arrives first wakes you; on a one-shot waitpoint the other is then answered "already resolved".

docs.title: Waiting on several jobs
docs.text:
Name the members and the waitpoint becomes a barrier:

wait_create({
  label: "T2 ladder",
  intent: "all three arms; wake me when they are all in, or as soon as one dies",
  members: ["arm2", "arm6", "arm8"],
})

Each job signals with --member arm2. A signal that names nobody, or a name that is not on the list, is refused with an error rather than counted, so neither a typo nor a forgotten flag can complete the set. By default the first failure wakes you immediately (fail_fast), and otherwise you are woken once, when all three are in — one turn, not three. quorum: 2 instead of the default "all" makes it a two-of-three barrier. A waitpoint that needs more than one signal delivers its wake three seconds after it completes, carrying every signal recorded by then. Once a one-shot barrier has fired, it is resolved, and a later signal from another arm is answered "already resolved" rather than counted.

--status progress records a heartbeat without resolving anything, for a job that wants to report milestones without waking anyone.

docs.title: What you get when it fires
docs.text:
A message naming the waitpoint, how long you waited, what reported, and the intent you wrote. The external payload is included but explicitly framed as data — anything holding the secret can write it, and it arrives in your transcript as a user turn, so it is never to be read as instructions.

If the deadline passes before the waitpoint resolves, you are told that instead — whether nobody reported, only some members did, or only heartbeats arrived, the notice says which. An agent left waiting on silence is worse off than one told nothing came. A monitor that reaches its deadline gets the same notice, saying how often it woke you and carrying any report that had not reached you yet.

docs.title: Seeing it in the UI
docs.text:
A waitpoint belongs to a session, so that is where it shows up — no separate dashboard to go looking at.

Above the composer. While a session is waiting on anything, a capsule sits in the row directly above the input, beside the task list: train-arm2 · 0/1 received · expires in 3h on desktop, the count of armed waitpoints on a phone. Click it for the full picture — the intent the agent wrote, quorum progress, member reports, every signal received so far with its source, and a cancel button — in a popover on desktop and a sheet on a phone. Several waitpoints show as N waiting items · <first label>. It renders nothing at all when nothing is armed, so an ordinary session is unchanged. Cancelling asks for confirmation first, because it stops the waiting, not the external job.

The panel shows armed waitpoints, and a fired or expired one only while its wake is still being delivered. Once delivered, the waitpoint has posted its own notice into the transcript; repeating it in a panel would tell the same story twice.

In the session list. A session waiting on an external signal carries a hollow ring next to its name — deliberately not the amber dot, which is reserved everywhere in Cortex for "blocked on YOU" (a pending question or plan approval). Waiting on a machine asks nothing of you, and should not compete for the attention of the one marker that does.

Three things worth looking for in the opened panel, each a way a wake can fail silently. Any of them, or a failure signal, also puts a dot on the capsule itself:

Badge Means wake limit reached (12/h) — the next wake waits until the hour clears The hourly cap is holding a wake back. Signals are still recorded, and the wake goes out — carrying everything that arrived meanwhile — once the trailing hour has room again. delivery retrying · N attempts A signal landed but the wake did not. Hover for the error. N/12 wakes this hour The budget is nearly spent (shown from two below the cap).

A failure signal shows as its own danger-toned badge. The signal secret is never shown: only its hash is stored, and the plaintext is handed out once when the waitpoint is armed.

Which waitpoints count as "this session's" is the union of two rules: the session armed it, or its wake will be delivered here. The second is what the notifier actually uses, so a waitpoint armed by an earlier session on the same channel (after !new, or on a re-run of a schedule) shows up on the session that will really receive it. The agent's wait_check and wait_cancel follow the same rule: a session sees and disarms its own waitpoints, never another session's.

docs.title: Housekeeping
docs.text:
settings.json key Default Lifetime waitpointTtlMs 7 days; expires_in_hours sets it per waitpoint, hard ceiling 30 days Sweep and collection interval waitpointSweepMs 30s; 0 turns the sweep off Wake cap per waitpoint waitpointMaxWakesPerHour 12 per sliding hour Wakes per waitpoint max_signals on wait_create 1; more turns it into a mailbox

The environment variables CORTEX_WAITPOINT_TTL_MS, CORTEX_WAITPOINT_SWEEP_MS and CORTEX_WAITPOINT_MAX_WAKES_PER_HOUR are read when settings.json does not set the key; see configuration.md.

wait_check shows what you are waiting on; wait_cancel disarms one you no longer care about — worth doing, since an abandoned waitpoint wakes you days later about something nobody remembers. A resolved waitpoint is kept for three days, so a late signal is told "already resolved"; after that its id is unknown. When session retention deletes a session, its armed waitpoints are cancelled with it, so a late signal cannot bring the session back.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The secret is a capability scoped to exactly one waitpoint: it can resolve that waitpoint and do nothing else. This is why the signal route does not take CORTEX_WEBHOOK_TOKEN — that token grants command execution on every connected device, and a training script has no business holding it.

Secrets are stored hashed, compared in constant time, and expire with the waitpoint. Payloads are size-capped: 64 KB per request or spool file, 2,000 characters of message and 16,000 of data. Unknown ids and wrong secrets share a budget of 60 misses a minute, after which the route answers 429, and each miss is logged as a warning in the daemon log, so a typo in a script is findable rather than silent.

docs.title: Cortex
docs.text: Cortex 是一个面向自主科研、自我改进循环和以天计长任务的智能体工作台。你给它一个带有成功标准的使命，它会规划工作，带着一组智能体在你的多台机器和 GPU 上执行，把每个结果以纯文件形式记在项目里，并对照你们约定的内容检查结果，只在需要你拍板时才来问你。

docs.title: 为什么选择 Cortex？
docs.text:
终端里的编程智能体围绕单个会话设计：一个任务、一台机器、一小时内做完。自主科研（Auto Research）和递归自我改进（RSI）需要的不止这些：一项研究要跑好几天，比其中任何一个会话都长；结果要留下来，一轮一轮地对比；工作要拆给多个智能体；实验跑在 GPU 服务器上，而不是智能体启动的那台机器上。

Cortex 把编程智能体（Claude Code，或者用你已经付费的 provider 跑 PI）作为长期运行的服务，专为这类工作而设计：

  • 任务跨会话接着跑 —— 使命、状态和决策以纯文件形式保存，而不是存在不断积累、逐渐失效的聊天记录里，所以新会话能从上一个会话停下的地方接着做。
  • 实验结果留得下来 —— 每个实验都有自己的记录：跑了什么、得到什么、说明什么；确认的结论和跨实验的模式也在旁边一并积累（记忆）。
  • 多个智能体协作 —— 主会话把有边界的工作交给子智能体和持久的 worker，它们各自从全新的上下文开始；主会话还维护一块实时看板，显示工作进行到哪里（团队模式）。
  • 智能体管理跨机器的模型训练 —— 智能体先看哪块 GPU 空闲，再在任意已连接的机器上启动训练和评测，不用轮询就能等它们跑完（跨机器、等待点）。
  • 这套环境本身也能改进 —— 技能、规则、钩子，乃至 Cortex 自己的源码，都是智能体可以修改的文件，边界由你写的安全规则划定。Cortex 本身完全是在 Cortex 里开发的。

docs.title: 特性
docs.text:
• 计划与审批 —— 不简单的工作从你批准的计划开始；提问、决策和需要签字的操作都以卡片形式出现，直接在原地处理（安全与审批）。
  • 子智能体与团队模式 —— 有边界的工作交给上下文干净的子智能体；开启团队模式后，一个会话可以带领持久的 worker 会话（团队模式）。
  • 用看板跟踪长任务 —— 长任务在对话旁边有一个实时状态页，展示状态、计划、需要你处理的事和已做出的决策（看板）。
  • 结构化项目日志 —— 每个项目以纯文件形式保留使命、路线图、状态、实验、知识、模式和决策（记忆）。
  • 定时任务与等待点 —— 安排 Cortex 定期扫描、摘编或巡查；会话发起的训练、构建或评测结束时，由等待点把它唤醒（调度、等待点）。
  • 跨机器统一代理 —— 通过 cortex-client 连接任意 Mac、Windows 或 Linux 机器；工作台显示每台机器的 CPU、内存、磁盘，以及每块 GPU 的负载和进程（跨机器）。
  • 可编辑的技能与插件 —— 技能就是普通的 SKILL.md 文件，Cortex 和你都可以编写、覆盖或还原它们，直接改文件或在设置 → 插件中操作；执行环境决定每个会话加载哪些插件、规则和工具（技能与插件、配置）。
  • 从源码重建自己 —— 用 CORTEX_REPO 指向一份源码 checkout 后，Cortex 会在代码变化时自动重建、重新安装并重启自己（热重建）。
  • 由 agent 操作的浏览器 —— agent 在服务器或你自己机器上的 Chrome 里打开、阅读和操作网页；你可以实时观看，遇到登录时接管（Agent 浏览器）。
  • Web、原生应用、聊天平台与终端访问 —— 浏览器工作台、Linux/macOS/Windows 桌面应用、Android 应用、Slack、飞书和 TUI 共用同一服务器。工作台把会话、worker、看板、审批、机器和项目记忆并排呈现。

docs.title: Cortex 使用方式
docs.text: 界面 适用场景 指南 浏览器工作台 无需安装客户端，从现有浏览器访问 浏览器访问 桌面应用 Linux、macOS 或 Windows 原生工作台 桌面与 Android 应用 Android 应用 移动端会话、项目与审批 桌面与 Android 应用 Slack 或飞书 对话式操作与通知 快速入门 TUI 全屏终端操作 CLI 参考

docs.title: 快速开始
docs.text:
桌面应用可以在 macOS、Linux 或 Windows 上无需终端地安装并启动 Cortex 服务器。使用终端时：

npm install -g @cortex-agent/server
cortex init
cortex ui enable
cortex daemon

服务器与聊天平台的详细设置见快速入门。服务器启动后，可在服务器上打开 http://127.0.0.1:3004 进入工作台，按浏览器访问从其他地方访问，或按桌面与 Android 应用连接原生客户端。

docs.title: Agent 浏览器
docs.text:
Cortex 里的 agent 操作的是真实的 Chrome：打开页面、阅读、点击、填表、截图。这个浏览器是 Cortex 在服务器上管理的那个 Chrome，或者某台已连接机器上的 Chrome；你可以在 App 里实时观看，页面需要人来处理时可以接管。

Agent 通过 cortex-browser 命令控制它，这个命令和其他工具一样在 agent 的 shell 里运行。内置的 browser skill （在 cortex-system 插件里）告诉 agent 什么时候用、怎么用，所以直接说「看一下这个页面」「给仪表盘截个图」「登录后看看」就够了。

docs.title: Agent 怎么用它
docs.text:
cortex-browser 就是连到 Cortex 所管理 Chrome 上的 agent-browser。 除 --device 外的所有参数都交给 agent-browser，所以命令集就是 agent-browser 的：open、snapshot、click、fill、 screenshot、get、eval 等。常见的流程是：

cortex-browser open http://127.0.0.1:5173
cortex-browser snapshot -i              # 可交互元素以 ref 列出：@e1、@e2 …
cortex-browser click @e2
cortex-browser screenshot ./after.png

与版本匹配的完整命令指南随二进制一起提供：cortex-browser skills get core（加 --full 列出全部命令和选项）。 cortex-browser 自己额外做了什么、拒绝什么，见 CLI 参考。

相对文件路径（screenshot ./page.png、pdf out.pdf、upload @e5 a.png）按 agent 的工作目录解析。不管截图来自哪台机器的 Chrome，文件都落在服务器上；agent 用 send_file 把截图发给你。

docs.title: 每个会话一个 tab
docs.text:
每个会话都有自己的 tab；worker 和 subagent 也各有一个，因为它们本身就是独立的会话。Tab 在多轮之间保留，agent 会接着上次的页面继续。 会话之间从不共用 tab，也看不到彼此的 tab。

一个会话连续 10 分钟没有调用 cortex-browser，它的 tab 就会关闭。下一次调用从空白页开始并会说明这一点，agent 再重新打开需要的 URL。 如果 Chrome 因为别的原因停了，比如崩溃或机器重启，下一次调用会重新启动 Chrome，同样接着进行。最后一个会话的 tab 关闭 10 分钟后， Chrome 本身也会退出。

登录状态保存在浏览器 profile 里，而不是 tab 里，所以登录过的网站在之后的 tab 和之后的会话里仍然保持登录。服务器上的 profile 是 $CORTEX_HOME/browser/profile/（默认 ~/.cortex/browser/profile/）；设备上则是运行 cortex-client 的用户主目录下的 ~/.cortex/browser/profile/。它们都与你日常使用的 Chrome profile 分开。

docs.title: 选择机器
docs.text:
• server（默认）是 Cortex 服务器上的 Chrome，在那里 localhost 指服务器。服务器有显示器时它运行在该显示器上，否则运行在虚拟 显示器上（需要安装 Xvfb）或以 headless 方式运行。App 里的实时画面和接管走的是 Chrome 的调试连接，所以哪种情况都能用。
  • --device <name> 改用某台已连接机器上的 Chrome：用它的 localhost、它的网络和它的登录状态。Cortex 通过该机器的 cortex-client 启动那个 Chrome，并经客户端的端口转发访问它的调试端口，所以那台机器上不需要额外开放任何东西。 那台机器上需要装有 Chrome 或 Chromium。

选择会一直生效：一个会话用过某台设备后，之后的调用不用再写 --device 也会去那里。换到另一台机器时，会话在上一台机器上的 tab 会被关闭。 你要求用你自己的机器，或者页面只在那台机器上存在时，agent 会选择对应的设备。

浏览器用不了时，cortex-browser 以非零码退出，并说明原因和下一步：设备离线或未知、Chrome 启动失败，或者你正在操作这个浏览器。

docs.title: 在 App 里观看
docs.text:
会话有浏览器时，对话头部会显示一个浏览器胶囊，标出所在机器和浏览器状态：启动中、启动失败、正在某个页面，或你正在操作。点击它会在停靠栏 打开该会话的 Agent 浏览器标签页，实时显示页面。命令面板（⌘K / Ctrl+K）把所有正在运行的 agent 浏览器列在 Agent 浏览器分组下， 在任何会话里都能打开。画面只在标签页可见时传输。

在手机上，对话的活动条会显示浏览器小标签，点开是该页面的只读画面。

docs.title: 接管
docs.text:
有些页面需要人来处理：登录、验证码、二次验证，或者 agent 关不掉的 cookie 弹窗。Skill 要求 agent 遇到这些时来问你，而不是设法绕过。接手的步骤：

  1. 打开该会话的 Agent 浏览器标签页，按接管。
  2. 直接操作页面：点击、滚动和按键都会送到页面上。标签页里的文本框会把文字输入到当前获得焦点的元素，从剪贴板粘贴也一样。
  3. 按交还，然后在对话里回复，agent 会在同一个 tab 里继续。

你操作期间，agent 的 cortex-browser 调用会被拒绝并提示「the user is controlling this browser」，agent 会等你。接管属于发起它的那个窗口； 另一个窗口也可以把接管转到自己这里。发起接管的窗口的画面消失 30 秒后（停靠标签页被关闭、页面重新加载、网络断开），或者 10 分钟内没有点击、 按键或粘贴，Cortex 会自动把浏览器交还给 agent。

docs.title: 配置
docs.text:
变量 默认值 用途 CORTEX_AGENT_BROWSER_BIN Cortex 随附的 agent-browser 二进制 cortex-browser 运行的 agent-browser 二进制的绝对路径。路径不存在时直接报错，不会退回其他二进制 CORTEX_BROWSER_BINARY 自动检测 服务器上浏览器使用的 Chrome 或 Chromium 二进制 CORTEX_BROWSER_DISPLAY 自动检测 服务器上浏览器使用的 X display，跳过 display 检测

Cortex 使用自己固定版本的 agent-browser，从不使用 PATH 上找到的那个，因此命令指南总是和命令一致。这些变量放在哪里，见 配置。

docs.title: Cortex 架构
docs.text: Cortex 是一个面向机器人学与 AI/ML 的自主研究智能体系统。它采用服务器-客户端架构：agent-server 编排工作——对话及其智能体运行、定时任务、聊天平台集成、Web UI 和 MCP 工具——而远程 agent clients 通过 WebSocket 连接，在远程机器上执行命令。关于这些子系统的深入说明，参见 memory.md、scheduling.md 和 mcp.md。

docs.title: 软件包
docs.text:
仓库是一个 pnpm workspace。其中两个包发布到 npm；其余的包要么被构建进这两个包，要么单独部署。

包 路径 用途 @cortex-agent/server agent-server/ 主服务器：Slack 与飞书适配器、Web UI 宿主、TUI 网关、LLM 编排、定时任务、MCP 工具。提供五个 CLI 可执行文件：cortex、cortex-browser、cortex-hook、cortex-evidence-export、cortex-signal。发布的包还携带构建好的 web 应用和客户端 bundle @cortex-agent/client client/ 轻量级远程智能体守护进程（cortex-client）。通过 WebSocket 连接，在本地执行 shell/文件命令 @cortex-agent/web web/ 基于 Vite + React 的浏览器应用，含桌面与移动端布局。构建到 web/dist，由服务器的 Web UI 宿主提供 @cortex-agent/desktop desktop/ Tauri v2 桌面与 Android 外壳。通过 cortexui:// scheme 提供 web 应用，来源是自带的副本，或从服务器下载的更新 bundle @cortex-agent/ui-contract packages/ui-contract/ 仅类型的重新导出，导出服务器的 Web UI router 和 DTO 类型，web 应用基于它编译 @cortex-agent/deepseek-relay-worker packages/deepseek-relay-worker/ Cloudflare Worker，为无法直连 DeepSeek 的主机做中转 插件 agent-server/defaults/plugins/ 包含技能的内置插件包（cortex-system、cortex-board、cortex-feishu）。不是 npm 包——运行时作为目录原地读取

docs.title: Agent-Server 架构：六层结构
docs.text:
agent-server/src/ 下的 agent-server 代码组织为六层（L0 到 L5），另有两个各自有规则的适配器目录。运行时每层只能从其下方的层导入；仅类型导入可以跨层。这些规则由 agent-server/.dependency-cruiser.cjs 在测试时强制执行——npm test 会运行 depcruise，出现任何运行时违规即失败（npm run test:quick 跳过这一步）。

L0  core/          → (no runtime dependencies)
L1  store/         → core
L2  events/        → core
L3  domain/        → core, store, events, platform, agent-adapter
L4  orchestration/ → core, store, events, domain, platform, agent-adapter
L5  entry/         → everything (composition root)

    platform/      → core, events
    agent-adapter/ → core, store, events

orchestration/ 还必须没有导入环。

  • agent-adapter/ —— 两个 LLM 后端的抽象（Claude Code 和 PI）。domain/runs/adapters.ts 是组装这些适配器的唯一位置。
  • platform/ —— 消息与传输层：Slack 和飞书适配器、TUI 网关、同时运行多个平台的组合适配器（adapters/）、Web UI HTTP 宿主（ui-http/），以及服务器上的 Chrome 和 agent-browser 进程调用（browser/）。

另一个目录 tui/ 是 cortex tui 运行的 Ink 终端客户端。它只通过 TUI 网关的 WebSocket 与服务器通信，共用网关的协议类型和 i18n 字符串，没有自己的分层规则。

docs.title: 第 0 层：core/ — 共享内核
docs.text:
其他各层共同依赖的共享内核：类型、路径常量、设置，以及内存中的运行与会话状态。它在运行时不导入其他层；可以导入它们的类型，hook bus 条目、环境定义这类 core 类型就是这样引用归属别处的结构。

文件 用途 paths.ts 规范路径常量：INSTALL_ROOT、DEFAULTS_DIR、DATA_DIR（~/.cortex/）、CONFIG_DIR、STORE_DIR（data/）、CONTEXT_DIR、PROJECTS_DIR、WORKSPACE_DIR（tmp/）、PLUGINS_DIR、PROMPTS_DIR、HOOKS_DIR、LOGS_DIR、AGENT_CWD、CLAUDE_CONFIG_HOME，以及守护进程 PID 文件和重启触发文件 settings.ts、settings-spec.ts config/settings.json 中的运行时设置：带默认值和旧变量的键 schema、校验、缓存快照和热重载（参见 configuration.md） utils.ts 工具函数：chunkText、formatDurationCompact、todayISO、listProjectDirs、readableTimestamp、npm prefix 解析 atomic-write.ts atomicWrite(filePath, data) / atomicWriteSync —— 写入 .tmp.<pid>.<ts>.<rand> 后 fs.rename；mutateFileAtomically 用于读-改-写 json-repository.ts 通用 JsonRepository<T> 基类：read()、write()、mutate(fn)、flush()。首次 I/O 时惰性清理孤立的 .tmp.* 文件。损坏 JSON 备份机制 async-mutex.ts AsyncMutex 类——基于 Promise 的互斥锁，用于串行化异步磁盘写入。在整个存储层中使用，防止并发写坏文件 log.ts createLogger(tag) —— 控制台 + 按日滚动的文件输出，保留 14 天 i18n.ts、locales/ 系统生成消息的英文与中文字符串；由 CORTEX_LANG 或 !lang 偏好选择语言 cli-utils.ts formatHelp、formatError、readStdinSync、readStdinBufferSync、cliError —— 共享 CLI 格式化 status-format.ts 纯格式化：computeElapsed、formatMetricsSuffix、buildSessionTag、buildUserProcessingMessage、renderTurnStatus rebuild-progress.ts 监督器发布到 daemon-rebuild.json 的热重建进度记录：纯步骤状态迁移（planRebuildProgress、startRebuildStep、finishRebuildStep、settleRebuildProgress），以及一个永不抛异常的读取 run-registry.ts RunRegistry —— 当前存活执行的唯一内存索引，以 executionId 为键、按频道建索引。向 EventBus 发布 agent.* 生命周期事件 session-holds.ts SessionHolds —— "会话是否忙"的另一半：回合已结束但后台工作仍在继续，带按所有者区分的句柄、替代与停止 session-state.ts sessionState(sessionId) / channelEngineBusy() —— 存活执行与 hold 的唯一汇合点，也是判断会话是否忙的唯一位置 agents/ 子代理角色加载（roles.ts），以及两个后端共用的委托 schema、模型选择和编排（subagent/） types/agent-types.ts Backend、AgentResult、AgentProgress、AskUserQuestionInfo，以及 todo、上下文用量、附件和通知的结构 types/environment-types.ts 执行环境类型：AgentDefinition（对应一个 config/environments/*.json 文件），以及一次运行打开时使用的 ResolvedEnvironment config-generator.ts 新安装的配置文件初始化，以及每次启动时写入的 MCP 配置 gateway-generator.ts API 网关 YAML 生成 models-generator.ts 默认模型与收藏 JSON 生成

docs.title: 第 1 层：store/ — 持久化
docs.text:
所有写操作都经 AsyncMutex 串行化，防止并发写入造成损坏。该层使用两种仓库模式：

  • 模式 A（JsonRepository 委托）：JsonRepository<T> 的简单 CRUD 包装。用于 schedule-repo、cost-repo、board-repo、waitpoint-repo、provider-state-repo 以及大多数其他仓库。所有写入都经过 atomicWrite()。
  • 模式 B（内存 Map + 即发即忘持久化）：读走同步的内存 Map，写走异步持久化链。用于 execution-repo，那里读延迟很重要，崩溃后数据陈旧可以接受。
文件 用途 outbound-queue.ts 基于 WAL 的持久化出站消息队列。30 分钟 TTL，200 条压缩，5 秒排空循环。合并对同一条消息的连续更新 conversation-ledger-repo.ts session-registry-repo.ts 的外观层——提供相同的按频道回合 API（initConversation、beginTurn、addResponseTs、completeTurn、rollbackTo），自身没有文件 session-registry-repo.ts 基于 JSONL 的 UUID 会话注册表，也是会话记录、频道→会话绑定以及按频道的对话头与回合的唯一所有者。回放仅追加日志（put/patch/delete-intent/delete-commit/bind/unbind/turn/conversation）、接纳会话，并在日志增长后压缩快照 conversation-history-repo.ts data/conversation-history/ 下按会话的 transcript JSONL，Web UI 据此渲染对话 execution-repo.ts 模式 B 仓库：startLocalExecution、completeExecution、failExecution、cancelExecution。启动时 markMissingRunningExecutionsStale 把已不存活的运行标为陈旧；超过七天的终态记录归档到 data/archive/ project-dir-repo.ts projectName → machineName → dirPath，支持反向频道查找 schedule-repo.ts 定时任务持久化。ScheduleTask 接口；schedules.json 与进程外的写入方共用 cost-repo.ts 费用存为 JSONL（仅追加），预算存为 JSON。启动时修剪超过 90 天的记录 models-repo.ts 同步缓存读取器。startModelsWatcher() 用于热重载 waitpoint-repo.ts、provider-state-repo.ts、board-repo.ts Waitpoint、提供商限流状态与恢复队列，以及看板注册表 team-inbox-repo.ts、team-outbox-repo.ts 团队 lead 与其 worker 之间的消息，跨重启保留 hook-registry.ts、hook-writer.ts 钩子注册表：内置声明之上叠加 config/hooks/，以及钩子开关背后的写入器 version-migrations.ts $CORTEX_HOME 的一次性升级迁移，启动时运行

docs.title: 第 2 层：events/ — 事件总线
docs.text:
同步、类型安全的事件总线，带 JSONL 日志。

文件 用途 event-types.ts CortexEvent 可区分联合，分组见下文，另加两个元事件（event-bus.handler-failed、event-logger.dropped） event-bus.ts EventBus 类 —— subscribe(type, handler) / publish(event)。同步扇出。异步处理器即发即忘。对 event-bus.handler-failed 有重入保护。提供用于 SIGTERM 排空的关闭钩子 event-logger.ts 订阅 '*'，1024 条环形缓冲区，100ms 刷新间隔，logs/events/ 下按日滚动的 JSONL，保留 14 天。由 config/settings.json 中的 eventLog 设置控制（旧环境变量 CORTEX_EVENT_LOG=off 作为已弃用的回退读取）

事件类别：

  • Session：session.message、session.message.delta、session.message.delivered、session.status、session.turn、session.turn.completed、session.todos、session.context-usage、session.context-compacted、session.rewound、session.decision、session.board、session.interaction、session.tool-images、session.debug.updated
  • Interaction：plan.submitted、plan.approved、ask-user.requested、ask-user.answered
  • Agent lifecycle：agent.started、agent.completed、agent.failed、agent.superseded
  • Auth：auth.required、auth.recovered
  • Board：board.updated、board.style-updated
  • System：system.notice、config.changed、llm.active-count-delta、rate-limit.changed、ui.mutate-invoked，以及 scheduler.tick（为 TUI 仪表盘声明；没有服务器组件发布它）

docs.title: 第 3 层：domain/ — 业务逻辑
docs.text:
最厚的一层。每个领域关注点一个子目录。

子目录 用途 agents/ 引擎选择、收藏、模型记忆、执行环境（agents/environments/）、子代理运行器和凭据：一次运行可以配置成什么。启动运行属于 runs/ runs/ 运行层：startRun 与 AgentRun 所有权对象、RunRequest 的引擎选择/spec/提示解析及其共享构建器（builders.ts）、后端中立的 RunEvent 流，以及 SessionEngines 池 sessions/ 会话生命周期与记录、会话钩子管道（onNew、onMessageEnd、关闭前）及可选的智能体注入、团队会话，以及保留期清理 executions/ 基于 store/execution-repo.ts 的执行注册表访问，以及存活执行的清理与停止 auth/ Claude Code、PI 和 Codex 的凭据与登录流程、认证状态与过期监视，以及登录后的网关同步 pi-providers/ 自定义 PI 提供商：cortex auth provider 背后的模型目录条目和网关路由 costs/ 费用追踪、网关管理、用量采集、账户读数与 banked reset、按提供商感知的速率限制 scheduling/ 持久化调度引擎，加上由设置驱动的内置作业控制器。Scheduler 热重载用户定时任务，每次触发都新开一个会话；记忆索引重建等内置作业拥有自己的守护进程计时器 waitpoints/ Waitpoint 服务：布设、信号解析、过期，以及唤醒会话的通知（参见 waitpoints.md） boards/ 看板服务、路径与 slug、重新渲染已打开看板的文件监视器，以及把决策投射到看板上 plugins/ 插件目录、内置与用户插件加载、技能投射，以及插件 MCP 服务器 projects/ 项目注册表：脚手架、扫描 context/projects/，以及项目元数据 memory/ 记忆/索引管理。index-regen.ts 从 YAML frontmatter 和访问日志重建生成的 index.md 文件（CLI：cortex memory regen）。上下文变更的文件监视器。AGENTS.md 扫描与注入，以及规则加载器 hooks/ 供 Web UI 使用的钩子注册表只读视图 monitor/ GPU 和磁盘资源监控 system/ 主机层面的事务：doctor 检查、更新状态与提示、系统通知及其历史，以及 rebuild-hold.ts —— 由监督器下推、供准入判断读取的"不开新回合"状态 browser/ Agent 浏览器的 broker（broker.ts）：每个会话一个租约，把会话绑定到服务器或设备上 Chrome 里它自己的 tab，空闲 10 分钟后关掉这个 tab，并记录用户的接管状态（见 agent-browser.md） remote/ 通过 WebSocket 的远程设备管理。基于 SSH 的客户端引导；客户端根据服务器推送的 bundle 自我更新 mcp/ 内置的 Cortex MCP 服务器及其工具模块（参见 mcp.md） ui-service/ Web UI 的后端：tRPC AppRouter（app-router.ts）、其 query 与 mutation 处理器，以及把实时事件流式推送给 UI 的事件总线订阅（subscribe.ts） tui-session/ TUI 网关的会话握手与切换 benchmark/ 生产基准证据：attempt 身份与日志，以及 cortex-evidence-export 背后的导出

docs.title: 第 4 层：orchestration/ — 消息路由和执行
docs.text:
将平台消息连接到领域逻辑。hook-bridge（本层的一部分）详见 hooks.md。

文件 用途 conduit-queue.ts 按 conduit 的串行 Promise 队列。确保每个对话同一时刻只运行一个回合，并允许 !cancel 丢弃排队中的尾部 orchestrator.ts 把每条入站消息交给 AgentRunner agent-runner.ts 默认智能体路径的准入：路由、回合中注入、排队，以及一个回合所需的会话与租约解析。回合本体属于 turn/turn.ts session-gateway.ts deliverToSession() —— 除入站平台消息外，所有进入对话回合的事物（web 发送、定时触发、智能体结果、恢复、waitpoint 唤醒）的唯一入口 session-events.ts 发布 Web UI 和 TUI 渲染的 session.* 事件：消息、增量、状态、回合、todo、上下文用量 runtime.ts PlatformAdapter + EventBus 的编排持有者，由组合根注入一次 conversation-request.ts prepareConversationRequest() —— 为普通聊天回合组装 RunRequest：智能体 spec 加首回合的环境信息块 turn/turn.ts Turn / openTurn() —— 一个对话回合的唯一所有者：状态消息、账本回合追踪、会话租约、startRun、观察者扇出、终态渲染、running:true/false 括号 turn/turn-prep.ts 调用方在 openTurn 之前要解析的内容：回合的文件、会话记录与使用租约 turn/terminal.ts 回合的终态渲染：状态封存、账本的回合完成、错误正文、错误会话持久化 turn/turn-tracking.ts 回合簿记中账本的那一半：开始、快照、接受，以及等待期间的替代窗口 turn/active-turns.ts 按频道的回合状态：回合注册的流式回调、编辑替代标记 turn/background-hold.ts "回合已结束但会话未结束"的统一 hold 生命周期：忙碌括号、SessionHolds 注册、运行订阅、六种终态判定 turn/hold-render-platform.ts 被 hold 回合在 Slack/飞书上的渲染——后台阶段运行期间的状态行及其封存 turn/hold-render-web.ts 被 hold 回合在 web 上的渲染——续写的正文、工具和通知，发送到会话事件流上 mid-turn-inject.ts、session-compact.ts、session-rewind.ts 把消息引导进正在运行的回合、按请求压缩，以及把对话回退到更早的回合 subagent-*.ts、team-*.ts 把后台子代理结果和团队 worker 报告投递到其父会话或 lead 会话 waitpoint-*.ts Waitpoint 信号接入、周期性清扫、从已连接设备排空暂存的信号，以及唤醒通知 session-retention-controller.ts 在启动时、每 6 小时以及保留期设置变更时运行会话保留清理 resume-dispatcher.ts 限流恢复队列：窗口重置后继续被用量限制中断的会话 busy-tracker.ts 追踪活跃 LLM 数量，向父守护进程发送 IPC busy/idle human-answer-backstop.ts 等待人工自由文本回复的频道的叶子注册表，每个进入会话的入口都会查询它，使回复被消费而不是开启新回合 routing/message-router.ts 平台消息入口：在适配器上注册入站消息处理器，并委托给 orchestrator routing/commands/ !command 处理器，每个命令族一个模块：cancel、channel、compact、cost、device、lang、login（含 login-custom）、mode、nvtop、orient、restart、schedule、sendfile、session、status、tail、usage（含 usage-reset）。index.ts 把命令词——!agent、!backend、!model、!thinking、!new、!resume、!usage 等——映射到这些模块 routing/webhook.ts 回环 webhook 服务器（WEBHOOK_PORT，默认 3001）：钩子回调、cortex-signal、cortex-browser 租约（browser-webhook.ts）、子代理、团队和看板回调 routing/hook-bridge.ts PreToolUse 钩子 → EventBus 桥接。发布 plan.submitted 和 ask-user.requested routing/hook-bridge-subscribers.ts 把问题或提交的计划转为交互记录的订阅者，各个界面将其渲染为卡片 interactions/ AskUserQuestion 流程、计划审批状态机、按钮/模态框动作路由

docs.title: 第 5 层：entry/ — 组合根
docs.text: 文件 用途 app.ts 组合根。加载 .env 并迁移旧设置，然后依次连接 EventBus → event logger → hook bridge → RunRegistry/plan approvals/busy tracker → platform adapters → outbound queue → auth watch → scheduler → commands → interactions → message handler → Web UI host → platform connect → client manager → webhook → memory watcher shutdown.ts SIGTERM 处理：一个有序的关闭步骤列表，前一步失败后续步骤照样执行，最后退出 daemon.ts 进程监督器。Fork app.js，监视 $CORTEX_REPO/src 以自动重建（设置了 CORTEX_REPO 时），监视 .restart 触发文件，带指数退避的崩溃恢复（1s→30s 上限）。发布逐步骤的重建进度，在 install/restart 之前等待 app 空闲，并在这段窗口内拦住新回合（见下文） daemon-notice.ts 下行 IPC 的 app 侧：把 rebuild-aborted 变成系统通知、把 rebuild-hold 变成准入侧的闸门，并在监督器断开连接时解除闸门 cortex-cli.ts、cli.ts cortex CLI 入口。分派到 init、config、auth、doctor、feishu、restart、setup-gateway、ui、client、install、schedule、memory、start、daemon、tui，各自在独立的 *-cli.ts 模块中实现（参见 cli-reference.md） browser-cli.ts、hook-cli.ts、signal-cli.ts、production-evidence-export-cli.ts cortex-browser、cortex-hook、cortex-signal 和 cortex-evidence-export 可执行文件 init.ts 交互式首次初始化 start-ui-http.ts、ui-http-gate.ts、ui-service-wiring.ts 在 CORTEX_UI_HTTP 开启时启动 Web UI 宿主，并连接它所提供的 UiService startup-helpers.ts 清理日志、确保 MCP 配置 startup-notify.ts 向管理频道发送启动私信 platform-connect.ts 启动各平台适配器。TUI 网关绑定完成后启动流程才继续；Slack 和飞书在后台连接，启动从不等待网络握手（出站消息走它们的 HTTP API，不走长连接）。连接失败会在 5 秒、30 秒、2 分钟后重试，之后报告为错误通知；60 秒后仍在连接的平台报告为警告

docs.title: 热重建：发布的进度与回合闸门
docs.text:
设置了 CORTEX_REPO 时，源码改动会让监督器重新构建各软件包、重新安装自身， 并替换 app 进程。构建分三条并发 lane 进行。其中一条是有序链—— 先 server，再 ui-contract，最后 web-typecheck——因为 ui-contract 重新导出 server 构建出的 类型，而 web 的类型检查依赖 ui-contract 的构建产物。另外两条 web-bundle 和 web-depcruise 只读 web 源码，一开始就与它并行。每条 lane 都会跑到底， 任何一步失败都会在安装之前终止这次重建，并发出一条点名每个失败步骤的通知。 有两个机制让重建既可见又安全。
